events.title: Saudi Pro League postpones matches after Asian Cup rescheduling
events.summary: League delays matches after revised Asian Cup dates create ‘additional flexibility in the domestic football calendar’. Matches in Saudi Arabia’s premier football league scheduled for the coming week have been postponed after the rescheduling of the AFC Asian Cup 2027, the Saudi Pro League (SPL) says. “The decision comes as part of a wider review of the ⁠⁠2026-27 league ⁠⁠fixture schedule, with the revised Asian Cup dates creating additional flexibility in the domestic football calendar,” the SPL said ⁠⁠in a statement on Tuesday, two days before the start of the match week. The postponement of the Asian Cup until December next year was announced earlier in the day after recent attacks on the kingdom. The 24-team continental tournament had been due to take place from January 7 to February 5. Asian football’s governing body announced the decision after “extensive discussions and close consultation with the Local Organising Committee (LOC) of the AFC Asian Cup Saudi Arabia 2027 and the Saudi Arabian Football Federation (SAFF)”. The tournament will now run from December 23, 2027, to January 21, 2028. An attack on Riyadh’s international airport last month killed at least 13 ‌‌people and wounded more than 300. Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility for the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. Further attacks on the airport in the span of a week killed at least five more people. “New ⁠⁠dates for matchweek 13 ⁠⁠will be announced once the review is complete.” The SPL has rescheduled several domestic league games this season for logistical ‌‌reasons, and last month’s AFC Champions League Elite clash in Riyadh between hosts Al-Nassr and Emirati ‌‌side ‌‌Al Wasl was postponed due to a threat of missile attacks. Kickoff was delayed after Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued a safety warning 15 minutes before ⁠⁠the scheduled start time.

events.title: Air India seeks more wide-body jets, sees profitability ‘very soon’, CEO says
events.summary: Air India CEO Tewolde Gebremariam speaking at the Aviation India event in New Delhi, on Nov 3. Air India wants to increase an order for wide-body aircraft as it seeks to boost international passenger traffic, chief executive Tewolde Gebremariam said on Nov 3, adding that the Tata Group-owned carrier would return to profitability “very soon”. The comments come three months after the former head of Ethiopian Airlines took charge of Air India , which is driving a sweeping turnaround while grappling with higher operating costs, geopolitical disruptions and losses. “We want more wide-body aircraft,” Gebremariam said at the Aviation India event in New Delhi, signalling the airline’s ambition to further strengthen its long-haul fleet as it pursues overseas growth. Air India has held talks with both Boeing and Airbus as it weighs the cost of running its older wide-body jets, said an industry source who sought anonymity for lack of authorisation to speak to the media. “The cost of operating old wide-bodies is high, and they’re not very efficient,” the source said, adding that newer aircraft would help the airline connect more cities and navigate the impact of Pakistan’s ban on use of its airspace. “There are so many cities they don’t connect,” the source added. Airbus said it does not comment on any discussion with its customers on their fleet plans, while Boeing did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Gebremariam did not respond when asked how many wide-body jets Air India seeks to order. Since returning to the ownership of India’s sprawling Tata Group conglomerate in 2022, the airline has embarked on a multi-billion-dollar transformation programme covering fleet renewal, cabin upgrades and network expansion. Tata owns about 75% of Air India, with Singapore Airlines owning the rest. It has been adding new aircraft and refurbishing older jets to improve service standards and compete more aggressively on international routes. REUTERS

events.title: Corporate America prepares for post-midterm Democratic backlash
events.summary: The witness-prep business is about to take off for Washington law firms. As Democrats appear poised to take the gavel, at least in the hearing-happy House of Representatives, the task of helping corporate executives prepare for their turn in the chair — a DC practice known as “murder-boarding” — will be in high demand. Democrats have been plotting for months about how to go after corporations that have courted Trump’s approval, Semafor’s Nicholas Wu reported earlier this year, citing missives sent to companies over things like ballroom funds, antitrust suits, and business deals involving the Trump family and one-time “first buddy” Elon Musk. “Companies that made investments or commitments at the president’s urging should prepare for scrutiny,” said J. Peter Donald, a former spokesman for the FBI’s New York field office and assistant NYPD commissioner who now advises companies in tight spots. “Everything will be on the table. CEOs should be ready to explain their decisions under oath.” It’s a good time for companies to prepay any outstanding law firm bills and book some time on CEOs’ calendars for mock grilling. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal. Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice. Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave . —Amit Katwala Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.” But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks. So one month in, who’s on board? —James O’Donnell This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday. events.title: Tech companies rummage for cash to fund the AI buildout
events.summary: Tech companies are turning over the couch cushions in their hunt for money to fund the AI buildout. Meta is prepping a big bond offering that includes its first-ever euro borrowing for up to $15 billion, people familiar with the matter tell Semafor, while Alphabet closed its second euro deal of the year. The tech giants that have run through US markets are now turning to other pools of capital. Alphabet this year issued its first-ever British sterling bond — a rare “ century bond ” that comes due in 2126 — along with deals that tapped Swiss and Japanese debt markets. For most companies, broadening lender bases is a test-the-pipes exercise to ensure that diverse funding is available if it’s needed. For hyperscalers today, it’s a globe-trotting bush-beating that’s crucial to funding the AI buildout that’s propping up their stock prices. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: How Florida Governor Ron DeSantis will shape his state’s 2026 midterm race
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms The outgoing governor and former presidential candidate has transformed Florida into a conservative policy vanguard. Few modern governors have left as deep a mark on Florida’s character as Republican Ron DeSantis. Across his two terms, the 48-year-old politician has overhauled the state’s political landscape, turning what was once a swing state into a Republican stronghold. list 1 of 4 Democrat Emily Gregory wins Florida seat in Trump’s Mar-a-Lago district list 2 of 4 New Florida map boosts Republican seats amid national redistricting fight list 3 of 4 Five key takeaways from Trump-Netanyahu meeting in Florida list 4 of 4 US-Israel ties: What Netanyahu and Trump will discuss in Florida The Florida governor has also established himself as a key national figure in United States politics. During the 2024 presidential race, he was considered one of the chief Republican challengers to President Donald Trump. DeSantis leaves office in January: Due to term limits, he cannot run in a third election for governor. But experts say his legacy as a hardline Republican will define the race to succeed him in Tuesday’s midterm elections. US Representative Byron Donalds is campaigning to defend the Republicans’ hold on the governor’s mansion in Florida, but he faces stiffer-than-expected competition from former Congress member David Jolly, a centrist Democrat. “Was [DeSantis’s position] going to alienate some voters? It definitely has. We’ll find out tomorrow if it’s enough to make a change,” Aubrey Jewett, a political science professor at the University of Central Florida, told Al Jazeera. A decade ago, DeSantis was hardly the household name he is today in the US. A former naval officer who served three terms in the US House of Representatives, the Republican was by no means a shoo-in for the governor’s chair when he first ran for office in 2018. The race was tight. Even with Trump’s endorsement, DeSantis only scraped past his Democratic rival, Andrew Gillum, by less than half a percentage point. At the time, Florida was a quintessential “purple” state, capable of leaning towards either Republican or Democrat. Under DeSantis’s leadership, however, the state took a rightward turn. The last Democrat to win statewide office in Florida was Nikki Fried, the former agricultural commissioner – and her victory came eight years ago. Ever since, Democrats in Florida have endured a dry spell, while the Republican margin of victory has grown. In 2022, for instance, DeSantis overwhelmingly won re-election by 19 points, the largest gap since 1982. He also became the first Republican gubernatorial candidate in 20 years to win the Democratic stronghold of Miami-Dade County. By Trump’s re-election in 2024, Florida’s reputation as a reliably red bastion was undeniable. Trump notched a decisive victory with 13.1 percentage points over former Vice President Kamala Harris in Florida’s presidential vote that year, a far cry from his wafer-thin 1.2-point advantage during the 2016 election. According to Florida’s Division of Elections, Republicans currently hold an advantage of 1.5 million registered voters over the state’s Democrats. That is a dramatic reversal from 2020, when Democrats held a registration advantage of at least 100,000 voters. Many experts credit DeSantis with spearheading this registration surge. Republicans have been attracted to the state by DeSantis’s platform of low taxes and light regulations, as well as his rejection of pandemic-era restrictions. Trump himself made the Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, his permanent residence in 2019, in a move widely speculated to take advantage of Florida’s favourable tax regime. Though Trump and DeSantis were briefly rivals during the 2024 Republican primaries, Jewett said the Florida governor has helped shape the meaning of “Trumpism”, the president’s political movement. DeSantis himself has held up Florida as a “blueprint for America’s revival”. Under his leadership, Florida has participated in Trump’s immigration crackdown and sought to purge public universities of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives. In April 2022, for instance, he signed into law the Stop Woke Act, which limited how race and gender were taught in public schools by barring instruction that portrayed any group as “inherently racist”. Part of the law was later struck down after advocates argued that it constituted censorship in violation of the First Amendment of the Constitution. Other DeSantis-era laws, like 2022’s Parental Rights in Education Act, curbed classroom instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity. “Those things have been cemented in Florida’s K-12 system,” Jewett explained. “There’s not a lot that the school boards could do, given that the governor has removed several people for policy disagreements.” Those laws, however, had wide-reaching impact across the US.

events.title: Most of our stuff is still on the Villa Vie Odyssey. We're on another cruise, waiting to see what happens next.
events.summary: Travel vloggers Dwight and Sheila Greene have been aboard Villa Vie Odyssey for over a year. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila Dwight and Sheila Greene have been living aboard the Villa Vie Odyssey for over a year. When it abruptly halted operations in Cambodia last week, they left most of their belongings aboard. They're now on another cruise, waiting to see what happens to the Odyssey. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Dwight Greene, 64, a Villa Vie Odyssey passenger from Fort Worth, Texas. He and his wife, Sheila, are travel vloggers. It has been edited for length and clarity. My wife, Sheila, and I have always loved to travel and have been on plenty of cruises. It was our friends who first told us about the residential ship . In May 2025, we flew to Acapulco, Mexico, and sailed for a week to Mazatlán through Villa Vie Odyssey's "try before you buy" program. We loved it so much that we decided we wanted to be a part of it. Six weeks later, we came home from a separate trip to Europe and had two weeks to pack for the move. We kept our house in Texas. We had been traveling with Villa Vie Odyssey for over a year. The couple, from Fort Worth, Texas, boarded the cruise ship in August 2025 when it was in Japan. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila We joined the ship in August 2025, when it docked in Yokohama, Japan. I had only been to Tokyo once before, over three decades earlier, so I was excited to return to this part of the world. We flew over with seven giant suitcases. The day the ship was supposed to arrive in Yokohama, it was raining. We put on ponchos and walked around, trying to see whether we could spot it. We came to a clearing on a bridge overlooking the water, and there she was. When we finally went aboard, I remember thinking it was the greatest day of our lives. We found a community aboard The Villa Vie Odyssey didn't feel like any other cruise we'd been on. What really got us was the people. On other cruises, nobody ever talked to us. It's like we were invisible. But on the Odyssey, people would come up and say, "Hello, welcome aboard. Let's introduce ourselves." We made friends in one week. A lot of people rotated tables, and we would eat dinner with different people each night. Sometimes we would just be walking by, and someone would say, "Have dinner with us." There was a buffet and a sit-down restaurant with tablecloths and silverware. We drank wine every day. The couple found a community aboard the Villa Vie Odyssey. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila We put on our own shows, too. I had been a stage actor, so when someone dropped out of a musical, they roped me into it, and it was a blast. Staying on the ship full time would have been too restrictive for us. We like to bop around. We use it like an aircraft carrier, getting off to do deep dives into other countries as it travels the world. Then, we'll come back to our "home," except it's in a cruise cabin . For example, when the ship changed its New Zealand itinerary in March, we got off in Dunedin with two friends, rented a car, and spent a couple of weeks traveling around the country before flying to Melbourne to meet the ship again. We had already set off on our own By the time the Villa Vie Odyssey halted operations in Cambodia last week, Sheila and I had already gotten off. They were already off the ship when the announcement came that the Odyssey was halting operations. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila The first time the ship docked in Sihanoukville in late September, we got off to travel through Cambodia. In early October, we met the ship again in Laem Chabang, near Bangkok, to pick up a few more things from our cabin. That was the last time we were aboard. By then, everyone knew the ship was having fuel issues , and people had started talking about it more seriously. While in Bangkok, we were also told that several ports would be dropped from the itinerary, leaving the Odyssey at sea with only a brief refueling stop. With little to no internet expected during that period, and no certainty that we'd be able to get off in time to fly to Singapore for a Royal Princess cruise we had booked months earlier, we decided not to stay aboard. We got off and traveled around Thailand instead, before making our way to Singapore for our cruise. The cruise we're on now is supposed to end in Singapore on November 10, around the time the Odyssey was originally scheduled to arrive. We thought, "They'll arrive, we'll arrive, and we'll just change ships." Now, the couple is on another cruise, and waiting to see what will happen with the Odyssey. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila That was the plan. Then, we got the announcement that the Odyssey was halting operations . We were fortunate that our travel plans were already in place, so we had somewhere to go. We knew other passengers were in a much harder position . When we got off in early October, we took the important stuff we needed. I left most of my things on the ship, including a full-size refrigerator and a big-screen TV we put up. I have been angry before, when I was younger, and I did not like the person it made me. Now, I am a positive person. I try to look for what is good in every situation. My wife and I are both that way — it's how we go through life. If the ship is in Singapore when we arrive in mid-November, we'd love to hop back on board. For now, we're waiting to find out what happens next. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ferrari raises 2026 guidance after Q3 earnings beat
events.summary: Ferrari raised its 2026 guidance after its third-quarter results topped Wall Street's expectations. The sports car maker cited stronger customer personalizations, lower-than-expected currency headwinds and its Formula 1 championship position as reasons for the guidance raise. Ferrari shipped 10,170 vehicles through the first nine months, 318 fewer than a year earlier, even as revenue and earnings increased. Ferrari on Tuesday raised its 2026 guidance after the sports car maker slightly beat Wall Street's third-quarter expectations. Here's how Ferrari performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 2.44 euros ($2.77) adjusted vs. 2.37 euros expected Revenue: 1.9 billion euros vs. 1.89 billion euros expected Ferrari raised its guidance to revenue of 7.65 billion euros, up from 7.6 billion euros; adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to 3 billion euros, up from 2.97 billion euros; and adjusted EPS to at least 9.85 euros, up from at least 9.68 euros. The automaker also upgraded its expectations for industrial free cash flow to up to 1.65 billion euros, up from previous expectations for at least 1.55 billion euros. This is the second consecutive quarter Ferrari has raised its 2026 guidance, despite vehicle shipments being lower by 318 units through the first nine months of the year, at 10,170 vehicles, compared with last year. The decline is led by fewer shipments to the Americas and China, Hong Kong and Taiwan. Ferrari said Tuesday that the guidance improvements were a result of stronger-than-expected customer personalizations, lower than anticipated currency headwinds and a second place finish in the Formula 1 championship. "Our order book now reaches into 2028, and we still have two more launches to come this year. In addition, we continue to create engaging events around the world to further tighten the bonds with our clients and partners across Racing, Sports Cars and Lifestyle," Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna said in a release. RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan said Tuesday that Ferrari's results were largely in line with Wall Street expectations. However, he said shares may be under "under slight pressure given some were hoping for a bigger guidance raise, but expect it to get better once folks realize these results are healthy." Ferrari's U.S. shares initially declined on the results before turning positive and were up roughly 2% during premarket trading.

events.title: Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing
events.summary: The AI bull market likely can't be led by the likes of Walmart and Eli Lilly. JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter is advising clients to remain on the defensive until there are clear signs of capitulation. Apple loses a key valuation advantage it held over the rest of the big-spending tech crowd. ChatGPT wishes me a happy birthday in my writing style. Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly. There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost. The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another. While this to-and-fro has so far protected the S&P 500 as a whole from an appreciable setback for months, it has left it stymied around levels that date back to May — before we got two earnings-reporting seasons showing 30% annual profit growth. A week ago here , I suggested the AI theme was nearing a make-or-break moment to stage a recovery or risk surrendering its leadership status and destabilizing the broader market. Thus far, this trade has failed to respond to moderate oversold conditions or a run of cosmetically strong hyperscaler quarterly results, further loosening its grip on the benefit of the doubt. In stressed markets undergoing soul-searching about the long-term bullish thesis, prices often need to travel further to find buyers with conviction while the market action must disappoint dip-buyers to extinguish complacency. Hard to know if we're there, but presumably we're now closer. The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday right at its 200-day moving average, off almost 11% from its record high. After an enervating failed Monday-morning bounce attempt, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished down another 3.8% and settled under the late-July low that was set as the Situational Awareness hedge fund was finished liquidating. "Markets did not get the memo that bearish seasonal pressure typically subsides in mid-October and instead ended the month with some of the most acute selling pressure that has been realized during the late-summer/early-fall period," notes JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter. He's advising clients to remain on the defensive "until we see clear evidence of a bottoming process on the charts or until there are clear signs of capitulation." This is a time-tested playbook, though many a sharp market pullback has ended without what would qualify as unqualified capitulation. The market action is winning some plaudits for the way non-tech stocks have held up better, many groups benefiting from the "quality" rotation while abandoned consumer cyclicals get a reprieve from easing oil prices and the slide in the 10-year Treasury yield back below 5%. This gives active managers plenty to do in playing against a highly concentrated and tech-dependent S&P 500. But I'll continue to argue that the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market. The AI-related stocks' weighting in the S&P 500 is off the highs but remains near 45%, according to Morgan Stanley. As the chart shows, AI has wobbled relative to the rest of the market during this uptrend before reasserting itself. But there's a trickier element to the current gut check: In prior phases of the buildout, the key limiting bottleneck gave investors something to buy in order to exploit it. The initial scarcity of GPUs meant to own Nvidia above all else from 2023 through 2024. When cloud capacity, power and cooling were found to be the crucial scarce resources, hyperscaler stocks worked and the AI-adjacent industrials were drastically revalued. Then memory emerged as the chokepoint and Micron and Sandisk went stratospheric. Now, as Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said, capital is the constraint and that not only leaves no asset to buy, but it raises the cost of capital broadly as the mega-caps go free-cash-flow-negative. Overlapping feedback loops and scrambled correlations across the markets and the real economy have further sapped investor conviction. Treasury yields no longer move with oil but largely with AI-capex sentiment, with both in retreat lately.

events.title: New national home listing database is taking on Compass in the battle for control of real estate information
events.summary: AGNT, HomeServices of America, Keller Williams and Real REMAX Group, four of the nation's largest brokerages, announced that they are creating a largely open and shared database (API) of listings for brokers. Open Real Estate is designed, according to its founders, to counter the increasingly fragmented residential listing market, and specifically private, off-market listings, which are favored by Compass, a brokerage behemoth. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Some heavy hitters in residential real estate just joined the fight over who can see residential property listings. Their goal, they say, is to counter private listings, which are becoming increasingly popular in certain markets. AGNT (which owns eXp Realty and NextHome), HomeServices of America, Keller Williams and Real REMAX Group, four of the nation's largest brokerages, announced that they are creating a largely open and shared database (API) of listings for brokers — and inviting all other brokerages to join it. Those who do must submit a new listing within one business day. There is, however, an option within the system for certain private listings. Open Real Estate is designed, according to its founders, to counter the increasingly fragmented residential listing market, and specifically private, off-market listings, which are favored by Compass, a brokerage behemoth. Compass is embroiled in more than half a dozen lawsuits with state and local Multiple Listing Services (MLS) involving listing rules and antitrust claims. "We want to ensure that for the American consumer, there's a complete data set that is capital T truth, that's reliable as to what is happening in the marketplace," said Leo Pareja, CEO of AGNT. "So whether it's MLSs fragmenting, pocket listings, walled gardens, whatever, the goal is to ensure that there's a complete data set for the American consumer, so buyers and sellers have the most amount of accurate information." Those who want to join the platform can do so with no initial charge or fees. Pareja said the four founders are going to make the investment into the infrastructure and the technology. Brown Harris Stevens, Lamacchia Realty, Samson Properties and Windermere are listed as initial participants. "It's clearly a clap back to Compass, firstly," said Jonathan Miller, a longtime housing market analyst and director of markets at StreetMatrix, a housing data and analytics company. "And it's absolutely better because Compass is literally hiding listings from competitors by design." Just after the announcement, Compass CEO Robert Reffkin posted a congratulatory message on X, saying that Compass is "excited that there will be a national real estate listing service that will return the power back to the creator of the listing — the homeowner and their trusted agent. This is good news for all agents and their clients, and we look forward to helping build the next chapter of listing services." When asked, Reffkin declined to comment further. Pareja's response to that: "We saw that, and we're grateful for his appreciation, and he's very much invited. We'd love to have him participate." While Reffkin's response may seem odd, given that Compass supports private listings, there is one part of the Open Real Estate platform that does allow for exclusives. It's called "participant view." A property that goes into that view is put into a part of the database, "where only agents that are associated with participating brokerages can see it, and it cannot be publicly marketed by anyone, including the listing agent and the listing brokerage," according to Open Real Estate's website. Pareja says that option will be used sparingly and largely for high-profile, celebrity home sellers who are trying to protect their privacy. Reffkin's response came at the same time another MLS, New York's OneKey MLS, joined the California Regional Multiple Listing Service's federal lawsuit against Compass. The organizations are asking the court to firmly establish that rules protecting the shared, public marketing of listings are lawful and pro-competitive, according to a release. It followed OneKey's rejection of Compass's demands to dismantle local cooperation policies. "This case raises questions that extend far beyond any one company or market," said Richard Haggerty, CEO of OneKey MLS in the release. "It goes to the core of how homes for sale are shared, how everyday buyers access that information, and how we protect a fair, equal housing market for everyone. We believe these issues demand clarity from the court, and joining CRMLS gives OneKey a direct, active voice in securing it.

events.title: AI agents are deciding who captures the value. Shoppers, workers and voters should have a say
events.summary: Ask an AI assistant to buy you a coffee machine on Amazon and you have stepped into one of the first legal fights over agentic commerce. Perplexity’s Comet browser can browse the store and place the order for its user. Amazon sued, arguing that the agent entered its store without authorization while disguised as an ordinary Chrome browser, and a federal judge in San Francisco blocked it. On Aug. 4, the Ninth Circuit vacated that order . Because the agent acts only when its user tells it to, the court wrote, “it is the user who ‘accesses’ Amazon’s computers.” In September the court declined Amazon’s request for a rehearing . The underlying case continues. The dispute matters to shoppers because it is about what they get to see. Search Amazon yourself and the results page mixes sponsored listings with organic ones, flagged in small type, and you can scroll past them. Send an agent and you get back a short list with a sentence of explanation. You do not see the products it dropped, and you cannot tell whether its ranking reflects quality or what a seller paid for placement. Perplexity framed its defense in those terms, accusing Amazon of being “more interested in serving you ads, sponsored results, and influencing your purchasing decisions.” Amazon’s position is that a store may decide which software comes through its door. Both companies are fighting over the same asset, which is control of the moment a shopper makes up their mind. The price itself is becoming as hard to read as the ranking. In December 2025, Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative asked 437 volunteers to buy the same groceries through Instacart . At one Safeway in Washington, D.C., a dozen eggs came up at $3.99, $4.28, $4.59 or $4.79 depending on the shopper. Instacart described the tests as limited and randomized, said they used no personal data, and ended them within two weeks of the report. The gap between the lowest and highest price for the same eggs was value moving from shoppers to the seller, and only the seller could see all of it. Cases like these are usually filed under consumer protection. They point to something larger. Each of us meets agentic AI as a consumer, as a worker and as a citizen, and in each role the same question is being settled: who captures the value that agents create. The public debate on AI and the economy has concentrated on productivity and jobs, on how much value AI will add. Far less attention has gone to how that value is divided, which depends on who controls the terms agents operate under. For workers, the division can already be measured. Researchers at the University of Oxford , working with the nonprofit Worker Info Exchange, analyzed more than 1.5 million trips by 258 Uber drivers in Britain between 2016 and 2024. After Uber introduced a dynamic pricing algorithm in 2023, passengers paid more per trip while drivers’ inflation-adjusted hourly earnings fell from over £22 to just over £19, before costs. Uber’s share of fares rose from around 25% to 29%, and on some trips exceeded half. Uber said it did not recognize the figures. The mechanism deserves attention whatever the exact numbers. One system sets what the passenger pays and what the driver earns, and it sees both sides of every trip. The passenger and the driver each see a single figure, and neither can tell how the other was priced. For citizens, the stakes are institutional. Friedrich Hayek’s defense of the market rested on the idea that prices emerge from countless decisions and belong to no one. The French philosopher Jean-Pierre Dupuy observed that this anonymity made market outcomes bearable, because a price set by no one offers no address for a grievance. Agentic pricing gives the price an address. When the Justice Department sued RealPage, it treated the vendor of the software that landlords used to set rents as a party to the coordination, alongside the landlords themselves. The proposed settlement announced in November 2025 bars RealPage from feeding its models competitors’ current nonpublic data and from training them on active leases. The rent on an apartment turned out to have an author. Inside companies, that author is harder to find, a problem two of us call “functional innocence” in our book IA et revenu (Ellipses, 2026): responsibility disappears across a chain of individually defensible decisions. Everyone involved can say in good faith that they decided nothing, which is why someone has to be named who answers for what the system does. These questions are being settled in court dockets and in the integration meetings where companies plug into assistants, and neither was designed for public deliberation. Where elected bodies have stepped in, the results have been modest and workable. New York now requires businesses that set prices with personal data to state, next to the price, “This price was set by an algorithm using your personal data.” In October 2025 a federal judge dismissed the National Retail Federation’s First Amendment challenge to the law. In Europe, the Platform Work Directive obliges platforms to tell workers when automated systems monitor them or make decisions about them, and member states must transpose it by Dec. 2, 2026. In July the European Commission ordered Google to open Android features to rival AI assistants. Disclosure is a start, and a real debate would go further using tools that already exist. The German economist Walter Eucken argued that competition is an order that has to be instituted and maintained, because a market left to itself drifts toward concentration. Applied to agents, that principle gives consumers a right to send the agent of their choice to any store they may lawfully enter, and to leave that agent taking with them what it has learned about them. The Ninth Circuit has addressed the first half of that right under a single statute, on a preliminary record. The principle also implies a duty of loyalty for agents that buy on our behalf. European law settled the equivalent question for financial advice in 2014 : an adviser who claims to be independent may not keep commissions from the providers whose products it recommends. An agent that shops for you should meet the same standard, or say plainly who pays it. Business leaders have good reasons to want this debate. Most companies sit on the seller’s side of an agent’s shortlist, and they gain when channels stay open and no single assistant can set the terms of visibility alone. Executives are consumers, employees and voters as well. The question of who captures the value of agentic AI is being settled now, one ruling and one integration at a time, and leaving it there means accepting answers that few boards and no voters were asked about. events.title: Who pays for AI’s $2.6 trillion build-out? Look to corporate budgets
events.summary: Good morning. By 2030, the AI ecosystem will need about $2.6 trillion in annual end-market spending to support data centers, chips, model development, and investor returns, according to a BCG Institute analysis . Enterprises would account for $1.8 trillion of that total, followed by consumers at $366 billion, hyperscalers’ internal use at $204 billion, and emerging technologies such as physical AI at $200 billion. The estimates represent global spending, excluding China, and reflect infrastructure costs concentrated mainly in the U.S., where most new capacity is being built. The $1.8 trillion is a measure of what the AI ecosystem would need from enterprises, rather than a forecast of actual spending. In one illustrative scenario, BCG estimates that companies could contribute that amount by reallocating $857 billion from existing technology budgets and adding $937 billion in new spending. That would put enterprise tech budgets roughly 13% above International Data Corporation’s IT spending forecast, with AI’s share of those budgets rising from 5% today to 25% in 2030. The scenario underscores how much the AI industry’s growth depends on corporate spending. For CFOs seeking additional AI investment, that means presenting boards with evidence of productivity gains, cost reductions, new revenue or competitive advantage, said Clark O’Niell, BCG’s global lead for AI, infrastructure and cyber. Some strategic benefits, however, may be difficult to capture in traditional ROI calculations. “The question isn’t just whether AI delivers an immediate financial return,” he said. “It’s also what the cost of falling behind could be.” That argument deserves scrutiny, too. Fear of falling behind can be a legitimate strategic consideration, but it shouldn’t become a substitute for a business case. BCG considers the AI build-out as more resilient than past infrastructure booms, partly because hyperscalers have financed much of their investment through cash flow rather than debt. But the ability to finance infrastructure doesn’t guarantee that it will generate adequate returns. O’Neill identifies two indicators worth watching. The first is how infrastructure investment is financed, with a sustained shift toward debt signaling greater risk. The second is whether deployed compute generates sufficient revenue. As frontier labs enter public markets, their disclosures could reveal whether revenue is keeping pace with compute costs. The economics leave limited room for disappointment. BCG assumes AI chips have an average five-year lifespan and estimates that each gigawatt of capacity coming online in 2026 must generate about $15 billion in revenue to cover its costs. Weaker-than-expected demand could trigger price wars and losses for model providers and data-center operators. For corporate buyers, those pressures have a practical implication. O’Niell advises most to avoid long-term price-per-token commitments as AI prices continue to fall.  Contract flexibility could help CFOs capture future cost reductions. The $2.6 trillion is achievable, O’Niell said, “but it’s not guaranteed.” And even if enterprises provide the spending, the question remains whether they will capture enough of the economic value to justify it. Sheryl   Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: MAS’ Future of Finance Institute starts operations with AI focus; names interim CEO
events.summary: Alan Lim, head of the financial infrastructure and AI office at MAS, will serve concurrently as the interim CEO of FFI. MAS launched the Future of Finance Institute on Nov 3 to focus on AI in finance, share practical experience, and support safe adoption of new technology. Alan Lim will be interim CEO while the institute builds programmes and partnerships. MAS said it will help anchor key capabilities in Singapore. FFI will work through PathFin.ai, BuildFin.ai and SafeFin.ai to spread AI knowledge, set good practices, manage risks, and later expand into tokenisation. SINGAPORE – The Future of Finance Institute (FFI) began operations on Nov 3 with a focus on AI in finance, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said. It will bring financial institutions together to share practical experience in implementing AI, develop good practices for deploying agentic AI, and strengthen the management of risks from the use of AI, said MAS. Its managing director Chia Der Jiun said: “(The FFI) will seek to anchor key capabilities in Singapore, and connect the ecosystem to accelerate innovation and support safe adoption of new technologies.” This comes as banks and regulators become increasingly concerned about the risks that rapid AI adoption may bring to the financial industry. He will lead FFI’s strategy and operations as it builds out its programmes and deepens partnerships in the financial and technology ecosystems, MAS said. The FFI was first announced in June , with the aim to accelerate the adoption of new financial technologies and catalyse innovation in the financial sector. To start, it will home in on three pillars: PathFin.ai, BuildFin.ai and SafeFin.ai. To share AI knowledge across the sector, it will build on the PathFin.ai programme and broaden the range of solutions available through its knowledge hub. FFI will also bring together financial industry practitioners to discuss common challenges and practical approaches in the adoption of AI. Under BuildFin.ai, FFI will work with industry players to develop guidance, good practices, industry standards, and common tools and infrastructure for deploying AI, with a focus on the safe use of AI agents in financial services. FFI will also focus on promoting sound AI risk management practices under SafeFin.ai. It will progressively expand into other areas of financial innovation, including tokenisation, MAS said. events.title: As a flight attendant, I wish passengers would leave the window shades open. I've got my reasons, but it's not up to me.
events.summary: Regardless of whether you feel the window shade should be open or shut during flight, I (not pictured) say the passenger in the window seat should get to control it. Dobrila Vignjevic/Getty Images As a flight attendant , I prefer open window shades — but the choice is up to those in window seats. I love watching the scenery and feel safer, as we all get more visibility into our surroundings. Unless we're stopped at a warm destination or the cabin is rowdy, I am team window shades up. When it comes to whether window shades should be open or shut during a flight, my answer is simple: Generally, it's up to the passenger in the window seat . The choice is theirs to make, unless there's an onboard issue or the crew has instructed otherwise. If I'm in the aisle, and the person in the window seat has the shade down during my flight, I'll be disappointed, but I'll respect their decision. When I'm on the job as a flight attendant, I typically prefer it when my passengers keep the window shades open, too. Generally, I feel safer leaving the shades open When the window shades are open, we can all have a better view of our surroundings. Leanna Coy; Ignatiev/Getty Images Since becoming a flight attendant four years ago, I appreciate having the window shades up even more, especially during takeoff and landing. It gives passengers and crew members more visibility and can improve their situational awareness, which is crucial in the unlikely event of an emergency or evacuation. A passenger might even be able to spot a potential issue before the crew does. If there were a fire on the aircraft's wing, for example, someone in the window seat might be the first person to notice. Many international airlines actually require window shades to remain open during takeoff and landing, and some US airlines encourage the practice, even though it is not mandated by the Federal Aviation Administration. It also gives all of us the chance to catch incredible views I've seen national parks from above and caught glimpses of the northern lights outside of plane windows. Leanna Coy On a less serious note, it makes me kind of sad when passengers don't care about seeing the view out of the window. Even just a few decades ago, being able to look at the world from the sky was a much rarer experience. Many people never get the opportunity to do so, either. I've been on more than 800 flights, but taking in the scenery and sights never gets old. I've gotten aerial views of Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, and Zion National Park on the way to Colorado, and the Grand Canyon en route to Las Vegas. When I land in New England in the fall , I love seeing the vibrant foliage from above. I've also spotted fireworks from the sky a few times when I've flown on holidays — and once, I even got to see the northern lights from the plane window. I would've missed all of these moments if the window shades were down. When I'm a passenger, my shade almost always stays up. I love catching a good view when I'm working, too. If there's a pretty sunrise or sunset, you might see me sneak over to an empty row of seats to snap a picture. Still, I can admit that — in some cases — it's best to leave the shades shut If I'm in the window seat, I'll be keeping the window shade open to enjoy the views. Leannna Coy To be fair, there are times as a working crew member when it can be nice for passengers to keep the shades lowered. On long flights, I've noticed that people seem calmer when the cabin is dark and are more likely to fall asleep. Selfishly, this makes my job a little easier as a flight attendant. I don't think keeping the window shade open when it's bright out is rude, though. Instead, I recommend that a passenger pack an eye mask if they aren't sitting in a window seat and know they'll have trouble sleeping in the daylight. Ultimately, there's really only one common scenario where I'll ask passengers to close their window shades, and it's when we've landed at a hot destination and are getting ready to deplane. Direct sunlight can heat up an aircraft while it's parked, so shutting the shades helps keep the cabin cooler for the next set of travelers. However, if we're cruising and the cabin's comfortably cool, I'd love for my passengers to keep those shades up. Are you team window shades open or closed? Who do you think should be in charge of the shade's position during a flight? Let us know in the comments — but first, read one former flight attendant's argument for keeping them shut . events.title: Apple shares slide after weak margin outlook; Palantir slumps 6% after earnings
events.summary: Apple and Palantir shares fell in premarket trading on Tuesday. The iPhone maker is reckoning with a global memory crunch and a scramble for computer components. Palantir shares fell on a slowdown in U.S. commercial total contract value bookings growth Apple and Palantir shares fell in premarket trading Tuesday after both announced earnings after the bell on Monday. The iPhone maker reported better-than-expected revenue in its fourth-quarter earnings, but fell short of estimates on iPad sales and issued a margin forecast that disappointed investors. Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates , with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time. Apple was last trading about 4% lower, and Palantir was down 6.5% in premarket trading. Apple's statement marked the first earnings report since John Ternus took over as CEO from Tim Cook in September. The company is reckoning with a global memory crunch and a scramble for computer components. Memory costs were higher this quarter than in the June period, the company said Monday. Despite the price surge, Ternus said Apple had just capped off its "best fiscal year ever." He told CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos that Apple's growth came despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. "The concern is profitability," said Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares. "Management pointed to memory as the main pressure, together with the cost of rolling out Siri AI. Memory shortages are also expected to limit Mac and iPad supply, as demand has run ahead of plans." Apple shares have risen 25% in 2026, ahead of other big tech names, but that premium leaves "little room for disappointment," Todorova added. Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said in its earnings report. But the company also reported a slowdown in U.S. commercial total contract value, or TCV, bookings growth, said William Blair in a Tuesday note. Investors will "no doubt be looking for evidence in subsequent quarters that 11% growth in U.S. commercial TCV bookings is a fluke of duration and not something structural," a Piper Sandler note from Monday said. "We believe that is the case and demand for PLTR's solutions still very much outstrip supply."

events.title: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
events.summary: Yum Brands beat Wall Street's quarterly earnings estimates and its revenue was in line with expectations. Taco Bell's same-store sales declined as a cyclospora outbreak tied to lettuce served at its restaurants weighed on traffic. During the quarter, Yum completed its divestiture of Pizza Hut. Yum Brands on Tuesday reported earnings that beat expectations, but a cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce at Taco Bell weighed on the company's same-store sales growth. However, Yum said Taco Bell, which the company considers a "growth engine" for its business, has since rebounded. "Since the end of September, Taco Bell U.S. has been outpacing the [quick-service restaurant] industry on same-store sales growth," Yum CEO Chris Turner said in a statement. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.56 adjusted vs. $1.49 expected Revenue: $2.05 billion vs. $2.05 billion expected Yum reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $1.62 billion, or $5.92 per share, up from $397 million, or $1.41 per share, a year earlier. Excluding gains from its divestiture of Pizza Hut and other items, the restaurant company earned $1.56 per share. Net sales rose 4% to $2.05 billion. During the quarter, Yum completed its divestiture of Pizza Hut. It closed the sale of the pizza chain's business in mainland China to Yum China on Aug. 7 and sold the rest of Pizza Hut to LongRange Capital on Sept. 1. The company's third-quarter results include Pizza Hut up until those dates. Excluding Pizza Hut, Yum's same-store sales were flat for the quarter as Taco Bell weighed on the company's overall results. Taco Bell's same-store sales declined by 4% as diners temporarily pulled back on visits due to the foodborne illness outbreak . Yum executives previously said the weekend of July 18 saw the most severe impact to sales, but sales trends have improved since then. Outside of the U.S., Taco Bell's much smaller international business reported same-store sales growth of 5%. KFC's same-store sales ticked up 1%, helped by system sales growth in China and Europe. The U.S., now the chicken chain's third-largest market, saw system sales shrink 6% in the quarter. Like Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes , KFC has struggled in the U.S. amid a wave of new competitors and more budget-conscious consumers.

events.title: Britain on notice: AI-powered ransomware attacks to arrive by 2028
events.summary: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. The warning accompanies its annual review and a separate assessment exploring how AI could change cyber threats over the next two years. The cyber arm of signals intelligence agency GCHQ did not provide much detail about what form this AI malware may take. However, it alluded to open source AI security tools that were initially intended to assist security researchers being repurposed for nefarious activity. Attackers are already repurposing such tools. For example, researchers are increasingly seeing widespread abuse of ARTEX, an open source, Chinese-made AI red-teaming platform, in attacks on UK registrar 123 Reg , Microsoft 365 , and others since its launch in July. In its pessimistic scenario for 2028, the NCSC envisages "a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks worldwide," with wider adoption of AI tools making attribution harder. China "has likely played a role" in supplying those tools in this future, "enabling them to hide their activities within the noise," the report states. It also considers a further threat: an autonomous attacker operating beyond its human operator's control. The NCSC says it "is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyberattacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint." Such attacks would likely complicate geopolitical relationships, owing again to attribution difficulties, making it easier for countries that order attacks on others to deny their involvement. The UK's plans for AI defense At a time when each Patch Tuesday seems to come loaded with record numbers of bugs , the NCSC acknowledges that AI is already changing vulnerability discovery and patching. The body is also exploring how AI could help defenders keep pace. Project DROMOS began earlier this year with a four-week pilot analyzing government code repositories, before expanding into selected operational environments. The Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) launched the project with the AI Security Institute and other departments. The NCSC says it uncovered hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities. The review also reaffirms plans for Cyber Shield, an agentic cyber defense system first teased in July. Cyber Shield is expected to be delivered in stages over the next five years. It will involve the NCSC providing defensive agents deployed by participating organizations with data that will strengthen national resilience to ongoing cyber threats. The NCSC will be running the scheme alongside the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), but acknowledged that this kind of automated defensive activity currently sits outside many organizations' risk tolerances, meaning it has a role to play in building trust in the system before adoption can go mainstream. As reported last week , the government has set aside £60 million to fund the initiative, and an additional £70 million to support a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre. The NERV Centre's job will be to identify and maintain an ongoing understanding of vulnerabilities across CNI organizations and the wider economy. Per last week's budget, £40 million will fund a National Agentic Security Unit responsible for responding to uncontrolled bots and other agentic mishaps, and £24 million was assigned to strengthen public sector defenses. An undisclosed sum will also help establish a new NCSC-managed AI Cyber Security Centre in Manchester to develop AI security expertise across government. In the meantime, NCSC CEO Dr Richard Horne is calling for organizations to "invest with urgency" in their security and resilience. "For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap," he said today, announcing the annual report. "We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. "The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all." Horne said organizations should treat the NCSC's Cyber Essentials certification as the starting point, but scale up resilience efforts in line with organizational size, complexity, and risk. The government also announced a 75 percent discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small, and medium-sized businesses applying for their first certificate. ®

events.title: SIA Engineering’s first-half profit falls 1.7% to $81.9m, with revenue down nearly 10%
events.summary: On a per-share basis, SIA Engineering’s earnings were down at 7.32 cents, from 7.45 cents a year earlier. SIA Engineering’s first-half net profit fell 1.7% to $81.9 million, as revenue dropped 9.7% to $658.6 million. It declared an interim dividend of 2.5 cents a share. Profit was hit by lower earnings from associated and joint-venture firms, higher finance charges and taxes. Revenue also fell because of weaker material sales. Operating profit doubled to $25.7 million on strong MRO demand and lower start-up losses. SIAEC expects steady demand, but warns of higher energy, freight and supply chain costs. SINGAPORE – SIA Engineering Company (SIAEC) reported a 1.7% year-on-year drop in net profit to $81.9 million for the six months ended Sept 30. This came as revenue fell 9.7% to $658.6 million. On a per-share basis, earnings were down at 7.32 cents, from 7.45 cents a year earlier. The group declared an interim dividend of 2.5 cents a share, which will be paid out on Nov 27. SIAEC said in a bourse filing on Nov 3 that the reduction in profit was due to a 10.7% dip in its share of profits of associated and joint-venture companies, coupled with lower interest income, higher finance charges and higher taxes. The $7.6 million drop in share of profits of associated and joint-venture companies, to $63.7 million in the first half, was attributed to higher costs incurred for capacity and capability expansion at an engine joint venture. This was only partly offset by higher output and profit margins of other associated companies. SIAEC expects such expansion costs to tail off in the next financial year, as facility development work is expected to finish by the end of that period. The group’s top line was affected by lower revenue from materials, it noted, adding that excluding materials, its revenue would have been 1.6% higher year on year. Group expenditure was down 11.6% at $623.9 million, in part due to the absence of an impairment cost recorded a year earlier. Operating profit doubled to $25.7 million, thanks to “healthy MRO demand” and lower losses at startup subsidiaries. For the second quarter ended Sept 30, group net profit rose $1.2 million year on year to $41.6 million, as group operating profit increased $5.6 million to $12.5 million as cuts in expenditure outweighed a dip in revenue. SIAEC said that demand for its maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) services remained steady in H1, with its line maintenance operations in Singapore handling 3.3% more flights year on year. Its Malaysian subsidiary, Base Maintenance Malaysia, opened its facility and first hangar in May and finished its first aircraft maintenance check for Air India in July. This is expected to broaden the unit’s customer base. The group also expanded its footprint in China with a 30% stake in Arport Aircraft Maintenance & Engineering (Fujian), which will provide services to airports in Xiamen, Fuzhou, Wuyishan and Longyan. In June, SIAEC signed a joint-venture agreement with Safran Aircraft Engines to establish a full shop for CFM LEAP engines. An existing joint venture in Singapore, Safran Landing System Services Singapore, opened a $22 million facility in September, raising its capacity by 40%. The group said demand for its MRO services will continue with the growth of air travel, especially in the Asia-Pacific, and particularly as older aircraft see delayed retirement due to slowdowns in new aircraft deliveries. The Middle East conflict has bumped up energy and freight costs, as well as continued supply chain bottlenecks for selected aircraft parts, SIAEC noted, adding that it “remains focused on driving productivity improvements, increasing operational resilience and maintaining cost discipline”. The company’s shares fell 1.3% or four cents to close at $2.94, before the results were announced. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Virgin Media O2 to cut thousands of jobs as it plans £800m cost savings
events.summary: Up to 25% of 16,000 workforce could go as telecoms group says it will increase use of AI in areas including customer service Virgin Media O2 is to cut thousands of jobs in an £800m cost-cutting drive as the telecommunications company aims to tackle its £22bn debt pile. VMO2, which is jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, said £300m of the savings target will come from job cuts that will reduce the company’s employee wage bill by 30% over the next two years. The company did not specify how many jobs this will equate to, but it could be as many as 25% of its 16,000 workforce. “While we will give a fuller update on the new strategic plan in the coming months, we are already progressing and making difficult decisions to prioritise investments and reduce costs which includes the size of our workforce,” said the VMO2 chief executive, Lutz Schüler. “Standing still and doing what we’ve always done is not an option and while many of these decisions are tough, they are necessary for our future success and growth. Virgin Media O2 must evolve, and the action needed to make that happen starts now.” The company, which said that most of the job losses will come from non-customer facing roles, said it intends to increase the use of AI tools in areas including customer service, network planning and fault management. It has offices in London, Reading and Dublin. The cost-cutting plans, which will save £800m annually by 2029, also include making savings by reducing the use of contractors and reviewing suppliers and supply chain contracts. Noel McClean, the deputy general of the Prospect union, said that the scale of the cuts will be “devastating” for staff and significantly impact the operation of the business. “The proposed 30% reduction in the VMO2 workforce [costs] will be devastating for those directly affected and will of course have an impact on colleagues remaining in the business,” he said. “Industry conditions are tough but this level of cuts will drastically alter the way VMO2 works. As a union we have vast experience of this kind of restructure and stand ready to work with the employer.” The Communication Workers Union (CWU) said it hoped the large-scale job cuts could be managed on a voluntary basis to minimise the impact on staff. “The most recent news, briefed out to the media, will undoubtedly leave members feeling stressed and worried about their long-term job prospects,” Stephen Albon, an assistant secretary at the CWU, said. “The CWU wishes to work with the company to mitigate these losses and will be urging the company to explore a voluntary approach to them.” VMO2 has also moved to reduce capital expenditure by halting investment in upgrading its network to full fibre, which is 50% complete, beyond existing commitments it has with partners. Instead the company will make a low-cost upgrade that will lead to most of the network that has not transitioned to full fibre being improved to 2Gbps speeds by the end of next year. The company also looks poised to slash its dividend, saying it is “reviewing options” relating to cash distributions to shareholders this year. The business said it expects to incur £250m in restructuring costs. The cuts were announced alongside VMO2’s latest results, which showed the company shed 23,300 broadband and 7,800 consumer mobile customers, in the quarter to the end of September. “The direction we’re setting today paves the way for the next chapter of Virgin Media O2: a company that will be leaner, clearer on priorities and faster in delivery,” Schuler said. The cuts were announced alongside VMO2’s latest results, which showed the company shed 23,300 broadband and 7,800 consumer mobile customers in the quarter to the end of September. events.title: Two police officers protecting polio workers in Pakistan shot dead
events.summary: The attackers, travelling on a motorcycle, opened fire on a police car in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Gunmen have shot dead two police officers protecting polio vaccination teams in northwestern Pakistan, a day after four officers protecting polio workers were kidnapped. The attackers, travelling on a motorcycle, opened fire on a police car in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Tuesday. A third officer was injured in the attack, which occurred as the officers were travelling to a nearby village to protect polio vaccination teams. list 1 of 3 How Kenyan volunteers hunt polio’s hidden trail list 2 of 3 Trump cuts WHO off from Gavi vaccine alliance funding list 3 of 3 Yemen’s health system could collapse in some areas, minister warns “Two police personnel were martyred and another was injured in the attack. However, no polio vaccination staff were present in the police vehicle,” police official Ali Rehman Khan told the AFP news agency. No one has claimed responsibility for the shooting, but similar attacks have regularly been carried out by the Pakistan Taliban, known by the acronym TTP, and other armed groups. These groups falsely believe that polio vaccination teams are part of a Western conspiracy to sterilise children. In a post on X, Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari said Tuesday’s shooting was “extremely regrettable and condemnable”. “Police personnel deployed to protect polio teams are performing a national duty; their sacrifices will not be forgotten,” he added. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is also where four officers protecting polio workers were abducted on Monday. They have yet to be found, and search efforts remain under way. Pakistan and neighbouring Afghanistan are the only two countries worldwide where wild poliovirus remains endemic. Pakistan reported 31 cases of the disease last year. The violence coincided with the launch of a targeted drive on Sunday to reach nearly 24 million children across 97 high-risk districts throughout the country. The same day, health authorities registered the country’s eighth polio case of the year in a 13-month-old girl from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP)’s Khyber district. KP remains the hardest-hit province with six cases, followed by two in Sindh. Polio is highly contagious and easily spreads between people. In extreme cases, it can lead to life-altering conditions, including paralysis.

events.title: Adipec: Welsh companies look to UAE for energy sector growth
events.summary: Welsh companies are looking to increase business with the UAE energy sector, with some already relying on the Middle East for more than half their sales. A Welsh delegation of more than 16 companies is attending Adipec in Abu Dhabi, representing fields such as electric energy, maritime vessels and industrial equipment. Holyhead Towing has operations in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar, and managing director Dylan Jones told The National the region now accounts for 70 to 75 per cent of its revenue. “We have eight vessels working here in support of the energy sector, predominantly oil and gas,” he said. “Also, infrastructure-type projects like land reclamation are quite big around Dubai and Abu Dhabi.” Attending Adipec is an ideal opportunity to meet customers in the one place, said Mr Jones. The Welsh government is supporting companies attending the exhibition through an export visit designed to help them meet customers and develop business overseas. Another Welsh firm, Tomoe Valve, exports about half its UK factory output to the Middle East, with the UAE accounting for its largest regional market. For the manufacturer, repeat visits to Abu Dhabi have helped build a market for products made in Wales. “The Middle East is obviously a large attraction for us,” the company's business development director Clive Johns told The National . “About 50 per cent of our capacity is exported to the Middle East from the UK factory.” Tomoe manufactures butterfly valves used to control the flow of liquid and gas through pipes. Its products were originally designed for the oil and gas industry, making the Middle East a natural market. The UAE now accounts for most of Tomoe Valve's regional business. Mr Johns said the Welsh government has always had some “very good” contacts in the Emirates, with the help of the British embassy. He now wants to develop work in Oman, Kuwait and Iraq. “Adipec is the place to do business in the Middle East, not just UAE,” Mr Johns said. The company entered the year with a strong order book, although projects have been taking longer to receive final investment approval amid regional uncertainty. “Stuff is still moving,” Mr Johns said. “But yeah, it [uncertainty] slowed things down.” As the UAE places increasing focus on localisation, the company is considering how domestic partners could take on assembly, testing and other work. Establishing its own factory would be expensive, Mr Johns said. However, he added they “definitely want to work with local Emirati companies”. For Clenergy EV, chief executive William David said growth in the region has created opportunities for charging infrastructure. “For us, the target market is any building that needs electric-vehicle charging infrastructure,” he said. Its priority at the exhibition is to find partners who understand domestic customers and can represent Clenergy. Mr David said Wales’s industrial history has continued to influence its energy businesses. “We were part of the Industrial Revolution. We had the coal mines transitioning to renewable power in Wales.” The company now intends to establish its business in the UAE's expanding transport and property market.

events.title: Car finance compensation payments explained
events.summary: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. Who could receive car finance compensation? The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much. Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan. Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders. How much compensation could victims receive? Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement. The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn. How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered. The FCA has announced some claimants might be offered an early settlement, but only if it as good as what would be paid under the current proposed central scheme. What do victims need to do to claim compensation? Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything. The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company. The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts. Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation . The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external . lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster some people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, if the agreement began on or after 1 April 2014 and you complained by 30 June 2026 some of those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027, if the agreement began before 1 April 2014 there are exemptions , external , and anyone who does not hear from their lender by the dates set out, isn't necessarily owed compensation those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees. FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers. When will drivers receive compensation and who will pay? Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027. But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme. Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed" . The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 February to 3 March.
