AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters New CEO John Ternus toasts record sales as soaring RAM costs threaten supplies and squeeze margins Raspberry Pi hikes prices again, barely a month after the last round 3 hours ago Darkbloom, which allowed Mac users to rent out their GPUs for AI inference, warns of low payouts 3 days ago PC chip plunge wipes out a quarter of Intel’s value 4 days ago Traces of new Pi hardware spotted in GitHub 5 days ago SK Hynix says memory shortages to persist until 2030 6 days ago Apple says it sold more Macs in fiscal 2026 than in any previous year, but soaring memory prices are threatening to spoil the Cupertino-based gadget maker's record-breaking run. The warning came during Apple's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, the first since John Ternus took over as CEO . "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus told analysts. Apple has already raised prices across much of its hardware lineup, including Macs and iPads in June and iPhones in September. Those increases, along with existing inventories and cheaper components elsewhere, have softened the blow. Unfortunately for Apple, memory prices haven't finished climbing. "For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs," Ternus said, adding that Apple expects to pay more for memory beyond the end of the year. Mac buyers haven't been deterred so far. Apple pulled in $10.8 billion from Macs in the September quarter, up 24 percent year-on-year, following $10.35 billion in the June quarter, up nearly 29 percent year-on-year. The MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro accounted for much of the latest growth. "We have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time," Ternus said. Whether Apple can keep enough of them on shelves is another matter. COO Sabih Khan said the company had already experienced supply constraints across iPhone, Mac, and iPad during the September quarter, largely because of limited availability of advanced chipmaking capacity. Now memory is taking over as the chief headache. "For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected," Khan said. Apple isn't sitting idle. Ternus revealed that its manufacturing purchase obligations jumped by $33 billion between June and September as it bids to secure supplies, although he offered no indication of when the memory crunch might ease. Higher memory costs are also squeezing Apple's margins. CFO Kevan Parekh said gross margin fell by roughly one percentage point between the June and September quarters, excluding tariff effects, entirely because of memory costs. The damage would have been worse without existing inventory, cheaper non-memory components, and those price hikes. Apple expects its gross margin to fall from 47.9 percent in the September quarter to between 45 and 46 percent in December, primarily because of higher memory costs. Costs associated with rolling out Siri AI will also weigh on the figure. Parekh said Apple had "reluctantly" raised hardware prices, but supply constraints made it too early to assess how customers were responding. Meanwhile, Ternus is keen to sell customers on the Mac as an AI machine, particularly for running models locally. "Mac mini and Mac Studio in particular are pushing the boundaries of local private AI," he said, pointing to workloads that previously would have been difficult to run on desktop hardware. Apple has also refreshed its Mac lineup with M6-powered machines and a touchscreen MacBook Pro, giving customers more reasons to upgrade, provided there's enough memory to build the things. Not that the wider business is struggling. Apple reported September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year-on-year, while iPhone revenue climbed 17 percent to $57.6 billion. Services brought in $31.6 billion, up 10 percent. Apple forecasts revenue growth of 7 to 10 percent in the December quarter despite the supply constraints.

events.title: Larry Ellison has crashed to 9th on the rich list after a $159 billion wealth decline in the past year
events.summary: Larry Ellison, the Oracle cofounder. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images Larry Ellison's net worth has fallen by nearly 50% over the past year. The Oracle cofounder is now the world's ninth-richest person. Oracle shares fell on Monday amid concerns about its AI spending. Larry Ellison has lost $159 billion, almost half his net worth, over the past year. The Bloomberg Billionaires Index shows Ellison's net worth has fallen by 49.2% to $164 billion, making him the world's ninth-richest person. He started the year ranked fifth — ahead of Mark Zuckerberg and behind Google's Sergey Brin. The 82-year-old's wealth is tied to his shares in Oracle, the tech company he cofounded in 1977. Its share price is down 39% since the start of 2026, and over 53% since November 2025. That included a nearly 9% drop on Monday as investors reacted to Oracle's announcement that it is issuing new shares and bonds to raise $20 billion. The stock fell another 1.5% in premarket trade on Tuesday. Investors are wary about the size of the raise, with growing concerns about how much Oracle is spending to build the data centers needed for its AI contracts, and whether it can deliver on the massive infrastructure expansion. The share sale would also dilute existing investors' stakes, and the added debt would heighten concerns about the company's already hefty borrowing. A broader tech sell-off has also reflected fears that the AI arms race is cooling. Google's parent company , Alphabet, had its worst post-earnings reaction last week, with its stock falling 13%. It's a sharp reversal from 2025, when Oracle stock surged on enthusiasm that it could become a major provider of AI infrastructure. In September 2025, Ellison was briefly the world's richest person as Oracle shares jumped some 40% in a single day. He is now barely in the top 10 on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, hanging on below Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Elon Musk remains the richest person in the world by a massive margin, though his net worth has fallen from trillionaire levels . In mid-September, Oracle began a fresh round of layoffs, as Business Insider first reported . The job cuts came as the company racks up debt to fund its AI spending and affected double-digit percentages on some teams. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Gen Zers you call when the chatbots are talking smack
events.summary: Megan Shears and Icy Wong didn't have traditional experience when they got hired at London reputation firm Michael Macfarlane Associates. Ayesha Kazim for BI A rich guy had a very bad day on the internet. An embarrassing incident involving a flashy car went viral. TMZ picked it up, as did local news. On Reddit, one commenter called the centimillionaire a "douchebag." That's all according to Div Churiwal, who runs Nexus Multimedia, a California-based reputation-management company that caters to wealthy clients. Churiwal won't tell me the client's name, so I try to reverse-engineer it from the clues he gives me. Google gets me nowhere. Neither does ChatGPT nor Gemini. Div Churiwal puts his legion of Gen Zers to work on one particular reputation-shaping platform: Reddit. Gilbert Flores/Billboard via Getty Images Making unwanted information harder to find is what his clients pay him for, especially at a time when AI is changing how people search for one another. "All we have to do is release a whole army of other information that would overpower what's trending," Churiwal says, citing podcasts, news articles, and Reddit threads as tools at their disposal. To do that, he employs two dozen Gen Z staffers who work to master the new rules of AI search , which is fast becoming the default. They're familiar with Reddit threads and a variety of other social media platforms, and fluent in the vernacular of the Extremely Online. While wealthy people have always paid professionals to manage their reputations , today, they face a new threat: managing what chatbots say about them. And the firms I speak with say that as a legion of young global elites emerges, they are finding new value in advisors who grew up in the digital world. "You don't want boomers writing Reddit threads where Gen Z is the audience," Churiwal, 34, says. Three reputation-management firms tell me that ultrawealthy clients are increasingly concerned about how chatbots portray them, as more people use AI tools to research someone before meeting them, doing business with them, or inviting them onto a board. "I've had clients where a single negative article has cost them, in one case, we think about $200 million US within just a few months," says Michael Macfarlane, the founder of London reputation firm Michael Macfarlane Associates. In this shifting landscape, his job has become "can you create an information environment in advance that mitigates the impact of that?" The good old-fashioned Google search that dominated recent decades provides a list of ranked links for users to click through and form opinions, often prioritizing major publications. Chatbots and AI search instead perform multiple related searches and synthesize a wealth of information from across the web into a write-up that spoon-feeds an impression of the person searched. When Macfarlane was coming up, the ideal reputation manager was a seasoned PR operator with a thick contacts book, someone who knew which newspaper editor to call and could try to land a flattering profile in The Wall Street Journal over a boozy lunch . Increasingly, though, Macfarlane finds himself relying on the judgment of employees born after the dot-com boom . Michael Macfarlane relies on his younger employees to help shape online discourse. Ayesha Kazim for BI "I'm 43," Macfarlane says. "There's stuff that I would admit that I'm not fully across that younger people are." He has a blunt name for his recruitment strategy : "Hire the children." His younger employees audit what LLMs say about clients, monitor the themes and sentiment associated with their names, and decide what sort of content could strengthen their reputations online, be it a podcast appearance or a series of long-form posts on social media. At Nexus, Churiwal puts his legion of Gen Zers to work on one particular reputation-shaping platform: Reddit. They spend most of their work hours starting and participating in Reddit threads about wealthy clients and the businesses they run. Reddit is a "huge tool," he says, because "it's one of the easiest peer-to-peer communication platforms for gauging how people feel about things." Churiwal believes that getting involved in those conversations can influence what AI chatbots surface about his clients, helping to overpower dirty laundry with freshly laundered content. On a negative post, he says, they might ask a dissatisfied customer or anonymous hater what went wrong, or respond on the client's behalf. Churiwal says they always disclose their affiliation. His workers' fluency in online culture, gives them an advantage over millennials like himself, he says. "Like, what's LARPing?" Around a boardroom table in London's Canary Wharf neighborhood , two of Macfarlane's "children" sit across from each other. Icy Wong, a 22-year-old analyst, spent her childhood between China, Hong Kong, and London. She wrote her undergraduate thesis on trust and credibility on RedNote, the Chinese social media platform. For Macfarlane, her multilingual background and fluency across Asian and Western online platforms make up for her lack of traditional experience. Advisors at Michael Macfarlane Associates encourage clients to lean into newer media formats. Ayesha Kazim for BI Opposite her sits Megan Shears, a 25-year-old associate who studied history at King's College London before doing freelance work in social media and fashion PR. Last year, Macfarlane messaged her on LinkedIn about a job. She recalls telling him, "I don't have the experience you're looking for." He hired her anyway. A year into the job, Shears has come to see her youth as an asset. An emerging generation of international wealth holders makes up a significant share of Michael Macfarlane Associates' clients. "The great wealth transfer is happening, and it's underway," she says. "You're going to be dealing with a lot of young billionaires and millionaires who are much more native than maybe their advisors give them credit for." A record 35 Gen Zers appeared on Forbes' 2026 World Billionaires' List, a rise that Forbes attributes to large startup funding rounds, the AI boom, and inheritances. By 2040, the children of billionaires will inherit at least $5.9 trillion, according to the UBS Billionaire Ambitions Report 2025. Pearl Lam, a 58-year-old gallerist with a signature deep-purple bouffant, is one of the eight children of the late billionaire real-estate tycoon Lim Por-yen. Hong Kong-born, Lam began curating exhibitions in her 20s and has since built a prominent career in the art world. When Michael Macfarlane Associates first audited Lam's online reputation, she says, it found that the version of her dished out by AI was stuck in an earlier chapter of her career. Pearl Lam wants her online identity to catch up with her professional ambitions. events.title: Grain under fire: Russian, Ukrainian Black Sea attacks threaten food supply
events.summary: Renewed strikes on Black Sea shipping threaten grain exports, drive up food prices and deepen global food insecurity. Kyiv, Ukraine – Three black naval drones resembling oversized plastic toys struck a freighter sluggishly navigating the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria on October 28. Aerial drones joined the attack, and explosions rocked the Liberian-flagged Contship Jet Monrovia, loaded with more than 400 terracotta-coloured containers. The vessel, travelling from the Israeli port of Haifa to Romania, listed and sank, but all 18 crew members were rescued, Bulgarian authorities said. list 1 of 4 Seven missing after two tankers catch fire off Romania’s Black Sea coast list 2 of 4 NATO to send additional patrol planes to Black Sea after drone attacks list 3 of 4 Russia’s alleged sabotage campaign in Europe raises fears of escalation list 4 of 4 Ukraine invests in firepower as it inflicts a new Russian casualty record The daytime assault was filmed by crew members, other ships and photographed by a French surveillance plane. The drones were Russian, Kyiv claimed, adding that the attack was designed to make the Black Sea unsafe for civilian ships, paralyse Ukraine’s exports of grain and further hobble its war-ravaged economy. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv’s forces conducted “no operations in this part of the sea, and this latest tragedy involving civilian vessels is another part of Russia’s effort to make the western Black Sea completely unfit for navigation.” The European Union’s delegation to Kyiv said in August that Russia is “systematically strangling Ukraine’s ability to feed the world.” It added that by targeting ports, shipping lanes, and agricultural infrastructure, Moscow is not just waging war on Ukraine, but also “weaponising hunger against millions in Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.” And while Europe’s food security is not at stake, the EU is “fully committed to continue supporting Ukraine’s access to international markets,” Paula Ritter-Moschutz, a spokeswoman for Agriculture and Customs at the European Commission, told Al Jazeera. “We are continuously assessing its implications for agriculture, global food security, and the economy,” she said. “We support the initiatives for a moratorium on Black Sea attacks.” At least 30 sailors have been killed or gone missing in the recent surge of attacks, according to Bulgarian and Romanian authorities and maritime tracking services. ‘A shadow deal was breached by Ukraine’ Moscow’s alleged campaign follows Ukrainian strikes on Russian freighters and oil tankers in the Black Sea and the adjoining Sea of Azov amid attacks on oil refineries, military plants and warehouses. Those strikes intensified in July, and Moscow’s suspected retaliatory attacks may have been prevented, observers say. “A shadow deal [not to strike each other’s cargo ships] was breached by Ukraine in the summer,” Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher with Germany’s Bremen University who analyses the Russia-Ukraine war, told Al Jazeera. Russian President Vladimir Putin “definitely liked the idea of completely ruining Ukrainian exports,” he said. “Putin did issue several warnings before systemic strikes on the Odesa group of ports began.” “If the attacks on [Russian] tankers continue, we will consider taking retaliatory measures against ships from countries assisting Ukraine,” Putin said in December. Russian farmers and grain exporters usually ship more than two-thirds of their harvests via the Black Sea. As a result of the lack of security, they are testing exporting grain through the Arctic port of Murmansk, though the distance between the farms and the buyers will significantly increase costs. Before Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, about a third of the world’s grain exports passed through the Black Sea, and Ukraine provided a tenth of global wheat exports and 15 percent of corn. Ukraine’s customers include Middle East and North African nations. Over the past 12 months, wheat prices rose by a fifth. Chicago wheat futures, a global benchmark for the wheat market, have gone up from $5.03 per bushel (35 litres) in October 2025 to $6.03 in October this year. The US-Israel war on Iran, global warming and a drought in South Africa have also contributed to the spike. Constant Russian strikes by jet-powered drones, cruise and ballistic missiles brought operations in Ukraine’s largest maritime hub, Odesa, to a halt. “Today, after the ports of Odesa are paralysed, there’s no way out. Hardly more than 50 percent of grain can be exported via land routes,” Viktor Honcharenko, president of the Association of Farmers and Private Land Owners of Ukraine, told Al Jazeera. “Lots of wheat remained on the fields, it’s not being harvested,” he said. The consequences will have a domino effect on Ukraine’s entire economy.

events.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
events.summary: Published 3 November 2026, 02:11 GMT The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month. The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday. Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders. The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market. As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits. The deal could have the following impact: Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment". Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July. Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his. Jon Walsh of Bio&Me said his firm had stopped exporting yoghurt due to vets' fees Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news". "We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop." The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned. "It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said. "You just kind of give up because you're losing money." In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue. "The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added. Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU. Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards". Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix". "The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added. Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules. "Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with Prime Minister Andy Burnham While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force. The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax. The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days.

events.title: Current price of oil as of November 3, 2026
events.summary: As of 6:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil is trading at $110.45 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s $2.15 below yesterday morning’s level and about $45 higher than where it stood a year ago. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $112.60 -1.90% Price of oil 1 month ago $106.48 +3.72% Price of oil 1 year ago $65.41 +68.85% Will oil prices go up? No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds. Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring. It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s delivered the first major oil shock when the Middle East slashed exports and placed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices fell in the mid-1980s due to lower demand and an influx of non-OPEC oil producers joining the market. Prices surged again in 2008 as global demand grew, but then crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand plummeted like never before—pushing prices below $20 per barrel. To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more. Check out our recent coverage: Ryanair’s CEO says fares could rise up to 20% next year because of the Iran war As Trump eyes new attack, Iran vows to retaliate beyond the Mideast While Americans turn against data centers, Brazil offers tax breaks and cheap power Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: Wall Street is bracing for a fresh wave of tariffs, Iran action (and potentially a government shutdown) after the midterms
events.summary: Though analysts have been wrong before, many observers expect the Democrats to claw back some political power in this week’s midterm elections. Despite that, Wall Street is expecting President Trump to double down on some of his less popular policies, following the vote. At the time of writing, Harvard University’s polling gives a 96% chance that the Democrats take the House, and a 78% likelihood of the Democrats taking both the House and the Senate. Goldman Sachs , for example, wrote to clients this morning that it expects President Trump to increase tariffs in the event the Democrats secure greater Congressional influence. Economists Alec Phillips and Abhay Duggirala reasoned that “Democrats have indicated they would seek to reverse some of President Trump’s tariffs, but we expect this to have a limited effect since the reversals would likely be focused on a few countries (e.g., Canada) or products.” “We expect President Trump to announce new tariff increases after the election that would more than offset those reductions, likely resulting in a rise in the US effective tariff rate of a little under 2pp.” Tariffs will also likely become an increasingly important revenue source in the coming months. The conflict in the Middle East, for example, is proving costly, and sits against a backdrop of $40 trillion in national debt with calls from budget hawks to reduce deficits to 3% of GDP from its current 6%. But any efforts to reduce these deficits will likely get bogged down in a more divided government, according to ING’s James Smith. He wrote to clients that fiscal gridlock will likely push attention back to trade policy and how to squeeze more revenue out of import relationships. “Remember tariffs?” Smith wrote. “After the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s emergency tariffs, temporary 10% blanket rates ultimately gave way to a more permanent structure under Section 301. The issue has since slipped remarkably far down the agenda.” Iran action The White House’s course of action in the Middle East, post-midterms, remains an unanswered question. As UBS’s Paul Donovan described it, the president may become more aggressive in the Gulf war “once freed from the pursuit of popularity.” According to a Pew Research study last month, just 14% of voters said they strongly approve of President Trump’s handling of the military conflict with Iran, with a further 20% said they “somewhat” approve. With voters disenchanted, Trump’s only remaining motivations for the conflict lie in national security and his personal legacy. “Where markets will want to focus is on the Republican reaction to the results,” said Donovan. “Does the Republican Party divide over MAGA-related issues, and does President Trump escalate hostilities in the Gulf War with wider economic consequences at home and abroad?” More broadly, the cost of paying for the action settles into longer-term divisions about the future of government spending. Recent reports on the costs of the Iran war now come to $47 billion, with the conflict initially outlined as a matter of weeks now stretching into months. “Republicans will likely attempt to pass a reconciliation bill along party lines in the coming weeks that could add substantially to defense spending and potentially address the debt limit, which will have to be dealt with before the late summer/fall of next year,” Deutsche Bank wrote to clients on Friday. “Recall, also, that federal government funding runs out on December 11 which will require bipartisan support for a continuing resolution to prevent a shutdown.” Trump signed the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act on September 2, which funded federal agencies through a 72-day window to December 11. events.title: Drivers may get compensation offers before car finance saga ends
events.summary: Published 3 November 2026, 09:45 GMT Drivers may be offered compensation from lenders ahead of the next legal battle in the car finance mis-selling saga. Regulator the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it would welcome lenders making settlement offers as long as customers were not given a worse deal than under its proposed central scheme. That scheme is facing a legal challenge, to be heard in February, with resulting compensation unlikely to be paid until late next year. But Barclays has confirmed it will make early compensation offers from now, with others expected to follow suit. The FCA said it would still only expect a minority of claimants to be made early offers, with most having to wait for the outcome of next year's court case. Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA's general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said: "Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. It's clear they want the choice. "Anyone who wants to wait can, and there's no obligation to agree to the offer. We'll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means." The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. But millions of drivers who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024 will be entitled to compensation after the loans were mis-sold. They mostly related to when car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. Average compensation payouts of about £829 are expected to be made related to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year Published 1 hour ago Compensation will cost the industry up to £9.1bn, including administrative costs. Individual payouts will vary, depending on the degree of harm each driver faced. With huge compensation payouts inevitable, some lenders have already set aside millions of pounds to cover the cost. Barclays has decided to start making compensation payments early, potentially to start clearing the cost off its balance sheet. It pointed out that claimants had already faced "a considerable wait". "By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude," said a Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson. "Each offer will be calculated using the FCA's redress scheme methodology. We will clearly explain how it has been calculated and what accepting a full and final settlement means, so customers can decide whether accepting the offer is right for them." The lender said claimants would start to be contacted directly "in the coming weeks". But it stressed not all customers whose complaints were acknowledged on or before 1 October 2026 would receive an early settlement offer. Guidelines on whether to accept an offer The FCA has published a factsheet to help drivers , external work out whether they should accept early settlements from lenders. It will include a list of lenders who are making early offers, to ensure claimants with other lenders are not scammed. The regulator said lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes: Being able to keep any payment, even if the final settlement under the central scheme after the legal challenges proved to be smaller Claimants would not be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge meant they would have been paid more Accepting an offer takes you out of the scheme and stops any further input from the financial ombudsman The Finance and Leasing Association, which represents lenders, said: "We want to see consumers receive the fairest outcome in as timely a way as possible and recognise that, in some cases, that may point to early settlement, while in others it may be appropriate to await greater legal certainty." But Kevin Durkin, solicitor advocate and director at HD Law, who represented Marcus Johnson who won his case in the Supreme Court, said he had "real reservations" that fair compensation would be offered. "These are only heightened by reports that just a small number of claimants will receive what could be lowball offers. I fear this is crumbs from the table, for some customers who are highly likely to be owed more, while the vast majority will receive no offer at all," he said. The main proposed FCA scheme remains partially suspended, pending legal challenges in February. Consumer group Consumer Voice said the proposed compensation scheme left "too many people short-changed".

events.title: I partied until 4 a.m. when I was in college. My Gen Z twins are home before midnight and work at 6:30 a.m.
events.summary: The author jokes his twins would rather work than party. Courtesy of the author My 20-year-old son told his grandfather he lives "a quiet life." His twin agreed. At their age, my Saturday nights ended with a kebab at 4 a.m. They're a different generation, and I'm proud of the people they've become. At dinner at my parents' house, my dad asked my 20-year-old twins , Charlie and Thomas, if they'd been going out. Thomas said he didn't really go out much. Charlie said, "I live a quiet life." My dad summed it up. "You aren't party guys," he said. That got us talking about how differently we used to spend our weekends. My dad proudly shared that his mother occasionally found him passed out on their front lawn . Their weekend starts with a 6:30 a.m. shift Since they were 16, both boys have worked in the produce department at the same grocery store . They start work early every Saturday and Sunday morning. Those were the hours they were given when they started, and they've stuck with them ever since. On weekdays, they fit their shifts around university, where both are doing well. Like most Australian students , they still live at home. They aren't antisocial. Both have girlfriends, go to the gym, play golf, and hang out with friends. Neither seems to think a good weekend requires a late night or a hangover. The author's sons' rarely drink. Courtesy of the author Legally, they've been old enough to drink here for two years, but they rarely do. Charlie spends plenty of Saturday nights with his girlfriend. But she goes out a lot more than he does, and when she's at a party, he offers to drive over late, pick her up, and take her home. Thomas goes out a bit more. He'll go to an occasional rave or a concert, but he's usually home well before midnight. My parents barely saw me on a weekend At university, I worked in a department store, but I never had an early shift. On Saturday nights, we'd start with drinks at a friend's house because it was cheaper than paying bar prices, then head to a club to drink, catch up, and dance. Or try to. Most nights ended with a kebab around 4 a.m., my late-night street food of choice. That's about two hours before my sons' alarms go off now. The one Saturday I was sick and stayed home, I told my friends it was my first Saturday night in for three years. My parents never minded my late nights out. Given his fondness for the front lawn, my dad wasn't in a position to. My wife, Cece, is American and went to LSU. She definitely enjoyed the party scene the school is famous for. She knows times have changed, but she's still surprised by how little the boys go out. Some of our friends have the opposite problem. Their kids spend too much money on alcohol, stay out late, and sleep all Sunday. Compared to that, I've got nothing to complain about. Even their birthday didn't count as a special occasion It takes something big to get them out. At their 20th birthday dinner, neither of them would have a beer with us or go to a bar. The author says his twins have a very different lifestyle to what he had in his 20s. Courtesy of the author Schoolies was one occasion. It's the Aussie version of spring break, and after high school, they traveled interstate with a big group of friends. A year later, Thomas spent six weeks in Europe and went out far more often than usual. For Charlie, it took Oasis . When we saw the band last year, his first concert, he suggested a few rounds of beers before they even came on. I was surprised. I'm extremely proud of them They've got jobs, great friends, and good grades. If I raised them to be too responsible, I've no idea how. They didn't learn it from their dad, Cece, or their grandpa. They're just a different generation from us, and most of the changes are good ones. I don't need them to end up passed out on anyone's front lawn. I'd just like them to occasionally come home late with a story they can tell their grandkids. So I ask if they're going out, and if they want a drink, I offer to drive. Most weekends, they say no. They've got work in the morning. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UK’s most polluting power plant could power country’s largest AI datacentre
events.summary: Drax’s FTSE 250 owner strikes £20bn deal to build infrastructure in what it says is site’s ‘next chapter’ Britain’s most polluting power plant could soon power the country’s largest datacentre under a £20bn deal to build AI infrastructure on the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire. The power plant’s FTSE 250 owner has struck a deal with the infrastructure investor Brookfield and ⁠and the AI infrastructure platform Radiant to develop a datacentre with an eventual capacity of more than 1 gigawatt that could begin operations by early 2028. In the initial phase, Drax will provide the datacentre project with land and access to the national power grid through existing connections on the site, but it hopes to begin powering the datacentre directly by the early 2030s. Drax said the development could attract more than £20bn ($26.8bn) in investment and represent “the next chapter” for the former power plant after ministers signalled plans to limit its power generation in the future. The Drax chief executive, Will Gardiner, said the project would “help secure the long-term future of the site and protect hundreds of jobs” while “supporting the north’s reindustrialisation and strengthening sovereign AI capability”. The largest power plant in the UK produces almost 5% of the country’s electricity by burning woody biomass pellets, making the site the single largest emitter of carbon dioxide, according to analysts. These emissions are not accounted for by the UK government because Drax claims the equivalent carbon emissions are absorbed by growing trees that provide the waste wood used to make the biomass pellets. However, the government promised that Drax would play a “much more limited role” in future after growing concerns over the company’s sustainability claims , and will have access to only half its current £2m a day subsidies from 2027 to 2031. The company hopes to clear the regulatory approvals needed to begin supplying the datacentre directly before 2031 to secure its future revenues. The news was welcomed by equity analysts, while the company’s market value climbed by almost 9% on the London Stock Exchange to almost £3bn. Under phase one of the project, the datacentre would be operational from the first quarter of 2028 with up to 100MW of compute capacity. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The deal has emerged a week after the government published a draft national policy statement on datacentres, which said they were “as fundamental to our economy as the railways and electricity networks on which we have long depended”. “We must take control over the development of datacentres in this country and ensure that the country and host communities benefit from them,” the government said. However, the UK’s congested grid infrastructur e and ambitious legally binding climate targets have raised questions over how a dash to build datacentres could be powered without relying heavily on expensive and polluting off-grid gas generation.

events.title: Higher oil prices boost Saudi Aramco profits despite disruption from attacks
events.summary: Saudi Aramco is reporting a 35% increase in third-quarter net profit, boosted by higher oil prices and the sale of a stake in a Malaysian company FRANKFURT, Germany -- Majority state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco on Tuesday reported a 35% increase in third-quarter net profit as earnings were boosted by higher oil prices and the sale of its stake in a Malaysian refining and petrochemical company. Net profit rose to $36.3 billion from $26.9 billion in the year-earlier quarter. Adjusted net profit, which leaves out the sale of a stake in PRefChem to Malaysian state oil company Petronas, rose 9% to $31.2 billion. The company also benefitted from high profit margins at its refineries turning crude into useable products such as diesel fuel. Saudi Aramco sold its oil for an average of $95.20 a barrel during the quarter, compared to $70.10 in the year-before quarter, the company said in a news release. Oil prices surged after the outbreak of the Iran war due to disruption of supply and uncertainty about the course of the conflict. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say After the war began in February, Saudi Aramco was able to use its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to maintain a significant share of its oil exports despite disruption of tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz due to the risk of Iranian attack. The pipeline was attacked Sept. 10 but has resumed flows. Saudi oil is now also being transported through the strait using a U.S.-protected corridor near the coast of Oman. Exports have continued despite attacks on Aramco facilities by Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. The company is a major source of revenue for the Saudi government as it invests in projects aimed at diversifying its economy. events.title: Long-term demand for LNG will continue to rise, Adnoc Gas CEO says
events.summary: Demand for gas will continue to rise as the world requires more energy to power the development of artificial intelligence, the chief executive of Adnoc Gas has said. Severe disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has shut down about one fifth of the world’s monthly liquefied natural gas supply since the Middle East conflict started in February, adversely affecting some countries in Asia, Shell said in its latest LNG outlook. But Fatema Al Nuaimi told Adipec on Tuesday: “Gas is going to continue to grow and demand is going to continue in the long-term.” Ras Laffan in Qatar, the world's largest LNG refinery, was severely damaged by Iranian missile attacks. QatarEnergy declared long-term force majeure on contracts with buyers in China, South Korea, Italy and Belgium. However, global demand for LNG is projected to increase by around 65 per cent by 2050, to nearly 700 million tonnes a year, Shell said in its report. A key driver for growth comes with the rising development of new data centres to power AI technology. “We have these new demand hubs from AI … about 9.5 million tonnes of LNG required just for SpaceX,” Ms Al Nuaimi said. “We are an ambitious nation when it comes to building AI hubs to attract the biggest names in artificial intelligence and for this to be materialised, energy is required.” Abu Dhabi is investing heavily in AI infrastructure to support the growth of the technology. Among the projects is the 1-gigawatt Stargate UAE project being developed by Abu Dhabi-based AI company G42 in partnership with technology giants OpenAI, Oracle and Nvidia. It will lie within the 5GW UAE-US AI Campus in Abu Dhabi. ⁠Ms Al Nuaimi called for flexibility and co-operation in ​managing gas contracts to adapt to changing market conditions. “Contracts are very rigid, written with terms and conditions, and no matter how you craft them, they are not fit for different circumstances that face us in the market. So it's important for us to be flexible and to work together eventually.” Adnoc Gas on Tuesday also announced the singing of a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG to France's TotalEnergies, as the Abu Dhabi company expands its share of the global market. The agreement comes as Adnoc scales up a new global LNG trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the commercial capabilities of Adnoc Trading . Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs as well as end customers in more than 20 countries.

events.title: How India pulled 500 million people out of poverty as inequality deepens
events.summary: India’s extreme poverty declined from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent between 2011 and 2023 according to the World Bank. Bengaluru, India — India lifted nearly 500 million people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, with extreme poverty dropping from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent in the world’s most populous nation during the period, according to a new World Bank report. The only other parallel in poverty reduction on this scale is China, which lifted more than 800 million people out of extreme poverty, though that was over a period of 40 years. list 1 of 3 How Ambani’s Jio became India’s second-largest company list 2 of 3 India’s largest dam planned to counter China faces Indigenous revolt list 3 of 3 India protesters march with 1km banner of deleted voters’ names Yet despite the substantial fall in poverty in India — home to 1.4 billion people — the income and wealth inequality gap has widened significantly since it opened up its economy in the early 1990s. According to the 2026 World Inequality Report, inequality in India remains among the highest in the world. We take a look at how India managed to almost eradicate extreme poverty, and at the contrast between that accomplishment and the deep economic inequality that remains in the world’s most populous nation. Based on a threshold of $3 a day, the World Bank said extreme poverty in India declined from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent between 2011 and 2023. Extreme poverty is defined as the minimum amount of money needed to afford basic essentials such as food, water, shelter and clothing. Estimating poverty metrics based on three official household surveys, the bank also said an estimated 496 million people have been lifted out of poverty as the share of India’s population living below the lower middle-income poverty threshold of $4.2 a day fell from 57.7 percent to 16.1 percent. The authors of the report, led by World Bank’s South Asia poverty economist Ayago Wambile, wrote that poverty in India is “projected to continue declining, albeit more gradually with the poverty rate at the $4.20/day line expected to fall from 14.2 percent in 2026 to 12.1 percent by 2028”. “This progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth, rising employment, especially among women, and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies,” they added. How significant is India’s poverty reduction? India lifting nearly 500 million out of poverty in 12 years has been lauded as “remarkable progress” by the World Bank. It added that the downward trend represents “one of the fastest poverty declines in the world”. To determine India’s poverty rates, the bank used Household Consumption Expenditure Surveys (HCES), which were conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), an Indian government body. A 2022 report, jointly produced by the World Bank and the Chinese Ministry of Finance, said China had lifted 800 million people out of poverty, a process that took 40 years. Last month, the World Bank also raised its economic growth forecast for India to 7.1 percent. In a post on Instagram on Sunday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi lauded India’s progress in tackling poverty. “A historic fall in poverty. A generational rise in opportunity,” he said. Last November, the southern state of Keralam, which has been governed either by a Congress party-led centrist coalition or an alliance of communist parties since independence, became the first in the country to officially declare itself free from extreme poverty. Keralam has the best education and health statistics of major Indian states. Santosh Mehrotra, a development economist with India’s now-abolished Planning Commission, and currently a visiting professor at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, noted that India is the only lower-middle-income country among the G20 nations, which are otherwise upper-middle- or high-income nations. “The absolute number of the poor in our country is still the highest in the world for sheer size of population. So therefore, if we are going to genuinely reduce the incidence of poverty and more importantly, the absolute number of the poor, then it makes a huge difference globally,” he told Al Jazeera. Coming from the World Bank, the credibility of the analysis that has concluded India’s success in reducing poverty so significantly is also beyond question, said Surjit Bhalla, former executive director at the International Monetary Fund. Any data that comes from the World Bank, he said, is the “gold standard”. Bhalla said the institution carries out a poverty analysis for every country using a per capita consumption level that is normalised globally by invoking purchasing power parity. How did India dramatically cut poverty? Economists point to a series of factors and programmes that might have contributed to India’s success in pulling record numbers of people out of poverty.

events.title: We have the most powerful technology in history, and we’re using it to stop hiring young people
events.summary: We hold the most powerful technology in human history, and so far corporate America is mostly using it to write marketing copy and cut headcount. Through September, U.S. employers announced 573,195 job cuts. Artificial intelligence was cited in 120,136 of them, more than any other reason this year, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas . Tech companies alone announced 165,925 cuts, up 54% from the same period last year. To be fair, total announced cuts are down 39% from the first nine months of 2025, and AI was cited in only about 9% of September’s cuts. The bigger effect is on hiring. Using ADP payroll data, Stanford economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen found that as of June, employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations was about 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with young workers in less-exposed jobs. A year earlier, the gap was 15%. They write that the adjustment works “primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations.” Companies aren’t firing junior workers; they are simply not hiring them. They’re using efficiency as the excuse. A great economy for whom? On paper, the economy looks powerful. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis . Spending on computer equipment, a soft landing for capital expenditure, was a main driver. But for the common citizen, this year has been anything but a soft landing. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year through September, and gasoline rose about 34%. Since the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, oil has gone through what the World Bank calls “the largest oil market shock in history.” In addition, workers now pay an average of $7,471 a year toward family health coverage, up 9% from 2025, according to KFF . Over roughly the same period, wages increased only 3.7%. Effectively, the people took a pay cut. The looming electricity and water crises The AI buildout is also competing with households for the same electricity. In PJM, the largest U.S. grid operator, the independent market monitor estimated that data centers caused 63% of the price increase in 2025/2026, about $9.3 billion in costs, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis . Pepco residential customers in Washington, D.C., saw bills rise about $21 a month starting in June 2025. Roughly $10 of that came from capacity prices. This is what makes me angry. None of these issues requires new technology to be solved. The models exist, the compute exists, and the capital is already being spent. What’s missing is a decision about where to point it. The American Society of Civil Engineers estimates a water main breaks every two minutes in the U.S., and about 6 billion gallons of treated water is lost daily. We could use AI to forecast load and balance the grid so data centers pay for the strain they add. We could use AI to find leaks in water systems. We could model drought before it reaches a farm, inspect bridges, harden supply chains, and cut diagnosis costs instead of raising premiums. In June, in the U.K., Northumbrian Water reported that a six-month trial using AI-powered acoustic sensors to help crews locate hidden leaks was saving nearly 6.4 million liters of water a day. This is the technology we must invest in and deploy immediately. San Jose Water installed 13,600 fixed acoustic sensors across its 2,400-mile network, and the system found 483 leaks and saved more than 400 million gallons of treated water. Plus, New Mexico’s LeakTracer satellite-plus-AI program identified 216 leaks across 181 miles of pipe in its first year. Completing the needed repairs could recover 328 million gallons and save about $505,000 a year. This must become the industry standard. Four steps to secure the future First, we must treat energy resilience as a national security issue. Data centers must be required via litigation to pay for the grid upgrades and capacity they drive. Families shouldn’t have to subsidize the infrastructure required by multibillion-dollar tech companies. AEP Ohio already requires new data-center customers to reimburse 100% of buildout costs if they cancel before energization. The company creating the demand, carrying the risk, must be fundamental. In my home state, New Jersey’s Data Center Fair Share Act was signed in July 2026, creating a separate rate class for large data centers. This requires them to cover their own infrastructure costs, demands financial guarantees covering at least 85% of requested load for 10 years, and lets them offset capacity obligations by paying for demand reductions elsewhere. This could save ratepayers more than $1 billion a year . Other states are moving in the same direction, with large-load tariffs imposing high minimum-demand charges and contribution-in-aid rules so residential customers aren’t charged if a project underdelivers or exits. Next, go after health costs at the source. Use AI to reduce the volume of unnecessary tests, procedures, and late-stage interventions rather than simply shifting higher premiums onto households. Start by capping excessive hospital prices in public employee health plans, with safeguards for vulnerable hospitals. Oregon capped in-network hospital payments at twice Medicare’s rates and saved an estimated $107.5 million over 27 months. Then require publicly funded health care AI projects to demonstrate lower costs without compromising care. Efficiency isn’t helping if the patient’s bill remains the same. Third, deploy AI to retrain people faster than it replaces them. By tying public incentives for AI investment and data-center build-out to measurable entry-level hiring and apprenticeship commitments, AI will create efficiency and jobs. As entry-level roles disappear for the benefit of only AI owners, the coming generations are being steered toward economic ruin. Tie public AI incentives to net-new paid apprenticeships and entry-level jobs, with payments after six and 12 months of verified employment and not simply after a training course. This isn’t some pipe dream; the blueprint exists. In July, the Labor Department awarded nearly $162 million through an apprenticeship program that links payments to verified retention and progression milestones. Reward employers for being job creators and builders. Going forward, any firm receiving tax credits, accelerated permitting, or public power-purchase support for AI capacity must fund or host a proportional number of paid apprenticeships or entry-level roles, with progress reported publicly. Finally, give public infrastructure the same AI investment private data centers get. One of the most impactful improvements AI could make is in utilities and water. events.title: Proposal for free bus service scrapped
events.summary: Stagecoach said any free bus service would need to be carefully explored to ensure there was capacity Proposals for a free bus service in Guernsey will no longer be considered for next year's budget, deputies who suggested the move have said. Deputies Sally Rochester and Ross Le Brun put the plan forward as an amendment to the 2027 budget , asking the Policy and Resources Committee for £1.9m to "enable the existing public transport service" to be made free of charge in a one-year pilot. They have now pulled the plans after "concern from [operator] Stagecoach" that increased passenger numbers could mean certain routes not coping with the additional demand. Rochester said she and Le Brun were committed to working with the Environment and Infrastructure Committee to explore plans for the future. Rochester also acknowledged the pilot would not be possible if buses were "at capacity". Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Speaking to BBC Radio Guernsey, she said: "This amendment was all about supporting those in our community that are facing cost of living challenges. "It was about delivering the transport strategy so you could have access to a free bus service - make their lives easier, make their lives better. "Now we're not going to be able to do that if the bus service is at capacity." She said the "logical conclusion is that we would need more buses" while Stagecoach's contract "would need to be expanded" to provide the additional capacity. Rochester said these elements are "what we'll be looking into and hopefully bringing this back some time in the future". A spokesperson for Stagecoach said it welcomed "any initiative that encourages more people to use public transport and recognise the potential benefits of making bus travel more accessible". But it said it was important that "any proposal to introduce free bus travel is carefully considered to ensure that sufficient capacity is available across the network to accommodate the additional passenger demand such a scheme could generate". The company added: "Our priority is to ensure that bus services remain reliable, accessible and able to meet the needs of all passengers, particularly on routes that already experience high levels of demand." The proposal was one of 30 changes put forward to next year's budget, scheduled for consideration on Tuesday. Other amendments put forward include efforts to secure money for States' committees faced with budget cuts, attempts to freeze fuel duty and cuts to overseas aid. events.title: 'Quiet quitting' could be hitting the economy - here's why
events.summary: The so-called "quiet quitting" trend where workers do the basic requirements of a job but refuse to do anything more might be hitting the economy, analysis has found. Over the last decade, Britons have become less engaged with the jobs they do and are less willing to put in extra effort, according to a Resolution Foundation report. The thinktank said this could partly help explain the slump in productivity since the pandemic. "This is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn't bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead," said Hannah Slaughter, principal economist at the Resolution Foundation. Quiet quitting was popularised on social media shortly after the pandemic . Frustrated by high demands, low pay, and a squeeze in living standards, many online posts said workers should only do what their bosses asked and nothing more. So you still show up for work, but no more helping out with additional tasks or checking emails outside work hours, instead focusing on work-life balance and "acting your wage". Yet, far from being just a talking point on TikTok, the Resolution Foundation said the findings in its report were "consistent" with the idea of quiet quitting. 'I was working 60 hours a week so I quiet quit' Published 31 August 2022 The percentage of those surveyed willing to go the extra mile to help their employer has sunk from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025, according to their survey of 4,656 adults. Meanwhile, those who were not even "fairly" satisfied with their roles has sank to one-in-four, the lowest level on record. In addition, workers are less likely than 10 years ago to say they have an interesting job, with 63% of those surveyed saying so, down from 74%. "Workers today are indeed a little less committed to their employers, and a little less intrinsically drawn to work in general, than workers were a decade ago," the report added. This shift over the last decade "may have contributed to weak productivity growth", which has slowed since the financial crisis and weakened again after the pandemic, the Resolution Foundation found. Workers were also more focused on pay than in the past, which it said was "perhaps unsurprising... given the flatlining living standards of the past decade". Sir John Curtice, politics professor and co-editor of the report, said the analysis does not mean that young people have "become more 'work-shy', nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs". "But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financially rewarding and have flexible work hours," he added. events.title: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
events.summary: Chief executive John Ternus was presenting his first Apple results since taking over from Tim Cook Published 3 November 2026, 00:29 GMT Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period. The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000. The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance". Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres. Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September. It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen . Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold. As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo. Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible". Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October. Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before. iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn). Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn. Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn. However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively. Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes. Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan. Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products. Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages. Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular. Watch: Would you buy Apple's $2,000 foldable phone? Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple. Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood". Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%. Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business. While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive". However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading. events.title: Anthropic’s third quarter results mean IPO math and history are not on its side, analysts say
events.summary: Anthropic’s IPO is looking like an increasingly expensive and risky bet after the company released third quarter financial results yesterday that showed its rate of revenue growth slowing and its expenses climbing at a faster pace compared to prior quarters. Several analysts Fortune spoke to said math and past experience are not in favor of Anthropic producing stellar returns for investors. That may explain why institutional investors are reportedly pushing the company and its IPO advisors to price Anthropic’s shares at the lower end of a $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation range that the company is seeking in its public stock offering. Even that may be too pricey, according to analysts. Any IPO valuation above about $1.41 trillion would ask Anthropic’s buyers to pay more than $40 for every dollar the company generated in revenue over the past year—a price level achieved by just 14 of the 4,110 IPOs that took place between 1980 through 2024, according to a study from Jay Ritter, director of the University of Florida’s IPO Initiative. What’s more, those IPOs delivered lower average returns than the broader market, Ritter said. Against the roughly $35.3 billion in revenue Anthropic booked over the past four quarters, a valuation range of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, would mean investors paying between $43 and $57 for every dollar of sales the company generated in the past 12 months. To justify a valuation north of $1.4 trillion, Anthropic needs a path toward annual after-tax profits of at least $100 billion, Ritter told Fortune . Only a handful of companies have ever earned that much in a year, he said, including Alphabet , Nvidia , Apple and Microsoft . In the third quarter, Anthropic’s revenue rose nearly 47% from the previous quarter, while compute and infrastructure expenses climbed about 77% to $9.9 billion. About half of that compute bill, roughly $5 billion, came from the company purchasing short-term capacity. Anthropic typically orders compute 12 to 18 months ahead, but is forced to buy more expensive short-term capacity when customer demand or research needs exceed what it has secured. The company attributed the decline in its adjusted operating margin to 15% from 19%, primarily to those short-term costs.  Tomasz Tunguz, founder and general partner of Theory Ventures, told Fortune that higher compute costs would put increasing pressure on Anthropic’s margins, although he noted that the company’s implied gross margin was still a healthy 85%. Gross margin counts only the cost of serving customers. It excludes the far larger sums Anthropic spends training models and on research, which are booked as separate operating expenses. The pressure on adjusted operating margins arrived sooner than Tony Trzcinka, an investment grade portfolio manager at Impax Asset Management, said he expected. “The key question is whether revenue can compound fast enough to absorb the future commitments and outpace compute cost,” he told Fortune . He expects the company’s existing obligations and interconnected relationships to limit its ability to borrow at the kinds of low interest rates available to investment-grade companies. This means if Anthropic does need to take on debt to fund its compute capacity, that money will be expensive, further weighing on margins. But paying more for compute can also help an AI company generate future revenue, Campbell Hutcheson, a senior researcher at Epoch AI, said. Frontier models, such as those Anthropic builds, can command premium prices and help improve the training and inference efficiency of other models, he told Fortune . Because revenue growth often depends on reaching a capability or product threshold first, as with ChatGPT and Claude Code, he said it can be rational for labs to pay a premium to get there first. Hutcheson said Anthropic continued to show “very strong growth, high gross margins” while investing heavily in AI research. With about $131.8 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments at September 30, Anthropic has resources to keep investing while it works to improve those economics. Its operations generated $6.6 billion in cash during the first nine months of the year. Ritter said those reserves, combined with IPO proceeds, would allow considerable investment. Trzcinka also views liquidity as a positive for bondholders, while watching for further spending commitments and any borrowing under the company’s revolving credit facility. In estimating what Anthropic could be worth to shareholders, Aswath Damodaran, a finance professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business, looked a decade ahead. His Oct. 28 valuation—which was produced prior to Anthropic releasing its third quarter results—assumed annual revenue reaching $1 trillion by 2036, a target operating margin of 27.5% and an estimated $100 billion in IPO proceeds. Those assumptions produced an equity value of about $1.475 trillion, which he described as at the lower end of the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion range. Damodaran told Fortune that Anthropic’s third-quarter figures gave him little reason to revise his valuation, calling them “the most telegraphed 3rd quarter number of all time.” His earlier post had already discussed slowing revenue growth and continued margin volatility, he said. “If my intrinsic value changed significantly based on this news story, it would be neither intrinsic nor value, just a pricing chase.” Ritter likewise saw no big surprises in the third quarter numbers, but his research highlights the risk of paying for exceptional growth in advance. In Ritter’s study, the 14 IPOs that commanded the kind of price-to-sales ratio that Anthropic is asking investors to swallow delivered returns averaging 15.4 percent below the broader stock market, measured from their offer prices over holding periods of up to three years, although some companies outperformed. Each company had at least $100 million in revenue over the 12 months before listing, adjusted for inflation to 2025 dollars. Anthropic has substantial upside potential, Ritter said, but “a lot of things have to go right” for its revenue and profits to grow enough to support such a high valuation. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
