events.title: Elon Musk, angry voters, and the AI backlash: What's at stake in the 2026 midterms
events.summary: RYAN MURPHY/Getty Images; BI The 2026 midterm elections are here. Elon Musk has spent record sums to try to help Republicans hold onto their narrow majorities. History and polls show it could be a big night for Democrats. Americans are angry about affordability. The 2026 midterms will show who else will join President Donald Trump in paying the price. Trump has become so unpopular that the map of competitive races extends to Texas, Ohio, and even Kansas. Once considered unlikely, Democrats could sweep Republicans out of Congress. With even one house, Democrats can create headaches that stretch far beyond the White House. The very tech and business elite that cozied up to Trump ahead of his return to power may soon find themselves in the thick of congressional investigations. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has already made it clear that he's ready for a fight. Here are the storylines we'll be watching as the midterm elections unfold. Cost of living Most registered voters in an October Gallup survey said the economy would be either very or extremely important to their vote. Forty-two percent said gas prices would be extremely important to their decision. Americans are shelling out more at the gas pump than they were a year ago, as the Iran war has pushed up prices. Other polls suggest the cost of living is a crucial issue. Consumer spending is still strong in the US, but that's partly because higher prices are driving up nominal totals. Plus, inflation is eating away at raises . Prices have risen faster year over year than average hourly earnings for six consecutive months. AI backlash Trump may be unpopular, but building data centers is becoming an even harder sell. Polls show AI is not the top issue in the midterms, but ask a voter about building a data center in their community, and you're liable to get an earful. Across the country, candidates from both parties are racing to portray their opponents as too supportive of data center construction. This may just be the beginning. Some in tech are worried that the backlash brewing now will boil over once the 2028 presidential primaries get underway. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Mark Schiefelbein/AP Elon Musk's gigantic bet Everything is bigger in Texas, including Elon Musk's checks. The SpaceX CEO has donated at least $448 million, a historic sum. Of that total, more than $215 million has gone to America PAC, his allied super PAC. Musk's donations have been rerouted to help Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. Polls show Paxton in danger of losing, a potential result that would make it extremely difficult for Republicans to hold their majority. When he's not cutting checks, Musk is using his megaphone on X to repeatedly blast Democrats and boost Paxton at all hours of the day. "It would be game over for America," Musk wrote on X on October 30, warning what could happen if Republicans lose ground during the midterms ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Some of the other major donors Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the billionaire founders of Uline, have donated $150 million, mostly to Restoration of America, a pro-Republican super PAC. Jeff Yass , the cofounder of the global trading and technology firm Susquehanna International Group, has donated $110 million, including $30 million to a group supporting Vivek Ramaswamy's Ohio gubernatorial campaign. Rounding out the $100 million + club is George Soros, for years one of the biggest Democratic megadonors, who has given $102 million, mostly to Democracy PAC, a Soros-linked super PAC that supports Democratic candidates. Google cofounder Sergey Brin has given $102 million — not in support of federal candidates but rather in hopes of stopping California's proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires. Brin is part of a handful of tech elites who have cut large checks ahead of the midterms. Ben Horowitz & Marc Andreessen, two legendary venture capitalists, have donated over $92 million combined, mostly to a super PAC that supports candidates friendly to the AI industry. OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, have donated $50 million, half of which went to the same pro-AI super PAC. Races to watch Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, walks past President Donald Trump Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Ohio Senate: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, an Ohio Democrat, has zeroed in on Sen. Jon Husted's previous support for data center development in one of the closest-watched Senate races. Husted has said the issue should be left to communities and no longer supports offering tax incentives for new data center construction. If Democrats want to flip the US Senate, they'll need to win in places like Ohio. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a "Toss-Up." Texas Senate: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, is trying to avoid losing a Senate seat that could decide control of the chamber. Musk has donated $158 million to the Senate Republicans' allied super PAC, which in turn was donated to a pro-Paxton super PAC. Thanks in large part to Musk's donations, the Texas Senate race is now the most expensive non-presidential campaign in US history. Democratic State Rep. James Talarico has blasted Musk, saying the world's richest man "is trying to buy this Senate seat." The Cook Political Report rates the race as a "Toss-Up." Michigan Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed Jeff Kowalsky/ AFP via Getty Images Michigan Senate: The focus of the Michigan Senate race is on just about everything else, but don't overlook AI. Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health official, has echoed Sen. Bernie Sanders throughout the campaign. El-Sayed's AI platform is not different. Like Sanders (and Trump), he wants the US government to have equity in frontier labs. El-Sayed also wants to force big companies like Microsoft to divest from AI giants like OpenAI. While that policy is unlikely to pass, El-Sayed has made it clear that if he wins, he intends to play a king-making role in the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries, where Michigan will loom large. Former Congressman Mike Rogers, the Republican hopeful, has called for a pause on data center development in the state. If Republicans want to hold the majority, Rogers will almost certainly need to flip the seat. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a "Toss-Up." Google cofounder Sergey Brin speaks with Trump Win McNamee/Getty Images California wealth tax: California may make some history of its own. Despite Gov. Gavin Newsom's opposition, advocates were able to get a one-time 5% wealth tax on those with assets over $1 billion on the ballot. If it passes, California, home to the most billionaires, would be the first state in the country to impose such a tax. The proposal has divided the tech community. Google cofounder Sergey Brin has spent over $100 million to try to stop it. events.title: We Can’t Predict What Will Happen on Election Day. But We’ll Be Here to Cover It.
events.summary: Early voting for the midterms in New York last month Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors spent staggering sums . Both parties moved to redraw congressional district lines . President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the results could be trusted even before a single ballot was counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit that said the federal government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious. Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger? As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future — not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future. Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something? Send Us a Tip And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the military to seize voting machines in states he had lost. The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as lawmakers gathered to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything was possible in the aftermath of elections. We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have detailed what experts will be watching . But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans for covering voting stretch back many months. Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history. We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument that Trump’s 2020 loss was “rigged” by his opponents. We examined how the Trump administration depleted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency , the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.” Another story looked at how delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural counties , typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general election. One of our most detailed election stories traced the career of Cleta Mitchell , a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies. Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts . But she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell will be among the people he listens to. We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an email: “​​​​What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate, transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private advocate. We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting, looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have particular expertise. Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000 out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. Texas taxpayers paid $3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany him. (Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign. Another opportunity arose from an investigation that was seemingly not related to the midterms: our examination of the Trump administration’s handling of the Justice Department. We began many months ago to look for promising cases that had been dropped and found out the FBI had been looking into pay-to-play allegations involving prominent Democratic and Republican members of Congress. The case included a bipartisan list of political figures such as Susan Collins , the Republican senator from Maine running in a closely contested race this year, and James Clyburn , a leading Democratic representative from South Carolina who’s also on the ballot this year. Our first story revealed that Collins helped a little-known defense contractor win millions in federal contracts while the company’s CEO helped bankroll her 2020 reelection effort through a donation made via a shell company. Our second story revealed that the FBI was looking into interactions that Clyburn and Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, had with the same contractor. Collins has denied all wrongdoing. “A donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Clyburn’s office said. events.title: Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge
events.summary: Euro cloud trade association CISPE can keep the identities of members backing its VMware merger challenge confidential from Broadcom following a ruling by the EU General Court. Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe filed an action last year seeking to annul the European Commission's approval of Broadcom's acquisition of the cloud and virtualization giant. CISPE believes the Commission erred in allowing the purchase to go ahead without imposing any conditions on Broadcom to protect the many European cloud providers and their customers who depend on VMware's software. Broadcom sought access to redacted information identifying members supporting the action, arguing that it needed the information to challenge the action's admissibility. CISPE says the ruling allows the case to proceed without disclosing those identities to Broadcom. "It is a procedural ruling on confidentiality rather than a decision on the substance of the case, but it removes the immediate obstacle to the action moving forward," a CISPE spokesperson told The Register . CISPE argued that identifying the members, which are or have been VMware customers, would expose them to a significant risk of retaliation because of Broadcom's market power. Those members had supplied information about their commercial relationships with VMware. As far as the case itself goes, CISPE says it warned the Commission that Broadcom would use VMware's pre-eminent position in the private cloud market to rewrite licensing terms and reshape the market in its favor. Just a month after Broadcom's acquisition concluded in November 2023, partners were informed that VMware's channel program was to end in early 2024, and that Broadcom was also ditching the majority of VMware's Cloud Services Providers , keeping only a select few that had the largest turnover. Despite Broadcom CEO Hock Tan publicly stating that inflating prices was not his strategy, that is what happened. AT&T says that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent price increase , for example. Meanwhile, nine out of ten respondents to a recent survey of VMware customers said they were considering moving to alternatives. CISPE, which represents 48 cloud infrastructure service providers across the EU, says fewer than 20 European providers remain authorized to offer VMware-based services, down from more than a thousand. Commenting on the latest ruling, CISPE Secretary General Francisco Mingorance declared it a good day for the organization and for the rule of law in Europe. "The case matters even more today than when we filed it. In the three years since the European Commission waved this deal through without conditions, Broadcom has dismantled the European VMware channel ," he said . "Those excluded have until 31 March, 2027, to sell their infrastructure or their customers to a competitor chosen by Broadcom, or to close. This is the foreclosure the European Commission was warned about." We asked CISPE what outcome it hoped to achieve, nearly three years after the acquisition closed. "The immediate objective is to have the Commission's unconditional clearance annulled, on the basis that it failed to properly assess the effect of the acquisition on European cloud providers and the VMware channel," CISPE's spokesperson told The Register . The Commission did impose conditions concerning interoperability with rival hardware, but CISPE argues these did not address the risks to cloud providers. "We appreciate that it's a long shot (although there is precedent)," the spokesperson continued. "We have (along with others) also filed a competition complaint with the Directorate-General for Competition against Broadcom for its actions post-merger." The precedent referred to is the EC approval given to the merger of Sony and BMG's music divisions in 2004, which was ruled to be not of "the requisite legal standard" two years later. The deal was subsequently reassessed and re-cleared. "Ultimately, we want to do whatever we can to bring Broadcom to the table to negotiate and ideally end some of its most egregious practices so that European cloud providers can once again support cloud customers in a commercially fair and viable manner," the spokesperson added. The Register asked Broadcom to comment The European Commission declined to comment on procedural matters . ®

events.title: China and Russia have hypersonic missiles. This $13 billion startup wants the U.S. to catch up
events.summary: For the last couple of months, when someone asked what I was working on, I’d mention in passing “a hypersonics startup,” and almost always got stopped: Wait, roll that back. The startup is Castelion, based in Torrance, Calif. and working to produce and scale low-cost hypersonic missiles. The term “hypersonic” may have a sci-fi ring to it, but the technology is very real, and there are many reasons to pay attention. As I write at the top of the feature published this past weekend :  The first thing to know about hypersonic missiles is that they’re air-rippingly fast. A hypersonic missile, definitionally, moves at least at Mach 5, or five times the speed of sound; one could cross the U.S. coast to coast in under 45 minutes. Unlike ballistic missiles, hypersonics are maneuverable and unpredictable to watchers, with an uncanny ability to fly low, change course, and skirt radar. The second thing to know about hypersonics is that China and Russia have them, and the U.S. doesn’t—not really. It’s not for lack of trying: Despite years of research costing billions and some successful tests, the U.S. has yet to fully field a hypersonic missile of its own due to testing complications and production issues . The tech’s been around, but it’s been expensive and difficult to produce at scale. That’s the chasm that startup Castelion, valued at $13 billion, is betting it can close, even if the defense giants have so far fallen short. “Humans have done it, just not Americans,” says Castelion CEO and cofounder Bryon Hargis. “I firmly believe it’s doable.” In 2022, Hargis, Andrew Kreitz, and Sean Pitt—all previously SpaceX executives—cofounded Castelion to help close America’s hypersonics gap. And the beginning was comically unpromising, a reality the three founders remain unflinchingly honest about. An example, from the story: In 2022, as Hargis, Kreitz, and Pitt were just getting started, they presented to the Defense Innovation Unit, the Pentagon’s tech acceleration division. It didn’t go well. “It was the tailish end of COVID,” said Pitt. “So, it was a video presentation, and we explained ‘we’re here to make low-cost missiles.’ They asked: ‘Are you going to compete with Lockheed?’ We said yes, and it was not a little laugh. There were a good number of people laughing.” Not anymore. Now, Castelion is valued at $13 billion and ranks easily among the most valuable defense upstarts in the world. The company’s also at the end of the beginning: With a notable customer in the U.S. Navy (and the program of record to match), Castelion is barreling towards 2027 with a strong need to ramp up and speed up—for the business and to meet a wildly unpredictable geopolitical landscape. It’s a story about long odds, deterrence, and urgency. But Castelion is also a prism through which we can understand what makes the defense tech boom necessary, challenging—and definitionally high-stakes.  Read the feature here.  A note on print… An abridged version of this feature will appear in our next print issue of Fortune , in the brand-new Term Sheet section! In our print issues moving forward, we’ll be spotlighting companies and trends in the private markets. Got an idea wacky or interesting enough for print? events.title: Wharton economist says his views on AI have 'radically shifted'
events.summary: Economist Sylvain Catherine said he spends $200 a month on his AI subscription. He's still worried about the industry's "wild level of uncertainty." David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images A Wharton economist and associate finance professor says he loves Claude, but he worries about the AI race's pace. Sylvain Catherine says today's AI can lift GDP without a push toward superintelligence. He says voters, not just AI labs, should decide how much risk society accepts. Sylvain Catherine loves his $200-a-month Claude — but he isn't convinced the race toward increasingly capable AI models is worth the risk. The economist and associate professor of finance at The Wharton School recent made waves in the tech community when he declared on X that his "views on AI have radically shifted" after watching interviews with industry leaders and experts. "I am deeply uncomfortable with the absolutely wild level of uncertainty around this prediction," he wrote on Sunday. "And to be honest, even setting the doom scenarios aside, I find the utopia scenarios of some industry leaders actually dystopian." My views on AI have radically shifted over the past few weeks, after spending way too much time reading about it and watching interviews of industry leaders and experts. First, I really love the tools. I spend $200 on Claude every month and the product is worth every penny for me. Probably even more. I think the existing tools can deliver significant increase to future GDP and help us solve major global challenges faced by humanity. However, I just cannot comprehend why the industry is not much more regulated, as its leaders and employees seem to request themselves. I meet a lot of people who have heard of the hugging face incident but don’t know the actual chain of events. If you don’t, you definitely should spend a least an hour reading about it. I also do not know why we need to follow the path that frontier labs are following, to develop ever more powerful models. It seems to me that they are enormous gains that are readily available if we deploy the current technology in economic and scientific organizations without pursuing a super intelligence that they say might kill us and more likely wreak havoc in society. I know a lot of people think these warnings are marketing tricks, and that’s a reasonable assumption. But I don’t see the point of taking such risks. My median scenario is that of many economists: AI will diffuse slowly and lift gdp growth by a percentage point or so, will cause some economic disruption on the way, but ultimately people will get new jobs and maybe work less. However, I am deeply uncomfortable with the absolutely wild level of uncertainty around this prediction. And to be honest, even setting the doom scenarios aside, I find the utopia scenarios of some industry leaders actually dystopian. And I think a large majority of the public would agree if they paid attention to what they’re saying. To their credit, they themselves agree publicly that they should not be the ones making these choices. A large majority of the public is now very skeptical of AI as a source of human progress, in particular among younger adults who use it the most. They should have a say. I don’t want to convince you of anything but to get informed about this topic, express yourself and vote accordingly. — Sylvain Catherine (@sc_cath) November 2, 2026 Catherine's post lands amid an ongoing debate over how to regulate AI's risks. AI skeptics like Gary Marcus applauded the post. "Sanity is finally starting to win out," Marcus — who has been highly critical of AI companies and their business models — wrote in response. On Monday, Business Insider's sister publication, POLITICO, reported that  OpenAI's top policy executive  is urging potential 2028 presidential candidates to develop a governing philosophy for AI, not just talking points. The memo obtained by the publication lays out questions including how society can share in the technology's benefits. AI leaders themselves have offered wildly different visions of the technology's future. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said AI could create so much abundance that money becomes useless ; meanwhile, other leaders, like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have warned that AI could wipe out as much as  50% of  entry-level white-collar work. Catherine said there's still a range of possible outcomes. He said he believes that AI "can deliver significant increase to future GDP and help us solve major global challenges." His own Claude subscription, for example, is "worth every penny." Catherine said his median prediction is that AI will slowly lift global GDP while stirring "some economic disruption" as employees find new kinds of work. In a worst-case scenario, some tech leaders' visions for the future could be correct — namely, the forecast he finds "dystopian." Catherine said he was surprised the industry had not faced more regulation, especially after OpenAI disclosed over the summer that agents in an internal cybersecurity evaluation escaped aspects of their testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face , an open-source platform. Ultimately, he said there's one main solution for finding the right policy prescription for AI: sending Americans to the polls. "A large majority of the public is now very skeptical of AI as a source of human progress, in particular among younger adults who use it the most," he said. "They should have a say." events.title: DoorDash tells employees not to connect with Instacart peers on LinkedIn. It’s an uncommon M&A ask
events.summary: DoorDash is telling employees not to connect with their counterparts at Instacart on LinkedIn. Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images DoorDash is telling employees not to connect with their peers at Instacart on LinkedIn. The directive comes after DoorDash agreed to pay $17 billion to acquire Instacart. It's an unusual ask during a deal, experts said. DoorDash employees might have to make fewer LinkedIn connections as a result of their employer's $17 billion deal to buy Instacart. The food-delivery service told employees as much in an internal question-and-answer document filed with the SEC on Thursday. "Can I connect with Instacart employees on LinkedIn?" reads one of the questions in the document. "Not at this time," the answer says. "Please do not request any new connections with any Instacart employees on LinkedIn, even if you have a prior relationship." The guidance shows that a pending takeover can change life inside the companies involved, sometimes for long periods. Merging companies must remain independent competitors, limiting employees' ability to coordinate or share sensitive information. The document tells employees not to accept LinkedIn connection requests from Instacart employees, and that the two companies must continue to operate separately until the deal closes. DoorDash and Instacart said they expect the purchase to close either at the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028. Companies planning a merger or acquisition will often take steps to prevent employees from engaging in so-called gun-jumping, or behaving as if the deal is already done, something that could thwart the deal before it's completed. This might include sharing competitively sensitive information, coordinating on pricing or bidding, or discussing jobs with people at the other company without authorization. "You're supposed to continue to act like independent competitors until the deal closes," said David Gelfand, senior counsel specializing in antitrust law at Cleary Gottlieb, and former deputy assistant attorney general for litigation in the antitrust division of the US Department of Justice. By asking employees to refrain from certain LinkedIn connections, the companies could be trying to prevent brain drain, said Chris Selland, a lecturer at Northeastern University's D'Amore-McKim School of Business. DoorDash and Instacart already compete in the same industry. Discussions between employees could lead one company to hire employees from the other — bringing valuable connections, such as customer contacts, with them. "That could blow up the whole agreement," he said. However, several M&A experts told Business Insider they'd never heard of employees at companies undergoing a deal being barred from connecting on LinkedIn or any other social media platform. DoorDash didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Whether Instacart and DoorDash are acting sensibly, or imposing an overly broad restriction on ordinary employee behavior is "a great antitrust examination question," said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman and the director of George Washington University's Competition Law Center. events.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
events.summary: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators .  Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.  A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).  Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.  The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.  A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.  During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.  There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.  Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.  Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.” One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.  It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.  “Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior. Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. events.title: US hits Qeshm Island, Pezeshkian signals more diplomacy: Iran war latest
events.summary: With the first US attack on Qeshm Island since June, Iran and the US are on parallel tracks towards both peace and war. Amid growing concerns about renewed attacks on Iran following Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, US forces have struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in what officials have reportedly described as a defensive measure. In the first attack since June on Qeshm Island, which serves as the primary platform for Iran’s “asymmetric” naval power , according to analysts, the US strikes come as both sides continue to adopt military and diplomatic postures. list 1 of 3 How will the Iran war shape the outcome of the US midterm vote? list 2 of 3 How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge list 3 of 3 China steps up Middle East diplomacy with Iran and Oman meetings Mediation efforts led by Qatar are continuing in a bid to avert a return to all-out war, which began on February 28 when the US and Israel launched strikes across Iran, triggering the closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz, surging oil and gas prices and massive damage to military, civil and energy facilities around the Gulf. What happened in the attack on Qeshm Island? Several explosions were heard on Qeshm Island late on Monday, as US media reported that the US military had carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz. The blasts came in rapid succession, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses told the agency they saw two planes flying over the island, located off Iran’s southern coast along the waterway. According to The Wall Street Journal, which quoted an unnamed official, the strikes on Monday night appeared limited and were not a resumption of a major operation. The Associated Press news agency also quoted an unnamed US official as saying Washington had conducted the defensive strikes against “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets”. The attack came after IRNA reported that the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had destroyed a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The US first struck a critical desalination plant on Qeshm Island on March 7 – one week into the war. The strike, which Tehran branded a “flagrant crime” against civilians, cut off freshwater supplies to 30 surrounding villages. It is, but it is fragile, and mixed messages are coming from both sides. Qatari mediators have been engaged in indirect talks with Iranian officials in recent days. They have passed messages between the two sides, but the talks appeared to come to an end on Monday with no news of a breakthrough. An official briefed on the talks told the Reuters news agency that Iran’s delegation had departed from Doha on Sunday, but that a draft proposal was still being circulated, without elaborating on the content. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi regarding a version of a draft US-Iran deal which has been under negotiation for the past eight days, an official told Reuters. Araghchi told IRNA on Monday: “Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals, and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington.” Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei also told a news conference on Monday that the “ball” was in the US’s court as Iran’s demands were “clear and logical”. He said the plan Iran submitted in September to end the war remained the focus of talks, but that the proposal could be shortened and implemented in “two days”, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to talks about Iran’s nuclear programme. On Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had given the government “certain authorities” over talks with the US, local media reported. The president added that Tehran would look to resolve the conflict through dialogue. Khamenei’s apparent approval of diplomacy marks a change since the breakdown of the June memorandum of understanding , which allowed a brief ceasefire and peace negotiations, when the supreme leader said the US could not be trusted. For the US side, Vice President JD Vance also told reporters on Monday that he was hopeful for a diplomatic solution – just hours before the strikes on Qeshm Island. “The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance said. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.” Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reiterated on Tuesday that Iran’s response to any US “miscalculation”, such as launching strikes, would be unpredictable. “The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit,” he said. What has Trump said about diplomacy? Oil prices dropped by more than 7 percent on Monday.

events.title: The US-China thaw may not outlive the Trump era
events.summary: Andy’s view The prospect of steep losses for Republicans in today’s midterms and the lame-duck presidency that ensues regardless raise a fundamental question about the outlook for a budding US-China détente. Can warming superpower ties outlive the Trump era? I wouldn’t count on it. It’s not that an election humiliation would crimp US President Donald Trump’s diplomatic style. On the contrary, there’s every expectation it would give him even greater incentive to build his legacy on the world stage. But the current thaw is so much an artifice of his own unabashed admiration for his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping. And a backlash is brewing. Trump boasts of a “great friendship” with the Chinese strongman — they’ve held two summits so far this year, with plans of another meeting in Shenzhen this month, and a fourth in Miami in December — speaks of a G2 to manage global affairs, and waves away strategic concerns that might strain the bromance. (Asked about reports that Chinese satellite imagery was used by Iran to kill US troops, Trump told reporters on Air Force One: “They basically do what we do.“) Yet US policy on China remains very much in play, and debates will surely heat up after the midterms as the race to succeed Trump gets under way across both parties. Although Republican hawks have largely fallen silent in Trump’s second term, within the Beltway a bipartisan tough-on-China consensus is intact. Foreign policy elites complain that Trump is ceding the Western Pacific to Beijing (Evan Feigenbaum of the Carnegie Endowment mocks the administration″⁣s “ reverse pivot from Asia ” as the Pentagon diverts warships and marines to the Gulf.) Tech hawks accuse Trump of throwing away the US lead in AI by greenlighting exports of advanced Nvidia chips to China, or turning a blind eye to illicit transfers. The Taiwan lobby is outraged at his transactional approach to the island. Moreover, such criticisms are likely to intensify if an angry Trump, smarting from midterm defeats, focuses even more of his attention on deal-making with Xi. Ali Wyne, a US-China specialist at the International Crisis Group, sees bipartisan frustration at Trump’s China policy winding up like a coil, ever more tightly as he gives ground to Xi, and eventually unspooling “violently and unpredictably.” The next president, Wyne told me, will inherit a weaker hand vis-à-vis China and is likely to be “far more permissive of competitive and even confrontational actions.” Certainly, Trump’s successor — from either party — won’t have nearly the same latitude to manage China ties; one former American diplomat calls the president “ his own China desk officer .” (Of course, there’s always a chance that Trump himself will flip before he steps down, as he did at the end of his first term when he blamed Xi for unleashing the pandemic on the world and wrecking his reelection chances.) The late Henry Kissinger, the architect of Nixon’s 1972 opening to China, observed that “America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” In Trump’s ardent pursuit of Xi, critics suggest the US president forgot that lesson. Once Trump goes, a return to a colder, harder, more calculating is in the cards. Notable In a recent op-ed for The New York Times, Thomas L. Friedman argues that as the world’s leading AI superpowers, with shared interests in safeguarding against AI’s risks, the US and China may be pushed toward “ mutually assured collaboration .”

events.title: What's on the line for health care in the midterms
events.summary: Voters are about to decide whether public backlash against the health care industry translates into meaningful policy shifts. Why it matters: Health care has never been more expensive, and it's not going to get any cheaper without significant intervention. The big picture: It's hard to see Democrats not making health care affordability a top priority in the next Congress, regardless of whether they win only a narrow majority in the House or sweep both chambers in a blowout. But the party isn't aligned on an agenda, and a strong showing by progressives could drag things leftward. Reality check: Any Democratic victory — no matter the size — will be tempered by the realities of split government, with President Trump still in office for the next two years. Larger Democratic majorities may bring greater leverage in negotiations over spending packages or raising the debt limit. And the boldest changes will probably be reserved for the campaign trail, as 2028 presidential contenders begin to vie for the party's nomination. Here's what we're watching: Medicare for All vs. moderates: What happens in Michigan's Senate race — and Maine's, to some extent — will almost certainly shape how much sway progressives have in the next two years. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has made Medicare for All central to his campaign, unabashedly supporting the idea in a race that could determine which party has control of the Senate next year. The same is true of Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine's Senate race, though Jackson has a lower national profile than El-Sayed. But Medicare for All supporters looking for a vote on the measure face an uphill battle : Despite the policy's growing popularity among the public, moderates unwilling to abolish private insurance will make up a sizable portion of any Democratic majority. The doctors-turned-politicians: Doctors are on the ballot in key races this year, and the question is how much public trust translates into votes. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who went to medical school but isn't a practicing physician, is one example. There's also pediatrician Annie Andrews, who's mounted a strong challenge to Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, and Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton, who has focused on pediatrics and preventive medicine. "We've seen in our research over the last six-plus years that [doctors are] among the most trusted potential candidates for office, hands down," said Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action. MAHA on the line: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s "Make America Healthy Again" movement has focused its attention largely on the Iowa governor's race in the final weeks of the election, going all in for Republican Zach Lahn, who's pledged to take on Big Agriculture interests and the use of farm chemicals. Calling it an "existential" vote, MAHA Action founder Tony Lyons told MAGA influencer Steve Bannon that the race will be "the test of what's possible in a state, of whether we can actually take the country back from these corrupt companies, from these corrupt politicians, and really protect people." California's tax plan: Golden State voters will decide the fate of a controversial one-time wealth tax on billionaires, with most of the proceeds to be used to fund health care services. The money is intended to partly make up for Republican cuts to federal Medicaid spending but the tax is opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, a likely 2028 Democratic presidential contender. The measure tests voter sentiment in one of the bluest states to tax the super rich in order to fund health benefits — a potential prelude to a national debate over expanding the federal government's role in health care and how to fund it. Abortion ballot measures: Voters in four states will determine what reproductive rights in their states look like, another round of post-Roe abortion policymaking via ballot initiatives. Nevada and Virginia will consider constitutional amendments protecting the right to abortion, while Missouri will weigh a measure backed by the state legislature to repeal a 2024 pro-abortion rights amendment. Idaho voters will determine the fate of a state law guaranteeing a right to abortion until fetal viability, generally considered to begin around 23 to 24 weeks into a pregnancy, or after that in the case of a medical emergency.

events.title: I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
events.summary: A flash flood along the Rio Ruidoso on July 30, 2025 Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that, I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.  The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso, it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town, damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues. The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three people — two of them children — lost their lives.  Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?  In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He found that, after the 2024 fires, experts warned the town of increased flash flooding risks . Initially, local and state leaders considered a relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable, first responders say the three deaths could have been avoided . The responders told Abe that village leadership left them understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding. The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall, disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism, the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.” My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable disaster. A crumbled trailer and debris from flash flooding in Ruidoso on Aug. 1, 2025 The crumbling house at the Riverview RV Park on Sept. 10, 2026 When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection centers.  Supplies inside a Salvation Army makeshift distribution center and a sandbag distribution point facilitated by the New Mexico National Guard last summer While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service. We knew we should take them seriously. Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin. Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it. A woman watches the Rio Ruidoso rise from inside a brewery in downtown Ruidoso last summer. Two people venture close to the river as a flash flood began to subside last summer. Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning? In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.  Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the previous year. Downtown Ruidoso on a Friday afternoon this summer A mule deer and an elk wander behind downtown Ruidoso. New growth on a burn scar above Ruidoso But Stephanie and Sebastian Trotter still carry the scars of the day. They lost their two children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4, in the Ruidoso flooding.  There is now a memorial for them and Benjamin “Tim” Feagin, the third person who died, at the RV park where they had been camped. But I wanted to see for myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.  I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.  Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s trickle. events.title: Deadly RSF drone attacks reveal deep divisions between Sudan and Ethiopia
events.summary: Deadly drone attacks in Sudan have led to fierce diplomatic disputes with Ethiopia, exposing complex regional rivalries and fragile border security. The Sudanese government’s allegations that Ethiopia is behind a deadly wave of unmanned aerial assaults belie a deep and longstanding rift between the two countries, which threatens to intensify internal conflicts in both. Sudan has officially lodged complaints with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over allegations that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary – which has been at war with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since April 2023 – is using Ethiopian territory to launch attacks against civilian sites, including power stations. list 1 of 3 As aid situation worsens, displaced Sudanese worry about warnings of famine list 2 of 3 Sudan files complaints against Ethiopia with UN over deadly drone spree list 3 of 3 Drone attacks extend campaign targeting Sudan’s power system Ethiopia’s alleged support for the RSF has triggered differences within the SAF on how to respond next, Sudanese border affairs specialist Abdul Kareem Al-Almin Ahmed told Al Jazeera. “The mutual accusations are many and almost daily, and the tension on the part of the Sudanese army has reached high levels, to the degree that made some voices inside the Sudanese army and the forces allied with it demand that Sudan declare war on Ethiopia based on these interventions,” Al-Almin told Al Jazeera. Suspected RSF drone attacks have heavily damaged civilian infrastructure in SAF-controlled areas. More than 90 percent of power stations in Sudanese cities have been rendered out of service due to drone attacks, and al-Almin said the technological capabilities of these weapons indicate significant external backing. “They are mysterious drones, drones that reach long distances, and almost all Sudanese lands are currently violated by these drones, which confirms that they are drones with a special characteristic and flight properties for a long range and have high destructive power,” Al-Almin added. A detailed report prepared by the Sudanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs alongside military intelligence claimed that 70 separate assaults involving 187 one-way attack drones were launched from Ethiopian territory between February and October. The frequency of these attacks seems to be increasing, with 28 attacks carried out by 97 drones in October. The use of armed drones has been catastrophic for civilians in Sudan, with 13 million people already displaced and thousands at risk of famine due to the war. Between February 15 and October 27, drone attacks killed 176 Sudanese soldiers and 484 civilians, according to a report compiled by the Transitional Sovereignty Council, which is linked to the de facto Sudanese leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the SAF. It identified Asosa Airport in western Ethiopia, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area, and the Bahir Dar airbase in Amhara as specific launch sites for drone attacks. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Saturday he was appalled by the use of drones in the war and condemned the catastrophic toll this was having on civilians. A drone attack on displaced families in Wad el-Mahi , near the Ethiopian border on October 3, killed 26 women and four children. Another drone attack in Nyala, in Sudan’s Darfur region, on October 26 killed at least 21 people and injured at least 40. The Sudanese military has repeatedly accused the Ethiopian government of aiding the RSF. Addis Ababa denies the claims and has in turn accused the Sudanese government of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front . The tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia extend beyond these drone attacks and allegations of support for rebel groups. They also involve a confrontation over water resources and strategic regional alliances. There have been ongoing tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), built by Addis Ababa on the Nile River. Egypt and Sudan rely heavily on the Nile for water supplies and, being downstream, fear the GERD threatens their national security and claim it breaches international law. “The Sudanese-Ethiopian file is a complex file, in which many factors have intertwined: The Renaissance Dam problem first … and the rapprochement between the Sudanese army and the Egyptian government,” Al-Almin said. The Sudanese government is also angered that the RSF is allegedly receiving support from Ethiopia, he added. But Badr Hassan Al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution expert, said fears of an escalation that could harm Sudan and Ethiopia are preventing an all-out confrontation between the two countries. In a study published by the Al Jazeera Centre for Studies, Al-Shafei wrote that “Khartoum’s interest lies in the stability of its eastern neighbourhood to avoid security threats and waves of asylum.

events.title: Nearly a third of sitting US senators belong to fraternities or sororities. See the full list.
events.summary: Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL), Mitch McConnell (R-KY), and Roger Marshall (R-KS) are three of the US senators with ties to Greek life sororities and fraternities. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images/Pete Kiehart/Bloomberg via Getty Images/Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Fraternities and sororities have cultural dominance on many US college campuses. Ties to Greek life organizations can last long after college and offer access to powerful networks. Nearly a third of the US Senate comprises Greek life alumns from across the nation. Beyond party affiliation, there are some lesser-known loyalties tied to lawmakers in Washington, DC . Greek life  fraternities and sororities , which often dominate social life in colleges and universities across the US, also have some of the strongest footprints in the Capitol. In the 119th Congress, just under a third of US senators are affiliated with a Greek organization, according to the Fraternity and Sorority Political Action Committee , which aims to "help more Greek alumnae get elected to the House or Senate for the first time." In years with congressional races throughout the country, the political action committee — often nicknamed the "Frat PAC" — can play a significant financial role. In the 2023-24 election cycle , the PAC raised over $900,000. Today, it has raised over $650,000 for the 2025-26 cycle, toward a $1 million goal. While funding goes toward the campaigns of Greek-life alumns, the committee does not align with one party over the other. FSPAC said that in the 2023-24 cycle, 52% of funds went to Republican candidates and 48% to Democratic candidates out of the 97 congressional campaigns it donated to. Beyond nationally organized fundraising, Greek life organizations also offer their lifelong members access to a network of powerful connections in the Capitol and beyond. events.title: What not to watch on Election Day
events.summary: Ben’s view National election days in the United States of America are biennial festivals of noise over signal. This is the day of maximal public attention to television and online news, on par with wars and natural disasters and the World Cup finals. Hundreds of millions of people are watching TV and YouTube closely, chattering and analyzing on social media. Media companies — like ours — will be there to keep you company, of course, in our case with superb analysis and a thoughtful afternoon livestream . And yet: There’s no other day where the volume of nonsense so outweighs the quantity of new information. In the old days of print journalism, before websites, social media, and even cable news required that reporters broadcast nonstop, Election Day was a blast. Political reporters could sleep late, have a long lunch, even catch a movie. In the afternoon, you’d drop by a polling place for a little “B-matter” — some color and an ambiguous quote or two to bulk out a story in the early edition. “Voters lined up around the block at P.S. 87 on the Upper West Side to cast their ballots. ‘It sure is crowded here,’ said Bob Smith, 70.” That sort of thing. Too Online The modern Election Day media contains three things: anecdotes about how many people are voting; anecdotes about chicanery and hoaxes; and, long after that, results. Early voting trends and stories about how long the lines are in reliably red or blue districts are tempting to use as data points — but are notoriously misleading. You can only vote once, and it doesn’t count more if it comes in early, rather than if you wait until Tuesday to stand on line. Then there are the anecdotes. One, inevitably, will be that a voting machine somewhere in the US is on the brink. The influencers will be all over it. X, in particular, is now hyper-charged to reward engagement. A video — real or manipulated — of a machine in Pennsylvania or Arizona appearing to refuse to accept votes for one candidate is engagement gold. When you see these posts, remember that the US election system is wildly decentralized, secure, and largely offline, and that this story circulates every year. There will also be hints and rumors of poll-site interference or intimidation. Both parties have a maximal incentive to play up anything like this, both as an early warning in case it’s real, and to motivate voters in any case. This is a global phenomenon: Recent elections in Israel and Brazil were marked by wildly viral claims of misconduct — foreign funding of Arab voters in Israel’s case, polls being kept open too late in Brazil’s — that evaporated the next day when they were no longer relevant. Media companies, of course, have our own incentives to keep you engaged. There will be nonstop panels on TV and livestreams, analysts repeating analysis of days-old polls, and — come afternoon — figures from exit polls suggesting that Hispanics are voting in large numbers, or that the economy is a major issue. (These exit poll analyses are both largely useless and often corrected in the days after the election, but they fill the air.) So, Election Day is a good day to sleep late, see (if you haven’t yet), and, of course … watch our livestream . Then when the polls start closing at 6 pm EST, the news arrives: Numbers start rolling in to replace the chatter. And, on their heels, often, litigation. Room for Disagreement There could be substantive news to follow if the Trump administration acts to disrupt voting on Election Day, as some suspect will happen. A group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates “have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has ‘war-gamed’ how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots,” ProPublica reports .

events.title: How AI giants could raise the cost of borrowing in Europe
events.summary: France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments. With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital. Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon , Google -owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued around $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros. Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars. Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING. Battle for investor capital heats up That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France , Germany and Italy , whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances. With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%. The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028. Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade. Could France's debt crisis spread across Europe? In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance." Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market." That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow. 'Bond abundance' helps drive up yields Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance." Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest. Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together. Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down. AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated European companies could also feel more pain Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022. The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period. Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments. Regional governments paying the price for AI The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom. A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise. "Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

events.title: Hong Kong economy’s surprise jump takes growth to five-year high
events.summary: Hong Kong’s property market has rebounded, helping lift the Asian hub’s growth to a five-year record. Hong Kong’s economy grew 5.2% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in five years, driven by stronger exports and better investment. GDP rose 5.1% in the first nine months of 2026, and the government said the outlook stays positive with AI investment and tourism support. The city raised its 2026 growth forecast to 3.5% to 4.5%, and Paul Chan said the full-year estimate may be lifted again as growth stays robust. HONG KONG – Hong Kong’s economy unexpectedly grew at a faster rate in the third quarter, taking expansion in the first nine months to the quickest in five years, thanks to a surge in exports and improved investment. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 5.2% from a year earlier, compared with a downwardly revised gain of 4.2% in the second quarter, according to advance estimates released on Nov 3 by the Census and Statistics Department. Over the first nine months of 2026, GDP grew 5.1% from the same period in 2025. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, the economy also exceeded forecasts and expanded 1.9%. “Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s economic outlook remains positive, with incoming data pointing to sustained growth momentum,” a government spokesman said in a statement, citing continued global investment in artificial intelligence and sustained growth in tourism among reasons for optimism. A surge in exports, powered by strong global demand for electronics amid the AI supercycle, has been a key driver of growth for the transshipment hub and gateway to China. Consumption and investment have also held up as the property market rebounds and infrastructure development for the Northern Metropolis gathers pace. The city’s government in August upgraded its forecast for GDP growth in 2026 to 3.5% to 4.5%, from 2.5% to 3.5% predicted in May. Financial Secretary Paul Chan said over the weekend that economic growth remained robust in the third quarter as investment continued to surge, adding that the official full-year projection may be revised upward again. Beijing has signalled its strong backing for the Asian financial hub, with Vice-Premier He Lifeng saying on Nov 3 that developing the city “remains a key strategy for China”. The national government will continue to endorse a free and open economic environment in Hong Kong, He said in a video speech to the Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in the city. events.title: Trump vanishes from GOP campaign ads
events.summary: Data: AdImpact; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Republicans on the ballot this cycle have all but stopped mentioning President Trump in their campaign ads , according to an Axios analysis of broadcast advertising data from AdImpact. Why it matters: Trump has tried to make the 2026 midterms a referendum on his presidency. His party has run the other way. The big picture: Ads from both parties in Senate, House and gubernatorial races have shifted from a heavy focus on Trump during the primaries to a much greater emphasis on the economy in the general election. Both parties have also leaned much more heavily into health care, with a noticeable increase among House Republicans. By the numbers: The drop-off is steepest among Republicans, and especially in House races. Trump appeared in 66% of House Republicans' primary ads but shows up in just 3% of their general election ads. In Senate races, Republican ads mentioning him fell from 77% to 22%. Governor's races saw the same shift: Republican ads mentioning Trump fell 34 percentage points. Democrats have also pulled back from Trump, though less dramatically. Trump appeared in 45% of Democratic primary ads, but just 18% of their general election ads. Zoom in: Republican candidates are mentioning some of Trump's signature issues less than during the primaries. The share of Republican ads mentioning immigration has dropped 20 percentage points in Senate races and 14 points in House races. Ads referencing law enforcement fell from 11% of Republican Senate primary ads to 6% in the general election, even as their mentions of crime increased. Data: AdImpact; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Between the lines: Candidates often lean on the country's most prominent political figure in primaries, then pivot to policy issues in the general election. But this year's drop-off stands out given how hard Trump has pushed to tie himself to the midterms. He has urged voters to pretend he's on the ballot and essentially demanded ads running during the Republican midterm convention in September feature him. Of note: In this analysis, primary ads are broadcast ads that aired before a race's primary. General election ads aired between the primary and Oct. 26. The trends may be even more pronounced in ads running through Election Day. The bottom line: Most Republicans have been too scared to tell Trump how unpopular he is, Axios reported . But their ad receipts don't lie.
