events.title: An artist says Meta’s bots overwhelmed her website and left her scrambling to protect her business
events.summary: A Meta crawler bot visited a San Diego artist's website more than 550,000 times in 48 hours, consuming nearly all of her site's traffic allowance. Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images A Meta crawler bot visited a San Diego artist's website more than 550,000 times in 48 hours. The bots are now using 100% of her site's traffic allowance, essentially taking it down. Meta told Business Insider that website managers can decide how our crawlers interact with sites. A San Diego-based artist wanted more people to visit her website. Instead, she said she got more than 550,000 hits from a Meta bot and is scrambling to keep her business online. Chelsea Paulus, a children’s author and illustrator, told Business Insider that an automated visitor overwhelmed her website’s hosting resources, forcing her to troubleshoot the problem with her hosting provider. “This has never happened before,” Paulus said. "It has been an incredibly stressful week, even with some of my technical knowledge to handle it." Paulus said she's operated her business for a decade and became a full-time artist last year. Before that, she worked in tech and web design, so she said she quickly realized something was wrong when the website traffic started piling up. "I do not believe this is any kind of intentional or malicious attack from Meta," Paulus said. "But small business owners need to be aware this could happen and be given tools to stop it." The fight to keep the webpage running On October 24, Paulus received an email from her hosting provider, SiteGround, warning that she had used 80% of her allocated CPU resources. Paulus's four websites share a single hosting plan supported by the Bulgaria-headquartered company. Paulus said that when she checked her website’s security dashboard the following Monday, she saw requests arriving several times a second. "I went to WordFence, and then I saw the continuous lines that kept popping up every second," Paulus said. "In WordFence, you can click on the details so you can see the IP address. I looked it up, and that IP address is from a Meta location in Dallas." She said the visitor identified itself as “Meta External Agent,” a fact later backed up by operators at SiteGround, her website host. According to Meta's developers webpage, a Meta External Agent "crawls the web for use cases such as training foundation AI models or improving products by indexing content directly." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Chelsea Paulus | Artist (@chelsea_ayna_art) Paulus said she occasionally runs Meta ads and had seen Facebook bots visit before, but this number of hits was something entirely new. "I edited my robots.txt file, and I put up a firewall, but those can also take 24 hours to take effect, and I needed to stop the bots immediately," Paulus said. "So I contacted my host." "They gave me some code to add to a hidden file on my website," she added. "This hidden file is not something that anybody who's a normal person running a website would want to touch, but that's the only way that we could stop the bots." The fix was temporary. By mid-week, Paulus said another Meta bot named "Meta Web Indexer" arrived, pushing her hosting resource usage to 100%. Meta's developer guide defines a "Meta Web Indexer" as a crawler that "navigates the web to improve Meta AI search result quality for users." The search for answers continues A Meta spokesperson told Business Insider on Monday that website managers control bot activity and referred to its "Meta Web Crawlers Developer Documentation" page for details on how each bot is used. "Like many companies, Meta uses web crawlers for a number of different purposes, and website managers can decide how our crawlers interact with their sites through tools like robots.txt," a Meta spokesperson said. "We provide publicly available guidance on ways to manage robots.txt for our crawlers, and we respect the preferences site owners set. SiteGround did not respond to a request for comments. According to a screenshot email exchange between SiteGround and Paulus, the company said that its "server-side protection" is already limiting these bot attempts . As of Monday, Paulus said her website is still struggling. She had to remove the webpage link from her Instagram profile to prevent the additional human clicks that could take the site offline entirely. Paulus said she doesn't have the means to pay to increase the traffic allowance for her site because bots are not customers and do not generate additional income. There are no laws that prevent an AI bot from crawling a publicly accessible website. She said she is also exploring Cloudflare's human verification tools to stop bots from reaching her site. The tool is free to use at the moment. "Meta needs to have guardrails in place to prevent this from happening," Paulus said. "Imagine if the unregulated AI keeps doing this, how long can platforms like Cloudflare continue to offer free services?" She added, "If this keeps happening, I would assume that small businesses are going to fork out more, either for higher usage or for programs to better protect themselves." events.title: At least 73 injured as Russia bombs Ukrainian hospital and power plants
events.summary: Medical facility was struck by Russian ballistic missiles and aerial bombs overnight. Russia has bombed a hospital in Kharkiv, injuring at least 73 people, while also carrying out several attacks on energy infrastructure across multiple Ukrainian regions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X that “the Russians directly struck a city clinical hospital. Seventy-three people were injured, and the cardiology department, where people were receiving treatment, was damaged.” list 1 of 3 Nuclear radiation in Russia, Ukraine? No, just hacked warning alerts list 2 of 3 Russia, Ukraine air raid alert apps hit by cyberattacks after truce ends list 3 of 3 Russian attack on Ukraine aid hub kills 31 as US announces new peace talks Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov confirmed on Telegram that the hospital sustained heavy damage in Monday night’s bombardment, with more than 1,000 windows shattered. Separately, Ukrainian energy sites were hit, including in Kharkiv, in what President Zelenskyy described as a “complex, massive attack”. “The main target was energy – power generation facilities and substations – in the Odesa, Cherkasy, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Chernivtsi, Chernihiv, and Rivne regions,” he said in a post on X. Zelenskyy added that Russia had launched 289 attack drones overnight, as well as 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles. This comes a day after at least 31 people were killed in a Russian strike on an aid distribution centre. The Russian Ministry of Defence said it had targeted electricity facilities in the Vinnytsia, ⁠Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions. In its statement, it said the sites supplied power to the Ukrainian army and military factories. More than 180,000 people were without power in the Zhytomyr ⁠region on Tuesday morning after Russian attacks, Governor Vitalii Bunechko said. Odesa has implemented scheduled power outages in response to the attacks. Meanwhile, two employees at a Russian oil refinery in Yaroslavl were injured during a Ukrainian drone attack that caused a fire at the site, according to Governor Mikhail Yevrayev. The latest exchange of attacks comes as the United States ramps up efforts to end the war, with a meeting between US, Russian and Ukrainian officials due to take place in Abu Dhabi next week. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said in a post on X late on Monday that the discussions would focus on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace”. Witkoff added that US negotiators would meet with representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Union and NATO in Brussels this week. He said the talks would focus on security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe’s post-war security architecture and economic opportunities to support Ukraine’s reconstruction. This comes as global attention turns to Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US. Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said these were arguably the most important elections in recent years for Ukrainians. “Since the Trump administration took office and the House and Senate flipped Republican, there have been no significant military aid packages for Ukraine. In comparison, Biden, during the early years of the war, you were looking at $60b in military aid for Ukraine,” MacAlpine said. “Europe has largely filled that gap but certainly Ukraine would like to resume that aid from the US. That’s been at the top of President Zelenskyy’s agenda for over six months now,” she added.

events.title: Is a post-midterm deal with Canada possible?
events.summary: Trade watchers are waiting for Tuesday’s elections to pass to ascertain whether a US-Canada deal is actually imminent. President Donald Trump’s repeated insistence that a deal is close “matters for a couple of key states” like Michigan , Washington Council Ernst & Young’s Blake Harden told Semafor. “So it’s hard to know if it’s the midterms that are motivating that from the White House and whether that calculus changes after.” Both countries have signaled little change in their positions since talks collapsed, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pledging “our teams will work over the coming weeks” to advance the ball. The US and Canada may have “more room to make a deal” post-election, Harden said, or “could actually get more dug in” without an “action-forcing event.” The White House is keeping details of talks closely held. “The Trump administration welcomes continued engagement with Canada as we work toward finalizing the details of a deal that will deliver meaningful results for the American people,” a White House official told Semafor. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: I'm an employment law attorney. Here are the 3 steps you should take if you're offered a buyout like Microsoft's.
events.summary: Craig Levey, an employment law attorney, shares the three things employees should do if offered a buyout. Craig Levey Microsoft is offering buyouts to about 60,000 of its employees. Employment law attorney Craig Levey said that buyout programs can be "writing on the wall" about future layoffs. He said employees offered a buyout should understand the offer and get a sense of future job stability before deciding. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Craig Levey, an employment law attorney and partner at Bennett & Belfort, P.C., based in Boston. The following has been edited for length and clarity. When companies offer employees buyouts — like Microsoft did last week to around 60,000 employees — those employees have a decision to make. Speaking generally, a buyout offer can be a decent thing to happen to an employee if they were planning on leaving the company in the short term, such as retiring or quitting to go to another job. If an employee feels like their job could be in jeopardy in the future, they may want to take a buyout so that they get money and benefits and not risk being laid off, in which case there may be no severance offer. In many situations, when a company offers a buyout program, the writing on the wall is that there will be additional layoffs in the future. (Editor's note: A Microsoft executive previously told Business Insider , "Never say never, but there's a lot of desire not to do big layoffs." Microsoft also said in a statement that "future workforce needs will continue to be based on business needs and priorities.") On the other hand, if you're an employee who's planning on staying with the company for the long term and you have many years of employment in the future, a buyout might not necessarily be a good thing because you're taking a small amount of money in the grand scheme of things and you then have to find new employment, which can be difficult in this job market . I'm an employment law attorney who routinely assists employees in negotiating their departure from employers, including through buyout agreements. Here's what to make sure you do if you're an employee offered the opportunity to be part of a buyout program. 1. Thoroughly understand the offer HR or legal will send you the offer, which typically includes a release of legal claims, a no-rehire provision, potentially a non-disparagement provision, and so on. You need to make sure you totally understand it; if not, hire an employment law attorney to explain it to you. Questions to ask include: How much am I being paid? Is it going to be a lump sum or installment payments over time? When will the payments be made? What are the benefits? When would I have to leave the company? How much paid time off would I receive when I leave? Would I qualify for unemployment benefits after I leave the company? Remember to research your state's unemployment rules ; every state's a little different, and you'll want to make sure you know whether you're going to be entitled to unemployment. 2. Try to get a sense of whether you might be laid off in the future Try to ascertain information as to whether your job is protected moving forward. Get a sense of whether, if you don't accept this buyout now, you'll be laid off in short order anyway. It's usually not something to ask HR or your supervisor because they either won't know that information or won't provide it. Some employees may have the approach of "I have nothing to lose" and just ask; it depends on the individual employee's comfort level. Try and get as much information as possible from the facts at your disposal. Get a feel from the environment around you, possibly speak with colleagues that you trust, and do a little research internally. Look back at documents that were sent by the president or CEO, like emails or letters. What state is the company in? Is it in dire financial need, so much so that you can reasonably predict that there are going to be additional layoffs in the future? Have they done several rounds of layoffs ? Perhaps they've done return-to-office mandates , which resulted in people resigning. Oftentimes, employees can get the vibe of the situation and understand if there's more trouble on the horizon or if the company's doing very well and has just decided to offer buyouts to a particular division because they're restructuring while the rest of the company is going to be unaffected. 3. Decide if you want to accept, reject, or negotiate the offer Trying to negotiate can be difficult if you don't have leverage. With Microsoft offering 60,000 people a buyout, it may be difficult for one single person to try to negotiate a higher payout. However, if you're an employee who does feel like you're being targeted, you should do an analysis to see if the company did violate the law; did they target you? Assess whether you're being targeted and discriminated against because of a protected class, such as age, gender, or race, or if the company's engaging in retaliation because you complained about something illegal prior. You may want to speak with an employment law attorney in your state, because that might be a situation where you could negotiate a higher amount. Be very cognizant of the deadline by which you have to either accept or reject the offer. To the extent that someone is thinking of accepting the offer and getting a payment, they may want to speak with their tax advisor or CPA regarding the tax implications of any payment, particularly as we reach the end of the calendar year in the next couple of months. At the end of the day, the buyout offer is a contract; you can either accept it or reject it. You don't have to sign it. However, if you feel like you're being forced into the buyout or you're being targeted, you should speak with an employment law attorney to understand your rights. Do you have a story to share about being offered a buyout and deciding whether to take it? Contact this reporter at janezhang@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

Nobody has the right version 4 hours ago Public bodies in the UK expect higher operating costs and energy charges as a result of climate changes and the transition to lower carbon energy, but few have a good picture of the risks, according to government auditors. A new report from the National Audit Office (NAO) says some public bodies expect financial impact from the risks they identified, although bodies were often not able to cost these – even approximately. "Bodies anticipate costs to arise from damage to assets and infrastructure, driven by physical damage from extreme weather, as well as from chronic shifts to higher temperatures and more precipitation. Bodies also expect higher maintenance and repair costs, potential asset upgrades, and transition costs. Many bodies expect increased operating costs, including energy charges. Bodies controlling significant property or infrastructure are particularly concerned with decarbonization and adaptation costs," the report stated. His Majesty’s Treasury (HMT) has set out rules for climate-related financial disclosure in larger central government bodies' annual reports, which produced their first set of reports for the 2025-26 financial year. Other rules for disclosure have been in place since 2022. However, the NAO found [PDF] that understanding of the risks in the impact of climate change – increasing temperatures, higher risk of flooding, higher winds and longer droughts – was poor, as was insight into costs of moving to a low-carbon economy. "Bodies did not articulate transition risks as well as physical risks in the strategy disclosures. In the disclosures we reviewed, while several transition risks were listed, few specifics were given, unlike physical risks, which were explained in greater detail," the report from the watchdog stated. "The transition risks most frequently identified included the financial cost of transition, and supply chain disruption. Anticipated transition costs included the costs of: switching to lower-carbon energy sources, including investments in new technology; complying with new regulations; and of fluctuations in the price and availability of materials, water, energy and specialist skills," it added. Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "UK public services will need to adapt to the impacts of climate change. Parliament needs clear information on the resilience of infrastructure, service provision and finances to climate change, and on how these risks are being managed." "Although public bodies are still learning how best to report their most pressing climate risks, the requirement on all large central government bodies to make such disclosures from 2025-26 is an important first step. We expect this reporting to become more useful over time." Earlier this year a report from Global Action Plan, a climate charity, claimed 84 percent of proposed datacenter developments were in areas that are already water stressed or projected to be water stressed by 2040.

events.title: Fired general accused of being source for Wall Street Journal, NYT
events.summary: The Pentagon's former top military planner is under federal investigation and may face a court-martial for allegedly leaking to reporters from the Wall Street Journal and New York Times, according to three sources familiar with the controversy. Why it matters: Former Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week after being accused of misconduct as part of the department's war on leaks. Sylvia failed four polygraphs and admitted to the incidents during two interviews on video that lasted more than a total of two hours, according to details from an internal Pentagon report shared with Axios. "The president has no tolerance for leakers, so Sylvia's termination is the first step in the accountability process, not the last," one of the sources said. Zoom in: Starting in the fall of 2025, the sources said, Sylvia gave information without authorization to reporters Michael Gordon of the Wall Street Journal and Greg Jaffe of the New York Times. Neither reporter is suspected or accused of doing anything illegal, improper or unprofessional in their reporting. Journalists often rely on confidential sources in reporting on issues that involve institutions where insiders aren't authorized to speak publicly. The report states Sylvia admitted to more extensive contacts with Gordon in 2025 and 2026, when the general allegedly shared classified information about Ukraine and Iran with the reporter. The Justice Department is investigating that. Only one discussion with Jaffe appears in the investigative report, concerning Hegseth's unexplained purging of military leaders. Sources said the unauthorized communication by Sylvia potentially violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice's prohibition of "conduct unbecoming of an officer." Behind the scenes: Sylvia allegedly admitted to first disclosing information to Gordon in the fall of 2025 when the two met in the Pentagon and discussed unspecified information about Ukraine, the sources said. After the Wall Street Journal and other outlets were barred from the Pentagon, Sylvia met Gordon at the Silver Diner in Arlington, Va., to give information about a book the reporter was planning to write, the report said. "Major General Sylvia relied on notes he took while reviewing a classified secret report to orally brief Gordon on assistance to Ukraine," said the report, which emphasized that Sylvia didn't receive clearance to discuss the sensitive information. A separate legal analysis of Sylvia's conduct alleged that the general also discussed "munitions stockpiles and high-level interagency discussions with Iran" that were classified, according to a source briefed on the document. Then, "sometime in June or July," Gordon sent Sylvia a message on the encrypted app Signal, the report said. "Sylvia is unable to recall exactly what was in that message" the report said. "But he believed it had something to do with Iran. He stated that he did not respond to the message and instead deleted it." While deleting the message, Sylvia allegedly told military investigators that "he believed he deleted the entire message thread with Michael Gordon. This erased Signal messages and Signal phone calls that would have been recorded in Signal on [Sylvia's] personal phone." Sylvia "indicated multiple times he was comfortable with what he told Gordon about Ukraine assistance," the report said without elaborating. The intrigue: Sylvia's case has led to some friction in the Pentagon after the Joint Staff initially issued a positive statement about the general immediately after he was terminated. The Joint Staff retracted its statement after senior Defense Department officials sent word that Sylvia had been fired for allegedly leaking. A source familiar with the investigation said the Joint Staff should have known better. "You don't get four polygraphs deep without the head of the Joint Staff being briefed at some point. Why wasn't he flagged, what red flags flared up?" the source said. "Their first statement, they gave him a farewell — you know, 'We wish you well in your future endeavors' — and had to retract that information after the truth came out," the source said. "So there's a level of culpability within the Joint Staff that I think is a critical part of this they need to answer for." What they're saying: The Joint Staff declined to comment and referred questions to the Justice Department. The New York Times and Wall Street Journal declined to comment. Sylvia could not be reached for comment. The Defense Department referred Axios to a statement by Assistant Defense Secretary Sean Parnell, who said last week that "classified information is not personal property. Leaking it for personal, political or professional gain is a betrayal of the trust placed in those responsible for keeping it."

events.title: How Hollywood mogul Tyler Perry makes and spends his massive $1.4 billion fortune
events.summary: As of October 2026, Forbes puts Tyler Perry's net worth at $1.4 billion. Eugenia R. Washington/Getty Images Tyler Perry is a billionaire thanks to his Madea franchise and sprawling Atlanta movie studio. Perry was the third highest-paid entertainer in the world in 2022. Take a look at how the Hollywood mogul makes and spends his massive fortune. Tyler Perry's entertainment empire made him a billionaire. The actor, director, writer, and producer joined the billionaire ranks of Oprah Winfrey, George Lucas, John de Mol, and Steven Spielberg in 2020. In 2022, Perry was the third highest-paid entertainer in the world at $175 million, Forbes reported. As of October 2026, his net worth is $1.4 billion, according to his Forbes profile . Perry's income streams include his film and TV library, investments, his ongoing content deal with BET, and Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Here's a look at how he makes and spends his fortune. Perry, 57, was born Emmitt Perry, Jr. in 1969 and raised in New Orleans. Tyler Perry with his mother. Michael Tran/FilmMagic/Getty Images Perry shared a close relationship with his mother, Willie Maxine Perry, who died in 2009, The Seattle Times reported. He is estranged from his father and, to distance himself from him, Perry changed his name to Tyler at 16. Perry did not finish high school but later completed his GED. He is now based in Atlanta and has a son with his former partner, model and activist Gelila Bekele. Tyler Perry and his then-girlfriend Gelila Bekele. Gary Gershoff/WireImage/Getty Images In December 2020, Perry revealed in an Instagram post that he and Bekele had split. "I'm 51, single and wondering what the next chapter in my life will look like," he wrote. Perry got his start in theater. Tyler Perry, winner of Outstanding Theatrical Film for "Diary of a Mad Black Woman" M. Caulfield/WireImage for BET Network When his first play, "I Know I've Been Changed," debuted in Atlanta in 1992, it opened to a mostly empty theater, according to his official website . Thirteen years and many other plays later, he released his first film, "Diary of a Mad Black Woman," in 2005, jumpstarting his Madea franchise. The movie made $22.7 million its opening weekend. One of Perry's best-known projects is the Madea movie franchise, in which Perry himself dresses as a woman and plays the titular role. Tyler Perry as Madea during a 2017 appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Andrew Lipovsky/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images In a 2017 appearance on the "Today" show , Perry said that playing the role happened by accident. When the actress playing a grandmother in his 2000 stage show "I Can Do Bad All by Myself" didn't show up, he had to take over her lines, and Madea was born. "That two minutes of Madea ended up being most of the show," he said. Perry made 13 Madea movies over 2 decades. Tyler Perry as Madea. Andrew Lipovsky/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images The final theatrical release in the franchise, "A Madea Family Funeral," made $27 million in its March 2019 opening weekend, Variety reported . In July 2025, the latest movie, "Madea's Destination Wedding," was released on Netflix. The highest-grossing Madea movie, "Madea Goes to Jail," brought in $90 million in total box-office earnings in 2009, Forbes reported . Perry's Madea franchise has grossed over $660 million. Madea movie posters. John Parra/Getty Images for Lionsgate His broader film collection has brought in over $1 billion in ticket sales. Perry and Lionsgate had a "first look" deal for 6 years from 2008 to 2014. Tyler Perry speaks at an event. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic Many of Perry's Madea movies were distributed by studio giant Lionsgate; later Madea movies were released on Netflix. In a first-look deal, the creator owns the copyright to his material. Perry maintains ownership of everything he has produced, including 1,200 TV episodes, over 20 films, and at least two dozen stage plays. Since parting ways with Lionsgate, Perry has inked partnerships with the Oprah Winfrey Network and Viacom, the parent company of BET. Tyler Perry and Oprah Winfrey. JB Lacroix/WireImage/Getty Images Perry created shows such as "The Have and Have Nots" and "If Loving You Is Wrong" for OWN during his seven-year partnership with the network, which ended in 2019. In 2017, Perry signed a contract with BET's parent company, Viacom (now Paramount Skydance Corporation), to produce exclusive original content for BET and other Viacom networks following his partnership with OWN. BET, short for Black Entertainment Television, was launched in 1980 to focus on programming for Black audiences. In a September 2020 profile, Forbes estimated that about $60 million of Perry's billion-dollar net worth came from his stake in BET+. Marcus Ingram/Getty Images for BET At the time, the company reportedly gave Perry a 25% equity stake in its  streaming service, BET+ , and paid him $150 million annually to produce new films and TV shows. Paramount Skydance acquired his stake in 2026 when BET+ was folded into Paramount+. Perry continues to produce original programming for BET, though the terms aren't public. Perry's shows "Sistas" and "The Oval" were the top two cable series for Black audiences in 2021. Forbes estimated that his 330-acre production studio in Atlanta, Tyler Perry Studios, is worth $280 million. Tyler Perry Studios. Paras Griffin/Getty Images In 2015, Perry paid $30 million for a plot of land on the grounds of the historic Fort McPherson army base, where he built his production studio. Perry has said the studio site was once a Confederate Army base. In a 2019 BET Awards speech, he said, "While you're fighting for a seat at the table, I'll be down in Atlanta building my own." The studio grounds feature 12 sound stages and 200 acres of greenspace. Marvel megahit "Black Panther" was one of the first movies shot at the studio's new stages. Directed by Ryan Coogler. Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures Perry took Architectural Digest on a tour of the property in 2019, which includes neighborhoods, mansions, and a replica of the White House. Perry has built an impressive real-estate portfolio over the years that consists of several multimillion-dollar properties. Tyler Perry. Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images Perry bought a 34,000-square-foot house in Atlanta in 2007 for $9 million. It has seven bedrooms, 14 bathrooms, a helipad, an infinity pool, and a tennis court, Architectural Digest reported. He sold the home to David Turner, an entrepreneur and evangelist, nine years later in 2016 for $17.5 million. Steve Harvey bought the house for $15 million in June 2020. In September, Perry listed his Beverly Hills mansion for $57 million and said that he was preparing to move to Puerto Rico. events.title: Venezuela seeks more investment in energy sector as it reforms hydrocarbon law
events.summary: Venezuela is seeking more international investment in its energy sector, with the partial reform of the country’s hydrocarbon law representing a “paradigm shift”, its hydrocarbons minister said on Tuesday. “The new framework allows private participation in primary activities through mechanisms such as the production and exploration contracts and provides guarantees such as dispute resolution and different frameworks that improve conditions for attracting this investment,” Paula Henao told delegates at Adipec in Abu Dhabi. Venezuela's oil sector suffered for years as a result of sanctions that hampered the flow of investment into the country. The oil-rich nation is seeking more investment since the ousting of president Nicolas Maduro earlier this year. Mr Maduro was captured and arrested in a US-led operation in January, with Donald Trump's administration taking control of Venezuela's oil industry. “The main obstacles to large-scale investment continue to be sanctions,” Ms Henao said. The country has signed 80 commercial agreements with international companies over the past year despite continuing challenges, she added. In September, Venezuela signed an energy agreement with France’s TotalEnergies. Details on the scope and value of the agreement were not disclosed. US company Chevron has also revealed plans to invest $7 billion to double its Venezuelan oil production to 600,000 barrels per day over seven years, while North American Blue Energy Partners plans to invest up to $100 billion across 17 Venezuelan oil projects. US oil producer Continental Resources also signed a memorandum of understanding with the state-owned oil and gas company PDVSA to jointly develop the Ayacucho 2 block in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt, one of the world’s largest deposits of heavy crude. Abu Dhabi’s XRG, Adnoc's international energy investment unit , was awarded an offshore natural gas project in the South American country alongside global oil major bp and Qatar’s UCC in August. Venezuela is one of Opec’s founding members, alongside Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq and Kuwait. Home to the world’s largest proven oil reserves, the country produces about 1.1 million bpd of crude, with most exports flowing to China and India, according to Rystad Energy. While that accounts for just around 1 per cent of global oil trade, the output is distinctive, with more than 67 per cent classified as heavy crude.

events.title: Charted: Why early midterm results can be misleading
events.summary: Data: AP via The New York Times and Axios research; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios The first votes counted Tuesday night will almost certainly look redder than the final result, and control of the House and Senate could take days to settle. Why it matters: Early leads can create false impressions of who's winning and suspicion when those leads vanish. Election night is really election week. By the numbers: AP didn't call control of the House until seven or eight days after Election Day in each of the past three elections . The Senate was settled by 10:44pm on election night in 2018 and at 12:06am the next morning in 2024 . In 2022, it took four days , and in 2020, it wasn't called until Georgia's January runoffs , two months later. State of play: Republicans hold 53 Senate seats . Democrats need a net gain of four for a majority. The red head start: In every national election since 2018, the House and Senate votes counted by 9pm ET were 4 to 9 percentage points more Republican than the final result, an Axios analysis of AP and Edison Research vote counts found. It's mostly geography. Fast-counting Florida and other right-leaning states report first. At 9pm on election night 2022, Florida accounted for 40% of all Senate votes counted nationwide. By 11pm, more House races had been called for Republicans than Democrats in all four elections, including 2018 and 2020, when Democrats won the House. The tilt fades, slowly. At 6am Wednesday, the national House count was still 2 to 3 points more Republican than the final, largely because California, Washington and Oregon count for days. Data: Axios research; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Zoom in: Each state tilts its own way, depending on which ballots and which counties it counts first. States that count early and mail ballots first tend to start bluer than they finish. States that count Election Day votes first start redder. Ohio, Nebraska, Texas, Kansas and Iowa start blue. Sherrod Brown and Bernie Moreno were tied at 9pm in 2024 with half of Ohio's votes counted. Moreno won by 4. Independent Dan Osborn led Sen. Deb Fischer at 11pm in Nebraska with half the votes counted in 2024. Fischer won by 7. Beto O'Rourke led Ted Cruz at 9pm in 2018 with nearly half of Texas counted. Cruz won by 3. In 2020, Kansas Republican Roger Marshall was down by 8 points at 9pm, even though he'd eventually win by double-digits. Michigan swings both ways. Elissa Slotkin led Mike Rogers by 13 points at 9pm in 2024, trailed by 3 at midnight and won by less than half a point. Maine starts red and counts slowly. In 2020, Susan Collins led by 18 points at 11pm with 16% counted. She won by 9. Alaska is the slowest and starts out redder. In 2020, Sen. Dan Sullivan led by 28 points at 6am ET with 37% counted. He won by 13. Election-night results include Election Day ballots and some early and absentee ballots. The rest are counted in the following days. Rural mail often goes through Anchorage, and weather can slow it, with domestic ballots accepted up to 10 days after Election Day if postmarked on time. If no one wins a majority of first choices, Alaska will run its ranked-choice tally on Nov. 18. Data: AP and Edison Research via The New York Times; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Watch the clock (all times ET): 6pm — The first votes: Parts of Indiana and Kentucky close, giving us the first House returns. 7pm — The red head start: Polls close in the key Senate states of Georgia, South Carolina and most of Florida and New Hampshire. Fast-counting Florida gives Republicans an early boost in House races. 7:30pm — North Carolina and Ohio close: Watch for early Democratic leads in Ohio that could shrink as more votes come in. 8pm — Four more key races: Maine closes, along with most of Michigan, Texas and Kansas, the rest of New Hampshire and Florida's Panhandle. 9pm — Peak red mirage: Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska close, along with the rest of Michigan, Texas and Kansas. Historically, the national House count looks most Republican between 9pm and 11pm. 11pm — The West Coast: California, Oregon and Washington begin reporting, bringing millions of votes and pivotal House races into the picture. The early Republican tilt should begin fading. About 1am Wednesday — Alaska: The last polls close, and initial results are expected. Election-night results include Election Day ballots and some early and absentee ballots, with others counted in subsequent days. The bottom line: Early leads aren't necessarily predictive. The closer the race, the longer voters may have to wait to learn who won.

events.title: New FCA rules bring ESG rating providers into UK regulation for the first time
events.summary: New UK rules for environmental, social and governance (ESG) rating providers will raise standards in the market, helping investors to make better informed decisions. The new framework brings ESG rating providers into FCA regulation for the first time, covering a market that plays an important role in investment decisions. The rules are designed to improve the transparency, reliability and comparability of ESG ratings, helping build confidence in the information investors rely on. The regime applies to firms or organisations providing ESG ratings and assessments to ensure reliability across the market. The FCA has published guidance to help firms understand whether they may be in scope. Laura Dawes, director of authorisations and sustainable finance at the FCA, said: 'Trusted information is essential for well-functioning markets. These rules will help improve transparency and raise standards across the ESG ratings market while supporting competition, innovation and growth. 'Firms should check now whether they are in scope and start preparing for authorisation. We'll continue to provide practical support to help them prepare.'The new framework introduces requirements covering transparency, governance, systems and controls, the management of conflicts of interest, and engagement with users of ESG ratings and rated entities. It is designed to be proportionate to firms' size and activities and is informed by international and existing standards. Firms that may be in scope should start preparing now. ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. The FCA will provide webinars and access to its Pre-Application Support Service to help firms prepare. Firms should now: understand whether the framework could apply to their activities review the final rules and guidanceconsider whether they need FCA authorisationstart preparing for implementationengage early with FCA support servicesNotes to editorsRead the FCA’s Policy Statement and final rules, PS26/22, ‘ESG ratings: final regime’.The new framework takes effect on 29 June 2028. From that date, firms providing ESG ratings in the UK will need FCA authorisation and to have the relevant permission before carrying on that activity, unless an exemption applies.ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027. We are staggering application periods and encourage firms to apply as early as possible within their window. ESG ratings generally assess how companies or other entities, assets, or financial products perform against environmental, social and governance criteria. They are used by asset managers, lenders, benchmark administrators and others to inform capital allocation decisions and manage risk, among other uses. The approach is shaped by international standards, including recommendations from the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO). The final rules follow the FCA’s consultation, CP25/34, which opened on 1 December 2025 and closed on 31 March 2026. The regulatory framework follows government legislation bringing the provision of ESG ratings within the FCA’s remit in October 2025. 95% of respondents to the government’s consultation supported the move. The regime regulates how ESG ratings are produced, governed and communicated. It does not prescribe a particular sustainability view or methodology. There is strong investor demand for ESG information. The FCA's Financial Lives Survey 2024 found 72% of adults with investments or a defined contribution pension wanted their investments to do some good as well as provide a financial return.

events.title: Three questions that will define AI's political power
events.summary: The 2026 midterms will offer the first test of voter sentiment on the AI race, offering a window into how a niche policy debate is transforming into a wedge issue ahead of a presidential campaign cycle. Why it matters: The results will reveal whether explicitly campaigning on AI regulation — or aligning with tech moguls like Elon Musk — is a winning political strategy or a liability for 2028. One thing is already clear: Candidates increasingly can't afford to have half-baked AI agendas. Here are three major questions about the future of AI politics and policy and the races we're watching on Election Day for answers. 1. Did AI break through? A different kind of AI political spending has emerged in the midterms. Instead of supporting or opposing candidates based on their AI positions, some groups want to make AI policy itself a campaign issue. Guardrails Alliance, a pro-regulation advocacy group, recently launched ads targeting Republicans and Democrats over their positions on AI in Arizona, Montana, North Carolina and California. The organization backed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who said AI was the most important issue heading into Election Day, tying it explicitly to jobs and affordability. Democratic group Tomorrow Together also launched ads against Republicans' AI track record in Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. Meanwhile, competing AI groups Public First and Leading the Future spent more than $50 million through affiliated super PACs in nearly 50 races, but their TV and digital ads largely avoided the very issue they're trying to influence: AI. These races could offer an early test of whether explicitly campaigning on AI is a viable political strategy heading into 2028. 2. Did Elon Musk help or hurt candidates? Elon Musk's political spending, involvement in DOGE and ties to the Trump administration have made him both a powerful political backer and a target for Democratic attacks. He was the biggest donor in the midterms by far, contributing more than $400 million. Races we're watching include: Texas' 10th District: Republican Chris Gober, who represented Musk in connection with DOGE, faces Democrat Caitlin Rourk. Kansas' 1st District: Democrat Lauren Reinhold has leaned into her experience with DOGE, criticizing Musk's influence over the federal government in her challenge against Republican Rep. Tracey Mann. Ohio Senate: Republican Jon Husted has benefited from spending by Musk's America PAC in his race against Democrat Sherrod Brown. Texas Senate: Musk-affiliated spending has made the contest between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton another test of the billionaire's political influence. These races could help answer whether Musk's money helped elect Republican allies or gave Democrats a useful target. 3. How loud will the AI safety movement be in the next Congress? A handful of candidates aligned with stronger AI safeguards could help determine whether the next Congress has a more vocal bloc pushing back against the industry's efforts to limit regulation. Races we're watching include: Michigan Senate: El-Sayed wants a new Cabinet-level federal agency to regulate AI and a ban on super intelligence. He has used Musk's political involvement to attack Republican Mike Rogers, who has benefited from Musk-affiliated political spending. Colorado's 8th district: Democrat Manny Rutinel sponsored the nation's first comprehensive AI bill. California's 11th district: Democrat Scott Wiener's AI transparency legislation was at the center of a regulatory fight that divided the industry, offering a preview of battles in Washington. Minnesota's 2nd district: Democrat Matt Little would add another voice to the push to ban data center construction and nondisclosure agreements at the national level. These are some of the races that will help determine the size and influence of the AI safety movement's congressional coalition, an important indicator of where the fight over AI regulation is headed in 2027 and beyond. The bottom line: Many factors will shape the outcomes of races across the country. But competing AI factions will be quick to claim victories, explain away losses and draw lessons about what worked ahead of 2028.

events.title: Elon Musk's next target: a major shake-up of America's wireless market
events.summary: Elon Musk is looking to shake up America's wireless industry, potentially bringing the first major new competitive threat in years to a business dominated by three companies. Why it matters: The cellular industry has seen enormous technological change, but relatively little disruption to its competitive structure. Musk has the money, spectrum and satellite network to attempt something different — though he faces daunting obstacles. Driving the news: SpaceX is assembling the pieces to become a major U.S. wireless carrier, potentially building its own terrestrial network and buying available spectrum. The moves are meant either to build the capability to bypass existing carriers or to bring them to the table for a deal that would allow Musk to strike a deal for wholesale access to their networks. Musk may have reason to move quickly while the current administration and its regulatory appointees remain in place, a reason some analysts have cited in the context of proposals for a merger between Tesla and SpaceX . What they're saying: Blair Levin, a former FCC chief of staff who now heads policy at Optimal Advisory, says Musk's financial resources distinguish him from previous challengers. "For the first time, there is an entity capable of scaring investors in the traditional big three," Levin told Axios. Unlike Dish, which faced serious financing constraints, SpaceX can draw on capital markets that have rewarded Musk's ambitious plans. The latest : SpaceX has held talks with EchoStar about acquiring Boost Mobile or gaining access to its network arrangements, according to a Washington Post report Monday. That could provide a quick route to customers and infrastructure, although approval of such a deal is far from a foregone conclusion if Musk's businesses are drawn into a regulator quagmire after the midterm elections. The Post reported that Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile have all rebuffed Musk's efforts to gain access to their networks. State of play: Musk also has a path to maneuver around them. SpaceX has agreed to multibillion-dollar spectrum deals , including a low-band variety useful for reaching customers indoors and supporting a traditional cellular network. The company could build its own network using towers and smaller rooftop antennas, though doing so would require substantial investment and time. The big picture: America's wireless industry has spent much of the past two decades consolidating. T-Mobile once played the scrappy challenger, shaking up the industry with aggressive pricing and the elimination of unpopular practices. But its 2020 acquisition of Sprint reduced the number of major nationwide carriers from four to three. Regulators tried to preserve a fourth competitor by requiring the sale of Boost Mobile to Dish Network, which planned to build a nationwide network. That effort never delivered the competitive alternative envisioned, leaving Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile firmly entrenched. The intrigue: Musk would be moving from a business where SpaceX enjoys enormous technical and economic advantages to one where the established players have spent decades building infrastructure, acquiring customers and learning how to serve them. In terrestrial wireless, the big three carriers have spent decades investing in towers, spectrum, indoor coverage and the countless small improvements that make their networks reliable. Building such a network isn't simply a matter of spending billions on infrastructure, Craig Moffett of MoffettNathanson said in a recent podcast interview. It also means catching up on decades of work filling in coverage gaps in stadiums, airports and other difficult locations. The catch: Even if Musk can assemble the necessary infrastructure, it's far from clear that becoming a nationwide wireless carrier would be a particularly attractive business. Moffett questions why SpaceX would want to enter an industry where even the established carriers struggle to earn attractive returns on their investments. Between the lines: Success will depend on fundamentally lowering the cost of providing service or creating something for which consumers are willing to pay extra. SpaceX has floated the idea of using Starlink rooftop equipment as small cellular base stations, potentially reducing some of the costs of building a traditional network. The political backdrop: Musk's plans come as Washington faces a potentially significant shift following Tuesday's midterm elections. While SpaceX is likely to face significant political and regulatory risks due to Musk's ties with Republicans, analysts aren't sure that will translate into opposing a wireless deal that adds competition to the market. The bottom line: Musk has repeatedly succeeded in industries where established players doubted his ambitions. But this time he's the outsider, trying to overcome the advantages of companies that have spent decades building the networks he wants to challenge.

events.title: Democrats could learn wrong message from a blowout victory
events.summary: Democrats are poised to romp in today's election — easily winning the House and, according to most forecasts, flipping the Senate too. Yet the party itself is less popular than the IRS . Even the GOP has a better brand. Why it matters: There's a difference between a blowout and a mandate. Confusing the two could tempt Democrats to overread the results and forget the serious credibility problem they still face heading into 2028. The big picture: Democrats have done a lot of things right to position themselves for a big night. They recruited candidates who've put red state Senate races that seemingly were beyond reach, within their grasp. Many of those candidates vastly outraised their Republican opponents. But polls across the board still show a lesser-of-two-evils election — or as one Republican tied to President Trump's political operation described it, a contest of which party voters hate more. Voters are more eager to disempower Trump than to empower Democrats. By the numbers: Just 29% of registered voters have a positive opinion of the Democratic Party vs. 38% who view the Republican Party positively, according to a pre-election NBC News poll . The same poll showed Democrats with a 7-point lead in the congressional generic ballot, 52 to 45. And nearly 6 in 10 voters who plan to back Democrats in the election said their vote is about stopping Trump and Republican policies — vs. 4 in 10 who said they were more motivated to help Democrats enact their policies, per an October CBS News/YouGov poll . Zoom in: Many Democrats say they're determined not to repeat the mistake they made after the last midterms in 2022. They defied predictions of a red wave and saw it as an endorsement of Joe Biden and their party — when voters actually were increasingly angry. The post-2022 takeaway ultimately laid the groundwork for Trump's return to the White House after the 2024 election. Democrats won the House in the 2018 midterms — and went on to impeach Trump the following year. This time, presumed House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) isn't talking about another Trump impeachment — his 100-day agenda is focused on affordability. Zoom out: Other Democrats warn that it's been easier to run against Trump when he's actually in office. Making him the face of the election didn't work in 2024, and it might not in 2028, either. At the Third Way gathering in South Carolina earlier this year, Democratic strategist Jim Messina told a crowd of operatives and party leaders, "We have no economic message. And if we don't get one, we're not going to win" in 2028. Flashback: The 2006 midterms also featured a Democratic uprising against an unpopular war and an unpopular president. Democrats flipped the House and Senate in a major rebuke of President George W. Bush. But the party that year had a net-positive party image of 4 points in NBC polling. Today, it's 23 points underwater. Two years later in 2008 — with anti-Bush and anti-war backlash still running hot — Democrats harnessed Barack Obama's talents and calls for "change" to win back the White House. But a midterm blowout in 2026, if it materializes, will offer no guarantee the party will find an equally talented standard-bearer in 2028. What they're saying: "It's not great for the Democrats ... for 2028," Bill McInturff, one of the pollsters who conducted the NBC survey, said of the Democratic Party's lousy image. "But I don't see it as a barrier for how well they can do in 2026 when midterms are about Trump and these economic numbers." The bottom line: Ultimately, many top Democrats believe it will take a new presidential nominee — and likely one who wins in November 2028 — to fully repair the party's damaged brand. Axios' Alex Thompson and Holly Otterbein contributed to this story.

events.title: A new way of measuring AI models suggests China's threat to OpenAI and Anthropic may have been overblown
events.summary: The DeepSeek logo on a smartphone Illustration by Omar Marques/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Artificial Analysis's revamped ranking widened the gap between top closed and open-weight AI models. Many tests are now private, but the firm also changed the tasks and how it weights them. Open-weight AI remains competitive in coding. Usage figures offer only a limited view of demand. Chinese AI models have fallen sharply behind American rivals in a closely watched ranking, raising fresh questions about whether the threat from cheaper, freely available AI technology has been exaggerated. Artificial Analysis, a prominent independent firm that measures AI performance, recently overhauled its testing system to better reflect how people actually use the technology. One crucial change: Many of the tests are now kept secret, making it harder for AI companies to train their models specifically to perform well on them. The results were striking. Artificial Analysis said the best so-called open-weight AI models had trailed the overall leader by just three points under the previous system. Under the new system, that gap widened to 12 points. The 12-point gap included Moonshot 's Kimi K3.1 Pro. Among models with publicly released weights, the leaders scored just 32 points, compared with 58 for the then overall leader, Anthropic 's Claude Opus 5.5. The findings could have major implications for the AI industry and the billions of dollars investors are pouring into it. Chinese companies have been releasing powerful AI models that other businesses can download and adapt, often at lower costs than American alternatives. This fueled concern that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic could struggle to charge premium prices for their proprietary technology. The new rankings suggest that threat may have been overstated, potentially strengthening the investment case for Anthropic's planned IPO and a possible future OpenAI listing. Sridhar Ramaswamy, CEO of Snowflake and a former Google executive, highlighted the significance of the testing change. "The day benchmarks went private, the open-model gap went from 3 points to 12," he wrote on X . "Were open models catching up, or was the test leaking?" "Benchmark hacking" His point: When AI companies know exactly how their technology will be tested, they can train it to excel at those particular tasks. That doesn't necessarily mean their models perform equally well in the real world. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other AI experts have called this "benchmark hacking." Keeping the tests secret makes these hacks harder. The new results suggest American companies have a bigger lead than previously believed, particularly in complex scientific tasks. Even Claude Haiku 5.5, a smaller Anthropic model, outperformed every AI model with publicly released weights. Even proponents of open-weight models admitted something has likely been awry. "I do think the previous index was flattering the open weight models too strongly," said Nathan Lambert , cofounder of Trillium Labs, which researches large language models, especially open-weight models. Smaller usage There's another reason to question the threat from open-weight AI models: How much are people actually using them? Dax Raad, cofounder of software development company OpenCode, recently examined traffic through OpenRouter, a popular service that lets developers access AI models from different providers. He estimated that almost all the previous day's DeepSeek traffic flowing through OpenRouter could be handled by a single rack of powerful Nvidia computers, costing roughly $6 million to $7 million. That's a surprisingly small amount of computing power given the enormous attention Chinese AI models have attracted. OpenRouter represents only a slice of the market, so its figures don't capture all demand for open-weight models. But Raad's broader point is important: Much of the industry's enormous AI infrastructure investment is being driven by major providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, rather than the smaller developers using open models. Consider the more than 1 billion people who use ChatGPT every month. These folks are using OpenAI's closed AI models all the time — potentially way more activity than is captured by AI gateway services such as OpenRouter. Two questions Together, the rankings and usage figures raise two questions about open-weight AI: Is it really as good as the leading American technology, and is demand as substantial as the hype suggests? There are important caveats. Trillium's Lambert said open-weight models remain highly competitive in areas such as software development, and can offer businesses greater control and potentially lower costs. Still, the new evidence challenges a powerful narrative that has shaped the industry: that Chinese AI companies are rapidly catching America's leaders and threatening their business models. For investors weighing the enormous valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic, that distinction matters enormously. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . events.title: See inside Amazon’s robot warehouse
events.summary: Jess Lynn Goss for BI; Rebecca Zissser/BI At Amazon's sprawling fulfillment center in Tracy, California, robots carry shelves, sort packages, and move carts toward delivery trucks. But this is not a fully automated operation. Thousands of people still work alongside the machines, picking and packing orders, loading trailers, clearing jams, handling damaged items — and stepping in when the automated system hits a problem it cannot solve. Business Insider toured the facility recently to see how warehouse work is changing as Amazon deploys more robotics technology. These photos and videos show how people and robots work side by side, offering a glimpse of a more autonomous future. This is the latest installment of Robonomics, Business Insider's series on the rise of robots and their impact on business, jobs, and everyday life. We've unpacked the investment boom in robotics and spoken to Amazon warehouse workers to see if machines were taking their jobs. This is the entrance to Amazon's robotics fulfillment center in Tracy, California. Jess Lynn Goss for BI Workers and visitors pass through security gates before entering. Amazon's robotics warehouse in Tracy, CA Jess Lynn Goss for BI The Tracy warehouse spans 1.4 million square feet, roughly the size of 23 football fields. Eugene Kim Amazon says its next-generation fulfillment centers are about 25% more productive, and support roughly 30% more skilled jobs. Jess Lynn Goss for BI At Tracy, employees stow items in fabric pods that Hercules robots carry to pick stations. Jess Lynn Goss for BI Hundreds of Hercules robots carry towering yellow inventory pods to employee workstations. Jess Lynn Goss for BI This is Robin, a robotic arm that picks finished packages from a conveyor. Jess Lynn Goss for BI The packages are then placed on Pegasus mobile robots. Jess Lynn Goss for BI The Cardinal robotic arm then loads the sorted packages into tall metal carts. Jess Lynn Goss for BI Proteus, a mobile robot, then carries the carts toward outbound trucks. Loading trucks still remains manual work, with employees arranging packages to make the most of the available trailer space. Jess Lynn Goss for BI This is what Proteus looks like up close. Jess Lynn Goss for BI Human process assistants oversee warehouse robotic systems, coordinating responses when a chute jams or a robot stops working. Jess Lynn Goss for BI Briana Brager joined Amazon about two years ago as an entry-level employee. Now, she's a process assistant who monitors the machines and responds when something goes wrong. Jess Lynn Goss for BI When a Proteus robot breaks down, it is sent to this diagnostic center for inspection and repair. Jess Lynn Goss for BI Another area of the warehouse is called "Jackpot," where the automated system sends packages that get lost. A human worker determines where each wayward package belongs and returns it to the correct flow. Eugene Kim The employee cafeteria at Tracy. The facility employs more than 3,000 people, up from roughly 1,000 when it opened in 2023. Jess Lynn Goss for BI Mohammed Khan started as an entry-level picker 12 years ago and is now a senior manager at the warehouse. He said robots streamline work without necessarily eliminating it. "It's not that the amount of work has changed, it's how we approach it." Jess Lynn Goss for BI Read the original article on Business Insider

Credit unions could benefit from several ideas put forward today by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) aimed at helping the sector grow, innovate and meet the changing needs of their members. Credit unions, which are member-owned and typically focus on savings and personal loans in a specific occupation, community or area, have over two million members in the UK. Building on the joint PRA and FCA 2025 Mutuals Landscape report, this discussion paper examines whether the regulatory framework remains proportionate as the sector evolves, and explores how credit unions can expand access to financial services and improve outcomes for the members they serve. Options the regulators are seeking views on include: Removing some requirements on internal audit and regulatory documents for smaller credit unions, cutting red tape without compromising stability; Creating a risk-based framework for larger, more complex credit unions, giving them more flexible capital requirements; Applying relevant rules for smaller deposit takers, such as the standardised approach for risk weighted assets, to replace the current simple leverage ratio they report on; Applying a simplified version of the Basel framework, streamlining capital add-ons for large credit unions with specific exposures, and applying a simple capital buffer for absorbing shocks in stress periods; What barriers there are to credit unions offering new products and services, including how shared-service organisations and third-party organisations can best support investment, technology and operational capability; Giving credit unions additional guidance on FCA expectations around working with third-parties to provide important services; Whether changes to FCA fees could reduce regulatory costs and support sustainable growth; Providing credit unions a path to convert into building societies, bringing the benefits of a framework more tailored to specific lending and a wider range of funding tools; Reviewing the current framework for solvent exit, providing further flexibility to transfer business or restructure in an orderly manner. Shoib Khan, Director of UK Deposit Takers at the Prudential Regulation Authority, said: “Credit unions are a vital part of our financial services sector, and we have scope to make their regime even more proportionate and growth-friendly. We want to have an open, transparent dialogue with firms, and I look forward to seeing their honest feedback.” Sheree Howard, Executive Director of Authorisations at the Financial Conduct Authority, said: “Credit unions provide valuable support to millions of members, including many who may otherwise struggle to access affordable financial services. As the sector evolves, it is important that the regulatory framework keeps pace, enabling credit unions to innovate, grow and meet the changing needs of their members while continuing to deliver good outcomes for consumers. We want to hear directly from the sector about what is working well, where barriers remain, and how the regulatory framework may need to adapt to support a strong, sustainable future for credit unions.” The regulators are encouraging firms to offer their feedback on the options presented and whether there are other options which have not been included. The possibilities at this stage give more options to firms with very different business models, growth trajectories and risk profiles.

events.title: Republicans keep Senate hopes alive, mindful of the majority’s power
events.summary: Republicans can lose up to three seats today and still keep the Senate majority. Any further losses, however, carry immense consequences. Most in the party are already clocking North Carolina as lost to the Democrats. Losing the Senate would deprive Republicans of control over President Donald Trump’s nominees — including lifetime judicial appointments. And provided the House flips Democratic, Republicans could see a procession of impeachment trials for Cabinet members — and perhaps even the president. “The two oldest members of the Supreme Court are both Republican [appointees]. We want to make sure that if one of them decides to retire, or both, in the next two years, that President Trump can make an appointment that will get confirmed in the United States Senate,” Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., told Semafor on Monday amid a day of campaigning in Iowa. Republicans can quickly table impeachment trials with a simple majority if they keep Senate control; just two years ago, a Democratic majority dismissed the impeachment of then-Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas. Next year, if Democrats claim the majority in both chambers, the GOP can’t expect quick dismissals. “We’re going to need to be able to make sure that those are dealt with quickly in the Senate and are not allowed to be dragged out, which is what you’d have with a Democrat majority,” Barrasso added. The national mood is poor, and Republicans are fighting it out deep in red territory. They are hoping a pair of eleventh-hour dramas in Alaska and Michigian — and their most battle-hardened incumbent — will help bail out their embattled Senate majority. Republicans’ best pickup opportunity at the start of the cycle has faded away in Georgia. But GOP leaders see Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers as fueling their best chance in Michigan since their last Senate win in 1994. Stevens’ endorsement “brings more energy and more attention to that race, and it’s going to help in Michigan,” Barrasso said. “That is going to be a positive influence for the Republicans in the race tomorrow, and in turn I believe is going to generate more turnout and more votes for Mike Rogers.” The last batch of Michigan polls still show Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Rogers, though they won’t take into account Stevens’ stunning turn over the weekend. If Republicans somehow flip the Michigan seat, Democrats would have to net five pick-ups elsewhere, which would mean winning a majority of races in eight GOP-held states: North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Maine, Alaska, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa. Alaska has been one of Democrats’ core focuses since the start of the year, and the race still looks close. Republicans are praying that enough Alaskans saw The New York Times’ story on Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign allies working to recruit a spoiler candidate who might siphon votes from GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. “The more people that know about the situation, I think the more it’s going to help Sen. Dan Sullivan. I believe he wins the race,” Barrasso said. Asked if Peltola would be seated if she wins, Barrasso demurred: “We’re not there yet. I believe Dan Sullivan is going to win.” He also predicted GOP Sen. Susan Collins would defeat Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine, holding a seat she has occupied since winning it in 1996. Barrasso has been to Kentucky, Iowa, Michigan, Texas, and Ohio over the past few days. He said that Trump’s rallies are critical to stoking turnout by the GOP base in a cycle that’s typically brutal for modern presidents. “Nobody can get out a crowd or energize a crowd like President Trump,” Barrasso said. — Burgess Everett

events.title: OpenAI pushes policy rebrand to a skeptical audience
events.summary: The News OpenAI’s attempt to rebrand data centers and set a new tone for AI policy discourse after the midterms is landing with a thud in some circles, including with members of Congress. The company’s latest policy push is multi-pronged. It involves calling data centers “compute campuses” and seeking community input on their buildouts. It likens AI rules to speeding limits for cars, arguing that AI helps people in their daily lives, and pushing for global AI standards, as Axios first reported. If initial reactions from AI safety advocates are any indication, AI and tech companies have a long way to go to convince both voters and Democrats, who will likely hold more power in Washington after Tuesday, that their efforts are sincere and not just an attempt at face-saving. “If they think they can change the AI debate with Orwellian name changes, they are setting themselves up for failure,” said Brad Carson, former Oklahoma Democratic congressman and co-founder and president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a group pushing for AI guardrails. “AI will be the number one issue in 2028,” Rep. Greg Casar, D-Tex., posted on X . “And anyone looking to OpenAI’s lobbyist for advice will lose.” Still, OpenAI’s top lobbyist, Chris Lehane, is betting the company’s refreshed positions — on data centers and AI policy that puts people in control of the technology — will be “durable,” even if it’s in a “lonely position,” he told Semafor in an interview. “People are going to wake up in November and December and January, and there’s going to be hundreds and hundreds of state bills out there. So does Congress and the White House want to cede control of all of this?” he said, adding that OpenAI plans to push for a mandatory AI testing bill that can get 60 votes by connecting members across the aisle. OpenAI still supports certain state AI laws as well, recently endorsing two frontier AI safety bills in California, he said. He also said OpenAI spoke with Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif. on the AI “kill switch” bill the Democrat proposed in July, and said he would soon have “next steps” on making OpenAI’s products safer for teen users. Lehane said OpenAI’s views are meant to offer an alternative to extremes around AI. He argued that embracing a middle path would avoid the US ceding ground to China by being outright opposed to data centers, echoing the White House’s argument for a light touch on AI regulation. His argument isn’t doing much to win over skeptics. “[Lehane is] trying to get the best deal out of the Trump administration that he can before Democrats take over,” Alex Bores, the New York State assemblyman who became a top target of the AI industry in his run for Congress, told Semafor. “But it’s nice to see him say this debate is about control, and that the American people need a stake in what’s happening.” Room for Disagreement If Democrats want to get anything done on AI policy next year, they’ll need to work with Republicans — regardless of control of Congress. And that will inevitably involve moderation and compromise, as well as working with AI firms. “I’d expect others to follow [OpenAI’s lead],” Joseph Hoefer, chief AI officer at Monument Advocacy, told Semafor. “This is where the political calculus is inevitably heading. The industry had a good run making the case for a lighter touch, but the polling shows the limits of that strategy … and a hands-off message gets harder to sustain when voters are asking who’s in control.” Hoefer said that for AI companies looking to buoy continued AI sector growth, “the goal is to give lawmakers a case for AI investment they can defend back home.”

events.title: Asda appoints former Morrisons boss as chief executive as sales struggle
events.summary: David Potts to take over immediately as executive chair Allan Leighton steps back to non-executive strategic role Asda has appointed David Potts, the 69-year-old former boss of Morrisons , as its chief executive with immediate effect as it continues to struggle to lift sales. The UK’s third largest supermarket said its 73-year-old executive chair, Allan Leighton, who has been running the business since 2024 , would now step back to a non-executive role focusing on “the long-term strategic agenda for the business”. Potts began his career on the shop floor at Tesco aged 16 and worked at the UK’s biggest supermarket for decades, eventually heading its UK business. He was then chief executive of Morrisons between 2015 and 2023, leaving after the supermarket group was taken private by the US investment house Clayton, Dubilier & Rice in 2021. Asda and Morrisons are struggling as they face heavy competition and high levels of debt . Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third largest supermarket, with about one percentage point separating them. Asda’s sales fell by 0.5% in the three months to 4 October, according to the latest figures from the market research group Worldpanel by Numerator, despite its efforts to trim prices and improve its ranges and availability of stock. The appointment of Potts comes after a long search for a chief executive by Asda and is a surprise move as Leighton had indicated he expected to fill the role with an internal candidate. Leighton said he was “really excited” to appoint Potts. “Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth and begun to establish Asda as ‘more than a supermarket’ through our Formula for Growth strategy. David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him,” Leighton said. Potts said: “Asda has long been a great business, one I’ve admired and traded against over many years. The colleagues are remarkable, some of the most passionate I’ve met. The business has made good progress but significant opportunities remain and I’m delighted and very proud to have been asked by Allan to lead the team. “Providing value to families across the UK has always been in Asda’s DNA and by making improvements to the shopping trip every week, which customers can experience and feel in their pockets, we will revitalise the business and bring benefits for all our stakeholders, including our 116,296 very hard-working colleagues.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He added: “Christmas is upon us and the business has a clear focus on keeping Asda prices locked low at this important time for our customers. I’m excited to get started.”
