events.title: Trump is going to get 'trounced' in the midterms — and knows it, Anthony Scaramucci tells CNBC
events.summary: President Donald Trump will get "trounced" in the U.S. midterm elections, according to Anthony Scaramucci. The former White House communications director also said the Republican party was facing a "civil war" after the result. He also said he was "bearish" when it came to the outlook for the Iran war. U.S. President Donald Trump will get "trounced" in Tuesday's midterm elections, former White House communications director and SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci told CNBC. Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday, Scaramucci said America is in the throes of a cultural and economic struggle, with the two main parties fighting to deliver "two different visions of where the country should go." "I think the president's going to get trounced, by the way, and I think he knows he's going to get trounced," he said. Trump's economic approval rating hit an all-time low last month, according to CNBC's All-America Economic Survey , with 65% of respondents disapproving of the president's handling of the economy, while 80% rated the economy as fair or poor. "You have one vote. You have one customer relations survey that you can do on the American president — that's at the midterms, and people are not happy," Scaramucci added. "He promised affordability, he promised no more forever wars, he promised transparency on the Epstein files," Scaramucci said on Tuesday. "He didn't deliver on any of that stuff, and so there's a lot of people inside MAGA that are now also breaking from him." The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request to comment. The White House previously told CNBC that Scaramucci's "relevance ended almost a decade ago." Scaramucci was White House communications director for 10 days in 2017, during Trump's first term. Prediction markets are now pricing in around a three-in-four chance of the Democrats winning control of the Senate in Tuesday's election. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls. Scaramucci 'bearish' on Iran breakthrough On the Iran war, Scaramucci said he was "bearish" on a potential diplomatic breakthrough after the ballot. "I don't see any alignment between the Iranians, the Israelis, and the Americans for a potential negotiated solution right now," he said. "If the Americans are going to ramp up the military strikes alongside of the Israelis ... I don't really understand how that's going to necessarily help the region either." The U.S. launched "defensive" strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island overnight, a U.S. official told MS Now. Trump previously said American forces would not attack Iran before the midterms. "Wars are very bad for business," Scaramucci told CNBC Tuesday. "They're not great for the stock market. So I would like to have a negotiated settlement, but there's nothing on the matrix where you see the concentric circles lining up, where these three groups would say, 'okay, that's a deal that all three of us are willing to accept.'" Scaramucci also said "disarray" within the Democratic Party had been "the best thing that has happened for Donald Trump." "And so, if he gets trounced here, there will be bicameral investigations that will be the main show because there's a lot of things that's going on in the administration that the Democrats are going to want to uncover," he said. "The Republicans, in my mind, I think there'll be a great intellectual civil war. The Republicans are going to have to reconcile where do they want to go. It's no longer the party of Ronald Reagan, certainly not the party of George W. Bush, but is it the party of Donald Trump after he leaves the stage?" Scaramucci added that it was going to take a long while to get away from the so-called MAGA movement. "There'll be DNA elements of MAGA in the next presidential candidate for sure, because looming large over that presidential candidate will be Donald Trump and several hundred million dollars of his PAC money, and so they're not going to want to get too far away from him in 2028. So there will be elements of MAGA, but I also think there'll be a civil war in that party," he said.

events.title: Russian strikes choke Ukraine’s economy as steel shuts down and grain exports stall
events.summary: Ukraine's economy is struggling as Russia's air war targets industries, logistics networks and ports needed for exports KAMIANSKE, Ukraine -- The furnaces are cold, the factory floor deserted, and twisted metal litters the grounds of Kamet Steel, a vast industrial complex that once helped power Ukraine’s economy but closed after a Russian attack . Across the country, grain — a key export — piles up in fields and silos as farmers struggle to find routes safe from airstrikes and wait for prices to rise. Russia’s intensified air campaign is slowly strangling Ukraine’s economy, targeting industrial and energy plants and the logistics networks, railways and export routes that keep it afloat. The near-daily strikes with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones disrupt production and drive up transport costs. As a result, Ukraine’s government faces a deepening cash crunch as the air war chokes its revenue from steel, agriculture and other key sources. The damage ripples across interconnected sectors just as Kyiv faces uncertainty over future U.S. support . Ukraine’s central bank last week forecast a 0.4% economic contraction in 2026, reversing its previous projection of 1.8% growth, due to the attacks and a surge in global energy prices. Gov. Andriy Pyshnyy said the bank had also raised its inflation forecast to 12.5%, from 10% in July. Ukraine spends some 40% of its gross domestic product on defense — far beyond what it can cover alone, notes Torbjörn Becker, director of the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics. Raising taxes only would bring in a fraction of what is needed. Missile strikes have halted steel production across Metinvest Group, the country’s mining and metals giant. Kamet Steel, in the industrial city of Kamianske, accounted for more than a quarter of Ukraine’s steel output in 2025. The complex employed thousands producing steel and pig iron for domestic construction. It also supplied semi-finished steel to Metinvest’s facility in Bulgaria for the market there and elsewhere in Europe. But five ballistic missiles struck the site on Sept. 5. Its closure has hurt Ukraine’s industrial economy, affecting construction, mining, engineering, energy and logistics. Ukrzaliznytsia, the national railway operator, relies heavily on steel transport and other freight revenue. Businesses that rely on the plant could lose jobs and face bankruptcy, said Oleksandr Tretyakov, Kamet Steel’s CEO. European Union trade restrictions could hinder recovery by narrowing the market for Ukrainian steel exports, he said. “This is the worst situation since the Second World War,” Tretyakov said, noting that steel once accounted for about 6% of Ukraine’s GDP. “It did,” he said. “Right now, it’s zero.” Agriculture accounts for up to 60% of Ukraine’s foreign currency earnings, making it critical to the wartime economy. But Russian attacks on Black Sea shipping have sharply reduced traffic through Ukraine’s deep-water ports just as farmers need cash to prepare for the next planting season. Ukraine’s Black Sea trade has collapsed with attacks on ports, vessels and logistics infrastructure, according to maritime data and analytics company Lloyd’s List Intelligence. There were only 21 ship arrivals at Black Sea ports in August, down about 90% from a year earlier. Soaring insurance premiums and the constant threat of Russian strikes deter shipowners. Dozens of sailors have been killed in attacks this year. “All our developments and all the innovations we achieved will be crossed out by this situation and we will need to start from zero later,” said Volodymyr Scavinskyi, trade director at Nibulon, one of Ukraine’s leading agricultural exporters. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Ship traffic from Ukraine's lower-capacity ports on the Danube River to the Black Sea has surged, even under the threat of Russian bombardment. But it is costly. The Danube delta's Sulina Channel is too shallow for the largest vessels, and dozens of ships often wait days to enter or leave the river. Record low Danube water levels due to drought also constrain the route. Barges that once carried 1,500 tons are loading only 800 to 900 tons, Scavinskyi said. Nearly twice as many barges are needed to move the same volume, raising costs. Transporting each ton of corn from central Ukraine to Spain cost up to $50 earlier this year. Now, it can reach $150, he said. “It’s still risky and you don’t have any guarantees that your voyage will be successful,” Scavinskyi said. For Olena Shelest, commercial director at HarvEast, a major agricultural holding, the immediate challenge is finding buyers. HarvEast is holding wheat in enormous silo bags, waiting for market prices to stabilize. But the grain must be sold by year's end to free up cash for next year’s planting.

events.title: A little-known biotech’s high-stakes cancer bet just paid off and its shares doubled
events.summary: Genmab shares have doubled in three months after three successful Phase 3 cancer drug trials in October. The Danish biotech is using royalty income from drugs such as Darzalex to fund a shift toward owning more of the medicines it develops and sells. CEO Jan van de Winkel said recent trial breakthroughs mark “a completely new era,” with petosemtamab emerging as a potential multibillion-dollar drug. Danish biotech Genmab has seen its shares double in three months after a string of major cancer drug trial successes, giving fresh momentum to its push to take greater control of the medicines it develops and sells. After nearly three decades spent building Genmab into one of Europe's prominent biotechnology companies, CEO Jan van de Winkel told CNBC on Friday the breakthroughs marked "a completely new era." Historically, Genmab made money from royalties from drugs it helped develop, including Johnson & Johnson's multiple myeloma treatment Darzalex and Novartis ' Kesimpta. Van de Winkel said Johnson & Johnson is expected to generate $16.5 billion to $16.9 billion in Darzalex sales this year, with Genmab receiving royalties of up to 20%. Genmab is now using that financial firepower to build a business that keeps a much larger share of the revenue from its own treatments. The biggest market reaction followed Genmab's Oct. 28 announcement that petosemtamab, combined with Merck's Keytruda, reduced the risk of death by 50% compared with Keytruda alone in a Phase 3 trial of patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer. The combination also significantly improved response rates and showed no new safety signals, according to Genmab. Van de Winkel told CNBC the combination "could potentially set a completely new standard" of care although he declined to say whether the survival data might hold up as the data mature, citing still unpublished full data. Days earlier, Genmab reported that its medicine Rina-S reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 71% and the risk of death by 57% versus chemotherapy in a Phase 3 ovarian cancer trial. Barclays analysts said the results exceeded investor expectations and suggested Rina-S could offer an alternative for patients ineligible for AbbVie's competing treatment Elahere, or whose cancer had progressed after receiving it. They cautioned, however, that cross-trial comparisons are limited. A third late-stage October win came from Epkinly, co-developed with AbbVie, which reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 51% when combined with standard chemotherapy in previously untreated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Analysts see significant commercial potential for petosemtamab, including beyond its initial target market. Jefferies analysts said the drug could generate $3.5 billion in peak annual global sales treating recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer, and estimated an expansion into locally advanced disease could add another $3.5 billion, an opportunity they believe investors have yet to fully appreciate. Declining to give specific numbers, van de Winkel said he expects petosemtamab to become a "multi-billion dollar drug." Genmab is due to report third-quarter earnings on Nov. 5. Genmab has built its business around antibody-based medicines, including so-called bispecific antibodies such as petosemtamab, which can bind to two different targets on cancer cells simultaneously. Petosemtamab targets the proteins EGFR and LGR5, and is designed to both disrupt signals that help cancer cells grow and to encourage the immune system to attack the tumor. Van de Winkel said Genmab's expertise in antibodies and their interaction with the immune system has also helped it spot promising medicines developed by others. It acquired petosemtamab through an $8 billion purchase of Merus in 2025 and Rina-S through a $1.8 billion acquisition of ProfoundBio in 2024. Those deals are also central to Genmab's changing business model. It fully owns petosemtamab and Rina-S, while splitting the commercial economics of Epkinly equally with AbbVie, much larger shares than with Johnson & Johnson and Novartis. "From now on I'm going to increasingly hold on to ownership of these new medicines," Van de Winkel said. Genmab now has 15 Phase 3 trials across its three lead compounds. "The model is beginning to be validated and click together," he said. "I think the market gets it at this point finally." The Merus deal underscored the scale of the bet. Genmab borrowed $5.5 billion to help fund the purchase, relying on its royalty income as a financial backstop if petosemtamab failed. Owning more of its medicines also means taking on more of the work of selling them. Van de Winkel said the company already has much of the necessary infrastructure in place, having built up commercial capabilities around existing treatments including Epkinly and Tivdak, co-developed with Pfizer .

events.title: Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station
events.summary: Brookfield is planning a data center with more than one gigawatt of capacity at a site in England. The asset manager estimated that the potential investment for the project could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion). Drax Group, which operates the power station the facility will be housed at, saw shares rise more than 8% on Tuesday morning. Brookfield is targeting a massive artificial intelligence data center in the north of England, as Europe scrambles to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs. Energy company Drax Group said Tuesday it has signed an agreement with Brookfield and the asset manager's neocloud platform Radiant to jointly develop an AI data center on the Drax Power Station estate in North Yorkshire. London-listed shares of Drax were up 8.8% in early morning trading. The project is initially targeting up to 100 megawatts of capacity to be operational from the first quarter of 2028, with an additional 500 MW of capacity to be brought online between 2028 and 2031. It is then looking to secure more than 1 gigawatt of capacity at the site by an unspecified date. Brookfield estimates total investment, including semiconductors, could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion), with an initial £2.5 billion investment in phase 1. "This is a unique opportunity for the UK's AI ecosystem to build at scale," Radiant CEO Mahdi Yahya said in a statement. "By designing, building and operating from the UK, it will give British researchers, startups and enterprises access to frontier compute at home." The first phase of Brookfield's project in North Yorkshire will use power from the grid and target commercial customers from early 2028. The initial phase is subject to planning, regulatory and network approvals from the government and relevant agencies, alongside securing a tenant for the project, Drax said in a statement said. The company added that final investment decisions are yet to be made. While the U.S. has surged ahead on developing the huge data centers needed to power AI, Europe has been slower to break ground on the facilities. The U.K. in particular has struggled with high energy costs and challenges with long waiting times for businesses to connect to the grid. In October, it was reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid. An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC at the time that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site." Unlike the U.K., the Nordics benefit from abundant power and available land. Countries in the region, like Finland, have seen major commitments to develop AI data centers this year. In September, Google said it would invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) into AI infrastructure in the country, marking the tech giant's largest single investment in Europe.

events.title: Listing review process to come fully under SGX RegCo in move to speed up listings
events.summary: From Jan 4, 2027, SGX RegCo will review the listing documents submitted by prospective issuers seeking to list on the mainboard and Global Listing Board. SGX RegCo will take over listing document reviews from Jan 4, 2027, aiming to approve complete applications within six to eight weeks and make Singapore listings faster. Issuers will submit prospectus and listing applications through one portal. MAS keeps exemption powers, while SGX RegCo handles the main review. The change follows consultation support from law firms and issue managers. SGX RegCo says it will keep improving the process and seek more market feedback. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s stock market exchange regulator will take over the review of the listing process, and commits to processing complete applications within six to eight weeks. The move, announced on Nov 3, follows a month-long consultation that ended on Nov 29, 2025, as well as a review group’s recommendations to simplify the listing process and encourage more companies to go public in Singapore. From Jan 4, 2027, Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) will review the listing documents submitted by prospective issuers seeking to list on the mainboard and Global Listing Board (GLB). The GLB lets eligible companies valued at $2 billion or more list on SGX and NASDAQ at the same time, using a single set of offering documents. Previously, prospective issuers had to engage SGX RegCo on their suitability to list and separately submit their listing documents to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) for review under a much longer process. Issuers will now submit both the prospectus and listing application to SGX RegCo via the regulator’s electronic submissions portal, which will serve as a central interface for reviews, document tracking and regulatory correspondence. Having a single touchpoint is expected to streamline the review process for applications while maintaining review quality, said SGX Re gCo. MAS will retain the power to determine and grant exemptions from prospectus disclosure requirements and will continue to oversee the regulatory responsibilities performed by SGX RegCo. Steps have been taken to ensure SGX RegCo is equipped and adequately resourced for its expanded responsibilities. These include broadening the range of qualified individuals who may be appointed as SGX RegCo directors, thereby incorporating a more diverse range of industry perspectives and insights at the board level. “Ensuring appropriate safeguards to maintain the independence of SGX RegCo board’s judgment will remain our priority,” SGX RegCo said. The regulator will also disband the Listings Advisory Committee (LAC). The LAC predates SGX RegCo, which was etablished to carry out the exchange’s regulatory duties independently of its commercial operations. SGX RegCo chief executive Tan Boon Gin said the changes will enable greater regulatory certainty for companies seeking to list on the SGX. “Singapore investors have become more sophisticated, and they have access to more information of higher quality. Equity investing has also become much more global in nature. This requires an evolution of our philosophies and roles,” he said in a statement. He added that under the exchange’s new disclosure-based approach, SGX RegCo will focus on ensuring that companies give investors the information they need to assess for themselves the merits of investing in a stock. Respondents to the consultation – comprising law firms and issue managers – were supportive of the changes, citing a more streamlined listing process, reduced regulatory touchpoints for issuers and improved market efficiency and competitiveness. At the same time, many highlighted the need for continual process improvements driven by ongoing market engagement, and the importance of accessing practitioner expertise in SGX RegCo’s work. SGX RegCo will therefore be solicit ing feedback from market participants as the changes are made and will assess the need for further enhancements. Robson Lee, director at Kennedys Law, noted that while having a consolidated gateway to review and process listing applications will expedite the process and shorten the time to market , “whether more and better issuers will be attracted to list on the Singapore bourse will primarily depend on valuations and liquidity, post-IPO”. Lee welcomed the regulator’s assurance that faster reviews would preserve listing standards and the requirement for full and accurate disclosures so investors can make informed decisions. Tan Kian Tiong, chief operating officer at SAC Capital, said the streamlining of initial public offering listing reviews under SGX RegCo is a “positive and practical step towards making Singapore’s capital markets more accessible and efficient”. He added that a more efficient review process will allow companies to better plan their fund-raising strategies and respond to market opportunities.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Memory crunch pushes 16GB Pi 5 to $385, more than triple its launch price, just a month after the last round of hikes Apple's Mac business is booming, but the memory market has other plans 1 hour ago PC chip plunge wipes out a quarter of Intel’s value 4 days ago Traces of new Pi hardware spotted in GitHub 5 days ago SK Hynix says memory shortages to persist until 2030 6 days ago Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger bets on Nagare Labs to vault the memory wall 8 days ago Raspberry Pi has announced yet another round of price hikes, this time adding $80 to the cost of its 16GB Pi 5, which now sells for more than three times its original launch price. The latest bump, announced by Raspberry Pi boss Eben Upton, takes the 16GB Pi 5 to a whopping $385. The 16GB Compute Module 5 variants are also getting $40 more expensive, although the Raspberry Pi 500+, which packs the same amount of RAM, has escaped this particular round. Upton blamed a familiar culprit: soaring memory costs, worsened by a lack of alternative suppliers for 16GB DRAM and ongoing shortages of other components. "Unfortunately, a lack of alternative supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoing component shortages, means we now need to make further price increases on some of our highest-density products," Upton wrote. It's becoming an expensive habit for Raspberry Pi customers. The 16GB Pi 5 cost $120 when it launched in January 2025, which seems almost reasonable now. Raspberry Pi added $25 in December, another $60 in February, and a further $100 in April . With today's $80 increase, buyers are being asked to cough up $265 more than they were less than two years ago, a price hike of 221 percent. And it's barely been a month since Raspberry Pi raised prices on its 2GB Pi 4 and Pi 5 models by $12.50 apiece, taking them to $67.50 and $77.50 respectively. The repeated markups come despite Raspberry Pi reporting record first-half results in September. Revenue jumped 90 percent to $256.9 million, while gross profit rose 79 percent to $59.4 million. Gross profit per board climbed 53 percent to $12.20, helped partly by memory purchased before prices went through the roof. That stockpile advantage has since largely disappeared. For customers unwilling to pay nearly $400 for a single-board computer, Upton advises buying something with less RAM, using an older Pi, or optimizing applications to make do with less memory. He also warned that some sellers are exploiting the shortages by charging inflated prices or offering products that aren't what they appear to be, urging customers to stick to approved resellers. “We’re aware that a few bad actors have been taking advantage of the current memory supply circumstances to sell Raspberry Pi products at inflated prices or shift products that aren’t what they seem,” he said. There is, apparently, some good news, as Raspberry Pi continues to insist the increases are temporary. "As we've said from the beginning, the current memory landscape is difficult but ultimately temporary, and we look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again," Upton wrote. That could be a long wait. Micron has previously warned that memory shortages could drag on into 2028 or beyond, so anyone hoping to see a $120 Pi 5 again probably shouldn't hold their breath.

events.title: UK and EU agree deal to remove Brexit checks on food and animal products
events.summary: Agreement to ease rules on food imports and exports is expected to come into force in first quarter of 2028 The EU and the UK have completed their deal to remove Brexit checks on imports and exports of food and animal products ranging from sausages and cheese to leather goods and flowers. A wider series of mini-deals expected to be sealed at a UK-EU summit on 20 November would also result in Britain once again contributing to the EU budget as the price of rejoining a single electricity market. It will prove a boon for British food exporters and will also mean smaller retailers in the UK such as delicatessens can return to buying smaller batches of cheese and wines, something that became impossible because of the cost of Brexit checks introduced in 2022. But sources say the sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal, largely agreed in May, will not be implemented until the first quarter of 2028 after the change in UK prime minister caused a six-month delay to the second EU-UK summit, now due to be held on 20 November. Last month the National Farmers’ Union said exports of British food to the EU had collapsed by a third since Brexit, with eggs, chicken and potato products worst hit. Sources said a 200-page text on post-Brexit food exports had “been settled and there will no further negotiation”. A draft of a joint statement to be issued by the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, and EU leaders on 20 November is to be discussed by EU ambassadors at a meeting in Brussels on Wednesday. It states the SPS deal would allow “the vast majority of movements of animals, animal products, plants and plant products between Great Britain and the crown dependencies and the EU to take place without the certificates or controls that are currently required”. It adds that the UK goods would also be exempt from a carbon pollution tax, known as the carbon border adjustment mechanism, as the bloc and Britain are already aligned on emmissions. Rejoining the EU’s single electricity market is designed to help stabilise supplies but will allow UK energy companies to sell into continental grids again. The draft joint text says: “We agree that the UK’s participation in parts of the EU’s internal market requires an appropriate level of financial contribution towards reducing economic and social disparities between the regions of the EU that reflects the degree of the UK’s participation in the EU’s internal market”. The deal has divided opinion among unionists in Northern Ireland, with Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist party, saying it does not go far enough and reflects what he sees as a “lack of ambition” by the government. The DUP, which is in turmoil after the MP Carla Lockhart’s decision to quit the party on Monday, supported Brexit but not the Windsor framework part of the withdrawal agreement because it cemented SPS checks on goods sold into Northern Ireland from Great Britain. Steve Aiken, the Windsor framework spokesperson for the rival Ulster Unionist party, gave a cautious welcome to the deal. “If the agreement goes ahead, checks on most agricultural goods coming from the rest of our nation will be significantly, but not completely, reduced,” he said. The SPS deal will be presented to EU ambassadors at a meeting on Wednesday that will discuss the first iteration of a joint statement to be issued by Andy Burnham and EU leaders on 20 November. The “zero text” of a joint statement, as it is known, also includes chapters on a widely expected youth experience scheme, but this is still being negotiated, and ambassadors are also due to discuss an 11th-hour proposal from the UK over tuition fees for young Europeans to break a deadlock in talks. Two weeks ago the European Commission was so concerned that the UK would not budge on its insistence that EU students should pay full international fees that the ambassadors discussed “decoupling” the issue and agreeing instead to negotiate on it separately for another six months. The SPS deal was largely agreed in May and published by the government to allow food producers time to prepare for the change. At the time, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said it expected the deal to be implemented in May next year. Defra has now briefed industry leaders that it may not be implemented until 2028, with a further six-month transition period for a handful of key products such as grains grown this year with fungicides not yet approved in the EU. The delay is caused by the UK’s need to “dynamically align” British food standards legislation with the EU’s. Although the UK has largely followed EU rules, it has diversified in some areas such as fungicides used to help crops grow in British wet weather. The legislation is expected to renew controversy over whether the UK is a “rule taker” rather than a “rule maker”, a key issue in Brexit.

events.title: ChatGPT creator OpenAI loses bid to block Singapore start-up’s GemGPT trademark
events.summary: OpenAI argued that the name “GemGPT” conflicted with its earlier registered trademarks, including ChatGPT and numbered GPT marks like “GPT-3”. OpenAI lost its bid to stop Singapore start-up Porolis Technologies from registering “GemGPT”. The tribunal said sharing “GPT” was not enough to prove confusion or bad faith. The Intellectual Property Office of Singapore ruled on Oct 28 that “GemGPT” should be seen as a whole name. It found the public would view it as a gemstone AI product, not an OpenAI service. Porolis, part of the B.P. de Silva group, won $10,000 in costs. The ruling said OpenAI may still prove “GPT” is distinctive in a future case with different evidence. SINGAPORE – ChatGPT maker OpenAI has failed to stop a Singapore start-up from registering the name “GemGPT”, after an intellectual property tribunal found that sharing the letters “GPT” was not enough to establish its case. Por olis Te chnologies, which uses artificial intelligence to assess gemstones , can proceed with registering the trademark following the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore’s (IPOS) decision on O ct 2 8. The start-up, part of the B.P. de Silva group , was also awarded $10 ,000 in costs, including disbursements. OpenAI’s five objections to the trademark application were all rejected. At the heart of the dispute was whether people in Singapore would see “GPT” as a part of OpenAI’s products and services, or simply a type of AI technology. Porolis had applied to register GemGPT for its AI-powered gemstone authentication and related software services. Principal assistant registrar Gab riel O ng found that, as at May 2 2, 20 23, when Porolis applied to register GemGPT, OpenAI had not established that the three letters alone identified its business. The assessment turned on public perception at that date, less than six months after ChatGPT’s launch on Nov 30, 2022. Porolis, found ed in 2022, develops technology to help determine the grade, authenticity and treatment of gemstones, using images and optical data. Its parent group has its core business in gemstones and jewellery. According to the decision, Porolis said it chose “Gem” to refer to gemstones and “GPT” to describe its use of generative AI models. GPT stands for “Generative Pre-trained Transformer”, a term referring to a type of AI model. Its service is neither built on nor powered by OpenAI’s models. Porolis said it developed its systems using data that it owns or licenses, including samples labelled by gemmologists. Why OpenAI lost the GemGPT trademark bid OpenAI argued that the name GemGPT conflicted with its earlier registered trademarks, including ChatGPT and numbered GPT marks such as GPT-3 and GPT-4. Its objections included the likelihood of public confusion, harm to its well-known logos and an allegation that Porolis had applied for the name in bad faith. But Ong found that ChatGPT and GemGPT had to be considered as whole names, rather than giving disproportionate weight to the letters they shared. Although some of the companies’ services overlapped, this did not outweigh the other factors pointing against a likelihood of confusion. “The ultimate impression given is that ‘GemGPT’ concerns an unrelated AI or technology product or service for gemstones,” he said. The public would not be likely to mistake GemGPT for OpenAI’s marks, or assume that they came from the same or related businesses, simply because both contained “GPT”, he found. OpenAI also failed to establish that GemGPT would weaken ChatGPT’s distinctiveness by causing consumers to associate the two. “In my view, blurring does not arise simply because both marks contain ‘GPT’,” Ong said. Comparing with Gmail: ‘Mail’ non-distinctive element Ong drew a comparison with Gmail: the fact that it is well-known would not, by itself, prevent another business from using the non-distinctive element “mail” for e-mail or traditional mail services. On the bad-faith allegation, OpenAI argued that Porolis had sought to ride on its own reputation. It pointed to the application being filed less than six months after ChatGPT’s launch. Porolis countered that knowing about ChatGPT was insufficient to establish bad faith, and that GPT described a type of technology used by others in the industry. Ong accepted that Porolis knew or must have known of OpenAI and ChatGPT. But this did not mean its conduct fell below acceptable commercial standards. “Against this backdrop, the mere fact that the Application Mark contains the letter string ‘GPT’ does not, without more, justify a finding of bad faith,” he said. He also stressed that the ruling did not mean OpenAI could never establish that GPT was distinctive. “At a future relevant date, based on some other evidence, it could be possible,” he said.

events.title: North Korea says it wasn’t behind the $6.3 billion Binance hack and claims the US blames it for 'all the cyber crimes'
events.summary: North Korea is denying being involved in the hack on Binance. Korea Summit Press Pool/Getty Images North Korea denies involvement in Binance's $6 billion crypto theft. Kim Yo-jong accused the US of using cybercrime allegations to harm North Korea's global reputation. Binance detected a $6.3 billion breach and said it would cover losses. North Korea has denied that it was behind the $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the FBI's allegation a "grave political provocation." In a Tuesday statement, Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said: "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident." The statement was carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency and republished by South Korea's Yonhap News Agency. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she added. Kim also said Washington was using cybercrime allegations to damage North Korea's reputation. She said the Trump administration had announced plans to confiscate illicit cryptocurrency and use it as a strategic reserve, and suggested that who ultimately received "the so-called stolen cryptocurrency" could offer "a clue about who is behind the hacking incident." This statement comes after a few days of disruption for Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. On October 29, Binance said it discovered unauthorized withdrawals worth about $6.3 billion. The company initially said the breach may have involved a compromised laptop used by a DevOps engineer, though it later said it had identified additional points of intrusion. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. The exchange temporarily suspended withdrawals and said about $3 billion in assets had been frozen as it worked to investigate the attack. On October 31, the FBI said North Korea was responsible for the theft and identified the alleged operation as "TraderTraitor," a name it has previously used for North Korea-linked crypto thefts. The agency said it had observed the actors converting stolen assets primarily into ethereum and warned industry companies to block transactions connected to listed wallet addresses. Binance began restoring withdrawals in phases on November 1 and said it saw a net outflow of about $3.64 billion in under 10 hours. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Oil prices pass $105 after US strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
events.summary: Oil prices edged higher on Tuesday after reports of a US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island revived concerns about an escalation of the conflict and further disruption at the Strait of Hormuz . Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil , was trading 2.03 per cent higher at nearly $107 a barrel at 12.52pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was up 1.75 per cent to 98.15 a barrel. The gains followed a sharp slide on Monday, when both Brent and WTI plunged more than 7 per cent, with Brent settling at $104.77 a barrel and WTI at $96.46 a barrel. US forces struck Iran ’s Qeshm Island on Monday night, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday. The WSJ cited US officials, who described the attacks as defensive measures aimed at preventing Iran from targeting commercial vessels in the strait. Iranian state media said there were several explosions on the island, which is at the mouth of Hormuz. It was the ​latest in a series of limited attacks carried out by the US in recent weeks, the WSJ report said. Smaller scale strikes have been carried out and kept secret to avoid indicating any US intent to resume its major military campaign against Iran , the report added. “Overnight US strikes renewed uncertainty, leaving crude near $105 per barrel this morning and the diplomatic opening vulnerable,” said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. The latest military action comes as the US goes to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections. It also puts the focus back on the risk of supply disruption, a day after US President Donald Trump reportedly said he wanted to give diplomacy with Iran more time before considering renewed military strikes. “For oil, the decisive question will be whether the midterm elections can align the political pieces to pave the way for more normal supply conditions – or push that prospect further away,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote. “The clearest downside scenario for crude is credible de-escalation of geopolitical tensions followed by improving supply flows. The clearest upside scenario is renewed disruption while inventories continue absorbing the shortfall.” While the US midterms could change expectations rapidly, “they cannot, by themselves, reopen shipping routes, repair damaged infrastructure or reverse the AI impact on broader economies”, she added. The Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route connecting the Gulf to global markets, carried about a fifth of the world's crude oil and natural gas supplies before the conflict began in late February. Oil prices hit a six-month high at the end of October on Hormuz strikes and the probability of the conflict escalating again after the midterm elections. "Energy prices have been at lofty levels for a while, at least from our perspective. Oil trading above $100 and European natural gas above €90 is difficult to reconcile with current market realities," said Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer. "We are in an extraordinarily noisy week due to the midterms, and in a phase where the complex energy supply chains are normalising. Given this setting, today’s exceptional market fever and wild price swings should not come as a surprise. We maintain our cautious view on oil."

events.title: Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices
events.summary: iPhone maker says decision to raise prices has offset some of impact, as revenues are stronger than expected Apple has warned of an “unprecedented” rise in memory chip prices, as it battles with datacentres to lay its hands on supplies. The iPhone maker’s shares fell in after-hours trading after it told investors that the higher prices will eat into its profit margins. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” John Ternus, Apple’s new chief executive, told a conference call on Monday, predicting that memory costs in the fourth quarter of this year would be even higher than in the previous three months. The tech industry has been gripped by “RAMageddon” for months , as demand for memory chips from AI datacentres has surged, driving up prices. Ternus said Apple’s decision to raise iPad and MacBook prices in June, followed by iPhone prices in September, had “provided some offset” for the company. Ben Barringer, the head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said Apple’s results were “OK, if on the disappointing side”. “Revenues were up 12%, driven primarily by iPhone sales and strong sales of Mac Mini, which users can use to apply agentic AI. China growth was robust which is pleasing to see, while iPad and wearables disappointed with services growing but lower than the group average at 10%,” he added. “There appears to be a lot of interest in the iPhone Duo, but it is early days yet with the product not yet on full release, but it is hoped that can help drive the next leg of Apple’s product innovation.” Apple’s shares were down 2.75% in after-hours trading on Wall Street. Apple posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal third quarter, giving Ternus an upbeat start to his tenure, which began in September. The solid results bucked a downward trend for tech companies this quarter, as companies including Alphabet, Amazon and Intel had disappointing quarterly results. Jacob Bourne, an Emarketer analyst, said record iPhone revenue and strong growth in China demonstrated the resilience of Apple’s business. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Apple earned $30.71bn (£22.89bn), or $2.10 a share, in the July-September period, up 12% from $27.47bn, or $1.85 a share, in the equivalent period a year earlier. Apple said its earnings included five cents a share from tariff refunds. Revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn from $102.5bn. Analysts, on average, were expecting earnings of $1.99 a share on revenue of $113.4bn, according to a poll by FactSet. While its rivals are facing investor uncertainty over huge investments in artificial intelligence, Bourne said Apple’s “tepid approach” to AI infrastructure spending had helped preserve its cashflow – while partnerships with companies such as Alphabet could help the iPhone maker strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers.

events.title: FCA sets expectations for firms making car finance settlement offers
events.summary: Research shows consumers want the choice, rather than wait for the legal challenges to conclude. Almost 9 out of 10 (89%) car finance customers who have complained or are considering doing so want the choice of an offer of compensation now, rather than waiting for the legal challenges to the FCA's compensation scheme to conclude. 86% would be comfortable making the decision, and 61% say they’d accept an offer in line with the scheme. Timing matters for many: 77% say receiving compensation sooner would make a great deal or fair amount of difference to their financial situation.The survey findings are being released today alongside the FCA's expectations for lenders who want to make settlement offers to those owed compensation under its scheme, while legal challenges continue. This comes as Barclays Partner Finance confirms it will make settlement offers to some of its customers owed compensation.The regulator supports lenders making settlement offers, as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme.Lenders will need to be clear with people about what accepting any offer means. This includes that they will keep any money received, even if the outcome of the legal challenges means they would have received less. However, they also wouldn’t be able to claim more later if the outcome of the legal challenge means they would have been paid more. As consumers can reject an offer and leave their claim to be dealt with under the scheme, these offers can’t be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service for review.Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said:'Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. And it’s clear they want the choice.'Anyone who wants to wait can, and there’s no obligation to agree to the offer. We’ll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means.'To help consumers make informed decisions, the FCA has published a factsheet (PDF) that lenders must share with customers when making settlement offers. Not all lenders are likely to make offers, and those that do may only make them to some customers owed compensation. The FCA will regularly update its website with lenders making settlement offers to help consumers check whether an offer is genuine. Firms are expected to notify the FCA if they plan to make offers.Payouts under the motor finance compensation scheme were due to start this year. The scheme is currently partially suspended, pending the outcome of legal challenges due to be heard between 16 February and 3 March 2027. Under the partial suspension, firms must keep preparing for the scheme and continue progressing complaints as far as possible, but do not need to calculate or pay compensation under the scheme until the legal process concludes.Anyone who is concerned about their car finance deal and has not yet complained should complain directly to their lender. There is information on the FCA website on how to complain for free. There is no need to use a law firm or claims management company, which may charge up to 36% of any compensation, including VAT.Notes to editorsResearch conducted by Kantar, surveying 1,000 motor finance customers online between 25 and 28 June 2026. Findings cited are based on a subset of 590 respondents who said they had made or were considering making a motor finance complaint.Barclays press release.Statement confirming motor finance legal challenge to be heard in February 2027.Statement on the partial suspension of the motor finance scheme and what it means for firms and consumers.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters EVENT: Distributed teams need to collaborate, but duplicated files, delays, and competing versions keep getting in the way Distributed teams need to collaborate on shared information, but duplicated files, delays, and competing versions keep getting in the way. Picture a video production team with editors in different cities. One person updates a project file, another keeps working from an earlier copy, and a third waits for a large transfer to finish. When teams need to collaborate on large files across locations, traditional storage and file-sharing arrangements introduce friction precisely where people expect technology to help. Collaboration shouldn't require detective work The hard part isn't merely moving a file. It's knowing who has the authoritative copy, when changes are available, and whether somebody else is still working on an outdated version. Consider a game studio preparing a build for review. A designer exports an updated asset, but a colleague pulls an older version from a synced folder. The mistake only becomes obvious when the pieces are assembled. The team must trace the mismatch, resend files, and repeat work. Sync-and-download workflows depend on a chain of uploads, downloads, and decisions about which copy is current. Under deadline pressure, that chain breaks. Delayed access means missed handoffs; duplicated files mean extra checking and sometimes rework. For IT, each workaround creates another question: where does the data live, who can access it, and how do teams maintain consistent controls? Adding another collaboration application doesn't resolve those underlying questions. The useful starting point is the workflow. Find out where teams copy data, where they wait, and what prompts them to work outside the shared system. These frustrations cut across industries, but the ways organizations respond aren't identical. Hearing how another team handled version confusion, access, and handoffs is often more useful than another abstract promise of seamless collaboration. That's the focus of The Register and LucidLink’s invitation-only dinner on November 24 at Covent Garden Hotel in London. events.title: Seventeen's Joshua and Jeonghan are showing on tour just how fun going to work with your best friend can be
events.summary: Seventeen's Joshua and Jeonghan hit the road on a besties' tour. Pledis Entertainment Seventeen's Jeonghan and Joshua are on tour together. This follows the release of their first unit album, "Dreamscape," on October 19. They're showing off just how fun it can be to be onstage with a friend of over 12 years. Joshua and Jeonghan, vocalists from the mega-band Seventeen, made a three-hour concert look like a good excuse to hang out with your BFF. Over a decade ago, the two were training to debut in K-pop . One was a doe-eyed Korean American with an acoustic guitar, fresh off the plane from Los Angeles ; the other a South Korean high schooler. Working and living together, they overcame cultural and language barriers to become what they are today: best friends, as they often say, for over a decade. Seventeen, the band they were training to be in, debuted in 2015 as a 13-member group . Now, the two bandmates are promoting their first unit album together under the name JxJ, which launched last month. The duo bring years of stage experience to the project — and, as they told Business Insider before the album's launch, they have "a different kind of chemistry" when they're together. Their first tour, "Journey Into Dreaming," is giving that partnership an entire evening's spotlight. Business Insider attended two of the tour's Incheon stops, which drew about 25,000 attendees across three nights from October 30 to November 1. Their new album gave the show several directions to go in Joshua and Jeonghan took the stage at Incheon's Inspire Arena for three nights. Pledis Entertainment Since JxJ's "Dreamscape" album dropped on October 19, fans of the two have been wondering what would make it into the concert set list. The album's seven songs have five duo tracks — all of which they performed live in Incheon. "Outside" opened the concert with its rhythmic bass line. "Like You" followed, taking the set into house. Later in the show, "One Plus One" brought R&B and soul into the mix, while the lead single, "12 o'clock," supplied dance-rock. And to round out the show, "No Looking Back," a rousing concert anthem, got the fans singing along. Incheon marked the first time that all four B-side duo tracks were performed live. Years of performing together gave them somewhere to start JxJ released their "DREAMSCAPE" album, a seven-track collection, on October 19. Pledis Entertainment Joshua and Jeonghan had to decide what they wanted a project built around the two of them to sound like. In their interview with Business Insider, the pair said conversations they'd had about the album's direction had helped them "understand each other's tastes on a deeper level." Together, they decided what they wanted to experiment with and what part of their tastes they wanted to put on display. Joshua brought out an electric guitar. Jeonghan took to the piano. Jeonghan and Joshua each performed two solo songs. Pledis Entertainment Those separate interests had a place in the concert, too. Joshua played the electric guitar during his solo set, which included the English version of "Baby Come Home" and the sexy alt-rock track,"Not Personal." Jeonghan served up sweet and lyrical styles, playing the piano during his solo ballad, "Coincidence," at the keyboard. "Coloring," a new solo song from "Dreamscape," was reminiscent of Japanese pop, and let the singer show off his cute but laid-back dance moves . Game time JxJ adopted a show flow from Seventeen's fan meetings, where the members play games on-stage Pledis Entertainment Then there were the games, in which the two competed to avoid penalties. Between songs, they traded banter, cheating their way through most of the challenges. Games included a retooled version of "Pictionary" and quizzes where they had to guess the correct placement of various plushies. The winners avoided viral TikTok dance challenges while wearing prop headbands — but they convinced each other to do the penalty together anyway. Seventeen's catalog supplied old favorites The duo picked some fan favorite group songs for their unit concert set list. Pledis Entertainment JxJ had plenty of group songs to pick from. They went with "Crazy in Love" and "Come to Me," Seventeen songs that haven't been performed live in years. For fans who miss the complete band, JxJ brought out some tracks from its most recent tour set list, like "Rock with You" and "20." Haley Yuen, a fan from the US, flew to South Korea to see JxJ for two nights. "Their chemistry on stage was like watching two longtime besties on stage having fun," Yuen told Business Insider. "This is my first time attending a unit concert. So it really allowed me to put all of my attention on the two and their dynamic." Making it big with your bestie The "DREAMSCAPE" album has sold hundreds of thousands of copies worldwide. Pledis Entertainment According to South Korean music tracker Hanteo, "Dreamscape" sold 804,949 copies worldwide during its first week, and topped its weekly album chart. In Japan, the album debuted at No. 1 on Oricon's weekly album chart dated November 2. Oricon estimated its sales at 65,558 copies. The album also topped Japan's Oricon Weekly Album Chart and Weekly Combined Album Chart, as well as Billboard Japan's Top Albums Sales. Hitting the road together JxJ will continue to tour Asia together over the next four months. Pledis Entertainment JXJ will be on the road together for another quarter — they're taking their show to Japan on November 21 and 22. They're also serving up plenty of content on social media. View this post on Instagram A post shared by SEVENTEEN (@saythename_17) They share a Pinterest account, JxJ Diary , that mixes mood boards with behind-the-scenes photographs. The pair told Business Insider the project was a "little gift" to fans. Further tour stops in Macau, Taiwan, and Busan are scheduled through February 2027. events.title: Australian central bank chief signals pause after split decision on latest rate hike
events.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia’s governor Michele Bullock says “we’re basically preserving our options” on whether to raise interest rates again next year. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85%, an 18-year high, in a 6-3 split vote. Governor Michele Bullock said, “We’re basically preserving our options.” Bullock signalled a pause, saying the latest hikes have not yet fully impacted the economy. The RBA still worries inflation may stay above 3% and expectations could become “embedded”. The tougher policy is slowing demand, lifting unemployment and hitting housing. Home values in major cities fell 1.4% in October, and recovery may not come until rate cuts in late 2027. Australia’s central bank governor Michele Bullock signalled a wait-and-see approach to further tightening after policymakers lifted the benchmark rate to an 18-year high, in a split vote that sent the currency lower. At a press conference on Nov 3 in Sydney, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) chief highlighted that the tightening to date in 2026 has yet to feed through to the economy, while reiterating the ongoing inflation challenge . Her comments came after the nine-member policy board raised the cash rate by a quarter-percentage point to 4.85%, extending the most aggressive tightening among developed economies. The RBA board voted 6-3 in favour of raising the key rate for a fifth time this year. It omitted a reference that it was willing to hike further if needed, a line that has been included in each statement since June. “I’d not be interpreting this as saying we’re not going up. I wouldn’t be interpreting it as saying we definitely are going up,” Bullock said in response to a question on why that wasn’t kept. “We’re basically preserving our options.” Emphasising that the impact of the latest rate increases have yet to be felt, Bullock said “the last couple haven’t even started to flow through yet”. She added tighter policy was already weighing on demand, which is starting “to slow relative to supply, and ultimately it’s going to come back into balance”. Markets and economists read the governor’s remarks as dovish. The currency fell against the greenback as traders pared to about 30% the odds of the RBA raising the cash rate to 5.1% in 2027, compared with an almost 50% chance it would do so by next May before the announcement. Australia’s move comes in a week when Sweden’s Riksbank may also hike and the Bank of England is expected to increase borrowing costs for the first time in three years, as economies struggle with the energy-driven inflation shock. While Bullock talked tough on inflation, she noted that the three dissenters on the board had put greater emphasis on the downside risks in the economy. “We think the RBA will remain on edge as we enter 2027 but keep rates on hold,” said Belinda Allen at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “The slowdown in the economy through next year, led by the consumer and the resultant lift in the unemployment rate should see inflation moderate from here and return closer to target in late 2027.” Consumer prices have shown little sign of easing back to the central bank’s 2-3% target band. RBA officials worry that inflation expectations may be starting to untether, with deputy governor Andrew Hauser noting that a growing share of firms think 3-3.5% inflation is “a new normal”, a scenario he described as “the central bank’s nightmare”. “Inflation is now expected to remain above 3% for the coming year and there is an increasing risk that higher inflation expectations will become embedded,” the RBA’s board said in its decision statement. “The board is conscious of the period in which inflation has been too high.” The central bank also on Nov 3 released its quarterly update of forecasts in the statement on monetary policy. It showed underlying inflation will come back inside the RBA’s target band about six months later than assumed in August, with the economy seen slowing next year and unemployment tracking higher. The RBA now judges financial conditions to be “restrictive” and said labour market conditions “remain a little tight”, despite a rise in unemployment. Sally Auld, chief economist at National Australia Bank, warned the RBA left itself little room for error given the forecasts imply a “Goldilocks” disinflation. This is “especially considering the RBA’s hawkish description of the inflation challenge at present,” she said. “While we are not forecasting further policy tightening from here, there is little doubt the RBA will be sensitive, and responsive, to any upside surprise in inflation in coming months.” In addition to the impact of surging fuel prices, Australia has become more inflation-prone due to very weak productivity. That’s forced officials to scale back the potential growth rate, the level of expansion the economy can sustain before it generates inflationary pressures. The RBA has failed to hit the 2.5% midpoint of its inflation target band since late 2021.

events.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
events.summary: Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un Published 3 November 2026, 00:56 GMT North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric". Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history. This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor. The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group. "The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said. Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack Published 3 days ago Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Published 4 days ago But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025. Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said. The country has consistently denied such claims. Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace". Kim Yo-jong: North Korea's heir apparent? Published 16 June 2020 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Video, 00:02:32 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Published 16 June 2020 Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack. Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users. The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday. The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday. That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes. "Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added. The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals. Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack. The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach. events.title: Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters 'Weight-Space Programming' fiddles with nerd knobs to boost benchmark scores AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes 16 hours ago Thieves pilfer environment variables from Trigger AI workflow tool 20 hours ago Researchers find bugs in 5 AI developer tools, with OpenAI and Microsoft flaws still unpatched 4 days ago Google's Gemini 4 Carbon looks like a diamond in the rough 5 days ago Please state the nature of the medical emergency: Google is building a robot medic for NASA 5 days ago The outputs of AI models are the result of a complex interplay between neurons, weights, training, and inference, and are therefore difficult to follow. But in some ways they're starting to look more like open books. Recent work by Anthropic safety fellow Joshua Fonseca Rivera has revealed how certain neurons in a neural network can be associated with a specific persona . Now, computer scientists from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) have found that frontier AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra can rewrite the weights of another model directly, as opposed to indirectly through training, and alter their behavior. "We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights," said Rikiya Takehi, a PhD student at MIT CSAIL, in a social media post . "Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly." To demonstrate that, Takehi and colleagues Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to make it better at math. Astra changed only 0.016 percent of the model's weights, reducing its reasoning loops and improving its math performance by as much as sixfold on the MATH-500 benchmark, while boosting its instruction-following score on the IFEval benchmark roughly threefold. There was no training using gradient descent ; Astra just revised the numerical values that constitute Qwen's weights. "All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops," the researchers wrote in a blog post . "It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming. "Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights." Astra's ability to program weights extends to being able to write a neural network from scratch, zero-shot. The researchers told Astra: "write, from scratch, the weights of a policy network that plays [Breakout] as well as possible." And it did so. Takehi suggests this technique shows promise for improving models without the consequences of catastrophic forgetting , which can occur when a model is revised to include new knowledge. More generally, the authors expect Weight-Space Programming will open the door to new ways to understand models and optimize them, and to implement recursive self-improvement. The technique may also prove useful for reducing model sycophancy and improving interpretability and alignment. The next step, the authors say, involves building a benchmark and a harness for carrying out Weight-Space Programming on LLMs. "We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline," they say.

events.title: John Lewis Christmas ad stars Kristin Scott Thomas as glamorous granny on a gift hunt
events.summary: Company tugs at heartstrings with Pickles the talking toy dog as it celebrates 20 years of blockbuster festive ads Review: Kristin Scott Thomas v Pickles the evil AI overlord puppy John Lewis has turned to a celebrity best known for playing aristocrats to put a playful but rather upmarket spin on the countdown to Christmas with this year’s festive ad, which features a toy dog called Pickles and a glamorous granny. Kristin Scott Thomas, known for playing upper-crust characters in films such as Four Weddings and a Funeral and the Apple TV show Slow Horses, is cast as Gloria, a grandmother searching for gift inspiration, with the tagline “don’t give up on giving”. In the 20th version of its blockbuster Christmas ad, the department store kickstarts the official countdown to Christmas by tugging at the heartstrings, with Pickles, voiced by the comedian Paul Whitehouse, challenging Gloria to “do better than cash” when choosing a gift for her grandchildren. Pickles drags Gloria out of the house on a last-minute mission to find gifts, and after rejecting options in other shops, she sets off on a magical tuk-tuk ride to John Lewis, where she snaps up some disco balls and fairy lights to create a “gran cave” to hang out with her grandchildren, Freddie and Maggie. Rosie Hanley, the marketing director of John Lewis, said the retailer had increased its spend on this year’s festive ad as the cost of production had risen and it wanted to “push the boat out” for its 20th year. However, she said the company was confident it would see “a really strong return on our investment” as it tries to grab shoppers’ attention before the Black Friday discount period later this month. She said the company had wanted the ad “to be more joyful” this year because “things are tough for lots of families”. Despite concerns among British households about higher energy bills and housing costs, Hanley said spending on Christmas-related gear at John Lewis was already up on last year. The ad, set to a Sam Fender version of the Rolling Stones song You Can’t Always Get What You Want, features a range of John Lewis products in different price brackets, including the £12.99 Fisher-Price pull-along toy dog and a £255 Weekend Max Mara top and matching £290 skirt worn by Gloria. The three-minute ad will launch on social media on Tuesday morning, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, before a 60-second version airs for the first time on TV in the ad breaks for ITV’s Coronation Street and Channel 4’s The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday evening. John Lewis will also erect a giant Christmas tree outside its store on London’s Oxford Street to mark the recent pedestrianisation of the road . The company said the numbers of visitors to its store on the street last week were up by more than a fifth on the same week last year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning This year’s ad, created by the Saatchi & Saatchi agency, returns to a formula of using a cute character – such as Monty the penguin in 2014 and Buster the boxer in 2016 – after two years foregrounding other family relationships. However, it has the twist of focusing on the relationship between Pickles and a grandmother rather than centring on cute children. Hanley said the ad was inspired by research which had revealed that 52% of grandparents give cash as presents because they are not sure what youngsters really want. “People want to give thoughtful gifts but can often lack confidence, so resort to giving cash,” she said. Now considered a national moment which invites social media comment and skits, the first big-budget John Lewis festive TV ad launched in 2007, soundtracked by a piece of music by Prokofiev. Previous John Lewis Christmas TV ads have been soundtracked by covers including the Smiths song Please, Please, Please, Let Me Get What I Want and Together in Electric Dreams by Giorgio Moroder and Philip Oakey. Last year’s ad included the 1990s club classic Where Love Lives by Alison Limerick. This year’s track, which features the choir from the John Spence community high school, which Fender previously attended, and the Easington Colliery Band, will be released on vinyl later this month, with proceeds going to Action For Children. Pickles the dog is based on an existing Fisher-Price pull-along toy called Little Snoopy that is celebrating its 60th year. The John Lewis ad launch comes hot on the heels of other festive ads for most of the big supermarkets that kicked off last weekend. Total ad spending across the festive period is set to reach £14bn, up 8.2% year-on-year according to the annual review by the Advertising Association and research group WARC. That growth is led by an 18.5% year-on-year surge in social media spend, while total TV spending is expected to be up by 1.6%.
