events.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmellow, and robotaxi Mooves. On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue, officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I. “After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.” The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years. Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.” As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said. However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025. Still Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.” Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it pour £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size. “Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.” Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S. Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.” “I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued. She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mistusi and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.” “I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch. She is based in New York City.

events.title: Cheap flights in Europe face a fuel cost reckoning as Ryanair’s CEO says fares could rise up to 20% next year because of the Iran war
events.summary: Americans planning next year’s summer Euro trip may want to start saving now as the Iran war pushes up fuel prices and the CEO of the world’s biggest budget airline warns that the continent’s notoriously cheap short-haul flights could soon become more expensive. Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said on CNBC following the company’s earnings call Monday that he expects European airfares to rise by 10%, and maybe even 20% next year, potentially dealing another blow to Americans hoping to visit multiple European destinations without breaking the bank. Americans made nearly 24 million trips to Europe in 2025, a 5% increase from the previous year. Summer is one of the busiest tourist seasons for the region, and this year the European aviation network handled an average of 35,959 flights per day between June and August, a 2.4% increase from last year, according to The European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation . But the Iran war, now in its ninth month, has disrupted global supply chains, including by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20% of the world’s oil passed before the war. That has driven up oil and jet fuel prices increasing the burden on airlines, for which fuel is the s econd-biggest expense behind labor. Ryanair, Europe’s largest airline by passenger traffic, shows what could be in store for travelers next year. Hedging (fuel) bets Ryanair has been more insulated from rising fuel prices than many of its rivals because of fuel hedging, the practice of locking in prices ahead of time to protect against market volatility. O’Leary said Ryanair has locked in a price of $67 per barrel for 80% of its fuel needs through March 2027, helping keep costs in check for now. Beyond that, though, only 25% of its fuel needs for the following fiscal year are hedged at about $95 per barrel, leaving the remainder exposed to higher market prices. Brent crude stood around $110 per barrel Monday, up 70% from a year ago . Ryanair said in its fiscal second quarter earnings Monday that its annual fuel bill will increase by about 2 billion euros next year (for the fiscal year ending March 2028). O’Leary said fares would need to rise 20%, or about 10 euros per passenger, to cover all of it, but even he said the increase in fares might not fully cover the additional expense. To close the gap, the company said it is reviewing costs, including temporary pay freezes for labor agreements that mature in April and lower crew ratios. O’Leary’s comments highlight another potential expense for Americans already dealing with increasing inflation , especially in the travel sector. U.S. airfares rose 22.4% in September compared with a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, about six times the overall inflation rate. The average domestic airfare reached $445 in the second quarter, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. Unlike Ryanair, major U.S. airlines abandoned fuel hedging years ago, leaving them more immediately exposed to surging fuel prices.  Fewer flights Pricier jet fuel could also mean fewer flights to choose from. Ryanair has already reduced its annual passenger target from 216 million to 214 million for the fiscal year ending in March, and said it expects winter traffic to stay flat as it limits exposure to more expensive fuel. O’Leary said competing European airlines are already cutting capacity, which could drive up prices as travelers compete for fewer seats. Still, the higher prices could actually benefit Ryanair. O’Leary argued that competitors facing even greater financial pressure will have little choice but to raise fares, which means his airline can do the same while also maintaining its low-cost advantage. “They are under much more pressure to get pricing up,” he said during the company’s earnings call.  O’Leary also said Ryanair could maintain or even widen its margins as competitors increase their fares. For travelers hoping to squeeze several European cities into one vacation, the consequences could add up. A 50 euro flight that rises 20% would cost 60 euros. While that might seem small on its own, multiple family members and destinations could add to the cost.  For his part, O’Leary warned that travelers thinking about waiting for a bargain next summer should instead look at tickets now. “I would encourage them all to book early, because the longer you wait, the higher fare you are going to pay,” he said.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
events.summary: 'I've always looked in bins for clothes' Published 3 November 2026, 00:41 GMT Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket. On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters. Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it. Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come. During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist. Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor." Darryl Baker takes the clothes for herself and her children, and to sell In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket. Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three. Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years. "I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever." Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds. "Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says. Jeff Ferrell sells some of what he finds, and gives away other items Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay. Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year". 'If something catches my eye, I'll grab it' While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online. Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on Instagram of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells. Millie Diamond turns dumped textiles and clothes into new outfits She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600. "I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it." Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes." 'I haven't bought shampoo for years' For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them. This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money." Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items. Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says. Charlotte Bayford gives some of her finds to charity But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law? Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita. "Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges. In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land , external . In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances. "In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says.

events.title: China’s ‘Lipstick King’ touts AI tokens in first for Singles’ Day festival
events.summary: Li Jiaqi, also known as Austin Li, hosting a live stream at the headquarters of MeiONE in Shanghai on Sept 7. Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of Alibaba’s QwenWork office AI service within half an hour during a Taobao Live broadcast on Nov 2. China’s Singles’ Day added AI token packages as a major new product, moving beyond cosmetics and home appliances. It is the first time such AI credits were sold widely in the festival. Alibaba’s Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of QwenWork in 30 minutes. The stream also sold AI laptops and workplace devices, with Alibaba and JD.com launching AI token centres. AI token sales rose 450% from the previous month, and AI laptop sales jumped more than 300% in the first hour. Analysts said users may stock up, but fast AI change could make prepaid plans risky. BEIJING - The Singles’ Day shopping extravaganza in China unveiled a new attraction for 2026 as it graduates beyond a long association with cut-price cosmetics and home appliances: computing credits used to access artificial intelligence tools. The launch is the first time AI token packages have been offered as a significant consumer product category during Singles’ Day, the world’s largest shopping festival originally held on Nov 11 each year. Top live-streamer Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of Alibaba’s QwenWork office AI service within half an hour during a Taobao Live broadcast on Nov 2, the company said. That is equivalent to about two trillion AI tokens, or units of text processed by AI models. “Chinese consumers are now very accustomed to using AI productivity tools,” said Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at tech research firm Omdia. Frequent users can run short of credits, he added, which makes extensive purchases during a sales period “a very reasonable action”. It was unclear how much the token plans were discounted from normal prices, however. First sale of AI products for ‘Lipstick King’ The live stream marked the first sale of AI products by Li, who earned the “Lipstick King” moniker for amassing a huge following while selling vast volumes of lipstick online. It showcased QwenWork token plans, AI-enabled laptops and workplace devices. Chen Yusen, an Alibaba Group vice-president and chief executive of QwenWork, also made an appearance. Li asked Chen if AI could be used to build a digital avatar of himself to chat with fans around the clock. While AI could not replace Li, Chen responded, he hoped it could handle everyday tasks for users, freeing them to spend time with their families. Alibaba’s Tmall has launched an AI Token Center for the Singles Day festival, offering consumer token packages from Alibaba Cloud, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Z.AI. Alibaba’s Tmall has launched an AI Token Center for the festival, offering consumer token packages from Alibaba Cloud, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Z.AI, the e-commerce giant said. JD.com has also introduced an AI token section bringing together services from companies including DeepSeek, Z.AI and ByteDance’s Volcano Engine. Sales of AI token plans from Oct 1 to Oct 20 soared 450% from the previous month, Alibaba said, while sales of AI personal-computer laptops surged more than 300% year on year in the first hour of the Nov 11 checkout period. Su said the tokens’ relatively long expiry periods could spur users to stock up, but warned that rapid changes in AI products may make consumers wary of prepaying for services at risk of being replaced or retired. Singles’ Day, which has run since 2009 in an effort to spur consumer spending, earned total revenue of 1.70 trillion yuan (S$327.3 billion) across platforms in 2025, according to third party data provider Syntun. events.title: China regulator tells banks to pause IPOs: Report
events.summary: The move follows a sharp selloff that saw the blue-chip CSI300 Index slumping 8.5% in October, its worst monthly performance in more than a decade. China’s securities regulator told banks to pause IPOs and large share sales, The Financial Times reported, citing three sources. The China Securities Regulatory Commission gave informal “window guidance” after meetings with investment banks, Reuters could not verify the report. The move follows an 8.5% October fall in the CSI300, while regulators also launched market support steps on Nov 2 to stabilise shares. BEIJING – China’s securities regulator has told investment banks to pause initial public offerings and has suspended large share sales by existing shareholders until markets recover, The Financial Times reported on Nov 3, citing three sources with knowledge of the discussions. The China Securities Regulatory Commission held meetings with investment banks and gave informal “window guidance” over the past few days, the report added. Large sales by existing shareholders have also been temporarily suspended until the markets have recovered, according to the report. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Chinese financial regulators did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comments. Persistent weakness in the world’s second-largest economy, weighed down by frail consumption, a prolonged property debt crisis and a steep tech stock selloff, has sapped investor confidence. Chinese regulators rolled out a handful of measures on Nov 2, from conducting swap operations to upgrading a lending facility for stock buybacks by listed companies, as part of efforts to stabilise struggling capital markets. The effort to steady its sliding stock market struggled for traction on Nov 3, with AI-related shares leading declines as investors judged the financial support measures insufficient. China’s blue-chip CSI300 Index and the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index both dropped more than 1% in early trade, before paring losses to 0.1% and 0.7%, respectively, by midday. REUTERS

events.title: RBA interest rates: Bullock says ‘pain now’ will prevent worse later as Reserve Bank hikes rates for fifth time
events.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia increases official cash rate to 4.85%, bringing it to highest level since 2008 RBA interest rates live updates: Reserve Bank cash rate decision Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has said that “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track”, after lifting official interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85% in a bid to combat persistent inflation. The RBA’s decision to hit mortgage holders for a fifth time in 2026 will intensify pressure on indebted households, but there were signs that the central bank will at least now wait through summer to gauge the impact of higher interest rates on the economy. The decision split the monetary policy board, as six members voted for a hike, while three were in favour of a steady cash rate. Financial markets halved the probability of another rate rise before Christmas to 12%, but continued to price in a roughly 30% chance of a sixth hike by May. Speaking to journalists shortly after the rate decision, Bullock said: “I know this is not the news that many Australians want to hear, but it is what’s needed to get inflation down.” “Inflation is too high, and our forecast suggests it will stay higher for longer. Some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track,” she said. The back-to-back hikes will heap more pain on over 3.3m households with home loans and turn the screws on a federal government under pressure for its economic management. The latest rate rise will lift the monthly interest payment on a $700,000 home loan by $107, according to Canstar, bringing the total rise in repayments over this year’s five hikes to $532. Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, said higher fuel prices due to the Middle East conflict were the “primary driver” for the recent inflationary surge. “Our budgets are not what’s putting upward pressure on inflation. But we can play a helpful role and that’s what we intend to do,” Chalmers said. With surveys showing Australians are increasingly inclined to blame the Albanese government for ongoing high cost of living, Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, said voters “deserved to hear the truth”. “Labor’s spending spree is driving up inflation, it’s driving up interest rates, and Australians are paying the price,” Taylor said. The RBA’s post-meeting statement removed an explicit reference to the need for further hikes – an omission that economists at UBS interpreted as “clearly dovish”. And with the cash rate now at its highest level since 2008, Cherelle Murphy, the chief economist at EY, said the RBA “is likely to take a wait-and-see approach over summer”, even as she said higher interest rates could not be ruled out. The RBA’s latest set of forecasts in its Statement on Monetary Policy (SOMP) showed a difficult period ahead for the economy. The forecasts suggested the country’s cost of living crisis would extend for another year, even as Australia struggles with below trend economic growth and climbing unemployment. Inflation will push higher through the final months of 2026 to about 4.5% and only return below 3% – within the bank’s 2% to 3% target range – by the end of next year, or nine months later than hoped. Global oil prices would ease over the coming 18 months, but still remain relatively elevated, according to the forecasts, suggesting limited relief from high fuel costs for motorists and ongoing high costs for businesses. “We view the risks to the inflation outlook as still skewed to the upside,” the report said. Alongside persistent cost of living pressures, the RBA also predicted weak economic growth through to the end of 2028. The economy would grow by 1.6% this year and by 1.3% in 2027. That would be well below an estimated potential growth rate of about 2%, but better than recent forecasts by bank analysts. And despite the risks associated with a housing downturn that “is one of the steepest over the past 50 years”, the central banks’ economists saw no evidence that the country was headed towards recession over the coming two years. Unemployment, now at 4.7%, would end next year at about 4.9%, before creeping over 5% in 2028.

events.title: Adnoc’s XRG to buy Australian LNG stake for $1.5bn
events.summary: XRG , the international energy investment unit of Adnoc, has agreed to acquire Shell’s stake in an Australian natural gas project for $1.5 billion, as the company seeks to diversify its portfolio amid disruption to global energy markets caused by the Iran war. Abu Dhabi-based XRG will buy the stake in Australia's North West Shelf LNG project, marking its first investment in the country's gas sector and opening up greater access to customers in the Asia-Pacific region, the company said on Tuesday. The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, will give XRG access to one of the world's largest integrated LNG developments, with liquefaction capacity of 14.3 million tonnes per year and 4.4 trillion cubic feet equivalent of remaining resources. XRG has been actively increasing its portfolio of investments globally and plans to double its asset value over the next decade. Launched in 2024 as an international lower-carbon energy and chemicals investment company, with an enterprise value exceeding $80 billion, it has acquired stakes in several global gas projects. The latest acquisition strengthens XRG's position in the Asia-Pacific region. The North West Shelf project has been operating for more than four decades and plays a key role in the country's domestic gas supply and energy exports. The asset has supported domestic energy supply, jobs, international trade, and Australia’s emergence as a leading global energy exporter, XRG said. “This investment advances XRG’s strategy to build a leading international gas business serving growing demand across Asia-Pacific. The North West Shelf combines immediate production, strategic infrastructure, and future upstream development opportunities, making it a strong fit with our long-term ambitions,” said Mohamed Al Aryani, president of international gas at XRG. “XRG understands the importance of balancing export success with local energy needs. We believe continued investment in the North West Shelf can help sustain domestic gas supply, support regional energy security, create jobs, and deliver lasting economic benefits for Australia.” XRG said the project offers a combination of existing production, strategic infrastructure and opportunities for future upstream development. The company, which is wholly owned by Adnoc , has an enterprise value of more than $150 billion and invests across natural gas, chemicals and energy solutions.

events.title: Aramco's profit rises as refining margins strengthen amid Iran war
events.summary: Aramco reported a 9% rise in third-quarter adjusted net income to $31.2 billion, exceeding analyst expectations. The oil giant's downstream business posted a 234% jump in adjusted earnings, driven by stronger refining margins. The company declared a $21.9 billion base dividend for the quarter, up 3.5% from a year earlier. Aramco reported a 9% rise in third-quarter adjusted net income on Tuesday on stronger refining margins. The Saudi oil giant posted adjusted net income of $31.2 billion for the quarter, up from $28.6 billion a year earlier. The figure exceeded the median analyst consensus estimate of $30.66 billion, according to the company. Aramco's downstream business, which processes crude oil into fuels and other products, posted adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of $10.3 billion, up 234% from a year earlier, driven by stronger refining margins. "Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security," Aramco CEO Amin H. Nasser said in a statement. Nasser said the company's operational flexibility and supply network enabled it to continue delivering energy to customers despite the disruptions. Aramco is also exploring additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to strengthen its global supply network. The company generated $28.2 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, up from $23.6 billion a year earlier. Aramco said its board declared a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, up 3.5% year on year, to be paid in the fourth quarter. The company also said its major upstream projects remained on track and highlighted its acquisition of a 49% stake in Saudi artificial intelligence company HUMAIN. – CNBC's Emma Graham contributed to this story.

events.title: Car slams through supermarket wall 'like a sonic boom'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supermarket owner's lucky escape after car slams through store wall Topic: Road Accidents and Incidents A supermarket owner says he is a "very lucky man" after a car reversed through his store on Sunday afternoon. Marc Schirripa was checking stock at the supermarket in Adelaide's west when the car slammed through a wall, sending shelves flying in the aisle where he was standing. Police say a 31-year-old woman has been fined for reversing "further than necessary". A worker at a supermarket in Adelaide's western suburbs has had a narrow escape after a car reversed through the building. Emergency services were called to the Woodville IGA supermarket on Port Road about 1:30pm on Sunday. The store's owner Marc Schirripa told 891 ABC Adelaide he was checking stock when the car ploughed through the wall of the store, sending shelving and packages flying. The car left a hole in the side of the building. ( Supplied: SA Police ) "It felt like a big wave shooting up behind me, hitting me from behind, pushing me up against the shelves," Mr Schirripa said. "It was like a sonic boom just flashing behind me. "A car reversed through the wall quite fast, smashed into the wall and blew everything on top of me." CCTV from inside the store captured the moment of impact in the aisle that included snacks and confectionery. Marc Schirripa was standing in one of the aisles when the car crashed into the store. ( 891 ABC Adelaide: Troy Sincock ) Mr Schirripa was examined by paramedics at the scene. Police said the driver, a 31-year-old woman, and her passenger were not injured. "She was a little bit shook up, and I'm OK," Mr Schirripa said. The aftermath of the crash. events.title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is rolling out into beta testing on Tuesday, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. The news was announced via a press release sent out via Apple in India, but the update has not yet rolled out in the U.S. market as of this morning. The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist. However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps. Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them. With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation. Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things. When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said. These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them. The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations. Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information. Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone. This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features. At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days. This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning, too. Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.

events.title: Aged over 50, experienced and looking for work. Will employers bite?
events.summary: Even as older workers are encouraged to remain in the workforce for longer, the question is whether employers are willing to hire them. Singapore will raise retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70 from Jan 1, 2029, as the Government backs plans to help older workers stay in work. Older jobseekers like Raj Bharij, Gurmit Singh Kullar and Jason say they face instant rejections, overqualification fears and long job searches after retrenchment or resignation. Data shows weaker hiring for older workers: 42% in their 50s and 39% over 60 found jobs within six months, versus 61% in their 40s; employers may still value contract roles and transferable skills. SINGAPORE – Raj Bharij lost his job in 2026 when his employer, a global bank, restructured. “I’m 50 years old,” he recalls thinking, when told of the retrenchment in April. “Is anyone going to actually hire me now?” Six months on and more than 100 applications later, the former transformation director is still searching for his next job. He has received “instant” rejections, within seconds, from some firms’ automated systems and radio silence from others. An artificial intelligence chatbot tasked with helping to refine his resume suggested he take five years off his age. Bharij and other mature job seekers whom The Straits Times spoke to believe that being older and more experienced has somehow made their job search harder. Their experiences highlight a question facing Singapore: Even as older workers are encouraged to remain in the workforce for longer, will employers be willing to hire them? Singapore will raise its retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70 from Jan 1, 2029 – one year ahead of an earlier target. This was announced on Oct 26, 2026, when the Government accepted recommendations from the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment aimed at helping older workers remain in meaningful employment for longer. The move comes as the Republic’s population ages . The share of workers aged 50 and above in the workforce grew from 34% in 2015 to 40% in 2025, and is expected to rise further, a report by the workgroup said. Gurmit Singh Kullar, 52, left his job as a marketing director in July 2024 after experiencing burnout. Re-entering the workforce after a six-month break has proven an uphill task. Many marketing roles these days, he found, merge what would previously have been three jobs into one, effectively denting the value of his past experience. He applied to more than 200 openings in less than two years. When he did not hear back from prospective employers, he widened his search to include more junior or mid-level roles that paid just half of what he had been earning. Still, they did not bite. Hiring managers sometimes commented he had too much experience. “Isn’t it better for you to have someone more qualified?” he wondered. He attended career counselling and a handful of courses to learn new skills, where he encountered other mature job seekers in a similar situation. “Have you heard this line from people, that you’re overqualified?” he was asked by a man who had been retrenched from the insurance industry. Older workers are taking longer than others to find new work after losing their jobs, data from the Ministry of Manpower shows. In the second quarter of 2026, 42% of people in their 50s and 39% of those over 60 found new jobs six months after a layoff, compared with 61% for those in their 40s. A study by researchers, including Lee Zeewan from the National University of Singapore, found that 47% of employers surveyed were likely to hire workers in their 50s, compared with 35% who were neutral and 18% who were unlikely to do so. That number fell to 33% for workers aged 60 and above, they said, in a paper published earlier in 2026. Kirsty Poltock, a country manager for Singapore at recruitment firm Robert Walters, notes that the difficulties which older job seekers describe come as the market grows tougher for candidates in general, and firms’ hiring slows. She surmises that the labour market has become “less forgiving about a mismatch” between job seekers’ existing experience and the skills which firms are looking for, but believes there are still opportunities for workers in their 50s, having regularly placed such candidates in new roles. Contract work is one area that could play to senior workers’ strengths, she said, as more companies hire for non-permanent roles on a one- or two-year horizon as the economic outlook weakens. People who can articulate how their experience can help firms transform their human resources or finance operations, for instance, are seen as valuable hires, Poltock added. As their search for new work continues, Bharij and Gurmit are also having to deal with the emotional toll that being unemployed later in life brings, after having grown accustomed to the rhythm of work over decades. “The loss of identity is massive,” said Bharij, who used to describe himself as someone who worked at a bank.

events.title: Poundland staff could be out of work for years if retailer collapses, founder says
events.summary: Steve Smith calls on owners to accept proposed buyout as 12,000 staff face uncertain future in run-up to Christmas The founder of Poundland has warned that staff at the retailer could be out of work for “years” if it collapses, as he called on the owners of the troubled chain to accept a proposed buyout deal. Steve Smith, who set up the firm with a store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, said: “Once these jobs are lost, they are lost” from Britain’s struggling high streets. His warning comes as the chain’s 12,000 employees face uncertainty over their future in the run-up to Christmas. Poundland’s future hangs in the balance after the retailer, which is controlled by the US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until 12 November while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the likelihood of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers have held back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade . Poundland’s management is scheduled to meet Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, on Wednesday as political pressure mounts on Gordon Brothers to accept an offer from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group rather than calling in administrators to break up the retailer. The restructuring firm is understood to believe that it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer. Smith – who sold his final shares in Poundland for £250m in 2006 – said he was prepared to support that offer but Martin Property Group did not need his cash. “It was my baby,” he said, adding that he had put in an offer when Poundland was first put up for sale but had not heard back and it was too late to now launch his own bid. “If they have got offers on the table, why is Gordon Brothers not taking it and saving all these people? Retail is hard out there and if these people lose their job it could be a couple of years before they get jobs again. They work week to week and need their wages,” Smith said. “It is not just 12,000 jobs. Poundland has more than 2,000 suppliers, some only deal with Poundland and some employ hundreds of people.” He suggested that as many as 30,000 jobs could be at risk in Poundland’s supply chain, stores and at other affected businesses on high streets around the country. “Poundland brings in 4 million to 5 million customers every week to towns and shopping centres and retail neighbours are going to suffer as well,” Smith said. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Now it has been restructured and is turning a corner and starting to do well.” It is understood that talks continue about a potential deal under which Martin Property Group has offered about £7.5m up front and the same again in deferred payments over the next two years. That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood. This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, a former owner of Poundland that holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

events.title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
events.summary: Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge. Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used. Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin , NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own. From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough. In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries. In the San Francisco Bay Area , LiveX is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Nemotron open models, and Omniverse and Metropolis libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces. Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services. In Wrocław, Poland , K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions. In Malaysia , ITMAX bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence, to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%. Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making. At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance. In Taiwan , Linker Vision and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour. Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities. At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities. Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services. Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a keynote address followed by a panel moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA. events.title: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount
events.summary: Blackstone President Jon Gray said AI infrastructure investment will require more equity financing as debt investors face concentration risks. Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman warned that scale could strain markets, citing an estimate of about $10 trillion in capital expenditure over five years. Gray said demand for computing power was outpacing supply amid financing and infrastructure constraints. The artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout will need more equity financing as lenders become increasingly exposed to the companies driving the buildout, Blackstone President Jon Gray said Tuesday. Speaking at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit, Gray said the scale of capital required for AI is creating concentration risks for debt investors, both across the sector and at individual companies. Unlike shareholders, who can benefit from a company's growth, lenders have limited upside as their returns are largely confined to interest and principal repayments, he said. Speaking at the same panel, Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman warned investors that the scale of AI financing could prove to be "too much" for markets to absorb. Roman said AI-related capital spending could reach around $10 trillion over the next five years, citing General Atlantic CEO Bill Ford's estimate. He added that about $550 billion in AI debt had been issued in various forms so far this year. Even with a mix of equity and debt financing, the amount required would be “gigantic,” Roman said, comparing it with a global corporate bond market of roughly $20 trillion. “At some point in time, it’s going to be too much,” he said. Global data center demand will require about $8.5 trillion in capital spending over the next five years, Goldman Sachs wrote in a report Monday. Gray said financing the buildout would require a combination of public markets, banks and private capital, with companies increasingly turning to structured transactions to limit the amount of debt they take on. Cash generated by hyperscalers would also fund part of the spending, he said. “The creativity is needed because the scale of capital is enormous," Gray said. Despite those financing challenges, Gray remained bullish on AI infrastructure, saying demand for computing power was “running well ahead of supply.” Spending on AI models across Blackstone’s portfolio companies had risen 20-fold over the past year as businesses saw financial benefits from uses including coding, customer engagement and content creation, he said. Meeting that demand remains difficult, however, as securing sites, permits, chips, power and capital becomes more challenging, according to Gray.

events.title: Chalmers promises to be 'helpful' on inflation but rejects blame for rate hike
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government will play 'helpful role' on inflation but not at fault, Jim Chalmers says Jim Chalmers pointed to evidence that public sector demand was easing. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Jim Chalmers says the government's budget is "not what's putting upward pressure on inflation" after a fifth rate hike this year. The Reserve Bank made the widely expected move on rates. The government has promised fresh savings in the mid-year budget update next month. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has again denied his budget is the cause of persistent inflation, after the Reserve Bank raised interest rates for the fifth time this year. Facing political pressure over the level of government spending, the treasurer seized on the bank's assessment that public sector demand was "weaker than expected" in early 2026, the period when inflation began its resurgence. "Public demand growth has eased quite substantially at a time when private demand has tripled," he said. "Our budgets are not what's putting upward pressure on inflation, but we can play a helpful role and that's what we intend to do." RBA lifts interest rates to try to dampen inflation The RBA lifts interest rates to the highest level in 18 years in a majority decision by its board. Mr Chalmers has promised fresh savings in next month's mid-year budget update, but could not say whether the savings would be enough to outweigh new spending, a feat the Albanese government has not managed in any of the five years it has overseen. "We take responsibility for our part of the fight against inflation," he said. "We're helping with the cost of living at the same time as we manage the budget responsibly." Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock maintained her longstanding practice of avoiding direct comment on the government's budget, saying overall demand, combining public and private, remained too high across the economy. "It's up to the government, the elected officials, to decide what they want to do with the budget," she said. "Independence is a two-way street. I don't tell them what to do with fiscal policy. They don't tell me what to do with interest rates." Public demand eases, but question marks over role of NDIS Ms Bullock said the decision on rates, which was not unanimous, was motivated by the ongoing consequences of the Middle East and domestic factors. The main domestic driver, though not the sole one, has been artificial intelligence investment. The bank's updated forecasts predict business investment will grow by 12 per cent this year and public demand by just 2.1 per cent. The "weaker" public result was partly due to "the ending of some temporary cost-of-living measures", a staff note explained. Also cited was a "moderation" in spending on defence, disability and aged care. The largest single category of savings by far under the Albanese government has been to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), with $36 billion saved over four years in the May budget alone. But fresh doubts have been raised over whether that saving can be achieved, after the publication of preliminary findings from the Australian Government Actuary that the $36 billion figure was subject to "considerable uncertainty". Though cautioning that he did not have "sufficient detail" to draw a firm conclusion about the costings, actuary Guy Thorburn noted several risks, including an assumption of the numbers of children with autism entering the scheme not yet borne out by reality. The government has not been specific about where further savings will be found in the budget. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said she was "looking across government" for ways to cut back, but that these would be "difficult decisions". "We have to respond to the economic circumstances we face … [But] we're also mindful of the fact we need to support people through this as well," she said. "I hear a lot of calls for cuts to government spending, I don't hear as many specifics about where." Could government spending cuts fight inflation? The Reserve Bank is tipped to increase interest rates tomorrow because of an ongoing concern that inflation is not under control. But is there an alternative? Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the government had a "spending addiction" and was fuelling inflation. "[It] will never pull in its belt, but it keeps telling Australians to pull in theirs. It stokes inflation, taxes inflation and spends inflation," he said. While public demand is growing much slower than private demand in the Reserve Bank's forecasts, the bank does expect it to grow faster than the economy overall.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Models are commodities, harnesses are the valuable part A whopping 3% of boardroom execs spy productivity and costs savings from AI 6 days ago Alibaba's Qwen AI caught trying to contact server in China 7 days ago IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem 12 days ago Nvidia woos wary Europeans with more open weights models 12 days ago The AI math isn't mathing as infrastructure spending forecast to outstrip expected revenue 20 days ago For-profit model-makers, many of which are spending billions on AI infrastructure, will be chasing revenue from just ten percent of steps involved in agentic AI workflows, according to analyst firm Gartner. “Nine in 10 agent workflow steps are routine, and open-weight models handle them at parity for a quarter of the price of the cheapest closed model,” the firm’s senior director Mark Petty and group vice president Raymond Paquet wrote last week in new document titled “Open-Weight Models Will Run 90% of Enterprise Agentic Workflow Steps.” “Typical operational workflows involve hundreds of routine executions, such as classification, tool calling, passing, validating and reconciling data,” the pair observe, before suggesting open-weight models “can handle hundreds of these routine steps for every one that needs frontier reasoning.” “Against the cheapest closed model at the same score, the open model costs a quarter as much. Against a frontier model run on every step, it costs as little as a twentieth,” the pair add. Those are the best-case numbers, because the analysts admit “Current open models can be more verbose and retry more often, so the saving per task against a frontier model is closer to five or six times.” That’s still a lovely saving, but the analysts rate it as the welcome by-product of moving to open models rather than an end in itself. “Years of workflow history are a large part of what an acquirer pays for in a SaaS company and every routine step sent to a frontier API moves a slice of it outside your perimeter,” the pair wrote. “Open-weights preserve your control. The cost saving is a bonus.” The two analysts therefore offer the following strategic planning assumption: “By 2030, 90% of enterprise operational agent workflow steps will execute on open-weight models.” They argue that enterprises will mostly adopt domain-specific open-weight models, because they do well “in scenarios where a small number of highly stable steps run millions of times a month.” Most models, however, are already commodities. Harnesses, the tools that run agents and manage agents, are the source of value in AI products, because one of their roles is to route work to the most appropriate model for a job, without users noticing any impact. A good harness saves money, imposes strong guardrails, and manages agent fleets. Less powerful harnesses leave users with more to do. The paper suggests frontier models will continue to have a role as the engine of research and development and are effectively capital expense. events.title: Brittany Snow says she learned to have a different kind of relationship with her father after his Alzheimer’s diagnosis
events.summary: Brittany Snow said her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in 2020. Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images Brittany Snow said her father's Alzheimer's has brought a "prolonged grief." But it has also made her appreciate the small moments they still share. Their relationship has taken a different shape, she said, but they're still close. Brittany Snow , 40, says her father's Alzheimer's diagnosis taught her to appreciate the time they still have. On Monday's episode of " Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard ," Snow spoke about her relationship with her father, who was 48 when she was born. "My dad and I had an interesting relationship growing up, and then when I was doing the soap opera when I was 12, it really shifted for me, and we got really close," the "Guiding Light" actor said. "We were so close." Snow said her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in 2020, and his condition is "pretty extreme at this point." "I shouldn't refer to it as 'we were close' because we are close, but you know, it takes a different shape," Snow said of her current relationship with him. She said navigating her father's illness has brought a mix of emotions, from sadness and grief to gratitude for the time they have together. "I got six years that I wouldn't have had if he got cancer or something like that, and I got to really be present in those years because I knew it was happening," Snow said. "I really don't take that for granted." She said her father's condition has brought a form of "prolonged grief," but has also given her time to make sense of the loss instead of being hit by it all at once. "You're sort of mining all the stuff before," she said. Snow has opened up about her father's diagnosis in past interviews. In a 2024 appearance on the " Broad Ideas with Rachel Bilson & Olivia Allen " podcast, Snow said leaving after visiting her father is difficult because he didn't understand where she was going. She added that she has to remind herself that he would want her to continue living her own life too. "It's a baffling disease to witness, but it's really, really interesting and beautiful to get to see someone still there, but in a different version of themselves," Snow said. events.title: Victorian farmers blindsided by approval of 155-turbine wind farm ahead of election
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian farmers blindsided by wind farm approval on eve of election caretaker period A 155-turbine wind farm has been approved for Victoria's north. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) The Victorian government has approved the controversial Meering West Wind Farm, which could include up to 155 turbines, a day before entering caretaker mode. More than 100 objections had been lodged and neighbouring farmers say their concerns have been ignored. The project's future could hinge on the November 28 state election, with the Coalition pledging to scrap the VNI West transmission line the project intends to connect to. The Victorian government has signed off on a large wind and battery project for the state's north, on the eve of entering caretaker mode ahead of this month's state election. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny signed off on a planning permit for the Meering West Wind Farm on Monday, just a day before the caretaker period came into effect. The facility to be built at Meering West, about 140km north-west of Bendigo, would be one of Australia's largest, incorporating up to 155 wind turbines. Construction on the project, which would deliver 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity and 1,000 megawatt-hours of battery energy storage, is due to start in 2029. Like other similar facilities, it has been deeply controversial among local residents, with many farmers rallying against its approval. The timing of the approval is further complicated by the facility's intention to tap into the VNI West transmission line, which is yet to be built and would be scrapped if the Victorian Coalition came to government. Tyler Nelson is one of many neighbouring farmers who have objected to the project. He said he was not surprised the government had signed off on it at the last minute. "I'm very disappointed, but at the same time I can't say I'm shocked with the behaviour of the Labor government," he said. "It's well established that there are a lot of projects being rushed through at the 11th hour and there's been a pretty poor process involved for quite some time." Tyler Nelson is among the many farmers who oppose the Meering West wind farm. ( Supplied: Tyler Nelson ) Mr Nelson said he and other neighbours had been unaware of the project until it was well advanced. "Most neighbours and those affected found out pretty late in the piece, once there were contracts and caveats in place," he said. Mr Nelson said more than 100 people had objected to the project, with concerns including noise, shadow, flicker, land devaluation, fire risk and impacts on the natural environment. He said their objections and requests, including removing turbines from the project footprint close to objecting neighbours, had not been adopted. The wind farm at Meering West would have 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity. ( Supplied: Pixabay / JACLOU-DL / License /File ) Mr Nelson was reluctant to comment on the community divisions the project had created. "I've tried not to let it affect me, but it's difficult not to," he said. "Communities that usually stand together and talk, when that's taken away, it seems a bit odd." Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most. Given the Coalition has committed to scrap VNI West, Mr Nelson said he hoped there would be a change of government on November 28, but he was not convinced it would leave the Meering West project dead in the water. "It would be nice to think that is the case, but what we're learning is we never know what's happening with backroom deals," he said. "Yes, scrapping VNI West is a good move by the Coalition, but what does it mean for this project? "It's my understanding that [project proponent Virya] will continue to develop on somehow, but I don't know what that looks like." The Victorian government, Meering West Wind Farm representatives and developer Virya were contacted for comment.

events.title: Russia is hiding anti-Starlink jammers in parking lots and trailers on the front lines: Ukraine drone expert
events.summary: A Ukrainian soldier operates a GARA long-range drone. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images A top Ukrainian drone expert says Russia is deploying more jammers to counter Starshield. These Volna Kupol Garant systems beam interference at specific satellites as they pass overhead. They first emerged in 2024, but Russia said this August that it's begun serial production of the system. Russia is rolling out more trailer-mounted jammers designed to prevent Ukraine's attack drones from connecting to SpaceX's satellites , according to a top Ukrainian analyst. Each jammer can provide point defense covering about 25 square kilometers, or about 9.6 square miles, said Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential advisor on drones. "Russia has covered nearly all important sites in Crimea with this type of EW and is increasingly deploying it along the front line," Beskrestnov wrote on Monday on his Telegram channel. He said the Kremlin was deploying the systems to counter Ukraine's use of Starlink over Russian-held territory. Ukraine's forces rely on the military version of the SpaceX service, Starshield, for strike and deep-recon missions. Starshield, as well as onboard artificial intelligence, has been crucial to helping Ukraine control mid-range attack drones and receive intel from recon drones flying behind Russian lines. Beskrestnov advised Ukrainian drone pilots to look out for truck or trailer parking lots as an "ideal place" for Russia to conceal its jammers. "Of dozens of trucks, three to six may have the system installed. Also watch for small trailers attached to passenger cars," he wrote. "The complex can even operate from generators," Beskrestnov added, saying that Ukrainian drone teams could look for polycarbonate panels, plastic sheeting, or greenhouses that can obscure the jammer. The system mentioned is the Volna Kupol Garant, which targets the satellite instead of the drone or ground terminal. It uses dish antennas to beam powerful radio interference at individual low-Earth-orbit satellites, aiming to create a local bubble in which satellite links such as Starlink struggle or fail to work as they pass overhead, per ODIN, the US Army's public database. Ukraine reported Russia's first use of the system in Kharkiv in 2024, but it's been deployed in greater numbers since the start of this year, as Starshield has increasingly allowed Ukraine to strike deeper into Russian-held territory with drones. In August, the Russian state media outlet TASS reported that serial production of the Volna Kupol Garant was underway to build more countermeasures. One jammer system typically consists of six trailers, each with two antennas. Ukrainian forces attacking jamming sites previously uploaded drone footage showing these trailers sitting neatly in two rows. But Beskrestnov said on Monday that Russia had recently developed versions that use only one antenna per trailer and was learning to spread them out and conceal them. Still, analysts believe one jamming system can target only a single low Earth orbit satellite at a time. Open-source trackers estimate that Starshield, which is owned and operated by the US, uses a constellation of at least 240 satellites. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Hope for house hunters amid slump as realtor warns optimism premature
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Perth property price slump provides glimmer of hope for homebuyers Vanessa Bray says a drop in Perth house prices has given her hope of finding a home for her family. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) Home buyers are hopeful a drop in Perth property prices will help them break into the market. New data shows the city's median dwelling value has fallen to $942,018, but that is still 68 per cent higher than it was five years ago. A Perth realtor warns the optimism of those trying to buy a home may be premature, saying the figures do not represent the true state of the housing market. After years of searching for a home as Perth property prices continued to rise at an unprecedented rate, Vanessa Bray finally feels like she has a fighting chance of securing one. The single mum has been buoyed by new figures showing Australia is tracking towards its biggest housing market downturn in 40 years, with Perth's house prices dropping 5.7 per cent over the last three months. Data from property research group Cotality shows Perth's median dwelling price has fallen to $942,018 — a drop of nearly $100,000 since peaking at more than $1 million in April. Meanwhile, economists at the Commonwealth Bank today released an updated forecast predicting Perth property prices would plummet 18 per cent from that April peak, before prices begin to stabilise in the second half of 2027. For Ms Bray, the easing market spells hope of finding a home for her and her sons. Vanessa Bray is feeling a lot more positive about buying a home in light of recent data. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "I can't even begin to describe the relief that I feel for myself and my kids that we could maybe have a home of our own," she said. "It's close. I feel like it will happen instead of the despair that I had that it was never going to happen." National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality. Ms Bray has been looking for a family home since she and her partner separated four years ago. She needs to find something in their school catchment while staying under the $850,000 cap needed to qualify for the federal government's Help to Buy Scheme. Ms Bray said her experience of trying to buy a home had been '"devastating" and like being on a "rollercoaster". "[I've gone from] thinking, 'right, this could finally be it. I'm going to make it. I'm going to have long-term security for me and my kids' to the devastation of 'I've missed out again'," she said. Perth's median dwelling price has fallen by almost $100,000 in six months. ( ABC News: Gian De Poloni ) While the recent slump in prices represents a glimmer of hope for those trying to break into the market, the softening represents a small dent in the meteoric rise in Perth's property prices, which have risen 93 per cent in a decade, including 68 per cent in the last five years. Perth realtor Kyle Peters warned the optimism of those trying to enter the market could be premature. Mr Peters said the recent figures were not a good representation of the true state of Australia's housing market. "It would be an interesting anomaly that a housing market would crash when we have a housing crisis and don't have enough houses for people to live in," Mr Peters said. "At the rate things were ramping up before, there needed to be some abatement, but certainly we [still] have a housing shortage." REIWA president Rob Mandanici said even if prices did not continue to fall on the same trajectory, the slowing market still provided benefits for those entering the market. REIWA President Rob Mandanici says the easing should give buyers some breathing space. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "They can take a little bit more time to make that purchasing decision and not feel that immense pressure to rush into a decision," he said. "The buyers themselves haven't disappeared, they've become more selective." House prices are falling all around the country. ( ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes ) Mr Mandanici said there was no doubt Australia was experiencing "a little bit of a market slowdown", but said the dip in prices did not amount to a crash. "We are seeing some prices across multiple Perth suburbs pull back, but a lot of those suburbs are coming off highs," he said. "We've got a lot of buyers sitting on the sidelines and I think today's interest rate decision will just give buyers the certainty that they want moving forward." On Tuesday the Reserve Bank increased interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, lifting the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, the highest it has been since 2008.
