events.title: Aramco posts 34% jump in third-quarter profit despite attacks on energy infrastructure
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's Aramco , the world's largest oil-producing company, has reported a 34 per cent annual increase in its third-quarter net income despite disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure in the kingdom. Net profit for the three months to the end of September rose to 135.94 billion Saudi riyals ($36.25 billion), up from 101 billion riyals for the same period last year, Aramco said on Tuesday in a statement to the Tadawul stock exchange, where its shares are traded. “Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security,” Aramco president and chief executive Amin Nasser said. “Despite challenges, the flexibility of our system and the strength of a supply network built over decades enabled us to continue delivering reliably to our customers through this extraordinary period.” Aramco's board approved a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, a 3.5 per cent year-on-year increase, which will be paid in the fourth quarter of this year. Revenue boost The annual quarterly increase was driven by higher revenue despite volatile global energy markets, where prices shifted according to geopolitical headlines. Total revenue for the reporting period rose to $140.5 billion, up from $111.6 billion recorded for the third quarter of 2025. “The increase in revenue was predominantly driven by higher prices of refined and chemical products and crude oil, partially offset by lower volumes sold of crude oil and refined and chemical products,” Aramco said. The company's increased quarterly income provides a boost for Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s biggest economy, which still relies heavily on the sale of hydrocarbons for revenue. Aramco, Opec’s biggest oil producer and the main driver of Saudi Arabia's industrial sector, has faced waves of missile and drone attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militants that have put pressure on government revenue. In October, a Houthi missile attack damaged Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran. The attack caused a fire in an administrative building in the complex. Several crude refining facilities, including those in Jazan in the west and Riyadh, have also been attacked in recent weeks, raising fresh concerns about Saudi Arabia’s energy industry and Aramco’s ability to continue supplying crude oil to its global clientele. The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks on vessels rose in October to the highest level since the US Iran-war began on February 28, is adding to oil exporters’ woes. Overseas storage To avoid Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has ramped up crude shipments from its main export hub at Ras Tanura. The kingdom has relied on its East-West pipeline to pump crude to its Red Sea port. However, the pipeline was temporarily shut down after missiles launched from Iraqi territory damaged a pumping station. Saudi Arabia, which is also facing a Houthi-enforced maritime blockade, is exploring more routes to keep servicing its customers in Asia. “We continue to explore additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to further strengthen our global supply network,” Mr Nasser said. While the East-West pipeline provides export flexibility, the company remains focused on operations and will continue to invest in projects, Aramco said. Production started at the company's Zuluf crude oil increment project in October. Major upstream projects, including Jafurah phase two, the Fadhili Gas Plant expansion, and the Dammam development project, remain on track, the company said. Aramco's capital expenditure of $10.5 billion in the third quarter is, however, lower than the $12.6 billion reported for the same period in 2025. “Backed by our strong balance sheet, we remain focused on the disciplined execution of priority projects … to unlock new opportunities,” Mr Nasser said. “This is how we will continue to meet the world’s evolving energy needs and deliver value for our shareholders and customers.”

events.title: Adnoc Gas to supply TotalEnergies with up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG in five-year deal
events.summary: Adnoc Gas has signed a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to France's TotalEnergies, as the Abu Dhabi company expands its share of the global LNG market. The deal builds on a long-standing partnership between the two companies and reflects growing demand for LNG and confidence in Adnoc’s ability to deliver reliable supplies, the company said on Tuesday. “ Global demand for LNG continues to grow, and Adnoc Gas is well-positioned to capture that opportunity,” said Fatema Al Nuaimi, chief executive of Adnoc Gas. “This agreement reflects the strength of our LNG business, the competitiveness of our supply offering and our ability to secure long-term partnerships that support growth, enhance resilience and create lasting value for shareholders.” Adnoc Gas has continued to execute its long-term growth strategy this year, despite operational constraints. The company awarded $8.2 billion in engineering, procurement and construction contracts, part of its largest capital investment, for the second and third phases of the Rich Gas Development project – $3.9 billion for Phase 2, and $4.3 billion for Phase 3, the company said in August. These contracts build on Phase 1, announced in June 2025. The Rich Gas Development is a multi-phase, $13.2 billion capital investment programme by Adnoc Gas to expand gas processing and liquid recovery infrastructure across the UAE. The latest move strengthens Adnoc Gas’s commercial position at a time when demand for LNG is rising across Europe and Asia. Asia remains the main destination for LNG, accounting for about 65 per cent of global imports in 2025, while Europe has become a major buyer as it replaces Russian pipeline gas and manages storage needs, according to the International Energy Agency’s latest gas market report. “Thanks to its perfect location between Europe and Asia, this new supply will enable TotalEnergies to confirm its position as one of the main LNG portfolio suppliers,” said Stephane Michel, president of gas, renewables and power at TotalEnergies. TotalEnergies is both a shareholder in Adnoc Gas and a partner in the Ruwais LNG project. Adnoc Gas said it expects the planned integration of the Ruwais LNG project to significantly increase its production capacity, supporting its ambition to become one of the world’s leading LNG suppliers. The agreement between Adnoc Gas and TotalEnergies comes as Adnoc scales up a new global LNG marketing and trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the trading capabilities of Adnoc Trading . The platform is aiming to reach 47 million tonnes per annum of marketable LNG beyond 2030, a level intended to place it among the world’s leading LNG marketing and trading businesses, Adnoc Gas said on Tuesday. Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs and supplies end-customers in more than 20 countries.

( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Journalist Kate McClymont has given evidence in the Alan Jones trial where she was questioned about whether her reporting on Mr Jones was profit-driven. Ms McClymont spoke with three of the five complainants in the trial for stories published in late 2023 and early 2024. Mr Jones's team has also accused her of "introducing" the words "go the grope" in her interview with one complainant. The journalist whose work sparked a police investigation into broadcaster Alan Jones has been questioned about whether she had a "profit motive" to run a series of stories about the former 2GB radio host allegedly indecently assaulting young men. Kate McClymont gave evidence on day 55 of Mr Jones's criminal trial at the NSW Local Court, where he has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. NSW Sexual Violence Helpline on 1800 424 017 NSW Victims Services on 1800 633 063 Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831 Child Protection Helpline on 132 111 MARS Australia (for men affected by rape and sexual abuse) on (07) 3857 1222 National Survivors Foundation on 1300 124 433 Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. The court has heard Ms McClymont, who is a multiple Walkley Award-winning journalist and the Sydney Morning Herald's chief investigative reporter, spoke to three of the five complainants in the trial for stories published in late 2023 and early 2024. The defence has sought to poke holes in Ms McClymont's original reporting of the allegations against Mr Jones, some of which have since been explored during days of evidence in his criminal trial. Mr Jones's team has also accused the journalist of "introducing" the words "go the grope" in her interview with one complainant, and has suggested her reporting influenced the allegations other complainants made later. Mr Jones's barrister started her cross-examination of the reporter on Tuesday. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC probed Ms McClymont about why she wrote the stories, suggesting to her that there was a "profit motive" in writing articles about a high-profile person. "The story has to sell papers, doesn't it?" Ms Bashir asked. "That's not my problem," Ms McClymont replied. "It is correct to say that higher readership numbers encourage advertisers to invest in advertising with the paper?" Ms Bashir asked. "As a general proposition, yes, but that is not my role." Ms McClymont agreed Mr Jones was viewed "by some people" as "conservative leaning". "Alan Jones is a very public figure in New South Wales? He's a divisive figure?" Ms Bashir proposed. "If you say so," Ms McClymont replied. The journalist was also asked whether any money or benefit was paid to any alleged victim of Mr Jones in exchange for their stories, which she denied. Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching relating to five men. ( ABC News: Abbey Haberecht ) Ms McClymont confirmed she spoke to and published the allegations of three of the complainants in this criminal trial. She said she had no contact with two other complainants, the high-profile athlete known as Complainant M and a former up-and-coming athlete known as Complainant J. Mr Jones's lawyers have argued throughout the trial that Ms McClymont is on one side of a media rivalry which was set on "destroying" Mr Jones. Ms McClymont can be heard asking the man. "He'd go the grope," Complainant C said in reply. That phrase became part of the headline of Ms McClymont's first article about Mr Jones, which was published in December 2023. Under questioning, the journalist agreed she "introduced" the words but said her interview subject repeated them, so she used them. "You used those words and then he repeated them?" Ms Bashir asked. events.title: Taiwan’s AI stock boom is making early-stage startups a harder sell
events.summary: Taiwan's stock market has surged this year as investors chase the country's broad AI supply chain. I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty Images Taiwan's stock market has surged as investors pile into companies powering the global AI buildout. The rally is giving local investors a liquid alternative to early-stage startup bets. For early-stage founders, that can mean looking abroad for capital. Taiwan’s AI stock boom is creating more ways for investors to profit from its chip supply chain, making early-stage startups a tougher pitch. Taiwan’s benchmark Taiex index is up more than 50% this year, making it the world’s best-performing major index after pulling ahead of South Korea’s Kospi. The gains extend well beyond Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., spanning chip design, advanced packaging, networking, and server companies. About 7% of Taiwan-listed stocks have doubled this year, compared with 3% in South Korea. That wider exposure has made Taiwan a preferred Asian AI trade. A September Bank of America survey found that 35% of fund managers expected Taiwan to benefit most from the next phase of the AI cycle, tying it with the US. Just 5% chose South Korea. For startups, the appeal of those public-market returns can reshape the funding calculation. For Anderson Chen, the founder and CEO of Operon Solutions, a Y Combinator-backed industrial AI startup, that calculus was part of what shaped how he raised money. Chen said he chose to raise Operon’s $700,000 pre-seed primarily from Silicon Valley investors, leaving room for Taiwanese friends and family to participate. “The market in semiconductors is just too good, and you can get 10X returns from the stock market,” Chen told Business Insider. In his view, even a successful startup IPO might generate only a two- or threefold return for investors. The hunt for a first check That creates a challenge for startups trying to build Taiwan’s next generation of winners. Caleb Chu, an early-stage investor and founder of Taiwan-based Nova Studio, which backs young founders, told Business Insider that the stock rally had drawn many Taiwanese investors toward listed shares and away from venture capital and startups. Findit, a government-commissioned platform that tracks Taiwan's startup ecosystem, found that seed and angel rounds made up 38.4% of investment deals by Taiwanese VC firms in 2021. By 2024, their share had fallen to 17.1%. By contrast, B- and C-round deals accounted for 39 deals, or 29.1% of the total, in 2024. Chu said Taiwanese investors had increasingly favored B- and C-round and pre-IPO companies, where the route to returns was clearer. Private-equity funds face a related, though not identical, pressure. A March report by KPMG Taiwan said TSMC’s share-price strength had created a “crowding-out effect” for private funds, as investors favored liquid public AI stocks over funds with longer lockups and less certain exits. US venture data shows a different, if still uneven, mix. PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association said early-stage dealmaking was more favorable for AI startups than for non-AI peers in the first quarter of 2026. In a separate report, they found that 87.5% of US venture dollars invested in the first half went to rounds of $100 million or more. “When you look at the statistics around the world, the world is leaning toward early stage because investors realize it can generate much higher returns. Taiwan is the opposite,” Chu said. For founders, that can mean looking abroad for early backing. Operon's Chen said fundraising had become easier overall for Taiwanese deep-tech startups seeking overseas capital, helped by Taiwan’s technical talent and semiconductor expertise. His startup's $700,000 pre-seed round closed within three days. “It's gotten easier to fundraise in general, but maybe not necessarily in Taiwan,” he said. events.title: UK job satisfaction at record low amid rising frustration over pay and flexible working
events.summary: Resolution Foundation study finds workers are less willing to go ‘above and beyond for employers than a decade ago’ Job satisfaction among UK workers has dropped to a record low, according to a study that shows a growing frustration with employers over pay and flexible working. Analysis by the Resolution Foundation thinktank shows that a lack of flexible working, insecure jobs and a loss of independence have undermined how workers feel about their employment. Based on the 2025 British Social Attitudes survey, the study found a sharp fall in satisfaction at work that translated into British workers being less willing to go “above and beyond for their employers than they were a decade ago”. Job satisfaction fell from 81% in 2015 to 74%, the lowest figure recorded in the British Social Attitudes survey since 1989, when the question was first asked. Fewer workers said they had an interesting job or one that offered the chance of advancement. The proportion of workers who said they would work harder than required to help their employer succeed fell from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025. The Resolution Foundation said its analysis would give policymakers an insight into how they could reverse decades of slowing productivity growth, low levels of job mobility and high economic inactivity among some groups, most notably younger people . Only 4% of workers said there was “little intrinsic value” from working – a figure that has remained flat over time. What has declined, the thinktank said, was the number of people feeling positive about the jobs they do. The proportion saying they have an interesting job fell over the decade from 74% to 63%. Hannah Slaughter, an economist at the foundation and co-author of the report, said there was a rise in the number of workers who said they suffered from low pay and this concern spanned all the pay scales. She said decades of low pay-rises and the spiralling cost of living was affecting the outlook of all groups, though the demand for greater flexibility was equally pronounced. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Workers increasingly want jobs that provide flexibility, independence and financial security. But many feel those expectations are not being met,” said Slaughter. “The result is rising frustration among workers, who report lower job satisfaction, declining willingness to go above and beyond, and a reduced appetite for full-time work. This ‘dissatisfaction drain’ is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn’t bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead.” Separate polling by Ipsos dating back to the 1980s supported the foundation’s study, with workers reporting much lower satisfaction this year than when the same question was asked in 1976 and 1986. In 1976 it found 83% were very or fairly satisfied with their work compared with 69% in 2026. John Curtice, the Strathclyde professor and pollster who is co-editor of the British Social Attitudes report, said the findings showed young people had not become more work-shy, “nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs. But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financial rewarding and have flexible work hours.”

events.title: ‘It brings soul into this sterile world’: the Birmingham clubbers fighting to save their patch – and Britain’s nightlife
events.summary: Digbeth is the city’s most thriving party district, but railway upgrades could tear it apart. Here, clubbers explain why they are doing everything to stop that happening H ouse beats ring out through the open air while a heaving crowd of young partygoers dance. Suddenly, they begin to chant: “Richard Parker, Richard Parker!” You might think he is the next DJ on the set list, but in fact he is the mayor of the West Midlands and this block party has been assembled to send him a message: leave Digbeth alone. It’s Sunday night and I’m in Birmingham’s trendy party district. It’s filled with bars, warehouse clubs and storied music venues. The 1,800-strong crowd of mostly twentysomethings at the Parker event fits right in. But buzzy scenes like this may soon be a thing of the past. Under plans proposed by the Midlands Rail Hub Alliance – including Network Rail, which owns and manages railway infrastructure in Great Britain – seven nightclubs, including XOYO Birmingham, Mama Roux’s and Club Colette, could be demolished from 2030. The aim is to expand a nearby viaduct, allowing more trains to run through Moor Street station rather than the more congested New Street, but striking a blow to the city’s nightlife. Ravers want Parker, who leads the region’s strategic transport agenda, to use his power to lobby against these plans. The proposal comes at a testing time for the industry. More than 26% of all late-night venues across the UK closed for good between 2020 and 2025, according to the Night Time Industries Association . Birmingham has been hit harder than any other major city, experiencing a 28% drop in the number of bars, clubs and other establishments where you might grab a late-night drink. But Digbeth, a former industrial centre where metal sheets, Typhoo Tea and Bird’s Custard were once manufactured, has stood strong as the city’s cultural bright spot – far cooler than Broad Street, Birmingham’s main clubbing strip, which has the vibe of a street-long All Bar One. It’s where some of the names now headlining electronic music festivals around the world caught the raving bug. The Birmingham DJ Fleur Shore, 30, has been coming to Digbeth since she was 15. “Here is where it all started for me,” she says from behind her decks. “Without Digbeth, I wouldn’t be where I am now. I get to go all over the world and do my job.” Shore has played gigs in the Argentinian countryside, the historic Plaza de España in Seville, Spain, and the mountains of Gran Canaria. But the UK has not always made it easy. “The UK is so strict,” she says. “They don’t embrace this part of people.” The Parker party is a way for young ravers to revolt, she says: “This country doesn’t value younger people who want to go out, let loose and socialise. When everybody’s all together, dancing to the same thing, it’s powerful.” The mooted demolition of Digbeth’s bars and clubs is just one example of the threats to British nightlife. In central London, a bitter battle is playing out between venues and the Soho Society, a community group aimed at “preserving the character of Soho”, which routinely objects to new bar and restaurant licences, often backed by Westminster council. Venues say the restrictions could “destroy Soho’s reputation on the international stage”, while the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, has criticised the council’s “breathtaking arrogance” . In Manchester, meanwhile, the famed music venue Night & Day cafe was threatened with closure after noise complaints from neighbours in new flats. After a three-year row, it was told to limit noise in the small hours. There is no doubt that noise can be a nuisance, but it is hard to understand how anyone who moves next to a decades-old venue in an area known for nightlife can claim to be shocked by it. The value of a good night out is being forgotten, says Shore: “There’s so much pressure in life. People come to these places to breathe, dance and not think about their problems. I feel like, the way things are going, we’re going to be a soulless nation.” Lina and Johnny, who are part of the crowd making its way down the Digbeth strip, agree. “People from all walks of life come together here to move our bodies and exist in harmony,” says Johnny, 24. “If this street is demolished, that will be a lot harder to do.” Lina, who is also 24 and a musician, says she has met “so many other beautiful, talented people” in the area. “Where would all these creative people go? It brings soul into this sterile world,” she says. Among a group who met only hours earlier are Hood Ssengendo and Daniel Wright. “The fact they want to demolish this whole thing is pointless,” says Wright, a 24-year-old music producer. “There is still a club scene, ravers and people that want to have a good time.” Ssengendo, a 25-year-old welder, says: “For most young people, this is their hotspot for a night out and to make friends.” For many marginalised communities, the district remains a safe haven for a night out.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Anthropic BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters OpenVDDK is reportedly already being used in production, at scale Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge 2 hours ago SUSE to cut one in ten employees because of... AI 22 hours ago 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50 2 days ago AlpineBSD announced – an AI-free FOSS OS 3 days ago Howler will have AI answer your questions, then burn the chat 4 days ago A cloud architect has created an open source alternative to VMware’s Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK), which the virtualization giant recently withdrew from public downloads. VMware describes VDDK as “a set of libraries and utilities that enable software developers to create applications that can access and manipulate virtual disks” and “a valuable tool for developers of storage and backup applications.” Users, along with VMware’s rivals, had another use for VDDK: migrating VMs to alternative virtualization platforms. In August, VMware restricted access to VDDK downloads to its partners, meaning VMware customers couldn’t access the tool and some of its rivals’ migration tools became less effective. Cloud architect Andrija Panić decided to do something about it. “Many tools that have nothing in common except VMware use the same small library to read a virtual machine’s disks: virt-v2v and nbdkit, the importers in Forklift/MTV, Proxmox VE and Apache CloudStack, and countless in-house scripts,” he told The Register by email. “When public VDDK downloads ended, all of them became harder to install and run.” “I didn’t think it was fair that people’s ability to move or protect their own data should depend on a download page.” He describes the project as “an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.” Panić told The Register he wrote the tool in Go, with a thin C layer that exposes exactly the same C interface, library name and symbol versions as VMware’s code. The tool cannot write disks, just read them for backup and migration purposes. In his email to The Register , Panić said he has successfully tested OpenVDDK on vSphere versions 6.7 U3, 7.0.3, 8.0.3, 9.1.1. He said that tests in his lab with the latter version, accessing OpenVDDK through vCenter on a standalone ESXi host, saw every disk read match. “Independent testers have reported successful use with Forklift (VMware to KubeVirt, cold and warm), MTV on OpenShift (cold and warm), a Proxmox VE pipeline and custom nbdkit-based tools,” the architect told The Register . “I've received reports of production use, including a German cloud provider migrating a large file server with V2K Migrate and a US-based company migrating to Apache CloudStack/KVM.” Panić was at pains to point out that the reports of successful use are “not independently audited customer endorsements or a guarantee of suitability for every production environment.” As is often the case with FOSS tools. OpenVDDK is not the only option for migrating away from VMware without VDDK. KVM-based OpenNebula has a tool called OneSwap that it says has a 96 percent success rate. Nutanix recently tweaked its “Move” migration tool so it can do the job without VDDK. Red Hat is working on a fix but has provided details of a workaround . Panić made OpenVDDK available under an Apache license, so perhaps Red Hat and others will find it useful as they re-jig their VM migration tools.

events.title: China to raise FX reserve requirement to slow yuan’s rally
events.summary: The People’s Bank of China said it would raise the foreign exchange reserve requirement ratio by 2 percentage points to 6% from 4%, effective on Nov 15. China’s central bank will raise the FX reserve requirement ratio to 6% from 4% on Nov 15 to slow the yuan’s strong rally and absorb US dollar liquidity. The move may remove about US$24 billion from the system and sent the onshore yuan down 0.37% to 6.6728 per dollar, its sharpest daily fall in six months. Markets see the step as mainly symbolic. The yuan has still risen more than 5% in 2026, backed by exports, trade surpluses and corporate FX sales. BEIJING - China is raising the amount of foreign currency that financial institutions must hold as reserves, in one of the strongest moves to slow the pace of a long rally in the yuan, setting the currency on course for its sharpest one-day drop in six months. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) said in a statement on Nov 3 it would raise the foreign exchange (FX) reserve requirement ratio (RRR) by 2 percentage points to 6% from 4%, effective on Nov 15. The adjustment would result in an extra US$24 billion (S$30 billion) being withdrawn from the financial system, according to a Reuters calculation based on official FX deposit data. The decision to raise the ratio is “aimed at strengthening the management of foreign exchange liquidity in financial institutions”, the PBOC said. The onshore yuan weakened as much as 0.37% against the dollar to a low of 6.6728 per dollar, the weakest level since Oct 23, following the announcement. And it looked set for the biggest one-day drop since May 15. Its offshore counterpart also followed the weakening trend. “The PBOC is responding to strong market-driven yuan appreciation,” said Marco Sun, chief financial market analyst at MUFG (China). “By absorbing part of the available US dollar liquidity in the banking system, it is attempting to reduce the momentum behind yuan appreciation and prevent the market from developing excessive one-way expectations.” The yuan has gained more than 5% against the dollar so far in 2026, reaching its strongest level since 2022 and becoming one of Asia’s best-performing currencies. Its strength has been underpinned by robust exports, big trade surpluses and heavy corporate FX conversion. The FX RRR hike on Nov 3 would be a policy reversal of the PBOC’s decision in September 2023 to lower the FX RRR, which was a move to stem the yuan’s rapid losses and capital outflows. However, market participants do not expect the move to reverse the yuan’s upward trend. Xing Zhaopeng, senior China strategist at ANZ, said the move was likely to “carry greater symbolic significance” for the market. Corporates’ heavier FX settlement into yuan had “resulted in the current imbalance conditions of excess supply over demand”, Xing said. He added that the increase in the FX RRR would not be enough to ease the oversupply. Separately, the PBOC lowered its midpoint rate for a second day in a row on Nov 3 to 6.7150 per dollar, 661 pips weaker than a Reuters estimate - its largest weak-side deviation since Sept 10. The central bank has been gradually strengthening its daily yuan official guidance in 2026, but at levels weaker than market expectations, suggesting it is seeking to manage the pace of appreciation, market watchers said. Meanwhile, PBOC deputy governor Zou Lan reiterated the central bank’s stance on the currency. “China has promoted high-level opening-up and insisted that the market play a decisive role in the formation of the exchange rate,” he told a financial forum in Hong Kong on Nov 3. events.title: I lived in Shanghai in my 20s. Now, at 34, I'm back in China to start a business.
events.summary: After college, Alex Greenberg moved to Shanghai, then returned to the US. Now, at 34, he's giving life in China another try. Provided by Alex Greenberg After graduating from college, Alex Greenberg moved to Shanghai to teach skateboarding. He planned to stay for a year, but "the city felt so alive" that he stayed for five. After a few years back in the US, he returned to China last month to start a company in Chengdu. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alex Greenberg, an American founder living in Chengdu, China, who runs Observed Media, a creative studio. He is also the creator of the Instagram account @shanghaiobserved. His words have been edited for length and clarity. As graduation from college in Vermont approached, I had no idea what I wanted to do with my life. I'd studied abroad in Australia during my junior year and knew I loved traveling, but I drew a blank on what to do next. Then, in November of my senior year, I received an offer to teach skateboarding in Shanghai. It was my only job offer; I hadn't applied to much else. Teaching skateboarding in China wasn't exactly what I pictured doing with a college degree, but I figured it would make for an interesting gap year . I arrived in January 2015 speaking zero Chinese. More than a decade later, China has shaped my career. When he arrived in China, he spoke zero Chinese. Provided by Alex Greenberg Shanghai felt like a place where anything could happen Shanghai had become a magnet for street skaters, and most of my friends came through skateboarding and the video production world. It was one of the best social periods of my life. I remember constantly thinking, "What am I doing? This is wild." I'd chosen this completely unexpected life, and somehow it was working. After my one-year contract ended, I expected to go home. But by then, I'd built a network and a life in Shanghai . Leaving didn't make sense. I also had the safety net of teaching English. The US job market felt like a mystery to navigate, so I stayed. Not knowing what I wanted to do became an asset Career-wise, I was throwing everything at the wall. I started juggling English teaching and private skate lessons. At the same time, I started Shanghai Observed on Instagram as a daily photography project for fun. There wasn't some grand business plan behind it; I was just walking around Shanghai and documenting the city. In 2016, I got an internship at PUSH Media and eventually worked my way up to project manager. We produced campaigns and events for brands like Adidas, Vans, and The North Face. Have you relocated abroad — especially to Asia — for career opportunities, retirement, or lower living costs? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. Meanwhile, Shanghai Observed continued to grow alongside my career. Today, it has over 280,000 followers and gets millions of views a month, mostly from people outside China who are curious about everyday life. It's never been my primary source of income; it's always been more of a passion project. But it opened a lot of doors. A trip home unexpectedly turned into years away from China I flew to the US for Christmas in December 2019 and planned to return after Chinese New Year. Then COVID hit, and I couldn't get back. I spent about 15 months living with my parents in New York. After that, I went to Kauai to work on a pineapple farm. I was only supposed to be there for three months. China still hadn't reopened, so I stayed in Hawaii for two years. I converted a school bus into a tiny home on a friend's farm, worked as a drone pilot, and spent my free time surfing, playing poker and casual baseball games, and having dinner at friends' houses. Then, in 2023, I moved to San Diego for a remote brand manager role. I had built an entirely different life and career in the US, but China never really disappeared from either, and I continued running the Instagram account. He converted a school bus into a tiny home on a friend's farm in Hawaii. Provided by Alex Greenberg Moving back started making sense By the end of my time in California, I was paying $2,400 a month in rent, including utilities, for a small one-bedroom place in Encinitas. I loved living near the ocean, but I started thinking about what the same money could buy me elsewhere. I realized I could base myself in China again, build my own media business, and have considerably more money left over to travel. This September, I finally moved back — but instead of returning to Shanghai, I chose Chengdu, a major city in southwestern China. Despite not having lived there before, I had friends there, the creative scene seemed exciting, and it's a much more affordable place to build my business and study Chinese . Shanghai has more opportunity, but also more competition. Chengdu's pace feels slowe r. The city prides itself on tea houses, long dinners, and relaxing. There's a real emphasis on quality of life and comfort. Right now, I pay 3,000 Chinese yuan, or $420 a month, for a furnished studio on a month-to-month lease. A bowl of noodles costs around $2, and a coffee costs $1.50. Greenberg says he wants Shanghai Observed, his platform, to remain a window into the human side of China. Provided by Alex Greenberg I'm running a creative studio on my own I'm producing stories for brands and creators. Shanghai Observed was where I learned how to do it; Observed Media brings it all under one roof. The thread connecting everything I've done — from skateboarding and sharing day-to-day life content in Shanghai to my days in California — has been paying attention to culture and turning it into stories people want to watch. Shanghai Observed is still where I experiment. It's a mix of my own photography and footage, submissions from followers, and content I discover through WeChat groups . When I first moved to Shanghai at 22, I thought I was taking a one-year skateboarding job while I figured out what I wanted to do next. Instead, that spontaneous decision shaped my friendships, my career, the business I'm building, and the way I see the world. More than a decade later, I'm 34 and back in China, starting another chapter. And, strangely enough, I have that same feeling I had when I first arrived: What am I doing? This is wild. Only this time, I have a much better idea of what I'm doing here. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.  Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).  The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.  It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).  But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.  So one month in, who’s on board? Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period. There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.  The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents). As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.  But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too. In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.  But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.   Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia. But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.  In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.  Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too . One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order , leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month. But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.  People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change. If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. events.title: Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation
events.summary: The move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold. The central bank has also upgraded its inflation projectons, saying that inflation is not expected to reach its 2%-3% target range till late 2027. This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, but other factors including AI-related investment is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said. Australia's central bank raised its benchmark cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008. The Reserve Bank of Australia's move was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year. In its statement, the RBA said that the move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold. This also comes as the country continues to grapple with high inflation, with the consumer price index rising 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August and marking its highest level since March. The central bank also said inflation is now expected to "remain elevated through much of 2027," and not expected to fall back into its 2%-3% target range till late 2027, three quarters later than previously forecast. This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, in addition to factors including AI-related investment, which is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said. In its September decision, RBA governor Michelle Bullock said that inflation is "too high," driven by higher oil prices from the Iran War and stronger domestic spending. "We're seeing signs that upside risks to inflation are materializing," she added, saying that additional hikes will come "if that's what's needed to get inflation down." Growth has slowed in the first two quarters of 2026. Australia's GDP rose 2.1% in the June quarter compared to a year earlier, down from 2.5% in the March quarter. The RBA is trying to bring inflation back under control while higher borrowing costs and cost-of-living pressures weigh on households and activity. When asked if she sees a recession for Australia, Bullock said that it is "not our base case at the moment."

events.title: SATS redeploys staff to baggage handling amid MOM probe into contracted firms
events.summary: Some SATS employees have taken on extra responsibilities or been temporarily redeployed to help the ground handler keep its baggage-handling operations running. SINGAPORE – Ground handler SATS has temporarily redeployed some employees and assigned others additional responsibilities to keep its Changi Airport operations running smoothly, amid investigations into possible work pass violations involving workers employed by its contractors and sub-contractors . In an e-mail sent to all staff and seen by The Straits Times on Nov 3, SATS thanked its employees for helping out and supporting the company through the “operational adjustments required in recent weeks”. “Some employees have taken on additional responsibilities or been temporarily redeployed to help ensure our operations continue to run safely and smoothly. Your dedication, flexibility and professionalism have been instrumental in maintaining service to our customers, and we thank you for your support.” The e-mail addressed to SATS employees also outlined a broader context on actions the firm has taken to “enhance verification process controls” to make sure contractor workers are deployed according to their work passes. “We are rectifying compliance deficiencies in accordance with MOM’s (Ministry of Manpower) guidelines,” said the company spokesperson in the e-mail, urging employees to reach out to team leaders if they have any questions or want to clarify facts after reading media reports on the investigation. A SATS employee, who did not want to be named, said employees, including those from non-operations departments, were encouraged to step up on a voluntary basis to help with baggage-handling services, especially to fill slots for the upcoming Deepavali long weekend. ST understands that employees who volunteer for additional 2½-hour block duties will receive $15 in NTUC vouchers, time off in lieu and transport allowance. SATS said on Nov 3 that it is regular practice for the company to invite employees across the organisation to volunteer their support during peak travel periods, and that the request for volunteers did not come as a result of the probe. The request for volunteers can include customer service and premier services ambassadors, as well as support for baggage services, added the SATS spokesperson. Vouchers or time off in lieu will typically be provided as a gesture of appreciation. “This provides colleagues from non-operational functions with opportunities to gain first-hand experience of front-line operations, while supporting operational teams and enabling front-line employees to take well-deserved breaks.” Responding to queries from ST, a spokesperson for Changi Airport Group (CAG) said it is working closely with SATS’ management team to “minimise the impact of the manpower situation on airport operations”. “CAG expects SATS and other operators at Changi Airport to strengthen the oversight of companies they contract with and to ensure that these companies comply with applicable manpower laws and regulations.” MOM said in a media statement on Nov 2 that it has identified around 270 workers, employed by SATS’ contractors and sub-contractors, whose deployment may not have been in compliance with work pass regulations. The ministry said it found Employment Pass holders deployed to perform baggage-handling services during a recent inspection. SATS’ share price fell 3.01% after the market opened on Nov 3, with about four million shares worth about $14.2 million changing hands as at 10.40am. Sharon Salim is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, with a focus on jobs, workplace culture and trends.

events.title: Interest rates highest since 2008 as inflation forecast to stay high
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts RBA lifts interest rates to highest level in 18 years to try to dampen inflation The RBA's monetary policy board has increased interest rates for the fifth time in 2026. ( Reuters: Jason Reed ) The Reserve Bank's monetary policy board has lifted interest rates by 0.25 percentage points. The decision lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent. It is the highest cash rate since late 2008. It is the fifth interest rate increase in 2026, and the RBA has left the door open for more rate hikes. The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 18 years, while acknowledging it will take much longer to drag inflation down than it was expecting a few months ago. It has increased rates by 0.25 percentage points, which lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent. The cash rate has not been this high in Australia since late 2008. It is the fifth time the bank has lifted rates in 2026. The brutal redistribution at the heart of the RBA's interest rate policy RBA officials argue the hit to borrowers' income isn't the main way rate rises lower inflation. But they often omit a key fact. The RBA board's decision to lift rates was not unanimous. Six members voted to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent, while three members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.60 per cent. The majority decision will be another blow to households with mortgages. But individuals who have high-interest savings accounts will see their savings accruing more interest after today's decision, if their bank applies higher rates to their accounts. In a statement , the RBA board said inflation was now forecast to remain high throughout much of 2027 and was not expected to fall below 3 per cent until late 2027, which is "around three quarters later than previously forecast". "This presents upside risks to inflation expectations," it said. In recent weeks, RBA officials have been signalling their intention to lift rates at today's meeting, arguing that they can not afford to see peoples' inflation expectations drift higher. The RBA wants annual inflation in consumer prices to be around 2.5 per cent on average over the cycle. "There is an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that maybe 3 to 3.5 per cent is the new normal [for inflation]," RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser warned last month . It takes between 12 and 18 months for a change in interest rates to flow completely through the economy, so we will not know what total impact this rate hike will have on economic activity until 2028. Economy slowing, house prices falling, unemployment rising The RBA Monetary Policy Board said the cumulative rate hikes this year have tightened financial conditions in Australia. It says the economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly this year, and the unemployment rate has risen. Why housing's the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds. Its new economic forecasts see growth in output slowing even further over the coming year, which is expected to reduce capacity pressures and help return inflation to target. It says employment is expected to keep growing, but the unemployment rate is projected to rise by more than expected. In August, it was forecasting the unemployment rate to average 4.8 per cent in the December quarter of 2028, but now it was forecasting it to average 5.1 per cent in that period. The unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent . But the RBA board has also acknowledged that there continue to be "heightened uncertainties" about the outlook for inflation and the economy. "The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast," it warned. "Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation. "A period of prolonged uncertainty may also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia. events.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience. On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories. Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing. Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October. In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries. Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing. That could limit Dreambeans’ appeal in India, where many people regularly switch between languages, including Hindi and English, often mixing the two in what is commonly known as Hinglish. Dreambeans’ dependence on information from users’ Google accounts also raises questions about privacy and data access. The app uses Google’s Personal Intelligence technology to draw on connected services and personalize its AI-generated stories. Those services can contain sensitive personal information that some users may not want to share with an AI app just to receive personalized content. Users can choose which Google services to connect to Dreambeans and disconnect them at any time, Oznur said. They can also delete their Dreambeans data from within the app. Moreover, Oznur asserted that information deleted from the underlying connected services is also removed from Dreambeans’ personalization system. Users, Oznur said, can tell Dreambeans to avoid certain subjects, including business-related information, and the app will try to adjust its stories accordingly. She added that Dreambeans is available only to personal Gmail account holders, not enterprise users, and that generated stories are visible only to the account holder. Dreambeans’ proactive approach also carries the risk of surfacing memories that users may find upsetting. Oznur acknowledged that Dreambeans could generate stories involving people who have died, for instance. She said users can tell the app to stop showing certain subjects, comparing the feature to controls in Google Photos that let users limit which memories appear. Oznur told reporters that Google is exploring ways to make Dreambeans more actionable, moving beyond personalized stories and recommendations to help users act on the app’s suggestions. Toyota is the major shareholder in a company called AISIN, a manufacturer of automotive components. Both companies are aware that cars are increasingly reliant on tech like image recognition, and that robotics and other forms of “physical AI” will need parts that overlap with cars. AISIN thinks existing chips aren’t a good fit for such roles, because they rely on external memory to store AI models and then generate a lot of traffic between a processor and the model. That traffic, the company contends, makes image recognition and other on-device uses of AI less effective. DRAM is also currently vastly expensive. The company’s response is a system-on-chip built on a 16nm FinFET process, an Arm Cortex A53 dual-core CPU, plus an Arm MaliG31 GPU. The chip includes built-in STT-MRAM, which stores both model weights and an operating system. AISIN and its research partners at Tohoku University say that approach means the chip can go from power-on to kernel startup in 65.7 milliseconds – 38 times faster than is possible if using external memory – and run the Tiny YOLOv3 object detection algorithm on the chip. “To effectively utilize the limited on-chip memory capacity, a hybrid multiplication architecture combining 8-bit and 16-bit multiplication was developed” according to a machine translation of Tohoku University’s announcement [PDF]. “By combining 16x16, 16x8, and 8x8 bit multiplication, the amount of weight data for the AI model was reduced by 53 percent, from 17.7MB to 9.36MB, while maintaining 16-bit precision.” AISIN is an established parts supplier and already sells to Toyota and other automakers but hasn’t said if or when it can get this chip into production. events.title: EQT seeks joint AI and data centre deals with Saudi and UAE sovereign investors
events.summary: EQT , Europe’s biggest private markets investment firm, is in talks with sovereign investors in the UAE and Saudi Arabia to explore joint artificial intelligence and infrastructure investment opportunities in the Arab world’s top two economies, its global chair has said. The company with $400 billion in assets, which has been raising funds from Gulf investors for decades, is keen to now deploy capital in the region , home to some of the biggest sovereign wealth funds in the world, Jean Eric Salata, told The National . “Here [in the UAE] I would say, and we've also been talking to Saudis as well, looking at opportunities there. Those are the two big areas that we're working on right now,” Mr Salata said of the continuing AI co-investment conversations with sovereign investors. “We're most excited about, which I think aligns with the strategic goals of the UAE, is the whole infrastructure, particularly data infrastructure and data centres, where we have globally one of the largest footprints.” The Stockholm private equity company plans to expand its AI infrastructure footprint in the Gulf through its portfolio firm EdgeConneX, which owns more than 106 data centres across 25 countries, he said. AI opportunity EQT, which currently manages more than $100 billion in digital and energy assets across markets, is the latest global investor looking to the rapidly developing AI and digital infrastructure sector in the region. AI has become a central plank of economic diversification efforts of the oil-rich Gulf economies that have already announced mega AI infrastructure projects. The UAE is leading the way with a planned five-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus in Abu Dhabi, which includes Stargate UAE – a massive 1GW computing cluster anchored by a $20 billion data centre investment. UAE Tech investors Khazna and G42 are working on these projects alongside global leaders such as OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia and Cisco, and investors such as SoftBank. Saudi Arabia, the largest Arab economy, has rolled out Project Transcendence, a $100 billion scheme to scale domestic AI and data infrastructure. The kingdom’s $1 trillion Public Investment Fund has also set up Humain to build out national cloud infrastructure in the country. Qatar’s sovereign arm, the Qatar Investment Authority, has also launched Qai, a $20 billion AI infrastructure partnership, to build out domestic GPU and data centre footprints. Since last year the three Gulf states have announced AI investment plans worth $120 billion, which exceeded 5 per cent of their gross domestic product, according to International Monetary Fund estimates. The sheer scale of investment required for AI development and data centres creates a huge opportunity for global investors such as EQT. The $1.3 trillion Blackstone Group has already struck a $3 billion deal with Saudi Arabia’s Humain, while tech giant Microsoft has committed over $10 billion towards data centres and related infrastructure across UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait through to 2030. “There are many conversations that are ongoing right now with potential partners, both here [in the UAE] and elsewhere in the region,” Mr Salata said. “This is a sector that is capital constrained and is really, if you think about the AI build-out, the core, the key constraint in building the infrastructure is actually physical. It's the physical constraint around chips, energy, and data centres.” There is no shortage of demand for compute, hence a very strong investment case for building the power generation capacity and rolling out data infrastructure, he said. “I think that's where a lot of investment opportunity is right now for providers of long-term capital that can invest on a 15-year investment horizon,” he said. UAE SWF partnerships EQT opened an office in Abu Dhabi’s ADGM in September, joining the roster of trillion-dollar investors and asset managers including BlackRock, State Street, Blackstone Group, PGIM , Nuveen and Capital Group . A base in Abu Dhabi gives global investors opportunities to expand in the region and work closely with sovereign funds, large family offices and institutional partners. EQT is already working closely with the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, and Mr Salata said the firm is keen to expand that relationship. “They are one of our most important partners, and we're very excited to be working with them in, I would say, ever-increasing dimensions. We not only manage investments for Adia in our funds, but we also do a lot of co-investing together,” Mr Salata said. Adia is one of EQT’s largest co-underwriters in some of the European firm’s largest deals to take companies private in Europe. In June, Adia, along with Abu Dhabi’s $385 billion sovereign investment arm Mubadala Development Company, joined EQT’s £9.5 billion acquisition bid for the UK’s Intertek Group. Over the years, EQT has executed several co-investment deals with Mubadala, including the 2022 acquisition of Envirotainer, a biopharmaceutical industry solutions company. In 2025, Mubadala took a $600 million stake in Nord Anglia Education, and has been “a significant partner of ours all over the world”, he said. Deeping ties Establishing its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi, Mr Salata said, was necessary to deepen its ties to the region, where it has active relationships with “many of the other sovereign wealth funds”. “The plan is to continue to develop those relationships regionally and use this office as a base to access them on a more regular basis,” he said. Forty EQT portfolio companies already have a presence in the Gulf, and with a local footprint, it expects more investments from regional sovereign investors to flow into those companies. “The logical place for us to start is with our existing portfolio companies,” Mr Salata said. “We really want to try and figure out how we can become more deeply involved in the investment ecosystem here,” he said. Over time EQT plans to bring more of its portfolio companies to the Gulf, and Mr Salata believes that the number will grow two or three-fold over the five to 10-year horizon. The sectors it seeks to invest in are “very much aligned with some of the longer-term trends in the region”, including infrastructure, education and health care, as well as technology and energy, where “the government policy is supportive”, he added.

events.title: Frantic Binance hackers created windfall for crypto traders
events.summary: Blockchain data firm Bitquery estimates the attackers lost about US$119 million through poor execution in their haste. Binance was hacked for US$6.3 billion, and North Korean hackers rushed to move stolen funds before stablecoins were frozen and withdrawals were halted. Their panic created sharp price gaps in Ether, TRX and other tokens, letting fast traders and bots make big profits from the chaos. Bitquery said hackers lost about US$119 million through poor execution, while Binance later restored withdrawals and said it had frozen about US$3 billion in affected assets. SAN FRANCISCO – For most crypto investors, the theft of US$6.3 billion (S$8.07 billion) from Binance was a reminder of the risks that still surround digital assets. For a small group of fast-moving trading firms and skilled investors, it was a chance to make a quick buck. As apparent North Korean hackers rushed to convert funds stolen from the world’s biggest crypto exchange, they accepted punishing prices. That handed well-prepared traders a fleeting but lucrative opportunity. Bitquery, a blockchain data firm, estimates the attackers lost about US$119 million through poor execution in their haste. “The hack created sharp price volatility and a single, large, price-insensitive seller moving through thin liquidity,” said James Aitchison, chief investment officer at Caerus Global Management. That aggressive, one-way torrent distorted crypto prices across disparate venues and blockchains, he said, adding: “We traded the event and found several attractive dislocations.” After gaining control of Binance funds on Oct 29, the attackers focused on getting rid of the stablecoin portion of the haul, knowing issuers would soon begin freezing those stolen tokens. Within roughly half an hour, they began aggressively swapping stablecoins such as USDT into other cryptocurrencies like Ether, which cannot be frozen, buying the tokens wherever they could and jacking up the price. Tether and Circle froze roughly US$1.8 billion worth of their stablecoins about 40 minutes after the main Ethereum leg of the hack began, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. Binance, meanwhile, stopped withdrawals while it investigated the breach. That disrupted the usual flow of money between trading venues and allowed price gaps that normally disappear in seconds to remain open far longer. Luca Parlamento, founder and chief investment officer of D2 Finance, said his firm spent the night “on the other side of the thief’s trades”. Parlamento said the attackers paid an average of about US$2,657 for Ether through decentralised exchanges such as Uniswap, well above the roughly US$2,300 price on Hyperliquid, a crypto derivatives platform. “The gap was ours to close,” Parlamento said. For traders with funds already sitting on such venues, the basic trade was straightforward: sell Ether where the hackers’ frantic buying had pushed the price unusually high and buy it where the price remained lower. Annanay Kapila, a former quant trader who runs derivatives exchange QFEX, was working in his central London office on the night of Oct 29 when he noticed that the price of Ether had skyrocketed on decentralised exchanges, reaching over US$3,000 in some cases. Kapila began to borrow large amounts of Ether on decentralised lending platform Aave, depositing stablecoins in return. He then sold his Ether on exchanges where its price was highest. Kapila said he made a 25% profit on the trades within five minutes. Crypto’s lack of persistent volatility in recent years means this kind of window is increasingly uncommon, Kapila said, with the last such event being when prices collapsed in October 2025. “Crypto’s been a little bit dead this year. Anytime there’s big dislocation, there are big opportunities,” Kapila said. “I’ve been around since 2021 where this was almost a weekly occurrence, stuff like this. But nowadays, it’s relatively rare.” The scale of the price gap showed the extent to which crypto’s typical market structure had been weakened. Achieving a fair price usually depends on traders being able to move coins quickly from one venue to another. Binance’s suspension of withdrawals also did not help, with locked funds preventing more traders from cashing in on the opportunity. The dislocations spread quickly to other tokens. One of the largest appeared on Tron, another blockchain network. Aitchison said the attackers swapped about US$234 million of USDT for 638 million TRX, Tron’s native token, in 16 trades. The average purchase price on a small venue called SunSwap was about 36.7 US cents, compared with a wider market price near 33 US cents. The buying briefly pushed the main trading pool as much as 18% above the broader market, and the gap took roughly 10 hours to fully disappear, he said.
