events.title: Another judge blocks DOJ ballot demands in California
events.summary: A federal judge on the eve of Election Day barred the Trump administration from demanding California officials set aside ballots from registered voters it suspects are noncitizens, finding the effort likely violates the Constitution. Why it matters: Courts had already rejected the Justice Department's attempts to force California to separate the ballots. Monday's ruling goes a step further, directly barring federal officials from making those demands even as DOJ turns to the Supreme Court to compel the state to comply. Driving the news: Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg ruled Monday that the Trump administration likely violated the Constitution by pressuring California officials to change how they count ballots. His order prohibits the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from demanding officials set aside ballots or depart from existing state election procedures based on federal lists of suspected noncitizens. Boasberg found that the Constitution gives states and Congress, but not the executive branch, authority over election rules. The federal ban on noncitizen voting does not mean the administration can rewrite those rules. By the numbers: The DOJ claims it identified more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens on California's voter rolls. After Boasberg ordered DOJ to turn over its list, an expert found that at least 22 members of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights — all known U.S. citizens — were wrongly included. The expert found another 66 members were almost certainly on the list. Boasberg found the expert credible and concluded the list's errors posed a real threat to eligible voters. What he's saying: "The President evidently believes that it would be good public policy for more stringent procedures to be put in place," Boasberg wrote. "No matter how strong that policy case may be, however, it does not justify overstepping the bounds of the Executive Branch's limited constitutional authority in this domain." The White House referred Axios to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. DHS and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. Catch up quick: In a separate lawsuit , DOJ sought to force California and Los Angeles County to segregate ballots from suspected noncitizens. A federal judge rejected that request Wednesday, as did an appeals court on Friday. Monday's ruling is different in that it restricts the federal government from making its demands rather than simply refusing to order California to comply. It also follows a broader nationwide temporary restraining order Friday that prohibits similar demands and threats of prosecution against election workers. Yes, but: Boasberg did not prohibit federal officials from investigating illegal voting or compiling lists of suspected noncitizens. Federal law makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and DOJ can prosecute people who knowingly break that law. But that doesn't give DOJ the authority to order states to change how they verify voter eligibility or count ballots, Boasberg wrote. California can continue following its election procedures while federal prosecutors pursue illegal voting, Boasberg said. What's next: The Supreme Court could still order California to set aside the disputed ballots.

( ABC Kimberley: Tom Forrest ) Customers across Australia are receiving scam messages following a data leak involving third-party booking provider RMS. Travellers to Western Australia's north say they were initially fooled by the phishing scams, as they included accurate details about upcoming accommodation bookings. RMS says investigations are continuing to assess the full scope and impact of the incident. A cybersecurity expert says scammers are using fear and "weaponising urgency", as holiday-makers and hotels in Western Australia's Kimberley are caught up in a global data breach. The breach, involving third-party booking provider RMS , saw hackers access names, booking information and contact details from across the country. Cameron Craig received a WhatsApp message regarding his upcoming booking at Cable Beach Club in Broome last week. The WhatsApp message sent to Cam Craig regarding his upcoming booking was a phishing scam. ( Supplied: Cam Craig ) The Sydney resident said the text requested him to provide his payment details through a link, or risk losing his booking. The message included details including the correct dates of his planned trip and his full name. Mr Craig said he clicked on the link and entered some of his credit card information but the session timed out. Cam Craig has been travelling to different destinations around Australia with his son. ( Supplied: Cam Craig ) He later realised the message was sent by an international number and the reservation code was different. Mr Craig said he alerted Cable Beach Club, which then notified guests. The resort has been contacted for comment. Kimberley Accommodation Group, which also uses RMS Cloud as its third-party reservation system, received reports from guests who had received similar phishing messages. Managing director Dannielle Hart said hackers used genuine booking details and asked customers to confirm card details or make a payment. Kimberley Accommodation Group owns venues across the region including the Kimberley Hotel in Halls Creek. ( Supplied: Facebook ) Ms Hart said the company was not able to comment on the number of customers impacted, or any customer financial losses at this stage. "Our advice to guests is not to respond to unexpected messages, click links, provide card details or make payments in response to communications about their booking," she said. RMS confirmed the unauthorised activity identified within the RMS environment had been contained yesterday. The provider said investigations were continuing as it assessed the full scope and impact of the incident. Cybersecurity lecturer Brianna O'Shea said phishing scams had evolved over time to become more convincing. "Early attempts relied on generic mass emails with obvious spelling errors, poorly designed fake logos and simple web links," she said. Brianna O'Shea says more accommodation providers could be affected. ( Supplied: Brianna O'Shea ) The Murdoch University academic said third-party systems were a "lucrative target" for hackers. She said the breach could also have implications for FIFO workers and independent bed and breakfasts, where RMS was used to support bookings in temporary accommodation. "This is just the tip of the iceberg," Dr O'Shea said. "It'll be up to the owners to reach out to their customers and provide them with that support.

events.title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1/A on Monday (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print. The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals. To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more. Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’” When the term RSI became popular earlier this year , many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove. But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below): In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified , and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data. However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.” Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category. Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grown leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly. As always, it depends on what they're wearing iFixit dismantles Apple's Duo: 'You'd better baby that screen' 8 days ago Singapore boffins weave a GUI into fabric, and it's machine washable too 11 days ago YouTuber built 30-frame-per-second grayscale Game Boy, then open sourced it for all e-paper displays 18 days ago OpenAI claims 100-plus secret files followed ex-employee back to Apple 19 days ago Microsoft unveils 'Surace' Laptop Ultra 26 days ago The next time you see a software engineer shaping silent words with their mouth, you may have to think twice before asking if they need a mental health day – they might just be wearing a pair of smart glasses that let them talk to their computer without uttering a sound. Subvocal is a Y Combinator-backed startup aiming to produce these glasses, and already has working prototypes to show off in YouTube videos, including one with YC partner Dave Lieb trying them out and being impressed enough to offer funding. The headset isn’t what the final version will look like, the company notes, which is good: The demo headset is obviously 3D printed and far from fashionable. Once the final product is available it should look a lot sleeker, based on mockups on the company’s website. It’s not clear when they’ll actually be released, though the preorder page says it’ll be sometime in Q1 2027 at an early bird price of $499. It’s not clear what the final full price will be. As for how the glasses work, the founders, Georgia Tech computer science students Aarush Yadav and Arnav Kumar, explain in a launch post on YC that the device uses low-powered radio waves projected from the glasses toward a wearer’s face. Those waves are distorted by muscle movements and the change in a person’s face shape as they speak or simply mouth words, which the duo said can be picked up and translated into written text. “We started working on this about four months ago after building the first version at a hackathon,” the pair explained in their YC post. “Since then, we’ve gone from a table full of electronics and antennas taped to our face to a semi-portable board and sleek glasses that can decode open-ended speech at 200+ WPM and a reasonably low error rate even at a small dataset scale.” This is just a proof of concept, and many key details are still missing, like the accuracy rate, battery life, whether it will paired with an app, or what-have-you. “The core thing we wanted to prove first was that the signal exists and that we can decode it,” Yadav and Kumar said. In a Hacker News post announcing the company, Yadav and Kumar explained that they started the project during the hackathon by focusing on using EMG electrodes attached to Yadav’s face. They didn’t win the hackathon, but apparently the demo was impressive enough to earn some initial funding from San Francisco VC firm Afore Capital. Shortly after that, the pair pivoted from EMG to RF sensing, as a commercial dictation product that required sticking electrodes to one’s face was unlikely to succeed. “Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge,” Yadav said. “First we built an extremely low-noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face.” They eventually got to the functional prototype they have now, and pre-trained the AI models doing the speech recognition to minimize setup time. According to the company, Lieb only had to read 20 sentences to calibrate the headset to his speech patterns. “We think silent speech can become the next interface for interacting with computers, replacing voice and the keyboard,” the company says of its goal. “Emails, prompts, messages, code, notes, commands, all at the speed of speech without bothering anyone around you.

events.title: Nine engineers, 1,211 code updates in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork
events.summary: Nine engineers, 1,211 pull requests in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork Plus a case study where we put everything together by moving our runtime from Python to Rust while live. In January of this year, a small team at Microsoft set out to build Copilot Cowork , an agentic execution layer that performs multi-step workflows on a user’s behalf. That result brings the powerful AI-assisted tools and capabilities developers have today to everyday knowledge workers, all with Work IQ , Microsoft 365 security and governance, cloud execution, and Microsoft’s multi-model architecture. This is the story of how the team took Copilot Cowork from an empty repo to worldwide GA in about four and a half months, then moved its runtime from Python to Rust while it was live. Agents wrote most of the code. Ways of working changed along the way, and the practices other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team: moving fast while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view. On October 21, nine engineers merged 1,211 pull requests into the main branch of the Copilot Cowork backend. That number would have sounded absurd to the team in January, when a handful of us made the first commit to an empty repo. Agents wrote most of the code, but engineers remained responsible for defining the work and judging the results. Our small team wrote clearer specs, set architecture and security boundaries, and focused its review on higher-risk changes, production impact, and cases where checks or reviewers disagreed. Automated checks and agent reviewers examined every change. Agents could propose changes, but they could not decide what was allowed to happen. We didn’t plan on working this way. But every few weeks, the agents got better, part of our process stopped working, and we adapted. Six practices emerged from those changes. They cover how we specify work, run agents within clear boundaries, test our checks, preserve what the team learns, shape the codebase for parallel work, and set limits on automated loops. They aren’t a recipe for matching our PR count. They are lessons other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view. We’ll end with the project that puts those practices to the test together: moving the live runtime from Python to Rust. Lesson 1: Write the spec before the code The first commit was made on January 13. From the start, agents wrote the code. In the first weeks, we learned that the agent was rarely what slowed us down. The bottleneck was not knowing exactly what we wanted. A vague request got us code that looked reasonable, survived a quick read, and then did the wrong thing. Fixing it took longer than writing a proper request would have in the first place. So we adopted a rule that still stands today: no code without a markdown spec written first. The spec covers three things: A good spec saves far more time than it costs upfront. But a weak one leads to rework a few days later. The faster agents became at implementation, the more important it became for us to be precise about intent, requirements, and what good looked like. Many of our specs start out spoken. Someone talks through a feature, and an agent turns that into a first draft of the spec, which the human then edits. I think this did more for our speed than any single model upgrade. We launched Copilot Cowork to our first enterprise customers in the Frontier program on March 30. Lesson 2: Run narrow agents inside clear boundaries The next step was running more than one agent at a time. Each works in its own copy of the repo, on one task, from one spec. One agent became five, and five became dozens. Merged PRs per month went from 257 in January to 2,754 in May. Our busiest week before GA had 783. Parallel work went better than we expected for two reasons: Narrow tasks: An agent with one well-defined task makes fewer mistakes than one asked to do a lot at once. Picking the model per task: We treated model choice as a quality-and-cost tradeoff, not a race to use the cheapest model. Some tasks warranted stronger reasoning; for others, a faster, less expensive model gave us the right balance. In Copilot Cowork, the model runs in a container without user credentials. A trusted host outside the container handles identity, policy, approvals, and tools, and every Microsoft 365 operation goes through the host. We didn’t want to limit what the agent could attempt, because a heavily restricted agent isn’t very useful . With our architecture, the model can plan and ask for anything, and the host decides what actually happens. That separation lets us increase the number of agents working in parallel without giving the model credentials or direct authority over operations. The host still applied identity, policy, approvals, and audit at the point of execution. Building that in at the start was much easier than adding it later would’ve been. It also helped in a way we didn’t plan for. The agent only talks to the host through a defined interface, so we could later replace the entire host without changing the agent—which we did when we migrated to Rust. We reached worldwide general availability on June 16, about four and a half months after the first commit, with several models and 16 plugins. Lesson 3: Make checks prove they checked something With agents writing most of the code, nine people couldn’t read every change, and waiting for a human review was becoming the slowest step for every PR. Several engineers each built their own review bot, modeled on how they review code themselves, and the bots competed. When one bot caught a problem another had missed, the bot that missed it got a new rule. Over time, each reviewer built up a large set of rules learned from its own misses. Each one has now been through at least10,000 generations; in each generation, the reviewer runs reviews, then reflects on what it missed and gets better at reviewing code. Today, a useful first review usually arrives within several minutes of a pull request being opened. On a sample of recent merged PRs, the median was about four and a half minutes. Slower, more specialized passes follow: One walks the call graph, looking for code that isn’t wired up and for tests that would still pass if the change were reverted One looks at operational problems like restart safety, metrics, and stale docs One reads every changed file end to end One checks behavior against the code being replaced The author gets quick feedback while the change is still fresh, and the detailed reading still happens. Of course, reviewer agents can still miss things. Once, a group of reviewer agents read a change in one of the most sensitive parts of the product. Each had been told to try to break it, and none found a problem. People on the team then read the same diff and found four blocking issues, all of which were fixed before it merged.

events.title: Trump cuts South Africa, Rwanda from AGOA trade program
events.summary: The News US President Donald Trump plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from African Growth and Opportunity Act eligibility next year, stripping both countries of duty-free access to the US market under Washington’s flagship Africa trade program. Trump formally notified Congress and both governments of his decision, the Office of the US Trade Representative said Monday, after an annual review determined Pretoria and Kigali have been engaging in “concerning and pervasive” practices inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria. These include “barriers that undermine American trade and investment” and practices that “pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said. The statement also cited corruption in South Africa, while its concerns about Rwanda extended to the rule of law, political pluralism, and human rights. The decision follows months of US tension with both governments. Washington has clashed with Pretoria over Trump’s claims of a “genocide” against white South Africans, which experts have dismissed, and is ending PEPFAR aid to the country. South Africa hoped to use its critical mineral resources as leverage in trade talks. South African Trade Minister Parks Tau said the “decision does not define the broader relationship” between the countries and that South Africa would continue pursuing trade, investment and shared economic opportunities with the US. The trade ministry said it had offered additional concessions and called it “unfortunate that the US is now raising new issues that have not been the basis for discussions.” With Rwanda, the dispute centers on the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo: The US sanctioned Rwanda’s military in March and its defense ministry last week, accusing them of backing M23 rebels and using minerals from rebel-held territory in their supply chains. Know More South Africa has the most to lose as AGOA’s largest beneficiary, exporting about $1.7 billion worth of goods under the program in 2025, including vehicles and agricultural products. Rwanda’s exposure is far smaller, with US imports from the country totaling about $44 million last year. Standard trade will continue, but affected exports could become more expensive, and the damage may spread across southern Africa and impact thousands of jobs . “The loss of AGOA will reverberate through the SADC region as several countries, including Lesotho and Botswana, are part of the South African supply chain that provides goods and products for the US under AGOA,” said Witney Schneidman, a former US deputy assistant secretary of state for African affairs. AGOA, established in 2000, is authorized only through the end of 2028, and Schneidman said this episode highlights the need to modernize it. “China, the EU and South Africa’s other partners don’t turn their trade relations ‘on and off’ as the US does,” he said.

events.title: AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes
events.summary: If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos. Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale. "Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation." Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps. To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as " Legal Zero-Days : A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and " Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System " [PDF]. The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace . Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well." Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code. The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications. Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world. To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm. For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid. Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made. "We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote. "In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves." Wendy Musell, a San Francisco-based employment law attorney and partner, told The Register that the use of AI in the legal field is expanding rapidly. "Some California Courts, including LA Superior Court, are testing the use of AI as law clerks," said Musell. "Generally law clerks would assist the Court by researching and drafting opinions for the judge's review. That means AI is serving that role in certain courts. Litigators now must consider how AI is analyzing motions and cases. "This is the case even where I personally have found different AI sources to appear to have a slant or bias, and often fail to accurately analyze legal issues. It was just a matter of time before AI came for the legislative process." Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register that Ringe's argument has some merit. "I think the methodology of using AI to identify potential statutory gaps is logical," said Goldman. "However, it will require careful human review to determine if the AI-identified gaps are in fact actually gaps. Statutory gaps also may have no legal consequence, or at least none of significance; and legislatures will often correct any major gaps once they are identified." Goldman said the idea that legislators should use AI during the drafting process is ambitious, at least in the short term. "Legislators often draft laws with a range of goals and priorities, and avoiding statutory gaps is rarely a high priority," he explained. "But many legislatures have legislative counsel who are responsible for converting draft bills into final legislative text, and I could see where legislative counsel could benefit from using AI to identify drafting gaps as part of their standard cleanup protocols." ®

events.title: Trump to Axios: "No rush" to decide on bombing Iran again
events.summary: President Trump told Axios in a phone interview Monday he's "in no rush" to decide whether to resume fighting in Iran . Why it matters: The midterm elections have been seen as an inflection point for Trump on whether to unleash a massive bombing campaign to try to bring the war to an end. But it appears the president, at least for now, will continue on dual tracks — letting negotiations play out while preparing to go back to war if he concludes a deal isn't reachable. What he is saying: "One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it," Trump said in the interview. Driving the news: Qatari mediators have written a draft agreement outlining a three-day sequence of confidence-building measures aimed at resuming direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, according to regional sources. A diplomat with knowledge of the situation said the Qatari mediators are waiting for feedback from the U.S. and Iran. Qatari mediator Ali al-Thawadi traveled to Tehran on Monday to continue talks on the draft agreement and the diplomat said progress is building. Trump is giving diplomacy a chance but is clear-eyed about the chances of reaching a deal. "We are talking to them. It's going fine. The problem with them is ... they try and tap tap tap [us along]. There's less urgency [on the Iranian side] than you think there would be, but they want to make a deal more than they ever wanted," Trump said. The latest: Hours after the interview, Trump posted on Truth Social: "Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK, down almost $10 a Barrel, A RECORD, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran. Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!" Between the lines: Trump is weighing three courses of action, backed by three different camps: 1. Make a deal: Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are urging him to move toward a deal because a renewed war might not change the situation for the better. Most Gulf countries support this position and have communicated that to Trump, sources say. 2. Go back to battle: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to resume combat, as does Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. They argue that Iran can't be trusted to make a deal let alone abide by one, and that Trump should finish the job militarily. 3. Maximum economic pain: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are advising Trump to maintain the "no war, no deal" status quo and allow the economic pressure campaign to continue, sources said. Ratcliffe told Trump that prolonged economic pain will induce Iran to make more concessions — or create enough instability inside the country that citizens revolt, a source with direct knowledge said. The CIA declined to comment. The other side: Iran's civilian leadership sounded hopeful on Monday about the prospects of reaching a deal. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei "granted the government certain authorities" to try to reach an agreement through diplomacy. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that the diplomatic exchanges "have become very intensive." "Qatar and Pakistan are playing very active roles as mediators. We have presented our conditions and our proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political rationality. If they choose genuine diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if they intend to engage in deception and military operations, they will face a response more painful and severe than in the past," he said. Araghchi said that if the U.S. accepts Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, then "negotiations will resume." "Otherwise, the current situation will continue, and Iran will not bow down," he said. The big picture: Russia and China are taking an active role in the effort to reach a deal. Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone Monday with Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Gen. Mohsen Rezaei. The two discussed the efforts to reach a diplomatic agreement. Rezaei, who is very close to Khamenei, was also the recipient of a letter Vance sent recently proposing to resume negotiations. Russia has also offered to be part of any nuclear agreement, including by receiving Iran's enriched uranium stockpile. At the same time, Rezaei's deputy visited Beijing on Monday and met with the Chinese foreign minister. China is also urging the U.S. and Iran to resume direct negotiations to end the war. What they're saying: Vance told reporters on Monday that he and Trump "feel pretty good about the prospect of reaching a settlement" with Iran. "We made some progress and we will see if we can make some more," Vance said. He added: "We haven't set deadlines (for resuming strikes). We want to make sure the Iranians don't rebuild or try to rebuild their nuclear program. We do think there is a pathway there but it requires a firm and verifiable commitment that they don't rebuild their nuclear program."

events.title: Why Relationships Still Matter in the Digital Age of Banking
events.summary: As technology reshapes trade finance and global commerce becomes more complex, Habib Bank AG Zurich’s Hong Kong CEO says the winning formula is not scale alone – but responsiveness, judgment and trusted relationships. When Sachil Dagur took charge of Habib Bank Zurich in Hong Kong in 2018, he saw a bank with valuable strengths already in place: a niche in trade finance, deep ties to the trading community and a footprint across markets important to its clients. The opportunity, he believed, was not to reinvent those strengths, but to connect them more effectively and help clients make better use of them. Dagur, CEO of Habib Bank Zurich (Hong Kong), had spent more than two decades at Axis Bank, including senior roles in India, Singapore and Hong Kong. His career gave him a close view of corporate banking across Asia and shaped his belief that, while technology and trade routes may change, clients still value sound advice, relevant information and someone who answers the phone. “If they know they can reach out and somebody’s going to pick up the phone or call back immediately,” he says, “it gives great comfort.” For Dagur, the future of banking is not a choice between technology and relationships. It is about using one to strengthen the other. According to Dagur, technology may have transformed banking, but clients still want a bank that understands their problems and offers solutions. Personal accessibility remains a competitive strength, with customers valuing clear points of contact. This relationship-led approach, he explains, is what builds loyalty. In fact, he notes that about 40 per cent of Habib Bank Zurich’s clients have stayed for more than a decade. Trust, however, is not built on goodwill alone, he says. It requires continuity, knowledge and delivery. “The continuity of people is the most critical part,” he says. Clients should not have to repeatedly explain their business to changing relationship managers. Staff must also understand banking products as well as the markets and industries in which their clients operate. “You would always love interacting with people who provide additional knowledge to you,” Dagur says. That knowledge is particularly important in trade finance, where clients may be exploring unfamiliar destinations, counterparties or supply chains. Habib Bank AG Zurich’s presence in 11 markets including Bangladesh, Turkey, Pakistan, South Africa and Kenya gives it local insight that can help clients assess opportunities and risks. Dagur takes a similarly pragmatic approach to technology. No bank can ignore digital change, but not every institution needs to be first in every innovation. “If a tiger is chasing you, don’t be the last guy,” he says. “If you can’t lead, at least hang around at the front end of the crowd.” For Habib Bank Zurich, this has meant digitising internal processes such as letters of credit and invoice discounting while monitoring blockchain-based trade finance. Dagur believes blockchain may become important, but adoption remains limited. The immediate priority, he says, is to ensure that internal processes can be fully digitised before moving further. The bank is not yet blockchain-ready, he says, but it is watching the space and will be ready when the market is. As supply chains shift and companies rethink trade routes, banks cannot control geopolitics. They can, however, help clients understand change earlier and respond more intelligently. For Dagur, knowledge will be a key differentiator. “What do you know better and faster than others?” he asks. “That is going to be the differentiator.” Habib Bank AG Zurich’s representative offices in Bangladesh, Turkey and China, alongside its presence in several other countries, help the bank build deeper market understanding and share relevant intelligence with clients. This can be valuable for Chinese companies as they seek overseas markets and trading businesses look for new destinations. The challenge is no longer simply to provide financing. Banks must help clients decide where to trade, whom to work with and how to adapt when conditions shift. Risk management, he notes, is central to that role. Dagur has placed greater emphasis on larger, highly rated corporate clients, regular staff training and sustained attention to compliance. Risk and compliance, he believes, cannot remain the responsibility of a specialist department; they must become part of the institution’s culture. “If risk and compliance becomes a culture, it becomes a non-issue,” he says. His view was partly shaped from his early days in a military school, where the motto was “Play the Game”: which translates to “If you’re playing the game, play by the rules that the game has.” In banking, that means compliance is non-negotiable. Rules governing anti-money laundering, liquidity and financial crime controls must be followed, and employees need to understand why they matter.

( Supplied: Fortescue Helicopters ) The Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) has grounded Sky High Helicopters for a series of serious safety breaches. CASA says the breaches included directing its pilots "not to accurately record the total time in service for aircraft operated by the company". The company's suspension comes a year after CASA warned the watchdog would crack down on helicopter pilots over safety regulations. An outback Australian helicopter company has had its fleet grounded and its air operator's certificate suspended immediately over a "serious and imminent risk to safety". Sky High Helicopters Pty Ltd, which trades as Fortescue Helicopters in Western Australia and Queensland, has been grounded by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA). In its findings published yesterday, CASA said the company had been operating with "a deliberately and systemically non-compliant safety culture". Fortescue Helicopters operates in Western Australia and Queensland. ( Supplied: Fortescue Helicopters ) Corporate documents show the chopper company was first registered in 2008, offering aerial mustering, charter flights and mining support from the Pilbara mining town of Newman. It also has other bases in Perth, Broome and Far North Queensland. Owned by WA cattle producer and pilot Weldon Percy, Fortescue Helicopters lists among its clients mining giants Fortescue Metals Group (FMG), Rio Tinto, Glencore and Hancock Prospecting. On its website, the business says it has a fleet of 22 aircraft. "Safety, for our pilots and clients is our number one priority," the company's website states. "We believe safety is a company culture, not just a practice." It is not yet clear how long Fortescue Helicopters' suspension will last. ( Supplied: Fortescue Helicopters ) Fortescue Helicopters is not affiliated with the similarly named FMG, although it lists the company founded by billionaire Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest as "an important client of ours". It is understood Fortescue has used Fortescue Helicopters on an ad hoc basis but it is not its primary provider. CASA said in its findings the company had committed a series of serious and systemic intentional safety breaches, including that its pilots had been "directed not to accurately record the total time in service for aircraft operated by the company". Other breaches detected by CASA included pilots being "directed not to record maintenance defects on aircraft maintenance releases" and operating "aircraft with outstanding maintenance requirements". It also said personnel at the company were being ordered to perform unauthorised maintenance activities and had failed to comply with the company's operations manual. CASA has previously pledged to crack down on safety compliance in the northern Australian chopper industry. ( ABC News: Michael Parfitt ) CASA also said "pilots' flight and duty time limits are regularly and deliberately exceeded" by the company. Mr Percy hung up when the ABC contacted him for comment. Fortescue Helicopters was also separately contacted but has not responded. Suspension follows safety crackdown pledge The grounding of Sky High Helicopters comes a year after CASA's chief executive Pip Spence warned the watchdog would crack down on helicopter pilots who tried to "game the system" over safety regulations . She made the comments in the aftermath of the month-long trial of celebrity crocodile wrangler and chopper pilot Matt Wright in the Northern Territory Supreme Court last year, in which he was sentenced to prison for five months. Wright trial exposes cowboy chopper culture The trial of celebrity crocodile wrangler Matt Wright unearthed a culture of helicopter maintenance and safety breaches by his company, which some say have been ongoing in Australia's north for decades. Wright's trial for attempting to pervert the course of justice heard accounts of frequent under-reporting of helicopter flying hours within the northern Australian aviation sector, with pilots regularly disconnecting the devices used to record their hours. Separate to his criminal trial, Wright's company, Helibrook, was grounded in late 2024 over numerous breaches , including failing to record accurate flight times, reckless operation of aircraft, and the falsification of maintenance records.

events.title: Trump pre-election pitch: Reflecting Pool, pipes and a new promenade
events.summary: President Trump extolled his administration's Reflecting Pool project , dug up debunked claims of vandalism and applauded the new White House helipad in a Monday pre-Election Day speech. The big picture: Trump's deep focus on remaking the nation's capital has taken center stage as the clock ticks down to midterm elections. Driving the news: "The pool is now better and more beautiful than it's ever been before, and we're very proud of it," Trump said in Monday's speech, adding, "We went through a lot with vandalism." But Trump's own Justice Department dropped vandalism charges against former Olympian David Hearn , whose case was later killed by a judge after prosecutors acknowledged that faulty installation caused the damage to the Pool. Trump added the administration was "giving serious thought" to renaming the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the "Trump Reflecting Pool," before later saying he was kidding. Throughout the speech, he held up printed images he identified as pipes, joints and other Pool materials. He also showed an image that appeared to show "8647" sprayed onto the base of the emptied pool, claiming "that was a Comey phrase" — a reference to his former FBI director and top foe. Zoom out: He also discussed his White House renovation projects, including the recently installed helipad and Scotts Miracle-Gro's lawn restoration after the UFC fight on White House grounds. Friction point: Trump's projects, including his D.C.-area arch and White House ballroom, have been broadly panned by Americans in polling. "This project should be a project that unites all Americans," Trump said Monday of the newly reopened Reflecting Pool, which stood empty for an extended period earlier this year. Zoom in: His pre-election pitch at times sounded more like a typical rally speech, where he touted his immigration policies and war with Iran while slamming Democrats as "a party that hates America." This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime," he said. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history." He also reiterated his pitch to distribute $5,000 checks should Republicans win in the midterms. What's next: After inviting Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to speak, Trump then touted his planned " triumphal arch ," detailed plans for a "promenade" from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River and teased his golf course renovation . "We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that you don't have enough time," Trump said. He ended his closing argument by lauding a "golden age," saying, "We were laughed at like we were stupid people. We were laughed at by every ruler, every president, every prime minister, every king, every queen. But they don't laugh anymore." Axios' Josephine Walker contributed to this report. events.title: Scoop: Senate GOP makes massive bet on streaming
events.summary: The top Senate GOP super PAC has nearly tripled its spending on streaming and social media platforms this election cycle to more than $200 million, Axios has learned. Why it matters : In a record cycle for ad spending, more political money is shifting to streaming, where super PACs have greater freedom to target voters, bargain and experiment — but platforms have more power to set the rules. In some states, streaming and social media have swallowed half of the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) budget, according to a source familiar with the group's spending. SLF's $200M+ total for the 2026 cycle (up from $71M in 2024) includes tens of millions of dollars funneled through the SLF-linked Texas PAC and its affiliated nonprofit One Nation. The other side: The top Senate Democratic super PAC declined to provide a dollar figure for their spending on streaming. "Senate Majority PAC invested more this cycle in digital communications than any previous cycle, running digital campaigns in 12 states," SMP communications director Lauren French told Axios. Zoom in : Streaming and social platforms offer campaigns the power to target more specific audiences compared to traditional broadcast, and make it easier to measure the impact. "Its way more surgical than a linear broadcast buy," Zack Roday, managing director at Think Big, told Axios. But platforms can also set their own rules around which types of ads they want to accept. Some, like Netflix and TikTok, don't allow any candidate or issue ads . Republicans have complained about restrictions on ads that include transgender issues on Disney-owned platforms. Between the lines: Super PACs often pay multiple times what a campaign pays for ads on broadcast TV and radio because of laws ensuring candidates get the lowest rates. Online, super PACs can negotiate directly — and use their fat budgets and sprawling election maps as leverage. SLF works with platforms like SiriusXM, Paramount, Hulu, YouTube and others to lock in discounts based on their overall spending plans, according to the source. Groups can also experiment with different lengths and formats for ads online, breaking the 30-second broadcast mold. What to watch: Streaming ads can also be trickier for outside tracking. While Meta and Google provide public data on political ad buys, not every platform provides that kind of visibility, Streaming buys aren't covered by the same FCC filing requirements as political ad reservations on broadcast TV and radio. Broadcast filings can offer a preview of a group's targets months in advance, but streaming reservations are much harder to see. Although AI is changing the game, and there is a growing industry of companies offering better tracking tools. Super PACs still have to report independent expenditures to the FEC through 24- and 48- hour reports. Zoom out: Strong grassroots fundraising has helped Democratic candidates crush Republicans in dollars brought in directly to candidates. The GOP is hitting back with cash-flush committees and super PACs fueled by ultra-wealthy donors. In addition to super PACs moving more money to streaming, the National Republican Senatorial Committee jumped on a court decisions to coordinate ad buys with campaigns — giving them access to the candidate rate. It also allowed NRSC to negotiate with streaming platforms on behalf of multiple campaigns. The bottom line: It's just the beginning on maneuvering on streaming and coordinated buys. "That is definitely going to be the story of 2028," Kenny Day, senior vice president at IQM corporation, told Axios. He said the Supreme Court decision on coordinated spending "was too late for either party to really take advantage of the allowance of coordinated spending" in the 2026 cycle. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to show that the more than $200 million total included money spent through Texas PAC (not that it excluded that spending).

Property price slump provides glimmer of hope for home buyers A story from our Perth team, where aspiring home buyers are hoping a drop in property prices will help them break into the market . After years of searching for a home as the WA capital's property prices continued to rise at an unprecedented rate, Vanessa Bray finally feels like she has a fighting chance of securing one. The single mum has been buoyed by new figures showing Australia is tracking towards its biggest housing market downturn in 40 years, with Perth's house prices dropping 5.7 per cent over the past three months. Data from property research group Cotality showed Perth's median dwelling price had fallen to $942,018 — a drop of nearly $100,000 since peaking at more than $1 million in April. Meanwhile, economists at the Commonwealth Bank today released an updated forecast predicting Perth property prices would plummet 18 per cent from that April peak, before prices begin to stabilise in the second half of 2027. For Ms Bray, the easing market spells hope of finding a home for her and her sons. Despair turns to hope for single mum on house hunting mission Analysis: Tough Christmas ahead as inflation, interest rates bite Money correspondent Jessica Irvine was down at the RBA this afternoon, going over their economic forecasts. She writes that the RBA has delivered its fifth, and potentially final, hike of the year, but it won't be an easy Christmas. Official forecasts released by the RBA on Tuesday show workers can expect their real pay packets to shrink this financial year, with wages rising just 3.4 per cent compared to a forecast 3.7 per cent rise in prices. And we'll end the calendar year with a headline inflation rate of 4.5 per cent — well above the RBA's target of 2 to 3 per cent, revised up from a previous forecast of 3.6 per cent compiled only three months ago. Mortgage minimum repayments are were already eating up 10 per cent of household disposable income ahead of this week's decision, figures from the Reserve Bank's Statement on Monetary Policy show. Once the full effect of September's and this week's rate hikes are factored into repayments, Aussie home loan payments will be sitting at the highest level since the pre-global financial crisis in late 2007 and 2008. events.title: British Gas resumes force-fitting prepay meters months after £112m settlement
events.summary: Regulators lift block on supplier, enabling it to install meters in homes of people unable to afford energy bills British Gas has resumed force-fitting prepay meters in the homes of people unable to afford their energy bills months after paying the largest settlement on record for sending debt collectors into the homes of vulnerable customers. The industry regulator has lifted a block going back almost four years that prevented British Gas from clawing back unpaid bills by fitting such meters in customers’ homes after extracting a settlement worth more than £100m from the supplier for its role in the prepay scandal at the height of the Russian gas crisis. The decision means that British Gas agents will be able to force-fit prepay meters in homes from this winter as households brace for some of the highest energy bills since 2023, when the supplier first came under fire over its treatment of vulnerable customers. Debt agents working for British Gas at the time had ignored signs of vulnerability in struggling households while fitting meters in their homes, according to an investigation by the Times, including those with severe mental health issues and physical disabilities. The scandal ignited outrage among fuel poverty campaigners and across Whitehall as the government spent billions to help cut bills for energy users and prevent a collapse of the supplier industry. Within a year of the scandal, the regulator lifted its industry-wide moratorium on force-fitting meters to allow some suppliers to restart the installations , although forced fittings in homes with young children or people over the age of 75 remain banned. The regulator said that installing a prepay meter under a warrant “should only be a last resort, with rigorous checks to ensure debt is recovered lawfully, proportionately and safely”. It said smart pay-as-you-go meters were “a positive choice for many customers, helping them stay in control of their energy use and reporting high levels of satisfaction”. Campaigners have said the timing of the change is likely to increase people’s fears of falling behind on energy bills this winter, and will add to the stress that households face. Simon Francis, a coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: “It’s almost as if regulators and ministers are failing to remember the lessons of the last energy price spike. “While more protections are now in place than in 2022, we know that magistrates are still approving bulk batches of applications for forced prepayment meter installs and some of the system failures identified in the original investigations are still happening.” British Gas defended its plan to claw back unpaid bills as household energy debt is forecast to exceed £7bn, adding more than £80 to the average household energy bill. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Our industry needs to protect and support customers who genuinely cannot afford to pay while taking appropriate action where people are able to pay but do not engage,” the company said. “We know many households are struggling with energy costs, and we offer significant support to those who need it most.” It said it planned to “engage early, offer targeted support and agree flexible, affordable repayment options” to struggling customers wherever possible, and that involuntary prepay meter fittings would “remain a last resort, with robust vulnerability and affordability checks”. Under Ofgem’s rules, all suppliers must make at least 10 attempts to contact a customer before a prepay meter is installed and carry out a welfare visit before installation. Meters should never be fitted in the homes of the highest risk customers, which include households with people over 75, under two, or those with severe health issues or medical equipment. A government spokesperson said: “This is a regulatory decision by Ofgem. We cannot allow past rogue practices to be repeated, where prepayment meters were wrongly installed in the homes of vulnerable people. We are closely watching to make sure companies protect their customers and act within Ofgem’s rules.” An Ofgem spokesperson said the regulator would continue to closely monitor suppliers and will “take action if we identify instances where our rules are not being followed”.

To model how packaging decisions impact the carbon footprint we have estimated the embodied emissions (EE) of a chiplet-based GPU that has been scaled in 2.5D and 3D using the imec netzero modeling platform. We doubled the number of compute units and high bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity in the 2.5D and 3D scaled systems and found that 3D scaling results in an 89% increase in EE, as compared to an increase of 141% for 2.5D scaling, positioning 3D scaling as an attractive solution to limit the embodied emissions due to GPU scaling.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Democrats weigh ‘lawfare’ against Trump
events.summary: David’s view Before there was the other Dan Sullivan, there was the other Mike Doyle. Four years ago, when longtime Pittsburgh Democrat Mike Doyle retired from Congress, a left-wing legislator named Summer Lee won the primary to replace him. Republicans nominated a local politician from the suburbs to face her who had a fortuitous name: Mike Doyle. Some voters were perplexed . The new Doyle’s lawn signs called him “the right Mike” without explicitly identifying him as a Republican — a moniker that would be a non-starter in the safely Democratic seat. Local Democrats got worried calls, asking why Lee was running against their beloved liberal congressman. The Democrat Doyle called an emergency press conference to clarify that he was not the Republican Doyle: “My name is on the ballot, but it’s not me.” Lee won, albeit by a smaller margin than other Democrats in her district had in the past. Nothing else came of the story. There was no federal investigation of the Doyle scheme; no demands not to seat Doyle if he won; no statement from the governor saying that he might not certify the election. All of that has unfolded in Alaska this cycle. The clandestine Democratic effort to recruit a candidate who shares the name of the state’s incumbent Republican senator could have major implications for what happens after Tuesday. The plot’s exposure damaged Democrat Mary Peltola, knocking her off-message, and now threatens her party’s chances of winning control of the Senate. President Donald Trump’s administration is investigating, and also sued to block the certification of the results should Sullivan lose — though a federal judge tossed out the suit over the weekend. Those efforts, along with the announcement of investigations into candidates within 60 days of the vote, show how the Trump administration is jettisoning unwritten norms at the Justice Department. The Alaska mess is weighing heavily on Democrats who hope to win control of Congress tomorrow. Victory in either chamber would mean a two-year license on oversight powers, empowering Democrats to subpoena the Trump administration and its allies in the private sector. There is a thirst for vengeance among some Democrats that is testing their public stance that they must restore standards blown up by Trump. There’s also a shared sense, among most Democrats, that following those standards has gotten them nothing, while Republicans have benefitted from bending the rules. “Donald Trump and [House Oversight Committee Chairman] James Comer have basically written a playbook on how to politicize investigations and attack political enemies and weaponize government,” said Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is in line to lead the House Oversight Committee in a Democratic majority. “[Attorney General] Todd Blanche? His whole job is just to grift for the president.” The argument over which party first used “lawfare” to get what it wanted is an old one. Democrats have long celebrated the Watergate investigation as an example of the Constitution and US legal system working as designed. Republicans are more likely to call the episode a coup against a president who’d just won a landslide. But the current debate begins, like so many irritating conversations, with the 2016 election. For all of Hillary Clinton’s errors, like telling coal miners that their jobs would vanish if she won, Democrats largely believe that she would have won the election against Trump had the FBI not abandoned its “60 day rule” and announced an 11th hour investigation into emails found on Huma Abedin’s laptop. Some believe that Barack Obama acted too timidly when Republicans refused to co-sign a letter warning of Russian interference in that campaign. Nobody has ever accused Trump of acting timidly. Ten years on, his Justice Department is still probing the origins of the Russia investigation into his first campaign. When Joe Biden replaced Trump, he kept on the US attorney who was investigating his son. When Trump replaced Biden, he sacked the prosecutors who’d worked on post-Jan. 6 investigations. Democrats felt like suckers. Biden publicly promised that his Justice Department would act independently. Privately, he was resentful of Attorney General Merrick Garland’s choices to hold off on investigating Trump until November 2022, after Republicans were more or less united in denouncing any Trump probe as “lawfare.” This is on many Democratic minds as they watch the Justice Department in Alaska — even though it’s not the only race where one party meddled in a way that might confuse voters. In Maine, a conservative PAC is sending out mail for a left-wing spoiler candidate for governor. In Ohio, a conservative PAC is doing the same for a socialist Senate candidate who could threaten Democrat Sherrod Brown’s chances. In Nevada, a conservative PAC… okay, you get the point. “They’re obsessed with meddling in elections,” Garcia said. “We have to put in place new rules and a new standard to get things back to a place where we don’t have the president trying to rig elections constantly.” In Pennsylvania, when I asked Gov. Josh Shapiro how Democrats should respond to Trump’s Justice Department, he was hopeful they would be the “party of law and order” — by showing that this was not the way to use the government’s bottomless resources. “I said every single day to our team and to the public that I enforce the law without fear or favor,” said Shapiro, referring to his six years as state attorney general. “That is not the case in the Trump administration.” Despite the ongoing debate of how far to go, Republicans are portraying a party intent on going after the president in order to rev up their base. “They’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress,” House Speaker Mike Johnson alleged . In reality, the impeachment articles filed by Democratic Reps. Al Green and Shri Thanedar failed to accumulate broad Democratic support, and neither man will be in Congress next year. I’d expect Democrats’ thinking to reflect what happens on Tuesday. To be sure, there will be investigations of the Trump administration and its allies. But the risk assessment of any new probe will depend on voters’ appetite for it. Voters haven’t really punished a party for launching an investigation that doesn’t go anywhere. At the same time, Trump hasn’t lost much support for pardoning corrupt politicians like Rod Blagojevich, Kwame Kilpatrick, or Chris Collins. I’m confident about one thing: No Democrat with a gavel is going to want to move on from Trump oversight. Notable For Fox News, Elaine Mallon looked at how Democratic investigations could do more financial damage to their Republican targets. In his Off Message newsletter, Brian Beutler argued that Democrats should treat Blanche’s investigations the way Trump treated Garland’s — as illegitimate electioneering.

events.title: Germany says lawmakers’ iPhones may have been hacked with spyware
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. The German government is warning politicians and public figures that they were targeted by government-backed spyware, days after Apple began sending out notifications warning victims that their iPhones may have been hacked. Germany’s federal cybersecurity office, known as the BSI, said in a note over the weekend that it had become aware that members of the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, and other unnamed notable individuals had received warnings from Apple that they may have been targeted by cyberattacks. Per the Financial Times , German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said the government in Berlin was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously,” but he did not say who in the federal government had been targeted, including whether German chancellor Friedrich Merz was among them. Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to people it thinks may have been targeted by spyware, which can steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information from their phones. This spyware often relies on zero-click exploits , which can hack individuals almost invisibly as they don’t require a victim to click on a link or open a file. Apple does not attribute attacks to specific governments or say whether someone’s phone has actually been compromised. For that reason, the BSI said that anyone who receives an Apple threat notification “should therefore assume that their device may have been compromised.” Others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple. Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, said in a post on X that he received a new threat notification warning that Apple had detected “another attack against your device,” after an earlier spyware attack targeted him in 2021. It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries. The episode highlights again the murky business behind a growing number of attacks against members of civil society. Governments rarely build these tools themselves. Many buy them from private vendors, often called “mercenary spyware” makers, the best known being Israel’s NSO Group, which sells the controversial Pegasus spyware. Germany’s own central federal law agency, the BKA, reportedly bought access to Pegasus in 2019. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Residents campaign for curfew at new Sydney airport due to noise
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Blue Mountains residents unhappy at noise from Western Sydney International Airport David Lysiak has lived in Warrimoo on the footsteps of the Blue Mountains for 44 years. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Residents living near the new Western Sydney International Airport are reporting increasing aircraft noise linked to the new Western Sydney airport. Blue Mountains resident David Lysiak says he worries about not being able to sleep at night as flights ramp up. An expert in air traffic managements says there are "no perfect options" when determining flight routes. Residents living in the Blue Mountains say they fear an end to the area's peace and quiet following last week's opening of the Western Sydney International Airport (WSI). The airport officially opened to domestic and international passengers on October 25 amid much fanfare. But a week later, concerns are being raised about aircraft noise. David Lysiak has lived in Warrimoo, a village in the lower Blue Mountains, for 44 years. Sydney's second airport officially opened on October 25. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) The retired grandfather and his wife raised four children there, and they have always loved the tranquillity. "It's just beautiful, quiet. Not many people. We have one shop, a general store," he said. "I just wander into the bush and go for a bushwalk, and take your bike down the trails … You ride through a blue gum forest and it's all accessible right from here." But he fears the serenity of the last four decades could be a thing of the past because his beloved town falls under the WSI flight path. Mr Lysiak is concerned for the future of Warrimoo. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Freight flights began operating from the airport around the clock in July. Mr Lysiak said he has heard the noise of some freight aircraft "quite distinctly". That sound is only going to become more frequent . International airlines Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, Fiji Airways, Qatar Airways and Vietjet Air have so far signed up with WSI, with flights expected to ramp up over the next couple of years. The airport has one active runway. ( Supplied: Australian government ) WSI has one runway, designated as Runway 05 or Runway 23, depending on the direction of use. Flights on Runway 23 arrive from the north-east and depart to the south-west over areas in the city's west and Blue Mountains. Flights on Runway 23 arrive from the north-east and depart to the south-west. ( Supplied: Australian government ) When Runway 05 is used, flights take off to the north-east and land from the south-west. Flights take off to the north-east and land from the south-west when Runway 05 is operational. ( Supplied: Australian government ) Weighing up if a trip from Sydney's new airport is for you The doors to Western Sydney International Airport are set to soon welcome commercial passengers. Airservices Australia has previously said that, where possible, Runway 23 would be prioritised during the day to minimise overflight and noise over residential suburbs to the north-east of the airport. Marek Bekier, a lecturer in air traffic management at the University of New South Wales School of Aviation, said there were always "trade-offs" when deciding on the best flight paths. "An air route connecting an airport to the wider airway system is not just a straight line in the sky," he said. "You have to think about it as a kind of three dimensional corridor that has to fulfil certain requirements. "No option is perfect. You will never find a new route that will basically satisfy the wishes and demands of everyone, so you always have to make some trade-offs." Community treated as 'collateral damage' Julius Timmerman, who moved to the Blue Mountains town of Lawson with his wife in 1996, said people in his community had been treated as "collateral damage". "I'm worried about not being able to sleep at night, just the effect on my amenity because we bought a house in the mountains in good faith that the area would remain quiet and peaceful," he said. "It's completely unfair that the people of Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains should be just treated as collateral damage for the sake of the airline industry." Julius Timmerman says he bought his house in the area thinking it would be quiet. ( Supplied ) He is one of hundreds of people in the community who want a rethink of the flight paths and have signed the Western Sydney Airport Community Impacts Alliance petition calling for a night-time curfew. "The main thing that we want is, as mentioned in the petition, a curfew from 11pm to 6am, which lines up with Kingston Smith Airport," he said.

events.title: Web host Squarespace lays off 19% of its employees
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Squarespace, the web company that helps customers build and host their own websites, is laying off about one-fifth of its workforce, in a move that will affect hundreds of jobs. Jeff Seedman, a public relations specialist representing Squarespace, confirmed the layoffs to TechCrunch. The Verge initially reported the layoffs. “Squarespace is restructuring its organization and reducing its global workforce by approximately 19%, representing around 300 employees,” said Seedman. “The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth.” Website building has changed immensely over the last few years as a result of the generative AI boom. “Vibe-coding” website builders, which only require simple prompts from users to spin up functional front-end designs, have largely upended the industry, making it possible for users to create sites with significantly less effort. These kinds of sites have become an increasingly central part of the website-building business. Last year, web host rival Wix bought Base44 for $80 million . Similar offerings, like Lovable, have generated significant investor interest; Lovable raised a $400 million Series C round in August that valued the company at $13.3 billion. Google also recently launched Stitch , a feature that allows users to swiftly generate user-interface designs. Squarespace has also begun a big push into AI. In 2024, the company launched an AI tool called Blueprint. The company also recently announced Forma, an upcoming AI native platform, whose waitlist users can join . Squarespace was founded in 2004 and went public in 2021 at a $10 billion valuation. However, the company struggled in the ensuing years to generate enthusiastic public market interest. Squarespace ultimately decided to go private again by way of a $7 billion private equity deal in 2024. An earlier version of this report incorrectly stated that Squarespace had not yet launched AI tools; the story has been updated. events.title: Hardware Defense Blocks Memory-Dependent Prefetcher Leakage (KU Leuven)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at KU Leuven and EURECOM published “SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching.” Abstract Excerpt : “In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture—without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.” Find the technical paper here . The New York Times sued Brave, the 11-year-old, privacy-focused browser company, on Monday, alleging it scraped the outlet’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Separately on Monday, the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel filed a similar lawsuit. Both were brought in federal court in Manhattan. The New York Times, which has also sued OpenAI and Perplexity over similar claims, likens Brave to a “supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content” for AI companies. “In this way, Brave acts both like a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers, and an AI ‘fence’ that sells stolen content to third parties,” the suit reads. It says Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages using an unidentified crawler, leaving publishers unable to block it. The suit also targets a Brave browser feature that bypasses paywalls and the company’s practice of blocking publishers’ ads while selling its own. Founded in 2015, Brave has raised roughly $250 million to date, according to private-market trackers. The Times seeks an injunction and damages. Brave did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
