events.title: 42AI comes out of stealth with $62.5M and a world model that can ‘predict human behavior’
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation? Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand. “A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision. 42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks. “When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.” “So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added. The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions.) Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured. 42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said. In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity. In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly. He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.) And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague. Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.

events.title: OPay’s US IPO withdrawal casts shadow over African fintech
events.summary: The News OPay’s abrupt withdrawal of its $304 million US IPO on Friday cast a shadow over one of Africa’s most ambitious fintech listings, after an undisclosed foreign regulatory inquiry derailed its New York debut. On Friday, OPay had priced its American depositary shares at $19 each, the bottom of its target range, valuing the company at just over $4 billion. But trading never began: OPay and its underwriters terminated their agreement around 3.30 pm New York time, saying it was no longer prudent to proceed with the offering. OPay, which primarily operates its payments service in Nigeria, did not identify the regulator or specify the subject of the inquiry. It described the jurisdiction involved as “immaterial to its core business” and said it expected the inquiry to be “concluded satisfactorily in the near future.” The withdrawal represents a setback for Nigeria’s fintech sector and the wider African startup ecosystem, which has spent years trying to persuade global investors that its young companies can scale into major, publicly listed businesses that return funds to investors. Know More OPay, which launched in 2018 as a payments company, also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge. A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bank’s Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPay’s board following the IPO. The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances, and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bank’s infrastructure, regulatory expertise, and presence to expand across Africa.

events.title: Following a sudden GOP slide, a top data scientist’s model gives Democrats 90% odds of taking the Senate as Kansas trends blue in major shock
events.summary: Data scientist Thomas Miller’s site handicapping outcomes for the U.S. Senate races now shows overwhelming odds that the Democrats will take control, numbers much more commanding than even the polls and prediction markets are showing. As of around 9 a.m. ET on Monday, Miller’s site, Virtualtout.io, gave the Democrats a 90% chance of winning at least 51 seats. In recent days, the GOP’s chances of keeping control of the upper chamber have virtually collapsed, dropping from 23% on Oct. 26 to under 10% now. A major reason from the quick downdraft, and a sign of the blue wave’s strength: Democrats now hold the lead in longtime red stronghold Kansas, and have turned Iowa into a virtual toss-up. Miller, a professor at Northwestern University, won kudos for correctly forecasting that Democrats would sweep the two Georgia Senate runoffs in early 2021, when the polls and pundits posited GOP wins in both. He scored again by calling a Trump win in 2024. His methodology: Miller starts by incorporating the “prices” posted on the two prediction markets boasting the highest volumes, Kalshi and Polymarket, and translates those numbers into probabilities of a Democrat or Republican win. He then deploys multiple time series that examine 10 to 12 underlying factors that drive the prediction markets, and continually crunches the numbers to forecast their impact going forward. Miller updates the probabilities every 10 minutes, and the numbers stream across the top of Virtualtout.io in a continuous band resembling a stock ticker. The NowCast also displays the change over the last 24 hours. Hence, his figures are far more current than the polls. “They all relate to voters’ perception of the performance of the Trump administration,” Miller told Fortune . “That’s the thread running through all the races. The factors include affordability, the economy, and the war in Iran, the issues that motivate voters. The states don’t move independently of one another. When voters’ view of those issues turns more negative, the Republican numbers drop on all the races.” In other words, Trump has effectively nationalized the battle for the U.S. Senate. Miller added that the impact of Trump’s tireless stumping is harder to assess. “People have come to expect certain things from Trump,” he said. “The way he behaves is not a surprise, it’s a continuous thing.” Most of what the president says on the Senate campaign trail, according to Miller, simply reinforces the view of Trump and his party that voters already hold. “Still, there’s no evidence he’s helping,” Miller said. “It doesn’t appear that his appearances are a positive.” One instance where his model found that Trump’s rhetoric backfired: The POTUS’s defense of the ad Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy ran in Ohio featuring the mother of his Democratic opponent Amy Acton severely criticizing her daughter. “Following Trump’s praise of the ad, we saw a huge drop in the Republican percentage,” Miller noted. Republican numbers have dropped big-time in almost all the key races He pointed out that in the last 10 days, “a lot of contests are moving a little bit” in the Democratic direction from day to day, but the cumulative gains are substantial. In the five elections where the Democrats have long harbored chances for a flip, the GOP stands below 30% in all of them, from a high of 28.4% in Alaska to a low of 2% in North Carolina. The Republicans’ best chance comes in Maine, where incumbent Susan Collins sits at 34.7%. In Michigan, the probability of a Republican flip via beating Abdul El-Sayed has faded from over one-third in mid-September to a current count of 24.5%. The Miller model now points to high possibility of Democratic wins in states that, until a few days ago, the GOP counted on as surely in their column. “Those are the races I’ve been watching closely, and the move toward the Democrats in the last few days is surprising a lot of people,” says Miller. In the Iowa run for an open seat, Republican Ashley Hinson held an almost 62% shot at victory as of Sept. 17. Now, she’s dropped to 51.6% as her opponent Josh Turek pulls almost even. In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall looked on track for easy reelection just two months ago at around 75%. His number’s dipped to 43.9% and suffered a 7.1% drop just in the past 24 hours. Miller highlighted that Virtualtout.io and its NowCast will keep running all through Election Day, and will be first to call races, mainly based on its analysis of the swings in the betting odds. Of course, the Republicans could hang on by keeping Kansas and Iowa, winning Maine where their odds are still decent, and defying the probabilities in Texas or one other key state. It’s a narrow path that in recent days now looks far narrower as Midwestern strongholds swing blue. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ryanair CEO anticipates European airfare prices up as much as 20% next year
events.summary: The CEO for Ryanair expects European airfare prices may climb as much as 20% next year as jet fuel prices rise The CEO for Ryanair expects European plane ticket prices may climb as much as 20% next year with the conflict in the Middle East ongoing. “So we’re facing 2027 where we have much higher oil prices... I think they’re going to get passed on in significantly higher airfares,” CEO Michael O’Leary said in a Monday interview on CNBC. The price of jet fuel has been extremely volatile after the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran . Jet fuel has risen even faster than oil during the war, reflecting both higher crude prices and tight supplies of the refined fuel that is one of the largest operating expenses for airlines. Carriers have cut some less profitable flights and raised fares and baggage fees, although major U.S. airlines said higher passenger revenue initially covered only part of their soaring fuel costs. Globally, jet fuel averaged about $99 a barrel on Feb. 27, the day before the war began , according to the International Air Transport Association’s Jet Fuel Price Monitor. Prices more than doubled to $209 by early April, fell for nearly three months and reached $195 a barrel in mid-September following their renewed ascent, IATA said, citing data from S & P Global Energy Platts. The global average jet fuel price is currently hovering around $196 a barrel. The IATA expects fuel to account for nearly one-third of airline operating expenses this year, up from about a quarter in 2025. Ryanair said Monday that it doesn't expect European short haul airfares to fully offset anticipated increases in its fuel bill for next year, so it is reviewing its costs and may have to impose temporary pay freezes, lower crew ratios and use more artificial intelligence to get further productivity for back office and support functions. events.title: Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges
events.summary: Victim organizations are losing millions of dollars in token charges as criminals hijack their corporate LLM access to steal expensive computing resources and AI services. These fraudulent charges from resource consumption can exceed $100,000 a day, according to a Monday report by Google's Mandiant incident responders, who saw cumulative charges at some organizations hit $1 million before the victim companies revoked intruders' access. "Whenever possible, threat actors want to use this technology to gain a scale advantage over defenders. They achieve that with agentic tools and by stealing tokens from unwitting third parties,” John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told The Register . “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks.” This tactic of hijacking access to LLMs is called LLMJacking , and it’s been increasing steadily over the past two years. In one extreme case, documented in an August report from CrowdStrike, a token thief sent about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. In one case detailed in the report, a group Google tracks as UNC6993 illicitly gained access to LLM API keys, then generated additional keys and enabled services within the victim’s cloud projects, racking up $100,000 in charges. The threat intel biz also documented a different token thief subscribing victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements to access advanced models on the victim company’s dime. The crook selected premium foundation models, launched high-volume inference streams, and used a “burn and rotate strategy” to bypass rate limits by creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the billing interface to monitor financial impact. In yet another incident, an intruder executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours using stolen third-party API keys to power a token routing service called Jet Night, according to a Monday report from Google. “Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably,” the report says. “For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month.” Jet Night has also admitted to multiple outages on its public Telegram channel, which the Google threat hunters note is “likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises.” Specialized LLMjacking roles As more criminals join the LLMJacking ecosystem, Google says it has documented a division of labor between the criminals that establish initial access to compromised cloud and AI services, and those that manage downstream monetization infrastructure, called “LLM Mixers.” In one case that Mandiant responded to in mid-2026, UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used this access to grant further access to a model API. The crooks also spun up a session hijacking page purporting to be an application portal to join a group of LLM users. “This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls,” the report says. Google predicts miscreants will “increasingly prioritize LLMJacking” compared to other types of resource theft like cryptojacking. And to prevent cloud LLM service abuse, the security firm says defenders should prioritize identity and access management plus supply chain security, and use a centralized secrets management platform to rotate keys and secrets. Also apply least-access privileges to users and service accounts, ensuring that they only have permissions necessary to complete their roles and tasks. And automate secrets scanning within codebases to identify and then remove any API keys and secrets added to source code. ®

events.title: SUSE to cut one in ten employees because of... AI
events.summary: One in ten employees at SUSE are facing the chop due to "automation and AI," according to a memo dispatched by management at the privately owned open source software biz. In an email to the 1,900 strong workforce on Monday - seen by The Register - CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen, the former Red Hat exec who joined SUSE in March 2023, confirmed the "difficult news." "We are announcing a reduction of SUSE’s global workforce of approximately 10 percent," he said. "These decisions are painful for our people, our culture, and our open source community, but they are necessary for us to adapt and build a sustainable, resilient SUSE for the long term." Van Leeuwen says the business, bought by Swedish private equity provider EQT, decided to cut jobs after scrutinizing its "future strategy, required capabilities, and team structures." The rest of the organization will get a look at the fiscal year 2027 strategy on November 16. He said in the message to staff: "What is clear is that automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate. AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work. We have seen this trend already both inside our sector and in the wider economy. This means that the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully. "We are adapting. Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years. This means we are accelerating investments in high priority areas, and deprioritizing others. These are hard, painful decisions to make, but necessary for our future." As The Reg reported in 2025, SUSE doubled down on AI . The specific roles at risk of redundancy were not outlined but SUSE claims it has considered where the people in those positions are "able to evolve, what they can stop doing, what they need to do more of - and decisions have been made on that basis." Staff caught up in the redundancies will be informed by November 4, employee representatives nominated the following day, and one to one meetings will begin at the start of next week. Van Leeuwen says in the internal memo that the job cuts are a "reflection of shifting organizational needs, not your talent or commitment. You have tackled hard infrastructure and open source challenges that power critical enterprise systems around the world. "Any organization will be fortunate to have your expertise." Back in September, we reported that the company was asking old hands if they would take "voluntary separation ." It seems not enough people chose to walk through the door, so instead, they're getting thrown through it instead. SUSE "geckos" in the Czech Republic may be glad they joined a trade union . Back in 2018, EQT bought SUSE from Microfocus for $2.5 billion. EQT floated SUSE on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange in 2021 with slightly disappointing results . A couple of years later, new CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen took over , and later in 2023, EQT chose to take the company private again . The commercial context is that in March SUSE's corporate owner EQT was reportedly considering selling it off again. ®

events.title: Nuclear threats and street brawls: Russia, Ukraine report attacks on their emergency alert apps
events.summary: Cyberattacks on both Russia’s and Ukraine’s emergency alert apps resulted in fake messages about missile and nuclear strikes broadcast to the public. Officials from both countries confirmed the attacks, which occurred at similar times, on Sunday evening. According to public statements and messages sent via social media, Ukraine’s alert app was hit first, with the country’s Air Force quick to dispel nuclear fears. "The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," it said via Telegram at around 2100 UTC. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel!" At around 0030 UTC on Monday, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations confirmed the country’s app had also been abused, with fake messages sent to citizens' devices. "Attention! The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," it said, also via Telegram. "Work is currently underway to patch the vulnerability and restore normal operation." The ministry issued an update around 90 minutes later, saying the app was once again functioning normally, and pointing out that an attack on the app was not the same as a compromise of the state’s national alert system. "Citizens are alerted through primary channels: regional and municipal alert systems (sirens, loudspeakers), communication networks (SMS messaging), and television and radio broadcasts. The mobile app is merely an additional, supporting information service," it stated. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Affairs also issued a public announcement reminding citizens about how to receive emergency warnings while its “Alarm!” app was down. These include enabling iOS and Android emergency alerts, state-controlled sirens, and other official sources, such as the official social media accounts of Ukraine's government. According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical attacks, and radiation hazards. Alerts about the threat of nuclear fallout from official government warning systems would normally lead to panic, however, one of the earliest messages sent to citizens was written in Russian and referenced the "Oreshnik" missile, which was an immediate signal that the message may not be genuine. Equivalent alerts sent to Russian citizens also warned of impending nuclear strikes "at all regions of Russia," referencing "P1-Sun," the name of a Ukrainian attack drone. Oleksander Merezhko, who chairs the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee and noted the suspicious Russian-language alert, told the BBC the attack was almost certainly part of Russia's cyber war . "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that," he said. "It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities." Russia has not explicitly blamed Ukraine for the attack on its app, and official sources say the app is running as normal. Ukraine's announcement of the alert app cyberattack came almost simultaneously with the official conclusion of a six-day ceasefire in Kherson. Russia agreed to the rare temporary suspension of conflict to allow hundreds of Ukrainians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Olehsky. Russia did not agree to a proposed extension of the ceasefire, which officially ended at around 2100 UTC – around the same time Ukrainians began receiving fake warning messages. ®

events.title: Tomb Raider’s creators on how the game changed their lives: ‘Skint staff were suddenly pulling up in sports cars’
events.summary: ‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’ Paul Douglas, lead programmer and co-creator I joined Core Design in the summer of 1994 and met Toby Gard, who showed me his concept sketches for Tomb Raider . He’d already come up with the title and drawn a mock-up box cover with a woman holding two pistols. I was working on a golf game called The Scottish Open when Toby persuaded me that we should pitch his idea to Jeremy Heath-Smith, Core’s co-founder, who gave us the go-ahead to make a prototype. If I had stuck to the golf game, I would have had a much easier life. We had a couple of brainstorming sessions, and settled on the game’s four main pillars: platforming, puzzles, combat and story. Combat was always the weakest element but we didn’t have time to improve it. We also came up with the plot and level themes, and whittled a long list of interesting archaeological locations, including Petra and Angkor Wat, down to four: Peru, Greece, Egypt and Atlantis. Lara was originally Latina and her appearance was more realistic, almost androgynous. We felt that more stylised movement would play better, so her physique changed to reflect that. She became a British mercenary and then, thanks to scriptwriter Vicky Arnold, an aristocrat who tracks down historical artefacts just for fun. Toby and I came up with the movement metrics by measuring out a hopscotch grid in the car park. Lara was three paces tall and each block in the game’s environment was four paces. All of the gameplay systems grew from those measurements and constraints. It was brutal getting it delivered on time. I took just three days of holiday in two years. Toby and I were in the office until 2 or 3am every day, including weekends, for the best part of a year. Toby made himself sick with the stress. We were on the cusp of 3D games going mainstream and the action-adventure focus made us somewhat unique. Then the marketability of Lara thrust Tomb Raider into the stratosphere. The game’s publisher, Eidos Interactive, took the character and ran with it. I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of the way Lara was sexualised. We never imagined Tomb Raider would blow up in the way it did. It was the right time, right place, and it was different from the competition. We showed that ideas that go against conventional wisdom – a female character will never sell! – can uncover new territory and find success. It was gratifying and humbling to see our hard work rewarded by so many people playing the game. We managed to bottle lightning, although I’m still carrying the scars of its creation. We developed most of Tomb Raider in a big Victorian building on Ashbourne Road in Derby. We sat there sweating our guts out in the summer and freezing cold in the winter. I was the only female developer, but that didn’t faze me. I felt respected and was almost seen as a sister by some – the team was like a family. It was a defining time in my life. Toby was lovely. Very eccentric and a bit of a genius. He’d put together a demo that was like a simple top-down version of Prince of Persia, with an Indiana Jones-like character jumping and tumbling from platforms. Although management thought no one would want to play a female character, they went with it. There’s a certain empathy you get from playing Lara. It’s probably the number of times she dies and that awful scream. She was taciturn and mysterious: a loner who played her own game and didn’t answer to anybody. Women hadn’t really been portrayed like that before. Giving Lara pistols enabled us to show off her acrobatic movement. She was mostly pursued by animals rather than people. Hearing a bat, or the growl of a bear, was much scarier than a gunshot. You felt at the mercy of the wild. And we pushed the 3D environment to its limits. We only had so much memory and processor speed, but we were clever with it, giving players the sense that they were in this vast, cavernous space that was actually lots of rooms bolted together. Before designing a level, we always had a team meeting where we’d come up with a rough schematic. We all enjoyed history. We chucked in whatever myths and legends we thought would be fun and interesting. Our imaginations ran wild – to the point where we threw a T rex into Peru! Eidos saw the potential of Lara, rather than the game, so they focused on her. That was the right thing to do, but I think it went a bit too far with what she was wearing or the poses she was put in for some marketing campaigns. They showed a lack of imagination by oversexualising her. I knew we’d made a great game, but it didn’t really sink in until I saw the sales figures. It was life-changing for all of us. People who were skint before were suddenly pulling up in sports cars. I was able to buy a house from the royalties. Lara is right up there with iconic characters such as Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog.

events.summary: African lenders launched a $5 billion energy bank focused on oil and gas projects, as the continent tries to break its costly dependence on fuel imports. The continent requires an estimated $200 billion annually in energy investment, according to the African Export-Import Bank and the African Petroleum Producers’ Organisation. It will support projects across the energy value chain, including exploration ​and production, as well as ​refining ⁠and distribution. events.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman does deals in Abu Dhabi amid fundraising
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is in Abu Dhabi, where he secured contracts to deploy AI products across government, the oil sector, and sovereign wealth management. The deals come as the ChatGPT maker is reportedly looking to lock down a mega funding round ahead of an IPO. The biggest of the four agreements is with ADNOC, which will deploy OpenAI’s Frontier platform for building and managing AI agents. The multi-year deal, signed with G42 subsidiary Inception42, will link decisions across oilfield development, production, refining, and trading, and will run on G42 infrastructure in the UAE. No financial terms were disclosed. The Abu Dhabi government is also working with OpenAI to make some of its policies readable by AI agents. Separately, Mubadala will apply OpenAI’s models to analyze potential deals. A consortium of UAE backers, including Mubadala-backed MGX, is expected to be the largest investor in OpenAI’s latest funding round — launched after the company delayed its IPO — and will get an option to lease new computing capacity in the region, the Financial Times reported. Altman’s appearance at ADIPEC is notable not only because Exxon and Chevron executives skipped this year over security concerns. His visit also comes as the AI industry faces power constraints amid the massive data center build-out. Asked onstage about his biggest challenge, Altman had a one-word answer: “Energy.” AI models will become more efficient and cheaper to deploy, he said, but the power needed to run them could keep costs high and slow down growth. — Kelsey Warner

events.title: Microsoft's Canada timezone troubles leave admins fixing calendars, pretending they're in Bogota
events.summary: Microsoft has discovered once again that few things strike fear into the heart of a software engineer quite like a government deciding to fiddle with the clocks. Parts of Canada stopped observing seasonal clock changes on November 1, leaving affected areas of British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba permanently on UTC-07:00, UTC-06:00 and UTC-05:00 respectively. Unfortunately, Microsoft's sprawling software empire hasn't entirely caught up. The company has confirmed problems across a chunk of its software estate, leaving some customers facing incorrect times, broken schedules and a collection of workarounds while Redmond catches up. Outlook users have been left with the most homework. Switching to the new Canadian time zones won't automatically update existing calendar entries, meaning that meetings scheduled after November 1 are potentially an hour out of whack. Microsoft advises users to change their Outlook calendar time zone, then update upcoming events and meetings to use it. For meetings involving other people, only the organizer can make the change. Recurring meetings come with an additional treat: changing the time zone resets any previously moved occurrences, which then have to be recreated. Anyone with a calendar full of recurring meetings may wish to put the kettle on first. Microsoft is working on an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet to remediate non-recurring meetings, but according to its guidance, that's not due until later this week. A fix for recurring meetings remains "in development," with an ETA yet to be confirmed. Things get stranger with Power Automate and Fabric, where Microsoft's temporary fix involves pretending you're somewhere else entirely. Depending on the product and province, that could mean Saskatchewan, Arizona or, for Manitobans, Bogota. Because apparently time zones weren't confusing enough already. SharePoint On-Prem customers, meanwhile, have to wait until November 10 for the correct time zones to arrive, while Power Pages users could see server-formatted dates appear an hour out until a service fix lands. Microsoft's current milestone for that is December 12. Admins dealing with the fallout aren't exactly delighted. One sysadmin on Reddit said Microsoft's guidance had been "terrible" and claimed to have written roughly 900 lines of PowerShell to change users' Outlook settings and manually adjust calendar events. Others described switching systems to Saskatchewan time while waiting for Microsoft's new zones to settle in. Microsoft published its guidance on October 26, less than a week before the change took effect, and was still adding affected products and workarounds four days later. Meanwhile, admins were urged to test calendars, recurring meetings, and schedules before the November 1 switch, leaving little time to find out what might break. If any of this sounds familiar, it's because time has caused trouble for Microsoft before . In 2022, Chile delayed its switch to daylight saving time by a week. Microsoft responded by warning that Windows clocks could be wrong, scheduled tasks could run at unexpected times, and timestamps on files, transactions, and logs could end up an hour out. Four years later, governments are still messing with time and software is still apparently objecting. ®

events.title: Gulf states united in call for diplomacy to end war
events.summary: Gulf officials at a summit in Bahrain talked up the need for diplomacy to solve the region’s security crisis, yet a sense of helplessness hung over the atmosphere. Unlike at the beginning of the year, when messages coming out of the Gulf were less aligned, officials and diplomats at the Manama Dialogue supported Qatar-led mediation efforts with Iran and were clearly against the US attacking it again, concerned that renewed bombing would lead to even more destructive consequences for their countries. There was, however, hardly any US presence to hear that message. The Gulf’s primary security partner sent its smallest delegation to the event in years, despite Bahrain hosting the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. “People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region,” Saudi Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Waleed Elkhereiji said, while also emphasizing that the kingdom was investing to boost its defense and deterrence capabilities. Urging diplomacy while also preparing for conflict is a reflection that the most consequential decisions for the Gulf are now being made elsewhere, and all it can do is steel itself for the fallout. Gulf countries “don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region,” said Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president. “But we are braced for the worst.” — Matthew Martin

events.title: Poundland's former owner offers to invest as minister prepares to meet board
events.summary: Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm Poundland has been given until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk. Poundland's founder has said he would invest in the firm and a government minister said she would meet the firm's board amid its administration fears. Steve Smith, who set-up the Walsall-based business, said he had attempted to contact owners Gordon Brothers having been "really surprised" to learn about them filing for administration when sales were up 11% on last year. The BBC understands that Business Minister Kate Dearden will meet with senior Poundland executives later this week to discuss the company's threatened insolvency. US-based Gordon Brothers said it was evaluating interest for the whole business and formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of it. Gordon Brothers, who bought the firm from Polish retail group Pepco last year for £1, has stopped funding the business and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG). The retailer has given the business until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk. Steven Smith founded Poundland in 1990 with the help of his father, Kevin Smith It's understood the meeting with Deardon will be predominantly a "fact finding" meeting with government sources conceding there is limited scope for the government to intervene in a commercial transaction albeit one that puts over 10,000 jobs and hundreds of stores at risk. The meeting was first reported by Sky News. There is no current meeting planned between the government and executives from current owners, US private equity group Gordon Brothers. Concerns have been raised that Gordon Brothers have declined an offer from another buyer to keep Poundland afloat in order to ensure repayment of £30 million loan it inherited after buying the company for £1. 'Poundland closure would leave a void in our town' Published 3 days ago How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant Published 4 days ago Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators Published 4 days ago Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government was "ready to support" staff as he also called for answers over why an offer to buy the business had been rejected. Smith, from Wolverhampton and who set up the firm in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, said he contacted the owners over the last three months but had no reply. He had thought that was good news as he assumed the firm must have had offers on the table. "And maybe I was a bit too late, but I'd certainly... with talking to the staff and how Poundland's performing at the moment, I'd certainly, if there's an opportunity, I definitely want to put some money back in there." He said he was still in touch with staff there at levels within the business and "even last week" sales were 11.2 % upon last year. "Although Poundland made a loss last year, they're going to make a good profit this year, so it's just crazy." Staff held a protest outside Poundland's Walsall-based HQ last week He warned that the two or three thousand suppliers to the firm only worked for Poundland so they would be directly affected by its collapse. "This is not just about 12, 000 jobs. I'm estimating more like 20 or 30,000 jobs," he added. The company has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and Smith said it had between four and five million customers a week, so with Poundland not being present on high streets would "cause a lot of other retailers to fall as well". Liam Byrne, chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee and Labour MP for Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North, said he felt the company could be saved and "the whole deal stinks to high heaven right now". "Because I think the issue that we've got is, you've got an owner that could well be trying to cut and run, to sell a business that is in fact a going concern in order to maximize their own profits and put in jeopardy 12,000 British jobs on the high street." "Our message today to government and to ministers is, do not leave this to the last minute, which is Thursday... please get on the case now to get everybody around the table to maximize every option to save as much of the business as possible," he added. In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it had not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole". "We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment." Gordon Brothers said: "While Martin Property Group had been identified as the preferred bidder by Poundland's management team, attention must now turn to other active bids." The interest, formal and indicative offers were being evaluated "with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders.

events.summary: Abu Dhabi Investment Authority , the emirate's sovereign wealth fund, has teamed up with aviation finance company Avolon and infrastructure investor I Squared Capital to launch an aircraft leasing infrastructure investment platform . The new platform, Constellation Aviation, will provide airlines with access to fleet capacity and investors with exposure to long-term contracted cash flows, the companies said in a statement on Monday. Once the transaction is completed, Constellation is expected to acquire a seed portfolio of aircraft from Avolon with a current market value of $1.4 billion. The seed portfolio includes 22 aircraft with an average age of about five years, on lease to 17 airlines in 15 countries. Constellation is expected to scale over time, the companies said. “Aircraft leasing is a resilient and growing sector supported by strong structural demand for modern aircraft,” said Khadem AlRemeithi, executive director of the infrastructure department at Adia. Adia, which does not disclose its assets, invests on behalf of the Abu Dhabi government and is the largest sovereign wealth fund in the Gulf, with assets touching $1.1 trillion, according to consultancy Global SWF. The authority makes direct and indirect investments in asset classes including equities, fixed income, infrastructure, private equity and property across continents. The sovereign investor said in September that it aimed to diversify its approach across sectors to manage risks. The aviation market is growing amid a continued rise in passenger demand, but airlines continue to face aircraft supply shortages and delivery delays, driving demand for leased aircraft to finance fleet renewal and expansion. In July, plane lessor Dubai Aerospace Enterprise (DAE) partnered with US-based Neuberger Specialty Finance to launch Mustang Aerospace , an aircraft leasing co-investment vehicle targeting up to $6 billion in assets over the medium term. DAE in April also agreed with Blackstone Credit & Insurance to launch a platform that will invest $1.6 billion annually to build a portfolio of commercial aircraft. “Aircraft manufacturers’ order books now stretch a decade or more into the future, and airlines rely on lessors with scale and aircraft delivery slots to grow their fleets,” said Gautam Bhandari, co-founder, managing partner and global chief investment officer of I Squared Capital . “Avolon has one of the largest order books with Boeing and Airbus and thus enjoys significant benefits of scale.” Avolon will retain a minority equity interest in the joint venture and serve as Constellation's exclusive aircraft manager and servicer, the statement said. The joint venture will be supported by a syndicated debt facility provided by a group of international banks.

events.title: Frozen part II: Hackers remotely defrost produce in Euro supermarkets ... again
events.summary: The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food wastage as a result of miscreants raising the temperatures to highs of 50ºC (122°F). In Belgium, around 40 Delhaize stores were affected after the attackers reportedly switched fridges and freezers into defrost mode overnight, between Sunday and Monday, resulting in stock issues. Diego Louwers, a Proxy Delhaize store manager in Overijse, near Brussels, told RTL Info that the consequences of the cyberattacks were "catastrophic," forcing the store to throw out the entirety of its fresh and frozen products. "We can't have anything worse in our line of work," he said. "We have to throw away all of our merchandise, and it's both heartbreaking and very complicated operationally." A Delhaize spokesperson said it took steps to ensure stores remain stocked, although fresh and frozen products are "temporarily somewhat limited." "On Monday, 2 November, we identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen of our stores," they said. "We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational and ensure that our customers can continue to do their shopping as usual. "In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centres are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores. "We are, of course, continuing to ensure that our products are stored and presented under optimal conditions, so that we can provide our customers with the quality and freshness they have come to expect from us." Around 15 Carrefour stores are also reportedly affected, as are sites operated by Intermarché, Spar, and Shop & Go stores located at Q8 service stations. Belgium’s De Laet & Van Haver chain of butcher shops reported temperature rises in its appliances too, but followed up with a statement on Monday saying there was no impact on its produce, and all stores remain open. Simultaneously, similar issues have affected Swedish grocery chain ICA, which confirmed attacks on a "small number of stores." "We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network," a company spokesperson said. "The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation." ICA did not respond to questions about the scale of food wastage nor when normal operations are expected to continue. One store, ICA Nära in Böda on Öland, said via social media that it is open today but has no fresh or frozen produce to sell. "Unfortunately, we are one of the stores whose refrigerators and freezers have been hacked," it said. "We are open as usual, but unfortunately we have no refrigerators and freezers to sell. "We have no status on when the refrigerators and freezers are expected to be up and running again." The store manager, Mats Olsson, told SVT that he arrived to work on Monday morning and was greeted by a puddle of water and freezers set to 55 degrees C – a tale echoed by other managers across the country. Coop stores are affected by similar attacks too, with six locations in central Sweden experiencing fridge-freezer issues, according to a company spokesperson. Likewise, at least 13 SuperValue stores in Ireland are also affected, with fresh and frozen food being thrown out, according to parent company Musgrave speaking to RTE . The news comes less than a month after various grocery chains in France resorted to discarding bucketfuls of produce after their appliances were remotely defrosted by cybercrooks . Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others were hit with cyberattacks in mid-October, and hundreds of stores across the chains were reportedly impacted. At least some of the affected stores were running outdated firmware on their Danfoss refrigeration controllers, and shortly after the attacks were confirmed, CERT-FR published an alert pertaining to numerous Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controller compromises . Other retailers, such as Coopérative U, confirmed they were not Danfoss customers. It remains unclear if the latest attacks across Europe used the same methods as those used for the disruption in France last month. None of the companies that spoke to The Register on Monday responded to questions about who was behind the intrusions. ®

events.title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
events.summary: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%. That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work. Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it. HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships. Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice. Build for adoption, not rationing Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code. As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them. events.title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts. This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process . —Grace Huckins Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. events.title: Getting a big head start on holiday shopping can benefit retailers and consumers alike
events.summary: Does it make sense to wait until late December to wrap up, like these California shoppers did in 2023? Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Amazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October . But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping. As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions , I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping. Why retailers get such an early start Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S. Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey . But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween . Some do this out of necessity : They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks. For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually . In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping. Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds . And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season. A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics , since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs. Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October. Early birds could buy these Christmas decorations at a discount on Oct. 17, 2026. Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies . Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees. In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1. Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas. The timing of holiday shopping varies whether you buy gifts online or in brick-and-mortar stores. Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images When buying early makes financial sense Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary. For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price. But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out. And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items. Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget , recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping. James Malm does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: ‘Bragawatts’ and why all data-center investing isn’t created equal
events.summary: The News For all the talk of AI bubbles and market crashes, Scandinavian private-equity giant EQT says it’s making a bet that regardless of what happens with the frontier labs, AI is still going to need a massive amount of power, energy, chips, and data centers. “All of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now,” said Jean Salata, global chair of EQT, which has $400 billion in assets under management. “A lot of people went out and signed tons of contracts with anybody — they call them ‘bragawatts.’ But signing something and delivering it on time, and with power connected, are two very different things,” Salata said. “Sophisticated investors understand that, but there’s a lot of things happening in the public markets where people are investing in things that they really don’t understand.” EQT is a unique animal in an industry where exits have dried up, a generational bet on software companies looks vulnerable to AI, and higher interest rates have broken the math of cheap leverage and multiple expansion. Since 2018, PE firms have asked their investors for $1.5 trillion more capital than they’ve given back, and the industry is sitting on nearly $4 trillion worth of businesses it can’t sell. EQT has largely stayed out of the private credit and insurance boom that has turned its US rivals into asset-gathering giants — a “beta business,” said Salata, an artisanally crafted Wall Street dig. And it has an unusual backstop: The Wallenbergs, Sweden’s most powerful business dynasty, helped found EQT in 1994 and remain its largest shareholder. The family’s patient approach to ownership is close to the long-hold model that much of private equity is now trying to reinvent. Q&A Liz Hoffman: For a long time, private equity firms could borrow cheaply, ride a rising market, and look like geniuses. It feels like the jig is up, and I know you have some thoughts on that . Jean Salata: Our industry needs to remember what we are meant to be doing, which is delivering returns for our clients. If we’re not doing that, we’re going to end up in a very difficult place. There’s been a lot of attention on the growth in assets under management, a business model that has really benefited from the tailwinds of the private credit run of the last five years. But we’re in an environment where the tide is going out and that means you’re going where there is real value being created. There are something like 10,000 private-equity firms out there. What should that number be? The industry already is consolidating and that will accelerate. This year the top 10 firms in the world have raised 50% of the capital. When you raise smaller funds, people don’t see the carry coming in and so they leave and you get zombie funds. EQT has chosen not to chase those credit tailwinds you mentioned. It doesn’t have the big lending business that Apollo, Blackstone, and others have ridden to huge AUM piles. Do you feel good about that decision? I think there’s a role for private credit, but the question is who’s best positioned to deliver that? We’re good at being an equity investor, being really close to the sectors that we invest in, bringing the best operational talent, bringing the technology and the AI capabilities that we have to the company. None of those are really relevant to the credit business. It’s an origination business. It’s a beta business. Best case scenario, you make 8% return on your money. So, the answer is yes, I think we are happy with the decision. But how do you resist the pressures to be a one-stop shop? Eventually there is a feedback loop. Second-quartile [performance] is, maybe, good enough. But when you start talking about third- and fourth-quartile returns, clients will either stop or reduce the amount that they invest with you. It’s hard to take anything public right now that isn’t a giant AI company and private equity’s track record on returning capital has been abysmal . How does the industry get out of this funk? There are a lot of assets for sale that need to find a home and there aren’t that many buyers. At EQT, we’ve been able to take advantage of where there are pockets of opportunity and liquidity. We had $33 billion of distributions to our investors in the last 12 months, and as a result, we’re continuing to attract capital. There’s this strange incentive structure in our industry, where you sell businesses that you otherwise wouldn’t want to sell because of this finite [fund] life. There’s a bit of frustration on the part of sellers that have sold assets because they need to go fundraising, only to see the buyers make like another 3x on it, which is why you’re seeing these longer-hold vehicles like evergreen structures, open-ended structures, continuation vehicles. But then isn’t the market saying that the 10-year closed-end fund is outdated and should probably go away? One of the reasons we bought [secondaries firm] Coller is we think there is a convergence happening between the primary market and the secondary market. There’s a case to be made for the secondary market essentially becoming the private equity market, as it is in the world of listed equities. Remember, the stock market is a secondary market. Yes, you have some IPOs, but the vast majority of the trading is in existing shares. Where we’re heading in private markets is not quite that extreme, but it’s going to be a much bigger part of the industry. There were $250 billion of PE secondaries deals last year. That’s doubled in the last three or four years and it’s probably going to double again in the next five. One other tension in PE right now is that everyone seems to be in the same trade — the AI trade . Are you worried about correlation? There’s no patents in finance. We’re all moving in a similar direction and it’s going to boil down to execution. A lot of this is about talent. There’s a shortage of really good talent that understands technology and AI, and the ability to attract, to afford, that talent becomes a question of scale. Tell me why all this AI investing is not going to end terribly. There’s a lot of noise right now about data centers — ‘it’s a bubble, the market’s crashing.’ But if you look at the fundamentals of what’s going on in the AI buildout with power, energy, chips, data center demand, we think it’s very fundamentals-based and a very, very attractive opportunity. I don’t want to say we stumbled onto it — the team deserves more credit than that — but we found ourselves in the middle of this in a big way because we were investing in power assets and in data center assets for cloud migration. The pre-AI generation of data centers. Yes. So all of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now. Now we are building the industrial AI core for the next generation of data centers, but we’re still only working with the hyperscalers. This is an important point; 92

events.title: Blackstone-backed data center operator tests AI debt fears
events.summary: The Scoop Wall Street is finding out just how expensive things can get in a matter of months. For a look at how much investors’ jitters are reshaping AI-related debt financing, look to QTS, an investment-grade Blackstone-backed data center operator, that just six months ago was weighing a deal to borrow $800 million at a rate of 1.7 percentage points over Treasurys. That deal never went through. And now, that same debt is being shopped to investors at 2.2 to 2.50 points above comparable Treasury yields for a nearly identical offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Both offerings involve the same company, same blue-chip Wall Street backing, and the same collateral — just for a lot more money. Blackstone declined to comment. As debt jitters spread and borrowing gets more expensive, it’s a lesson in just how much sentiment has shifted in such a short amount of time. Know More On Friday, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it no longer expected Anthropic to get an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its IPO, a reversal of previous guidance about the frontier lab, which is raising billions of dollars to finance its AI buildout. And investment-grade SpaceX’s $40 billion debt launch saw its pricing widen out — reaching an expected 8.75% yield for the riskier portion of its recent debt deal, up from where pricing was discussed just a week earlier, Semafor reported .

events.title: Anthropic's IPO prospectus is big on promises, short on answers to tough questions
events.summary: It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Man n and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode. For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors. In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is. A lightly edited transcript is below: Brandon (00:03) Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register 's Kettle podcast. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter. Welcome guys. Tobias Mann (00:34) Good to be here. Tom Claburn (00:34) Good to be here. Brandon (00:36) So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb . Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO. Tobias Mann (00:56) Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy. Brandon (01:18) Right. Tobias Mann (01:18) The S-1 definitely did that. But on the numbers side of things, the takeaway for the market was kind of interesting because there were some people looking at the numbers and going, "OK, this actually seems reasonable." Their operating losses were only about 700 million dollars. Brandon (01:40) I think on 16.3 billion net [revenues], right? That was what they reported. Tobias Mann (01:46) Right. Brandon (01:47) Now they also mentioned, I think, and I was going to ask you about this, $80.7 billion total losses, but I understand that was an accounting adjustment of some kind. Did they mention in the IPO what that meant specifically? Tobias Mann (02:01) Not specifically. It's a little fuzzy, and it's always kind of like this. Brandon (02:07) Of course it is, right? Tobias Mann (02:09) Anthropic's business is extremely cash heavy, and so they had to go to partners and say, "Hey, we need capital in order to pay for compute to train these models. We can either take it in debt or you could also get repaid in valuation, our equity." And so I believe a large part of that loss is they're trying to write off a lot of the equity that they're going to have to pay off when they do go public. And so I do believe that's the lion's share of that loss. Because it does look huge, but when you think about how companies go public and how they raise capital as startups, it's not really that surprising. It's just a huge number because Anthropic is arguably the largest IPO in US history at this point. Brandon (03:02) Right. But bottom line is their actual day-to-day business losses were $693 million....It was $1.2 billion, I think, for the first half of the year or same time last year or something like that. So it's gone down. Tobias Mann (03:17) Yes. Tom Claburn (03:17) And they're trying to go out at two trillion now? Is that the number? Tobias Mann (03:25) Well, the number kind of depends on whether they're going to be able to sustain this. I was going to mention for the first time ever, their revenues outpaced their compute expenses two to one. This has never been true in the company's history, and it's one of the reasons that people are feeling more confident about this. The issue that really comes from all of this, and what has gotten missed somewhat in the more rosy interpretations of the S-1, is that they also are signed up to have to repay upwards of 800 billion dollars and counting of compute commitments out through the next two decades or so. Brandon (04:12) You outlined in your story just a whole host of people they owed billions of dollars to for compute. Like you said, it would be great. That $16.3 billion in [revenue] would be great if those compute costs were going to hold steady, right? But they're not. They're going to keep climbing and there are a lot of bills that are going to be due. So, profitability is relying on making more than that nearly trillion dollars in compute obligations, and that's a big if. I think the inference costs have dropped pretty significantly over the year, on average.
